Cracking the Systems Programming Interview

Cover

About this book

This book addresses systems programming in Rust.

Systems programming encompasses software that operates directly against hardware and operating system interfaces: data structures whose memory layout governs cache behavior, concurrent programs that coordinate shared state across threads, and network services that parse and transmit bytes over sockets. Writing reliable software at this layer requires understanding how memory is allocated and accessed by the processor, how the operating system schedules threads, and how data crosses the kernel and network boundaries.

Rust provides direct control over memory layout and execution cost while enforcing memory and thread safety at compile time. Whenever the compiler rejects an unsafe pattern in this text, we analyze the exact invariant that failed and the design change required to satisfy it.

The material progresses from foundational language mechanics to production systems primitives. The opening chapters establish bindings, file I/O, and standard collections. The middle chapters implement core data structures and analyze their memory footprints. The later chapters cover concurrency, networking, kernel interfaces, and production transport protocols. Each chapter introduces the underlying mechanism first, traces a concrete example by hand, walks through the implementation incrementally, and concludes with the complete, compilable program.

Several programs appear in multiple iterations. When an initial design exhibits a correctness bug or performance bottleneck, we diagnose the root cause and trace the structural change in the revised version.

Who should read this book

This book is written for programmers who have basic familiarity with Rust and want to apply it to systems engineering.

Readers should be comfortable with fn, let, if, match, struct, enum, Vec, and String, and should have prior exposure to ownership and borrowing (for example, from The Rust Programming Language). Prior knowledge of explicit lifetime annotations, trait implementations such as TryFrom, smart pointers (Rc, Arc), atomics, unsafe Rust, or async runtimes is unnecessary; each mechanism is introduced in the chapter that first requires it.

No prior background in operating systems or networking is assumed. Whenever a chapter relies on a hardware or kernel mechanism, such as CPU cache lines, virtual memory paging, or file descriptors, that concept is derived from first principles before it appears in code.

What you will learn

Working through this book builds the ability to:

  • apply Rust collections and iterators to algorithmic problems over arrays, strings, and associative maps
  • design domain types that enforce invariants and reject invalid state at program boundaries
  • implement linked lists, trees, graphs, and caches in safe Rust
  • choose between Box, Rc, and arena-backed vectors (Vec) for node-based data structures
  • evaluate data structures with statistically sound, reproducible benchmarks
  • analyze how CPU caches, false sharing, and page faults govern runtime performance
  • construct locks, concurrent queues, and thread pools from atomics and condition variables
  • parse network protocols safely and build servers backed by OS threads and epoll
  • trace how an asynchronous executor drives a Future to completion

How this book is organized

The book is organized into ten parts, each building on the mechanisms introduced earlier.

Part 1, First steps

  • Chapter 1 covers bindings, shadowing, functions, recursion, and loops, and benchmarks three implementations of Fibonacci numbers.
  • Chapter 2 covers files, directories, and command-line arguments, along with Result and the ? operator.

Part 2, Collections and algorithms

  • Chapter 3 applies vectors, strings, and hash maps to foundational array and text algorithms.
  • Chapter 4 details iterators, references, and explicit lifetime annotations.
  • Chapter 5 covers binary heaps and priority-ordered collections.
  • Chapter 6 covers recursion and dynamic programming, concluding with workloads that leverage GPU memory and parallel cores.

Part 3, Modeling data and ownership

  • Chapter 7 designs types that reject invalid values using structs, enums, and structured error types.
  • Chapter 8 covers pointer and ownership types: Box, Rc, RefCell, Weak, Arc, and Cow.
  • Chapter 9 implements linked lists and benchmarks four distinct storage layouts.
  • Chapter 10 merges multiple sorted streams into a single ordered sequence.
  • Chapter 11 covers trees and tries.
  • Chapter 12 covers graph representations and traversals.

Part 4, Memory and the machine

  • Chapter 13 implements an LRU cache and compares the performance of two node storage layouts.
  • Chapter 14 partitions a cache across sharded locks and distributed nodes.
  • Chapter 15 covers memory allocation, CPU caches, virtual memory paging, CPU scheduling, and system calls.

Part 5, Concurrency

  • Chapter 16 covers operating system threads, atomic operations, and synchronization locks.
  • Chapter 17 implements concurrent queues for inter-thread work distribution.
  • Chapter 18 implements bounded and work-stealing thread pools.
  • Chapter 19 covers rate limiting, bounded retries, and idempotent operations.

Part 6, The network

  • Chapter 20 covers network addressing, TCP sockets, and two server architectures.
  • Chapter 21 parses and serves HTTP/1.1 traffic.
  • Chapter 22 implements an asynchronous executor alongside two HTTP clients.

Part 7, The kernel boundary

  • Chapter 23 maps files into virtual memory, compares mmap against read, and transfers file data directly to sockets with sendfile.
  • Chapter 24 inspects the process file descriptor table and constructs ls | wc -l using pipe, fork, dup2, and execvp.
  • Chapter 25 covers edge-triggered epoll, the readiness stalls caused by missed edges, and kernel modes that share a single listener across threads.

Part 8, Under the locks

  • Chapter 26 implements a futex-backed mutex, counts its kernel transitions, and runs two memory-ordering litmus tests.

Part 9, Production networking

  • Chapter 27 traces TCP connection teardown and the socket states left behind under heavy server load.
  • Chapter 28 adds TLS and mutual TLS using certificates generated at startup.
  • Chapter 29 implements a bounded client connection pool with connection reuse.

Part 10, Compact implementations

  • Chapter 30 provides ten concise implementations sized for timed technical interviews, each cross-referenced to the chapter containing its full treatment.

Appendix A provides a Rust reference sheet covering common compiler diagnostics and idioms. Appendix B contains the complete benchmark report. Appendix C preserves the extended borrow-checker derivation for Chapter 10.

Conventions

Inline code appears in monospace font, such as this. Programs are presented in numbered listings, typically a few lines at a time, with each caption citing the source file and line range. Every chapter concludes with the complete listing for each program.

Program output follows the command that produced it. Benchmark measurements state the hardware on which they were recorded; absolute timings will vary across machines.

Key technical terms appear in bold where first defined.

Three callout styles appear throughout the text:

NOTE: Supplementary background or implementation detail that is optional for following the main narrative.

TIP: A practical engineering technique ready for direct application.

WARNING: A subtle failure mode that compiles cleanly, or runtime behavior that diverges from common expectations.

Each chapter concludes with a concise summary and a set of exercises.

About the code

All source code resides in the rust-interview-lab directory of the repository at https://github.com/arpanpathak/cracking-the-systems-programming-interview. The codebase targets Rust edition 2024 and builds with rustc 1.96.0. Listings in the text are included directly from the source files without modification.

Library modules with unit tests live under src/problems/, runnable binaries live under src/bin/, and the data structures benchmarked in Chapters 9 and 13 live under benchmarking_examples/.

Execute the test suites and binaries from the rust-interview-lab directory:

cargo test --lib                        # the library's unit tests
cargo test --bin http_server            # the tests inside one program
cargo run --bin tcp_echo_server         # run one program
cargo run --release --bin benchmark     # benchmarks, always in release mode

Building the book

The book sources reside in the cracking-the-systems-programming-interview directory:

make art        # the chapter plates and the cover (needs rsvg-convert)
make figures    # the diagrams (needs Graphviz)
make html       # the browser edition, in book/
make pdf        # the print edition, in build/
make serve      # the browser edition at http://localhost:3000

About the cover

The cover depicts the Chief Mechanic of the Ferrous Works inside a workshop of interlocking gears. The crates are labeled Arc, Mutex, epoll, and Box, with the chain terminating at a crate marked unsafe. Each chapter opens with a member of the same crew operating a machine that reflects the chapter’s technical focus.

ChapterMechanicMachine
1Riveta gate marked TRY_FROM that rejects parts of the wrong shape
2Ledgera filing cabinet, a stack of pages, and an offset counter
3Binsnumbered bins fed by a hashing hopper
4Shacklea chain on a crane, one link opened with take()
5Conveyorthree belts feeding a heap and one output belt
6Brancha manifold of pipes laid out as a binary tree
7Valvepipes and valves wired into a weighted graph
8Coga train of gears, each half the size of the last
9Drawera rack of crates, the oldest leaving by an eviction chute
10Turntablea ring of shards around a hub gear
11Gaugea board of page frames and a cache-miss gauge
12Spindlethread spools on one axle, and a padlock
13Carousela conveyor queue and a ring-buffer carousel
14Foremana job hopper feeding four worker robots
15Throttlea token bucket under a refill valve
16Signala radio mast and a socket panel
17Couriera pneumatic tube delivering a request to status-code slots
18Flywheela flywheel driven by poll, with futures on a rail
19Drilla drill press and a checklist

The plates are generated by tools/art.py.

Bindings, functions, and loops

This chapter covers

  • How a let binding works and where its value resides in memory
  • Shadowing an identifier, and how it differs from in-place mutation with mut
  • Recursive functions and their stack-frame allocation behavior
  • Replacing direct recursion with an iterative loop and with a memoization table
  • Measuring execution time with Instant, and passing functions as arguments

Every compiled program maps source-level identifiers onto concrete storage locations and control-flow frames. In Rust, lexical bindings, explicit mutability, and deterministic stack-frame reclamation govern how values occupy memory across function invocations.

Two programs illustrate these foundational mechanics. The first binds a single identifier to three values of distinct types in sequence, contrasting lexical shadowing with in-place mutation of a mutable slot. The second evaluates Fibonacci numbers through direct recursion, constant-space iteration, and memoization, demonstrating how recursive call trees consume stack memory and how algorithmic structure dictates asymptotic execution time.

Four definitions establish the memory model used throughout:

  • A binding associates an identifier with a typed value; for example, let x = 5; binds x to 5.
  • A lexical scope is the syntactic region in which a binding remains valid, delimited in Rust by { and }.
  • The call stack is the contiguous LIFO memory region holding activation records for active function invocations.
  • A stack frame (activation record) is the fixed-size slice of stack memory allocated upon entering a function to store its parameters, return address, and local bindings.

1.1 A binding is a name for a value

Upon function entry, the runtime allocates a stack frame sized statically from the types of its local bindings. Fixed-size scalar bindings occupy adjacent slots within that frame: a u32 requires 4 bytes, whereas a usize requires 8 bytes on a 64-bit architecture.

Dynamically sized types such as String partition their representation across the stack and the heap, a dynamically managed memory pool obtained from the system allocator. Because string length varies at runtime, the UTF-8 character bytes reside in a heap-allocated buffer, while the stack frame holds a three-word header consisting of a pointer to that buffer, the current byte length, and the allocated capacity.

Upon function return, the stack frame is popped and every local binding undergoes deterministic destruction in reverse declaration order. Dropping a String deallocates its backing heap buffer automatically.

1.2 Shadowing: one name, several values

Declaring a second let statement with an identifier already in scope does not overwrite the original value. Instead, it creates a distinct binding that reuses the identifier, hiding the earlier value from subsequent statements. Rust terms this mechanism shadowing. The original value remains alive until the enclosing scope exits, though it is no longer reachable by name.

Because each shadowed binding is an independent variable, its type can differ from the previous binding. Figure 1.1 traces the identifier value across three bindings of three different types.

Listing 1.1 implements this three-step sequence.

Listing 1.1 One name, three types. src/bin/shadowing.rs, lines 27 to 41

fn demonstrate_shadowing() -> String {
    // First binding is an integer.
    let value: u32 = 7;
    let mut log = format!("integer: {value}");

    // Shadow the integer with a String. The old integer is gone.
    let value = value.to_string();
    log.push_str(&format!("\nstring: {value}"));

    // Shadow the String with a usize computed from it.
    let value = value.len();
    log.push_str(&format!("\nusize: {value}"));

    log
}

Tracing the three let value statements in order clarifies how evaluation proceeds:

  1. let value: u32 = 7; initializes a u32 binding.
  2. let value = value.to_string(); reads the u32, allocates a String containing its decimal representation, and binds value to that String. On the right-hand side, value still resolves to the u32 because the new binding enters scope only after the initializer finishes evaluating.
  3. let value = value.len(); reads the byte length of the String and binds value to the resulting usize.

None of these bindings require mut because every value remains immutable after initialization. By contrast, log accumulates output lines via push_str, so it is declared let mut log, allowing the unit tests to verify all three intermediate states.

Figure 1.2 (left) depicts the conceptual stack frame after the third binding: three distinct slots exist, with only the final slot remaining accessible by name.

1.2.1 When shadowing helps

Shadowing is well suited to staged data transformations where an input arrives in one representation and must be converted into another. For example, numeric input from a user arrives as raw text; once parsed, the unparsed string is no longer needed and can be shadowed by the parsed integer:

let count = read_line_from_user();   // a String, for example "42"
let count: u32 = count.trim().parse().expect("a number");

After the second line, count has type u32. Subsequent code cannot accidentally reference the raw string because its identifier has been rebound.

1.2.2 A value captured earlier keeps its old value

A closure or reference created prior to a shadowing let remains bound to the original variable:

let x = 1;
let show = || println!("{x}");
let x = x + 1;   // a new x
show();          // prints 1

Because the second let allocates a new binding rather than modifying the first, the closure continues to observe the original x.

WARNING: Writing let x = x + 1; inside a loop body introduces a new binding scoped exclusively to that single iteration. On the next iteration, the outer x retains its original value. To accumulate state across iterations, declare let mut x outside the loop and update it with x += 1.

1.3 Mutation: one value that changes

When a single storage location must change over time, declare the binding with mut. The type remains fixed, and every assignment overwrites the same stack slot in place.

Listing 1.2 A counter that changes in place. src/bin/shadowing.rs, lines 43 to 53

fn demonstrate_mutation() -> String {
    // If you need to mutate the same binding's value (same type) without
    // creating a new binding, mark it `mut`.
    let mut count = 0;
    let mut log = String::from("mut count:");
    for _ in 0..3 {
        count += 1;
        log.push_str(&format!(" {count}"));
    }
    log
}

The header for _ in 0..3 executes the body three times while discarding the loop index with the wildcard _. Each iteration increments count in place and appends the updated value to log. Figure 1.2 (right) illustrates the single slot for count across its four states.

Table 1.1 summarizes the behavioral differences between shadowing and mutation.

Shadowing (let x = ... again)Mutation (let mut x, then x = ...)
Creates a new variableyesno
Can change the typeyesno
Needs mutnoyes
A closure that captured x earlier seesthe old valuea compile error if it is still in use

1.4 The first complete program

Listing 1.3 presents the complete shadowing.rs binary, including its entry point and unit tests.

Listing 1.3 The complete program. src/bin/shadowing.rs

// ============================================================================
// Variable shadowing vs mutation
//
// Ported from the Rust playground repo (`shadowing.rs`).
//
// What this demonstrates:
//   - Rust allows a new `let` binding with the same name as an existing
//     binding. This is called **shadowing**.
//   - Shadowing can change the value *and the type* of a variable without
//     declaring it `mut`.
//   - The old binding is no longer reachable after the shadowing `let`.
//
// Where this appears in practice:
//   - Rust SDK code often shadows parsed/deserialized values to convert them
//     from raw input to typed domain values:
//
//       let raw = request.header("X-GPU-Count")?;
//       let raw: u64 = raw.parse()?;   // shadow with a typed value
//
//   - Shadowing is also useful after unwrapping an `Option`/`Result` when the
//     guard value is no longer needed.
//
// Run:
//   cargo run --bin shadowing
// ============================================================================

fn demonstrate_shadowing() -> String {
    // First binding is an integer.
    let value: u32 = 7;
    let mut log = format!("integer: {value}");

    // Shadow the integer with a String. The old integer is gone.
    let value = value.to_string();
    log.push_str(&format!("\nstring: {value}"));

    // Shadow the String with a usize computed from it.
    let value = value.len();
    log.push_str(&format!("\nusize: {value}"));

    log
}

fn demonstrate_mutation() -> String {
    // If you need to mutate the same binding's value (same type) without
    // creating a new binding, mark it `mut`.
    let mut count = 0;
    let mut log = String::from("mut count:");
    for _ in 0..3 {
        count += 1;
        log.push_str(&format!(" {count}"));
    }
    log
}

fn main() {
    println!("=== Shadowing ===");
    println!("{}", demonstrate_shadowing());

    println!("\n=== Mutation ===");
    println!("{}", demonstrate_mutation());
}

// ============================================================================
// Tests (cargo test --bin shadowing)
// ============================================================================
#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn shadowing_allows_type_changes() {
        let log = demonstrate_shadowing();
        assert!(log.contains("integer: 7"));
        assert!(log.contains("string: 7"));
        assert!(log.contains("usize: 1"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn mutation_requires_mut_binding() {
        let log = demonstrate_mutation();
        assert!(log.contains("mut count: 1 2 3"));
    }
}

The unit tests reside in a module annotated with #[cfg(test)], which instructs the compiler to compile this module exclusively during cargo test. Inside the module, use super::*; imports the parent module’s items into scope, and each test verifies the formatted log output with assert!.

Running the binary and its test suite from the rust-interview-lab directory produces:

$ cargo run --bin shadowing
=== Shadowing ===
integer: 7
string: 7
usize: 1

=== Mutation ===
mut count: 1 2 3

$ cargo test --bin shadowing
running 2 tests
test tests::mutation_requires_mut_binding ... ok
test tests::shadowing_allows_type_changes ... ok

With single-frame storage established, nested invocations introduce a second dimension of stack management: activation-record accumulation during recursion.

1.5 A function that calls itself

The Fibonacci sequence begins with 0 and 1, and each subsequent term is the sum of the two preceding terms:

n012345678
fib(n)01123581321

This recurrence translates directly into a recursive function, a function that invokes itself.

Listing 1.4 Fibonacci by recursion. src/bin/cs_fib.rs, lines 8 to 15

use std::time::{Duration, Instant};

/// Exponential: fib(n) recomputes fib(n - 1) and fib(n - 2) from scratch.
fn recursive(n: u64) -> u64 {
    if n < 2 {
        n
    } else {
        recursive(n - 1) + recursive(n - 2)
    }
}

Inputs 0 and 1 form the base case, returning n directly without further calls. For any n >= 2, the function makes two recursive calls and sums their results. Because if is an expression in Rust, its evaluated branch serves as the function’s return value without an explicit return statement.

1.5.1 Counting the calls

Tracing recursive(5) reveals significant redundant work: recursive(5) invokes recursive(4) and recursive(3), and recursive(4) invokes recursive(3) a second time. Figure 1.3 illustrates the complete call tree.

Evaluating n = 5 requires 15 calls. Because the call tree for n contains both the tree for n - 1 and the tree for n - 2, the total call count grows by roughly a factor of 1.618 per increment of n. At n = 30, the function executes approximately 2.7 million calls; at n = 90, the call count exceeds 1019.

1.5.2 What each call uses on the stack

Every active invocation allocates its own stack frame containing its parameter n and return address, and releases that frame upon returning. Consequently, the stack never holds the entire call tree simultaneously; it holds only the active chain of pending calls. Figure 1.4 depicts the deepest stack state reached during recursive(4).

Direct recursion therefore incurs two distinct costs: exponential time complexity O(\varphin) caused by overlapping subproblems, and linear stack depth O(n) proportional to the input parameter. Although a depth of 90 frames is negligible, linear recursion depth exhausts the call stack on large inputs.

1.6 The same numbers with a loop

Computing the next Fibonacci number requires only the two preceding values. An iterative loop can maintain those two values in registers or stack slots and advance them one step per iteration.

Listing 1.5 Fibonacci with a loop. src/bin/cs_fib.rs, lines 17 to 24

/// Linear time, constant space.
fn iterative(n: u64) -> u64 {
    let (mut previous, mut current) = (0u64, 1u64);
    for _ in 0..n {
        (previous, current) = (current, previous + current);
    }
    previous
}

The declaration let (mut previous, mut current) = (0u64, 1u64); destructures a tuple to initialize both bindings in one statement, with the u64 suffix fixing the integer width.

Inside the loop, (previous, current) = (current, previous + current); updates both bindings simultaneously. Rust evaluates the entire right-hand tuple using the pre-update values before writing to the left-hand targets, eliminating the need for an explicit temporary variable.

Tracing iterative(5) confirms the state transitions:

after pass0 (start)12345
previous011235
current112358

After five iterations, previous holds 5, which equals fib(5). Because the loop executes n iterations using two fixed-size integers, its running time is linear in n and its memory usage is constant.

1.7 Recursion with a memory

To preserve the recursive formulation while eliminating redundant recomputation, each subproblem result can be recorded upon first evaluation and retrieved on subsequent visits. This technique is memoization, and the auxiliary lookup table storing evaluated subproblems is a cache.

Listing 1.6 Fibonacci with a cache. src/bin/cs_fib.rs, lines 26 to 41

/// Linear time, linear space: recursion plus a cache of subproblem answers.
fn memoized(n: u64) -> u64 {
    fn go(n: u64, cache: &mut [u64]) -> u64 {
        if n < 2 {
            return n;
        }
        let index = n as usize;
        if cache[index] == 0 {
            cache[index] = go(n - 1, cache) + go(n - 2, cache);
        }
        cache[index]
    }

    let mut cache = vec![0u64; n as usize + 1];
    go(n, &mut cache)
}

Three Rust constructs appear in Listing 1.6:

  • Nested function definitions: go is declared inside memoized, restricting its visibility to the enclosing function. Unlike a closure, a nested fn does not capture local variables from its enclosing scope.
  • vec![0u64; n as usize + 1]: This macro allocates a heap-backed Vec initialized with n + 1 zeros. The cast n as usize converts u64 to usize, Rust’s pointer-sized indexing type.
  • &mut [u64]: A mutable slice provides a borrowed, writable view into the vector’s contiguous elements. Passing the cache by mutable slice allows every recursive call to share one table without copying it.

On each invocation, go handles the base cases first and then inspects cache[index]. A zero entry indicates an uncomputed value, prompting two recursive calls whose sum is stored in the table before returning.

Using zero as an empty sentinel is valid here because fib(n) is strictly positive for all n >= 2, and smaller inputs return before consulting the cache. Figure 1.5 depicts the cache contents after memoized(6) completes.

With memoization, every subproblem from 2 to n is evaluated exactly once, reducing execution time to linear in n. Memory consumption remains linear in n for both the heap cache and the n active stack frames.

Animation 1.1 contrasts memoized(5) and recursive(5) side by side. The call tree on the left records every invocation, while the stack on the right tracks only the frames currently awaiting a return value.

1.8 Timing the three versions

To compare all three implementations quantitatively, the program wraps each invocation in a timing helper.

Listing 1.7 Timing a function and printing the result. src/bin/cs_fib.rs, lines 43 to 51

fn timed(label: &str, n: u64, operation: impl Fn(u64) -> u64) {
    let start = Instant::now();
    let value = operation(n);
    report(label, n, value, start.elapsed());
}

fn report(label: &str, n: u64, value: u64, elapsed: Duration) {
    println!("  {label:<10} fib({n:>2}) = {value:<20} in {elapsed:?}");
}

The parameter operation: impl Fn(u64) -> u64 accepts any function item or closure that maps a u64 to a u64, enabling main to pass recursive, iterative, and memoized directly by name.

Instant::now() samples a monotonic clock that never moves backward, and start.elapsed() computes the interval as a Duration.

In report, format specifiers control column alignment: {label:<10} left-aligns the label within a 10-character field, {n:>2} right-aligns n within 2 characters, and {elapsed:?} invokes Duration’s debug formatter, which automatically scales units to nanoseconds, microseconds, or milliseconds.

1.9 The complete Fibonacci program

Listing 1.8 combines all three implementations, the timing harness, and the verification loop in main.

Listing 1.8 The complete program. src/bin/cs_fib.rs

//! Three ways to compute Fibonacci: naive recursion, iteration, and memoization.
//! The first shows why exponential blowup happens; the other two fix it.
//!
//! Run with: cargo run --bin cs_fib

use std::time::{Duration, Instant};

/// Exponential: fib(n) recomputes fib(n - 1) and fib(n - 2) from scratch.
fn recursive(n: u64) -> u64 {
    if n < 2 {
        n
    } else {
        recursive(n - 1) + recursive(n - 2)
    }
}

/// Linear time, constant space.
fn iterative(n: u64) -> u64 {
    let (mut previous, mut current) = (0u64, 1u64);
    for _ in 0..n {
        (previous, current) = (current, previous + current);
    }
    previous
}

/// Linear time, linear space: recursion plus a cache of subproblem answers.
fn memoized(n: u64) -> u64 {
    fn go(n: u64, cache: &mut [u64]) -> u64 {
        if n < 2 {
            return n;
        }
        let index = n as usize;
        if cache[index] == 0 {
            cache[index] = go(n - 1, cache) + go(n - 2, cache);
        }
        cache[index]
    }

    let mut cache = vec![0u64; n as usize + 1];
    go(n, &mut cache)
}

fn timed(label: &str, n: u64, operation: impl Fn(u64) -> u64) {
    let start = Instant::now();
    let value = operation(n);
    report(label, n, value, start.elapsed());
}

fn report(label: &str, n: u64, value: u64, elapsed: Duration) {
    println!("  {label:<10} fib({n:>2}) = {value:<20} in {elapsed:?}");
}

fn main() {
    println!("small input, all three should agree");
    timed("recursive", 20, recursive);
    timed("iterative", 20, iterative);
    timed("memoized", 20, memoized);

    println!("\nrecursive cost grows quickly");
    timed("recursive", 30, recursive);
    timed("iterative", 30, iterative);

    println!("\nlarge input: recursion alone would not finish");
    timed("iterative", 90, iterative);
    timed("memoized", 90, memoized);

    for n in 0..20 {
        assert_eq!(recursive(n), iterative(n));
        assert_eq!(memoized(n), iterative(n));
    }
    assert_eq!(iterative(30), 832_040);
    assert_eq!(iterative(90), 2_880_067_194_370_816_120);

    println!("\nall checks passed");
}

Near the end of main, a loop verifies that all three implementations produce identical outputs for every n below 20, terminating via assert_eq! on any discrepancy. Two final assertions validate fib(30) and fib(90) against known reference values.

Executing the default debug build with cargo run yields:

$ cargo run --bin cs_fib
small input, all three should agree
  recursive  fib(20) = 6765                 in 90.908µs
  iterative  fib(20) = 6765                 in 567ns
  memoized   fib(20) = 6765                 in 10.826µs

recursive cost grows quickly
  recursive  fib(30) = 832040               in 11.124774ms
  iterative  fib(30) = 832040               in 542ns

large input: recursion alone would not finish
  iterative  fib(90) = 2880067194370816120  in 937ns
  memoized   fib(90) = 2880067194370816120  in 5.749µs

all checks passed

The recursive timings confirm the growth analysis from Section 1.5.1: increasing n from 20 to 30 multiplies runtime by roughly 120, matching 1.618^10 ≈ 123. At that growth rate, recursive(90) would require millennia, so main omits it.

Although both memoized and iterative scale linearly with n, memoized runs slower because it allocates a heap Vec and incurs recursive call overhead, neither of which the loop pays.

NOTE: fib(93) is the largest Fibonacci number representable in a u64; iterative(94) overflows. Debug builds trap integer overflow with a panic, whereas release builds wrap around in two’s complement arithmetic without signaling an error.

Summary

  • A let binding associates an identifier with a fixed-size slot in the active stack frame. A String stores its UTF-8 bytes in a heap-allocated buffer referenced by a three-word stack header (pointer, length, capacity).
  • Lexical shadowing introduces an independent binding that may assume a different type while leaving prior bindings immutable and unreachable by name. Closures capturing an earlier binding retain their reference to the original storage slot.
  • Declaring a binding with mut enables in-place mutation of a fixed-type storage slot.
  • Each active recursive invocation allocates a stack frame; unmemoized recursive Fibonacci recomputes overlapping subproblems, yielding exponential runtime and linear stack depth.
  • An iterative loop maintaining only the two preceding recurrence terms computes fib(n) in O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
  • Memoization caches evaluated subproblems in an auxiliary table, reducing recursive Fibonacci to O(n) time at the cost of O(n) heap space and O(n) stack depth.
  • impl Fn(u64) -> u64 accepts any function item or closure matching that signature, and Instant samples a monotonic clock for elapsed-time measurement.

Exercises

  1. Add a call counter to recursive, print the invocation count for n from 1 to 25, and verify that consecutive counts grow by approximately 1.6x.
  2. Modify memoized so the cache stores Option<u64> rather than treating 0 as an empty sentinel. Explain why 0 is a valid sentinel for Fibonacci numbers but unsafe for functions that can legitimately return 0.
  3. Update iterative to return Option<u64> using checked_add, so that iterative(94) returns None rather than overflowing.
  4. Run cargo run --release --bin cs_fib and compare the optimized timings against the debug output above.

Files, paths, and the command line

This chapter covers

  • How a program interacts with the kernel and storage subsystem when reading a file
  • Result and the ? operator for structured error propagation
  • Path and PathBuf, alongside whole-file and line-oriented reading strategies
  • Appending, copying, renaming, and deleting files, and classifying I/O error kinds
  • Listing directory entries and traversing nested directory trees
  • Cursor-based file pagination and typed command-line argument parsing

Interacting with persistent storage and process arguments requires crossing the privilege boundary between user space and the operating system kernel. Unlike pure in-memory computation, every kernel-mediated operation can fail because a path may not exist, permissions may be denied, or underlying storage may return an error.

Rust encodes recoverable failures explicitly through the Result type, preventing callers from overlooking error conditions. Building on Result and the ? propagation operator, the sections below develop path manipulation, buffered I/O, atomic file mutations, and recursive directory traversal, culminating in two complete utilities: a stateless cursor-based file paginator and a typed command-line argument parser.

Three operating system abstractions govern all file I/O:

  • The kernel is the privileged core of the operating system responsible for mediating hardware, virtual memory, and filesystem access.
  • A system call is a controlled trap from user space into the kernel requesting a privileged service, such as opening a file or transferring a byte range.
  • A file descriptor is a small non-negative integer allocated per process by the kernel to identify an open file table entry; subsequent I/O system calls reference the file through this integer.

2.1 What happens when you read a file

User-space processes cannot access storage hardware directly. Every file read is mediated by the kernel through a sequence of system calls, as illustrated in Figure 2.1.

Reading a file proceeds in three stages:

  1. open requests access to the path; the kernel verifies permissions and returns a file descriptor.
  2. read requests bytes from that descriptor; the kernel copies data from its page cache (fetching from disk on a cache miss) into a user-space buffer.
  3. close notifies the kernel that the process has finished with the file so the descriptor can be reclaimed.

Rust’s standard library wraps these system calls in safe abstractions, reporting any kernel error through Result.

2.2 Result and the ? operator

Result is a two-variant enum representing either a successful value or a failure:

enum Result<T, E> {
    Ok(T),    // the operation succeeded and produced a T
    Err(E),   // the operation failed with an error of type E
}

For I/O operations, the error type is std::io::Error, and io::Result<T> is a standard type alias for Result<T, io::Error>. Accordingly, fs::read_to_string(path) returns io::Result<String>, yielding either the decoded text or the underlying OS error.

Handling every fallible call with an explicit match quickly obscures control flow when a function chains multiple I/O operations. The ? operator eliminates that boilerplate. Appending ? to any Result expression performs one of two actions (Figure 2.2):

  • On Ok(x), the expression evaluates to x and execution continues.
  • On Err(e), the enclosing function immediately returns Err(e) to its caller.

Because ? performs an early return on error, the enclosing function must itself return a compatible Result type. For this reason, the binaries in this chapter declare fn main() -> io::Result<()>. When main returns an Err, the Rust runtime prints the error message to standard error and exits with status code 1.

2.3 Paths

A path identifies a file or directory, such as /tmp/data.txt. Rust splits path handling across two complementary types: &Path is an unsized, borrowed slice of a path, while PathBuf is an owned, heap-allocated buffer that can be mutated in place. Their relationship mirrors &str and String (Figure 2.3).

Listing 2.1 Building paths and taking them apart. src/bin/path_buff.rs

use std::path::{Path, PathBuf};

fn main() {
    let dir = Path::new("/tmp");
    let file = dir.join("data.txt");

    let mut buf = PathBuf::from(dir);
    buf.push("nested");
    buf.push("file.txt");

    println!("file: {}", file.display());
    println!("buf:  {}", buf.display());
    println!("parent: {:?}", buf.parent());
    println!("file_name: {:?}", buf.file_name());
    println!("ext: {:?}", buf.extension());
}

Path::new("/tmp") constructs a borrowed &Path view without allocating. Calling dir.join("data.txt") allocates and returns a new PathBuf, whereas PathBuf::from(dir) copies the base path into an owned buffer that push extends in place.

$ cargo run --bin path_buff
file: /tmp/data.txt
buf:  /tmp/nested/file.txt
parent: Some("/tmp/nested")
file_name: Some("file.txt")
ext: Some("txt")

Inspectors such as parent, file_name, and extension return Option because not every path contains those components; for instance, the root directory / has no parent. Formatting a path for display requires calling display(). On Unix systems (Linux and macOS), filesystem paths are arbitrary non-NUL byte sequences that need not be valid UTF-8; display() substitutes replacement characters for any non-UTF-8 sequences during formatting.

WARNING: Passing an absolute path to join or push replaces the entire base path rather than appending to it; Path::new("/srv").join("/etc/passwd") resolves to /etc/passwd. When constructing paths from untrusted input, reject absolute paths and .. traversal components before joining.

2.4 Reading a file

2.4.1 The whole file at once

For small files, the most direct approach loads the entire file into a single String.

Listing 2.2 Write a file, then read it back. src/bin/read_write_file.rs

use std::{
    fs,
    io,
    path::{Path, PathBuf},
};

// `&Path` accepts both a `&Path` and a `&PathBuf` argument; `&PathBuf` would not.
fn read_content_of_file(path: &Path) -> io::Result<String> {
    fs::read_to_string(path)
}

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    fs::write("hello.txt", "Hello, Rust!\n")?;

    // `join` builds a new PathBuf and leaves `base_dir` unchanged.
    let base_dir = PathBuf::from(".");
    let joined_path = base_dir.join("hello.txt");

    // `push` mutates the PathBuf in place instead of returning a new one.
    let mut mut_base_dir = PathBuf::from(".");
    mut_base_dir.push("hello.txt");

    let text = read_content_of_file(&joined_path)?;
    println!("File contents (via .join()):\n{}", text);

    let text_inplace = read_content_of_file(&mut_base_dir)?;
    println!("File contents (via .push()):\n{}", text_inplace);

    Ok(())
}

fs::write creates the file (or truncates an existing one) and writes the provided bytes, while fs::read_to_string opens, reads, validates UTF-8, and closes the file in a single call. Appending ? propagates any failure directly out of main.

Because read_content_of_file accepts &Path, both PathBuf arguments constructed via join and push coerce automatically via Deref, printing identical contents.

Loading an entire file into memory works well for configuration files, but is unsuitable for multi-gigabyte logs, which require streaming line by line.

2.4.2 One line at a time

Streaming a file line by line requires wrapping the File in a BufReader. Figure 2.4 contrasts buffered and unbuffered reads.

Listing 2.3 Numbered lines through a buffered reader. src/bin/readfile_line_by_line.rs

use std::{
    fs::File,
    io::{BufRead, BufReader},
}; // BufRead brings `lines()` into scope.

fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let file = File::open("log.txt")?;
    let reader = BufReader::new(file);

    for (i, line) in reader.lines().enumerate() {
        let line = line?;
        println!("{}: {}", i + 1, line);
    }

    Ok(())
}

BufReader::new(file) assumes ownership of the File and pairs it with an 8 KiB user-space buffer, amortizing kernel-crossing overhead across multiple line reads. Because lines is defined on the BufRead trait, that trait must be imported via use std::io::BufRead;.

Each iteration of lines() yields an io::Result<String> stripped of its trailing newline; because a read error or invalid UTF-8 sequence can occur mid-stream, every item must be checked individually. The statement let line = line?; unwraps the String by shadowing the Result binding. Chaining enumerate() pairs each line with its zero-based index, which the formatter shifts by one (i + 1).

Animation 2.1 traces this loop over a 12-byte, three-line file, counting read system calls with and without a buffer.

2.4.3 Reusing one buffer, and skipping bad lines

Because lines() allocates a fresh String on every iteration, high-throughput scanners avoid per-line heap allocations by reading repeatedly into a single reusable buffer.

Listing 2.4 One reused buffer, with invalid lines skipped. src/bin/read_large_file.rs

use std::{
    fs::File,
    io::{self, BufRead, BufReader},
};

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    let file = File::open("large.txt")?;
    let mut reader = BufReader::new(file);
    let mut line = String::new();

    while match reader.read_line(&mut line) {
        Ok(0) => false, // EOF, stop
        Ok(_) => {
            process(line.trim_end());
            line.clear();
            true // keep reading
        }
        Err(e) if e.kind() == io::ErrorKind::InvalidData => {
            eprintln!("skipping bad line: {e}");
            line.clear();
            true
        }
        Err(e) => return Err(e), // return works inside the condition
    } {}

    Ok(())
}

fn process(line: &str) {
    println!("{line}");
}

reader.read_line(&mut line) appends the next line, including its delimiter, into line and returns the byte count read. The loop uses the while match ... { ... } {} idiom, placing the match directly in the loop condition with an empty body {}; each match arm evaluates to true to continue scanning or false to terminate.

Table 2.1 summarizes the four outcomes handled by the match.

read_line returnsMeaningWhat the loop does
Ok(0)end of the filestops
Ok(n)a line of n bytesprocesses it, clears the buffer, continues
Err(e) with kind InvalidDatathe line is not valid UTF-8 textprints a message, clears, continues
any other Erra real read failurereturns the error from main

Because read_line appends to the existing string, the loop must call line.clear() after each iteration; omitting clear() would cause the buffer to accumulate the entire file while keeping its allocated capacity.

The InvalidData branch can resume safely because read_line has already consumed the malformed line up to the newline delimiter. Testing against a file containing invalid UTF-8 bytes on its second line confirms this behavior:

$ printf 'ok\n\xff\xfebad\nfine\n' > large.txt
$ cargo run --bin read_large_file
ok
skipping bad line: stream did not contain valid UTF-8
fine

2.5 Writing and changing files

2.5.1 Appending

Whereas fs::write truncates and replaces a file, appending to a log requires opening the file in append mode via OpenOptions.

Listing 2.5 Appending lines to a file. src/bin/append_to_file_open_options.rs

use std::{fs::OpenOptions, io::Write};

fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let mut file = OpenOptions::new()
        .create(true) // create if missing
        .append(true) // always write at the end
        .open("log.txt")?;

    writeln!(file, "New log line")?;
    writeln!(file, "Another line")?;

    Ok(())
}

OpenOptions configures open flags before issuing the open system call: create(true) creates the file if absent, and append(true) sets the OS O_APPEND flag so the kernel positions the write offset at end-of-file and writes the payload atomically. As a result, concurrent processes appending to the same log file do not overwrite one another’s records.

The writeln! macro formats text into any type implementing std::io::Write (such as File), requiring use std::io::Write; in scope.

2.5.2 Copying, renaming, and deleting

The standard library provides dedicated functions for copying, renaming, and removing files. Listing 2.6 creates a file, copies it, renames the copy, and deletes the original.

Listing 2.6 Copy, rename, remove. src/bin/copy_rename_delete_file.rs

use std::{fs, io};

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    fs::write("a.txt", "hello")?;

    fs::copy("a.txt", "b.txt")?;
    fs::rename("b.txt", "c.txt")?;
    fs::remove_file("a.txt")?;

    println!("Done");
    Ok(())
}

Upon completion, a.txt has been unlinked and c.txt contains hello. Each operation maps directly to one or two underlying system calls.

fs::rename provides an essential durability guarantee: when source and destination reside on the same filesystem, the rename is atomic. Concurrent readers observe either the complete old file or the complete new file, never a partially written state. Reliable file updates exploit this property by writing the new contents to a sibling temporary file and then renaming it over the target path.

2.5.3 Telling one error from another

Every io::Error carries a platform-independent kind (io::ErrorKind), such as NotFound or PermissionDenied, enabling callers to handle specific failure conditions distinctly from unexpected I/O errors.

Listing 2.7 Matching on the kind of an error. src/bin/file_error_handling.rs

use std::{fs, io};

fn read_file(path: &str) -> Result<String, io::Error> {
    fs::read_to_string(path)
}

fn main() {
    match read_file("missing.txt") {
        Ok(text) => println!("{}", text),
        Err(e) if e.kind() == io::ErrorKind::NotFound => {
            eprintln!("File not found");
        }
        Err(e) => eprintln!("Error: {}", e),
    }
}

The second arm uses a match guard (if e.kind() == ErrorKind::NotFound) to isolate missing-file errors while letting all other errors fall through to the third arm. Because main returns () rather than io::Result<()>, it handles every Result variant explicitly instead of propagating with ?. Executed in a directory without missing.txt, the program prints File not found.

2.6 Directories

A directory maps entry names to filesystem objects: regular files, subdirectories, or symbolic links. A symbolic link is a directory entry that stores a pathname pointing to another target path.

2.6.1 One level

Listing 2.8 enumerates the entries of the current working directory and distinguishes subdirectories from regular files.

Listing 2.8 Listing the current directory. src/bin/list_directory.rs

use std::{fs, io};

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    for entry in fs::read_dir(".")? {
        let entry = entry?;
        let path = entry.path();

        if path.is_dir() {
            println!("[DIR]  {}", path.display());
        } else {
            println!("[FILE] {}", path.display());
        }
    }
    Ok(())
}

fs::read_dir(".") returns an iterator yielding io::Result<DirEntry> items, since reading directory entries can fail mid-iteration. Calling path.is_dir() queries the kernel for metadata via stat, following symbolic links to report the type of the link target.

2.6.2 Every level

Traversing nested subdirectories applies the recursive pattern from Section 1.5, invoking walk on every subdirectory encountered.

Listing 2.9 Walking a directory tree. src/bin/recusrive_directory_walk.rs

use std::{fs, io, path::Path};

fn walk(dir: &Path) -> io::Result<()> {
    for entry in fs::read_dir(dir)? {
        let entry = entry?;
        let path = entry.path();
        let file_type = entry.file_type()?;

        if file_type.is_dir() {
            println!("[DIR]  {}", path.display());
            walk(&path)?;
        } else {
            println!("[FILE] {}", path.display());
        }
    }
    Ok(())
}

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    walk(Path::new("."))?;
    Ok(())
}

Here walk calls entry.file_type() rather than path.is_dir(). Unlike is_dir(), file_type() does not follow symbolic links, reporting a symlink to a directory as a symlink rather than a directory. Refusing to descend into symlinks prevents infinite recursion when a symlink points to an ancestor directory. On Linux, file_type() is also faster because the getdents system call typically returns the entry type alongside its name without requiring an additional lstat call.

Recursion depth equals the directory nesting depth. Because practical filesystem hierarchies are shallow relative to default thread stack sizes, stack overflow is rarely a hazard here.

2.7 Project: reading a large file one page at a time

Consider a backend service storing millions of newline-delimited job records in a flat file, serving them to clients one page at a time. Alongside each page, the service returns a cursor, an opaque token the client sends back to request the subsequent page.

Representing the cursor as the exact byte offset where the next page begins makes the service stateless: any server replica with access to the file can fulfill the next request directly from the cursor without retaining per-client session state.

2.7.1 The page type

Each response page bundles its vector of lines with the byte offset of the following page.

Listing 2.10 The Page type (lines 1 to 9). src/bin/file_pagination.rs

use std::{
    fs::File,
    io::{self, BufRead, BufReader, Seek, SeekFrom},
};

struct Page {
    jobs: Vec<String>,
    next_cursor: Option<u64>, // Byte offset where the next page starts
}

Page stores the decoded lines and an Option<u64> for next_cursor, where None signals that the end of the file has been reached.

2.7.2 Counting bytes to find the next cursor

Computing the next cursor requires care. Querying the underlying File’s current seek position after reading three lines yields the wrong offset: as illustrated in Figure 2.4, BufReader prefetches up to 8 KiB on its first read, advancing the kernel’s file offset well past the third line (Figure 2.5).

To maintain an exact byte offset, read_page accumulates the byte count returned by each read_line call (Listing 2.11).

Listing 2.11 read_page (lines 11 to 38).

fn read_page(path: &str, cursor: u64, page_size: usize) -> io::Result<Page> {
    let mut file = File::open(path)?;
    file.seek(SeekFrom::Start(cursor))?;
    let mut reader = BufReader::new(file);

    // Optimization which preserves as large as the max mage size
    let mut jobs: Vec<String> = Vec::with_capacity(page_size);
    let mut offset = cursor;
    let mut line = String::new();

    while jobs.len() < page_size {
        // Clear the previously read line
        line.clear();

        match reader.read_line(&mut line)? {
            0 => break,
            bytes_read => {
                offset += bytes_read as u64;
                jobs.push(line.trim_end().to_string());
            }
        }
    }

    let at_end = reader.fill_buf()?.is_empty();
    let next_cursor = if at_end { None } else { Some(offset) };

    Ok(Page { jobs, next_cursor })
}

read_page opens the file, seeks directly to SeekFrom::Start(cursor), and wraps the descriptor in a BufReader. Preallocating with Vec::with_capacity(page_size) avoids reallocations while collecting the page’s lines.

Initialized to cursor, offset increases by the exact byte count returned by each read_line call, including the trailing newline bytes. Calling line.trim_end() strips line terminators before storing the string, while leaving offset aligned to the exact byte boundary of the next record.

Detecting end-of-file on a full final page requires one extra check. If the file ends immediately after the last line of the page, next_cursor must be None rather than pointing at EOF. Calling reader.fill_buf() exposes unread bytes in the buffer (refilling from the file if empty) without consuming them; an empty slice confirms EOF and sets next_cursor to None.

2.7.3 The complete program

In Listing 2.12, main drives the paginator as a client, requesting three-line pages until next_cursor becomes None.

Listing 2.12 The complete program. src/bin/file_pagination.rs

use std::{
    fs::File,
    io::{self, BufRead, BufReader, Seek, SeekFrom},
};

struct Page {
    jobs: Vec<String>,
    next_cursor: Option<u64>, // Byte offset where the next page starts
}

fn read_page(path: &str, cursor: u64, page_size: usize) -> io::Result<Page> {
    let mut file = File::open(path)?;
    file.seek(SeekFrom::Start(cursor))?;
    let mut reader = BufReader::new(file);

    // Optimization which preserves as large as the max mage size
    let mut jobs: Vec<String> = Vec::with_capacity(page_size);
    let mut offset = cursor;
    let mut line = String::new();

    while jobs.len() < page_size {
        // Clear the previously read line
        line.clear();

        match reader.read_line(&mut line)? {
            0 => break,
            bytes_read => {
                offset += bytes_read as u64;
                jobs.push(line.trim_end().to_string());
            }
        }
    }

    let at_end = reader.fill_buf()?.is_empty();
    let next_cursor = if at_end { None } else { Some(offset) };

    Ok(Page { jobs, next_cursor })
}

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    let mut cursor = 0;

    loop {
        let page = read_page("src/bin/large_file.txt", cursor, 3)?;

        println!("--- page ---");
        for job in &page.jobs {
            println!("{job}");
        }

        match page.next_cursor {
            Some(next) => cursor = next,
            None => break,
        }
    }

    Ok(())
}

Against a thirteen-line input file, the program emits four full pages followed by a single-line final page:

$ cargo run --bin file_pagination
--- page ---
First Line
Second Line
Thrid Line
--- page ---
4
5
6
--- page ---
7
8
9
--- page ---
10
11
12
--- page ---
13

TIP: If the underlying file can be rewritten or rotated between requests, a previously issued byte offset may land mid-line. Embedding a file generation or version identifier alongside the byte offset in the cursor allows the server to detect and reject stale cursors.

2.8 Project: command-line arguments

When a process is launched with command_line_args --name ada --count 2 --verbose, the operating system passes an argument vector (argv) of strings (Figure 2.6). Index 0 holds the executable’s path, and subsequent entries hold the remaining tokens in invocation order.

The following program parses that raw string sequence into a typed configuration struct or returns a descriptive error message.

2.8.1 The options and their defaults

All program configuration resides in a single struct whose Default implementation supplies fallback values for omitted flags.

Listing 2.13 The options (lines 1 to 17). src/bin/command_line_args.rs

use std::{env::args, process::ExitCode};

/// The options this program understands.
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
struct Options {
    name: String,
    count: u32,
    verbose: bool,
}

impl Default for Options {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Self {
            name: String::from("world"),
            count: 1,
            verbose: false,
        }
    }
}

Options defines one field per supported flag. Implementing Default centralizes the default configuration, while #[derive(Debug, PartialEq)] enables assertion comparisons in unit tests.

2.8.2 Parsing

The parser consumes arguments sequentially and populates Options, rejecting unknown flags, flags missing their value, and non-numeric counts.

Listing 2.14 parse (lines 21 to 47).

/// Turn the arguments after the program name into `Options`.
fn parse(arguments: impl IntoIterator<Item = String>) -> Result<Options, String> {
    let mut options = Options::default();
    let mut arguments = arguments.into_iter();

    while let Some(argument) = arguments.next() {
        match argument.as_str() {
            "--name" => {
                options.name = arguments
                    .next()
                    .ok_or("--name needs a value")?;
            }
            "--count" => {
                let value = arguments
                    .next()
                    .ok_or("--count needs a value")?;
                options.count = value
                    .parse()
                    .map_err(|_| format!("--count needs a number, got {value:?}"))?;
            }
            "--verbose" => options.verbose = true,
            other => return Err(format!("unknown argument {other:?}")),
        }
    }

    Ok(options)
}

Accepting impl IntoIterator<Item = String> decouples parsing from std::env::args: the production binary supplies the process argument iterator, while unit tests pass in-memory string slices.

The loop drives iteration explicitly with while let Some(argument) = arguments.next() rather than a for loop. Flags such as --name and --count must consume the following token from the same iterator inside the loop body, which a for loop prohibits because it holds exclusive ownership of the iterator for the duration of the loop.

The expression arguments.next().ok_or("--name needs a value")? combines two steps: ok_or converts None into an Err, and ? returns that error immediately. The --count arm adds integer parsing via .parse(), using map_err to attach the offending input text to the error message.

Rejecting unrecognized tokens rather than ignoring them ensures misspelled options fail loudly at startup.

2.8.3 The exit code

Listing 2.15 connects argument parsing, execution, and process exit status in main.

Listing 2.15 main (lines 49 to 68).

fn main() -> ExitCode {
    let options = match parse(args().skip(1)) {
        Ok(options) => options,
        Err(message) => {
            eprintln!("error: {message}");
            eprintln!("usage: command_line_args [--name NAME] [--count N] [--verbose]");
            return ExitCode::FAILURE;
        }
    };

    for index in 0..options.count {
        if options.verbose {
            println!("[{index}] hello, {}", options.name);
        } else {
            println!("hello, {}", options.name);
        }
    }

    ExitCode::SUCCESS
}

A process communicates completion status to its parent shell via an exit code, where 0 denotes success and any non-zero value signals failure. Returning ExitCode from main lets the program emit custom diagnostics before exiting. args().skip(1) discards the executable path at index 0. On parse failure, main writes both the error and a usage line to standard error via eprintln! and returns ExitCode::FAILURE (1).

2.8.4 The complete program

Listing 2.16 The complete program, with its tests. src/bin/command_line_args.rs

use std::{env::args, process::ExitCode};

/// The options this program understands.
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
struct Options {
    name: String,
    count: u32,
    verbose: bool,
}

impl Default for Options {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Self {
            name: String::from("world"),
            count: 1,
            verbose: false,
        }
    }
}

/// Turn the arguments after the program name into `Options`.
fn parse(arguments: impl IntoIterator<Item = String>) -> Result<Options, String> {
    let mut options = Options::default();
    let mut arguments = arguments.into_iter();

    while let Some(argument) = arguments.next() {
        match argument.as_str() {
            "--name" => {
                options.name = arguments
                    .next()
                    .ok_or("--name needs a value")?;
            }
            "--count" => {
                let value = arguments
                    .next()
                    .ok_or("--count needs a value")?;
                options.count = value
                    .parse()
                    .map_err(|_| format!("--count needs a number, got {value:?}"))?;
            }
            "--verbose" => options.verbose = true,
            other => return Err(format!("unknown argument {other:?}")),
        }
    }

    Ok(options)
}

fn main() -> ExitCode {
    let options = match parse(args().skip(1)) {
        Ok(options) => options,
        Err(message) => {
            eprintln!("error: {message}");
            eprintln!("usage: command_line_args [--name NAME] [--count N] [--verbose]");
            return ExitCode::FAILURE;
        }
    };

    for index in 0..options.count {
        if options.verbose {
            println!("[{index}] hello, {}", options.name);
        } else {
            println!("hello, {}", options.name);
        }
    }

    ExitCode::SUCCESS
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    fn parse_args(arguments: &[&str]) -> Result<Options, String> {
        parse(
            arguments
                .iter()
                .map(|value| value.to_string()),
        )
    }

    #[test]
    fn defaults_apply_when_there_are_no_arguments() {
        assert_eq!(parse_args(&[]).unwrap(), Options::default());
    }

    #[test]
    fn a_value_option_consumes_the_next_argument() {
        let options = parse_args(&["--name", "ada", "--count", "3"]).unwrap();
        assert_eq!(options.name, "ada");
        assert_eq!(options.count, 3);
    }

    #[test]
    fn verbose_is_a_flag() {
        assert!(
            parse_args(&["--verbose"])
                .unwrap()
                .verbose
        );
        assert!(!parse_args(&[]).unwrap().verbose);
    }

    #[test]
    fn a_value_option_without_a_value_is_an_error() {
        assert!(parse_args(&["--name"]).is_err());
        assert!(parse_args(&["--count"]).is_err());
    }

    #[test]
    fn a_non_numeric_count_is_an_error() {
        assert!(parse_args(&["--count", "many"]).is_err());
    }

    #[test]
    fn an_unknown_argument_is_an_error() {
        assert!(parse_args(&["--colour", "red"]).is_err());
        assert!(parse_args(&["extra"]).is_err());
    }
}

Inside the test module, the parse_args helper converts &[&str] literals into owned String iterators so each test case stays concise. The suite exercises default values, individual flags, missing values, invalid integers, and unknown options.

$ cargo run --bin command_line_args -- --name ada --count 2 --verbose
[0] hello, ada
[1] hello, ada
$ cargo run --bin command_line_args -- --count many
error: --count needs a number, got "many"
usage: command_line_args [--name NAME] [--count N] [--verbose]
$ echo $?
1

The -- separator instructs Cargo to stop parsing flags for itself and forward all subsequent arguments directly to the compiled binary.

Summary

  • User-space processes access storage exclusively through kernel system calls; the kernel page cache retains recently read file blocks in physical memory.
  • Result<T, E> encodes recoverable success or failure. The ? operator propagates Err variants immediately to the caller, requiring the enclosing function to return a compatible Result.
  • &Path and PathBuf provide borrowed and owned filesystem path representations; public APIs should accept &Path to avoid unnecessary allocation.
  • fs::read_to_string loads small files in a single operation, whereas BufReader amortizes system-call overhead for large streams. Reusing a cleared String with read_line eliminates per-line heap allocation.
  • OpenOptions with append(true) sets O_APPEND for kernel-synchronized end-of-file writes, and same-filesystem fs::rename provides atomic file replacement.
  • Inspecting io::Error::kind() enables targeted recovery for specific failure classes such as NotFound or InvalidData.
  • Calling entry.file_type() avoids dereferencing symbolic links during recursive directory traversal, preventing infinite symlink cycles.
  • Stateless byte-offset cursors must accumulate exact byte counts returned by read_line rather than querying the underlying file descriptor’s buffered seek offset.
  • Accepting an abstract iterator in a command-line parser decouples parsing from std::env::args for unit testing, while returning ExitCode from main reports completion status to the parent process.

Exercises

  1. Rewrite walk iteratively using an explicit Vec<PathBuf> work stack, tallying file counts and total byte sizes grouped by file extension.
  2. Implement atomic_write(path, bytes) by writing to a temporary file in the target directory, calling sync_all() to flush data to storage, and atomically renaming it over path.
  3. Extend the pagination cursor with a version or modification-timestamp field, returning an error if the file changes between page requests.
  4. Extend the command-line parser to accept --name=ada syntax in addition to --name ada.

Vectors, strings, and hash maps

This chapter covers

  • Quantifying algorithmic work using Big-O notation
  • Memory layouts of Vec, String, and HashMap
  • Finding matching pairs in linear time with a hash map
  • Using a vector as a stack to validate brackets and track a running minimum
  • Traversing arrays with two indexes: in-place reversal, sliding windows, and interval merging
  • Binary search on rotated arrays, in-place matrix rotation, and linear-time substring matching

Algorithmic efficiency depends jointly on asymptotic operation counts and the physical memory layout of the underlying data structures. Rust’s three foundational standard collections (Vec, String, and HashMap) provide contiguous array storage, UTF-8-validated byte buffers, and open-addressed hash tables with predictable performance contracts.

The opening sections establish two prerequisites: asymptotic Big-O complexity notation for comparing scaling behavior, and the stack-versus-heap memory layout of each collection. With these cost models explicit, the subsequent algorithms remain concise while making their time and space bounds transparent.

The implementations are organized by reusable algorithmic paradigm rather than by surface domain. Table 3.1 maps each section to its underlying technique and target problems.

SectionTechniqueProblems
3.5look things up in a hash mapfind two numbers that add up to a target
3.6a vector used as a stackcheck brackets; a stack that knows its minimum
3.7two indexes moving toward each otherreverse a string; find three numbers that add to zero
3.8a window that slides along a stringlongest piece of text with no repeated letter
3.9sort, then walk oncemerge overlapping ranges
3.10halve the search each stepbinary search in a rotated array
3.11transform in placerotate a square grid
3.12reuse what you already matchedfind text inside other text

3.1 Counting the work an algorithm does

Two implementations can compute identical outputs while differing by orders of magnitude in execution time. Selecting between competing designs requires a formal notation characterizing how work scales with input size.

Algorithmic work is quantified by counting elementary constant-time operations (such as comparisons, arithmetic instructions, or array accesses) as a function of input size n, where n typically denotes the length of an array or string. Consider three operations on an array of n integers:

  • Reading the first element requires 1 operation, independent of n.
  • Summing every element requires n operations, one per entry.
  • Comparing every element against every other element requires roughly n × n operations.

Big-O notation expresses asymptotic growth by retaining only the dominant term and dropping constant multipliers. The three operations above are written O(1), O(n), and O(n²), where O(n) (“order n”) indicates runtime growing linearly with n.

Table 3.2 illustrates how sharply these complexity classes diverge at scale.

nO(1)O(log n)O(n)O(n log n)O(n²)
101about 310about 33100
1,0001about 101,000about 10,0001,000,000
1,000,0001about 201,000,000about 20,000,0001,000,000,000,000

A modern processor executes on the order of one billion simple operations per second. At one million elements, an O(n) algorithm completes in roughly a millisecond, whereas an O(n²) algorithm requires on the order of fifteen minutes.

The same notation characterizes auxiliary memory consumption. An O(n)-space algorithm allocates storage proportional to the input size, whereas an O(1)-space algorithm uses a fixed amount of extra memory regardless of n.

NOTE: O(log n) arises whenever each step discards half of the remaining search space. Halving one million elements reduces the range to a single element in roughly 20 steps, since 220 ≈ 1,048,576. Section 3.10 applies this property to binary search.

3.2 How a Vec stores its elements

A Vec<T> is a dynamically resizable, contiguous array. Its elements occupy adjacent addresses in a single heap allocation. On the stack, the Vec header stores three machine words: a pointer to the heap buffer, the count of initialized elements (length), and the total number of elements the current allocation can hold (capacity). Figure 3.1 depicts a vector of four i32 values backed by a six-slot allocation.

Contiguous storage makes indexing O(1): the address of v[i] is computed directly as base_ptr + i * size_of::<T>(), independent of the vector’s length.

When push is called on a full vector (len == cap), the vector must reallocate a larger heap block, as illustrated in Figure 3.2.

Although an individual reallocation copies n elements in O(n) time, doubling capacity on each growth ensures reallocations occur infrequently. Averaged across any sequence of pushes, each push performs constant work, a guarantee termed amortized O(1).

When the final element count is known ahead of time, Vec::with_capacity(n) reserves the full heap block upfront, eliminating intermediate reallocations altogether.

WARNING: Because push may reallocate and move every element to a new heap address, holding an element reference such as &v[0] across a v.push(...) would create a dangling pointer. Rust’s borrow checker rejects such code at compile time.

3.3 How a String stores text

A String wraps a Vec<u8> with one additional invariant: its byte sequence must always be valid UTF-8. UTF-8 is a variable-width character encoding in which ASCII characters occupy 1 byte while other Unicode scalar values occupy 2, 3, or 4 bytes. Figure 3.3 illustrates the byte representation of "café".

This variable-width encoding has three direct consequences in Rust:

  • s.len() returns the byte length rather than the character count ("café".len() equals 5).
  • s.chars() decodes and yields Unicode scalar values sequentially from the underlying bytes.
  • Integer indexing (s[3]) is forbidden at compile time because an arbitrary byte offset can land in the middle of a multi-byte character (such as byte index 4 in Figure 3.3).

3.4 How a HashMap finds a key

A HashMap<K, V> maps keys to values with O(1) expected lookup time through three steps (Figure 3.4):

  1. A hash function deterministically maps the key to a 64-bit integer.
  2. Selected bits of that hash index into a bucket within an internal table.
  3. The map inserts or locates the key-value pair starting from that bucket.

Distinct keys can hash to the same bucket (a collision), as keys 7 and 11 do in Figure 3.4, requiring key equality checks to resolve the entry. By resizing the table whenever its load factor exceeds a fixed threshold, HashMap keeps probe chains short, maintaining O(1) expected time for insert and get.

By default, Rust’s HashMap initializes its hasher with a per-process random seed to prevent algorithmic-complexity (HashDoS) attacks crafted to collide in a single bucket. As a consequence, iteration order over a HashMap is non-deterministic across executions.

With asymptotic analysis and collection memory layouts established, the following sections develop eight canonical algorithms, contrasting baseline designs against collection-accelerated implementations.

3.5 Finding two numbers that add up to a target

The problem. Given a slice of integers and a target sum, return two distinct indexes whose elements sum to the target. For [2, 7, 11, 15] and target 9, the result is (0, 1), since 2 + 7 = 9.

The baseline approach. Testing every pair (i, j) with i < j examines roughly n(n - 1) / 2 pairs, yielding O(n²) time.

The hash-map approach. Scanning the slice once, each element num requires a known complement target - num. Storing previously visited values and their indexes in a HashMap reduces the complement query to an O(1) lookup.

Tracing [2, 7, 11, 15] with target 9:

PositionNumberPartner neededIn the map?Map afterward
027no{2: 0}
172yes, at position 0answer: (0, 1)

Listing 3.1 Two Sum with one pass and a hash map. src/problems/two_sum.rs

//! Two Sum: find the pair of indices whose values add up to a target.
//!
//! Use a `HashMap` for one pass: O(n) time, O(n) space.

use std::collections::HashMap;

pub fn two_sum(nums: &[i32], target: i32) -> Option<(usize, usize)> {
    let mut seen = HashMap::with_capacity(nums.len());
    for (idx, &num) in nums.iter().enumerate() {
        match seen.get(&(target - num)) {
            Some(&prev) => return Some((prev, idx)),
            None => {
                seen.insert(num, idx);
            }
        }
    }
    None
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn finds_pair() {
        let nums = [2, 7, 11, 15];
        assert_eq!(two_sum(&nums, 9), Some((0, 1)));
    }

    #[test]
    fn returns_none_when_missing() {
        assert_eq!(two_sum(&[1, 2, 3], 100), None);
    }
}

Key details of the implementation:

  • The parameter nums: &[i32] is a slice, a borrowed view over contiguous i32 elements compatible with arrays, vectors, and subslices.
  • HashMap::with_capacity(nums.len()) preallocates enough buckets to avoid rehashing during the scan.
  • nums.iter().enumerate() yields (usize, &i32) pairs, and the pattern (idx, &num) copies the i32 out of its reference.
  • seen.get(&(target - num)) probes for the complement by reference.
  • When the complement exists, the function returns both indexes immediately; otherwise, it inserts (num, idx).

Performing the lookup before the insertion prevents an element from pairing with itself: for target 4 and [2], inserting before looking up would erroneously return (0, 0).

The function returns Option<(usize, usize)>, running in O(n) expected time and O(n) auxiliary space.

WARNING: Computing target - num in i32 can overflow near the bounds of i32 (for example, when num == i32::MIN and target > 0), causing a panic in debug builds. Widening to i64 or calling target.checked_sub(num) eliminates overflow.

3.6 A vector used as a stack

A stack is a last-in, first-out (LIFO) sequence where insertions and removals occur exclusively at one end (the top). Vec serves directly as a stack: push appends to the top, pop removes and returns the top element, and last inspects the top without mutating the vector. All three operations run in amortized O(1) time.

3.6.1 Checking brackets

The problem. A bracket string is balanced if every opening delimiter is closed by the matching delimiter type in proper nested order. "{[()]}" is valid, whereas "([)]" is invalid because ] closes while ( remains open.

The strategy. Scan left to right, pushing every opening bracket onto a stack. Upon encountering a closing bracket, pop the top of the stack and verify that it matches the expected opener. After the scan completes, the stack must be empty. Figure 3.5 traces "{[()]}".

Listing 3.2 Valid Parentheses. src/problems/valid_parentheses.rs

//! Valid Parentheses: classic stack problem with idiomatic pattern matching.
//!
pub fn is_valid(s: &str) -> bool {
    use std::collections::HashMap;

    let mut stack = Vec::with_capacity(s.len());

    // Maps each closing delimiter to the opening delimiter it must match.
    let expected = HashMap::from([(')', '('), ('}', '{'), (']', '[')]);

    for ch in s.chars() {
        match ch {
            '(' | '[' | '{' => stack.push(ch),
            // Every other character, including one outside the six delimiters,
            // must close the top of the stack.
            _ => {
                if stack.pop().as_ref() != expected.get(&ch) {
                    return false;
                }
            }
        }
    }

    stack.is_empty()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn valid_cases() {
        assert!(is_valid("()"));
        assert!(is_valid("()[]{}"));
        assert!(is_valid("{[()]}"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn invalid_cases() {
        assert!(!is_valid("(]"));
        assert!(!is_valid("([)]"));
        assert!(!is_valid("("));
        assert!(!is_valid(")"));
        assert!(!is_valid("(("));
    }
}

The lookup table expected, constructed via HashMap::from([...]), maps each closing bracket to its required opener.

The match expression partitions characters into two arms: the first pushes opening brackets, and the second compares two Option<&char> values:

  • stack.pop().as_ref() pops the top opener and converts Option<char> to Option<&char> so both sides share the same type.
  • expected.get(&ch) returns Some(&opener) for any closing bracket.

Any mismatch returns false immediately, including an extra closing bracket on an empty stack (None != Some(...)). After the loop finishes, stack.is_empty() rejects any unclosed openers. The unit tests cover balanced inputs, interleaved mismatches ("([)]"), lone closers (")"), and unclosed openers ("((").

WARNING: If a non-bracket character arrives while the stack is empty, both stack.pop().as_ref() and expected.get(&ch) evaluate to None, causing is_valid("a") to return true. Production validators that may encounter arbitrary characters should match non-brackets in a dedicated arm to skip or reject them explicitly.

3.6.2 A stack that knows its minimum

The problem. Design a stack supporting push, pop, top, and get_min (returning the current minimum element), each in O(1) time.

The strategy. Scanning the stack on every get_min call costs O(n). Maintaining a parallel auxiliary stack (mins) that records the running minimum at each depth makes get_min an O(1) lookup: every push appends the updated minimum to mins, and every pop pops both stacks in lockstep.

Tracing pushes of -2, 0, and -3 followed by a pop:

Operationvaluesminsget_min()
push -2[-2][-2]-2
push 0[-2, 0][-2, -2]-2
push -3[-2, 0, -3][-2, -2, -3]-3
pop[-2, 0][-2, -2]-2

Listing 3.3 Min Stack with a parallel stack of minimums. src/problems/min_stack.rs

//! Min Stack: O(1) push, pop, top, and get_min.
//!
//! We keep a parallel `mins` stack. Each push stores the current minimum at that
//! point in history, so pop is symmetric.

#[derive(Debug, Default)]
pub struct MinStack {
