    values: Vec<i32>,
    mins: Vec<i32>,
}

impl MinStack {
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        Self::default()
    }

    pub fn push(&mut self, val: i32) {
        match self.mins.last() {
            Some(&min) if min <= val => self.mins.push(min),
            _ => self.mins.push(val),
        }
        self.values.push(val);
    }

    pub fn pop(&mut self) -> Option<i32> {
        self.mins.pop();
        self.values.pop()
    }

    pub fn top(&self) -> Option<i32> {
        self.values.last().copied()
    }

    pub fn get_min(&self) -> Option<i32> {
        self.mins.last().copied()
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn stack_tracks_minimum() {
        let mut stack = MinStack::new();
        stack.push(-2);
        stack.push(0);
        stack.push(-3);
        assert_eq!(stack.get_min(), Some(-3));
        assert_eq!(stack.pop(), Some(-3));
        assert_eq!(stack.top(), Some(0));
        assert_eq!(stack.get_min(), Some(-2));
    }

    #[test]
    fn handles_duplicates() {
        let mut stack = MinStack::new();
        stack.push(1);
        stack.push(1);
        stack.pop();
        assert_eq!(stack.get_min(), Some(1));
    }
}

#[derive(Default)] synthesizes MinStack::default() with two empty vectors, which new() delegates to.

Inside push, self.mins.last() inspects the current minimum. The match arm Some(&min) if min <= val uses a guard to re-push min when the incoming value is not smaller; the fallback arm _ covers both an empty stack and a new strictly smaller minimum, pushing val.

Using <= rather than < preserves correctness when duplicate minimum values are pushed: popping one copy leaves the second copy reflected on top of mins, a case verified by the handles_duplicates test.

Both top and get_min call .copied() to convert Option<&i32> into Option<i32>, returning owned integers to callers.

3.7 Two indexes moving toward each other

Problems that inspect both ends of a sequence simultaneously can maintain two indexes, start and end, advancing them inward until they cross. Because at least one index advances per iteration, the traversal completes in O(n) time.

3.7.1 Reversing a string in place

The strategy. Swap the first and last bytes, then move inward one position from each end until the two indexes meet (Figure 3.6).

As noted in Section 3.3, a String must preserve valid UTF-8; reversing individual bytes of a multi-byte character would corrupt the encoding. Consequently, Rust exposes mutable byte access only through String::as_mut_vec, which is marked unsafe. An unsafe block designates code whose memory or type invariants cannot be verified statically by the compiler and must instead be upheld by the author; here, the required invariant is that the buffer remains valid UTF-8 upon exiting the block.

Listing 3.4 The reversing function (lines 1 to 14). src/bin/reverse_string.rs

fn reverse_str(s: &mut String) {
    // SAFETY: s._as_mut_vec() is unsafe because it exposes the inner mutability to it's character buffer, and we must ensure
    // to leave valid UTF-8. We enforce ASCII only characters.
    assert!(s.is_ascii());
    let bytes = unsafe { s.as_mut_vec() };

    let (mut start, mut end) = (0, bytes.len() - 1);

    while start < end {
        bytes.swap(start, end);
        start += 1;
        end -= 1;
    }
}

The function enforces the UTF-8 invariant upfront via assert!(s.is_ascii()), panicking if any multi-byte character is present. Because every ASCII byte is a self-contained single-byte UTF-8 sequence, any permutation of ASCII bytes remains valid UTF-8, allowing the unsafe block to wrap a single method call.

Inside the loop, bytes.swap(start, end) exchanges the two endpoints while start < end, leaving the center byte of an odd-length string untouched.

Listing 3.5 The complete program, with its tests. src/bin/reverse_string.rs

fn reverse_str(s: &mut String) {
    // SAFETY: s._as_mut_vec() is unsafe because it exposes the inner mutability to it's character buffer, and we must ensure
    // to leave valid UTF-8. We enforce ASCII only characters.
    assert!(s.is_ascii());
    let bytes = unsafe { s.as_mut_vec() };

    let (mut start, mut end) = (0, bytes.len() - 1);

    while start < end {
        bytes.swap(start, end);
        start += 1;
        end -= 1;
    }
}

fn main() {
    for value in ["abcd", "abc", "a", "rust"] {
        let mut s = String::from(value);
        reverse_str(&mut s);
        println!("{value:>6} -> {s}");
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn an_even_length_string_is_reversed() {
        let mut s = String::from("abcd");
        reverse_str(&mut s);
        assert_eq!(s, "dcba");
    }

    #[test]
    fn an_odd_length_string_keeps_its_middle_byte() {
        let mut s = String::from("abc");
        reverse_str(&mut s);
        assert_eq!(s, "cba");
    }

    #[test]
    fn a_single_byte_is_unchanged() {
        let mut s = String::from("a");
        reverse_str(&mut s);
        assert_eq!(s, "a");
    }

    #[test]
    fn the_buffer_is_reused() {
        let mut s = String::from("abcd");
        let capacity = s.capacity();
        let address = s.as_ptr();
        reverse_str(&mut s);
        assert_eq!(s.capacity(), capacity);
        assert_eq!(s.as_ptr(), address);
    }

    #[test]
    fn reversing_twice_restores_the_string() {
        let mut s = String::from("interview");
        reverse_str(&mut s);
        reverse_str(&mut s);
        assert_eq!(s, "interview");
    }

    #[test]
    #[should_panic]
    fn non_ascii_input_panics() {
        let mut s = String::from("café");
        reverse_str(&mut s);
    }
}

The unit test the_buffer_is_reused captures the string’s capacity and heap pointer before and after reversal, confirming zero reallocation. non_ascii_input_panics is annotated with #[should_panic] to verify that the ASCII precondition rejects "café".

$ cargo run --bin reverse_string
  abcd -> dcba
   abc -> cba
     a -> a
  rust -> tsur

WARNING: On an empty string, bytes.len() - 1 underflows usize, triggering a panic in debug builds. Production implementations must return early when s.is_empty().

3.7.2 Three numbers that add up to a target

The problem. Find every unique triple of integers in an array that sums to a given target, without emitting duplicate triples.

The strategy. Sort the slice in ascending order first. Fix the first element at index i, then search the remaining suffix with two converging indexes: left = i + 1 and right = len - 1. Sorted order determines which pointer must move at each step:

  • If the sum is below target, increment left to increase the sum.
  • If the sum exceeds target, decrement right to decrease the sum.
  • If the sum equals target, record the triple and advance both indexes past any duplicate values.

Sorting costs O(n log n), and each of the n fixed elements triggers an O(n) two-pointer scan, yielding O(n²) overall time.

The outer setup sorts the slice and iterates over each unique first element:

// Import the variants directly into scope
use std::cmp::Ordering::{Equal, Greater, Less};

pub fn three_sum(numbers: &mut [i32], target: i32) -> Vec<(i32, i32, i32)> {
    numbers.sort_unstable();

    let mut results = Vec::new();
    let target = i64::from(target);

    for i in 0..numbers.len() {
        // Skip a first value that was already used, so triplets stay unique.
        if i > 0 && numbers[i] == numbers[i - 1] {
            continue;
        }

        let (mut left, mut right) = (i + 1, numbers.len().saturating_sub(1));
        // ...
    }
}
  • Importing std::cmp::Ordering::{Equal, Greater, Less} allows concise pattern matching on comparison results.
  • Skipping numbers[i] == numbers[i - 1] prevents duplicate triples anchored on the same first element.
  • numbers.len().saturating_sub(1) safely yields 0 on empty slices without unsigned underflow.

For each fixed index i, the inner loop converges left and right:

pub fn three_sum(numbers: &mut [i32], target: i32) -> Vec<(i32, i32, i32)> {
    // ...
    for i in 0..numbers.len() {
        // ...
        while left < right {
            // Widen to i64 so the sum of three i32 values cannot overflow.
            let current_sum = numbers[i] as i64 + numbers[left] as i64 + numbers[right] as i64;

            match current_sum.cmp(&target) {
                Less => left += 1,
                Greater => right -= 1,
                Equal => {
                    results.push((numbers[i], numbers[left], numbers[right]));

                    while left < right && numbers[left] == numbers[left + 1] {
                        left += 1;
                    }
                    while left < right && numbers[right] == numbers[right - 1] {
                        right -= 1;
                    }

                    left += 1;
                    right -= 1;
                }
            }
        }
    }
    // ...
}
  • Accumulating the triple sum in i64 prevents signed 32-bit overflow when summing values near i32::MAX or i32::MIN, as exercised by does_not_overflow_on_extreme_values.
  • Matching on current_sum.cmp(&target) maps Less, Greater, and Equal directly to the pointer updates.
  • After recording a match, two inner while loops skip consecutive duplicate values at left and right.

Listing 3.6 Three Sum, with its tests. src/problems/three_sum.rs

//! Three Sum: every unique triplet of values that adds up to a target.
//!
//! Sort, fix the first value, then close in on the other two with two pointers.
//! Sorts the caller's slice in place: O(n^2) time, no extra space beyond the result.

// Import the variants directly into scope
use std::cmp::Ordering::{Equal, Greater, Less};

pub fn three_sum(numbers: &mut [i32], target: i32) -> Vec<(i32, i32, i32)> {
    numbers.sort_unstable();

    let mut results = Vec::new();
    let target = i64::from(target);

    for i in 0..numbers.len() {
        // Skip a first value that was already used, so triplets stay unique.
        if i > 0 && numbers[i] == numbers[i - 1] {
            continue;
        }

        let (mut left, mut right) = (i + 1, numbers.len().saturating_sub(1));
        while left < right {
            // Widen to i64 so the sum of three i32 values cannot overflow.
            let current_sum = numbers[i] as i64 + numbers[left] as i64 + numbers[right] as i64;

            match current_sum.cmp(&target) {
                Less => left += 1,
                Greater => right -= 1,
                Equal => {
                    results.push((numbers[i], numbers[left], numbers[right]));

                    while left < right && numbers[left] == numbers[left + 1] {
                        left += 1;
                    }
                    while left < right && numbers[right] == numbers[right - 1] {
                        right -= 1;
                    }

                    left += 1;
                    right -= 1;
                }
            }
        }
    }

    results
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn finds_all_unique_triplets() {
        let result = three_sum(&mut [-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4], 0);
        assert_eq!(result, vec![(-1, -1, 2), (-1, 0, 1)]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn skips_duplicates_on_every_position() {
        assert_eq!(three_sum(&mut [0, 0, 0, 0], 0), vec![(0, 0, 0)]);
        assert_eq!(three_sum(&mut [-2, 0, 0, 2, 2], 0), vec![(-2, 0, 2)]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn supports_a_non_zero_target() {
        assert_eq!(
            three_sum(&mut [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 9),
            vec![(1, 3, 5), (2, 3, 4)]
        );
    }

    #[test]
    fn returns_nothing_when_no_triplet_exists() {
        assert!(three_sum(&mut [1, 2, 3], 100).is_empty());
        assert!(three_sum(&mut [1, 2], 3).is_empty());
        assert!(three_sum(&mut [], 0).is_empty());
    }

    #[test]
    fn does_not_overflow_on_extreme_values() {
        assert_eq!(
            three_sum(&mut [i32::MAX, i32::MAX, i32::MIN], i32::MAX - 1),
            vec![(i32::MIN, i32::MAX, i32::MAX)]
        );
    }
}

3.8 A window that slides along a string

The problem. Compute the length of the longest contiguous substring containing no repeated characters. For "pwwkew", the maximum length is 3 (corresponding to "wke" or "kew").

The strategy. Maintain a sliding window start..=end invariant to contain exclusively distinct characters. As end advances one character at a time, if the incoming character already lies inside the current window, advance start immediately past its prior occurrence. Recording the maximum window width across all positions yields the answer.

A HashMap<char, usize> maps each seen character to its most recent character index. Figure 3.7 depicts the window state in "pwwkew" when the third w is processed.

Listing 3.7 Longest substring without a repeated character. src/problems/sliding_window.rs

//! Longest substring without repeating characters.
//!
//! Sliding window with `HashMap<char, usize>`; the window start is monotonic.

use std::collections::HashMap;

pub fn length_of_longest_substring(s: &str) -> usize {
    let mut last_seen = HashMap::with_capacity(s.len());

    let (mut start, mut longest) = (0, 0);

    for (end, ch) in s.chars().enumerate() {
        if let Some(&previous) = last_seen.get(&ch) {
            start = start.max(previous + 1);
        }
        longest = longest.max(end - start + 1);
        last_seen.insert(ch, end);
    }

    longest
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn examples() {
        assert_eq!(length_of_longest_substring("abcabcbb"), 3);
        assert_eq!(length_of_longest_substring("bbbbb"), 1);
        assert_eq!(length_of_longest_substring("pwwkew"), 3);
        assert_eq!(length_of_longest_substring(""), 0);
    }
}

When last_seen.get(&ch) finds an earlier index previous, start = start.max(previous + 1) advances the left boundary without ever moving it backward. The .max(...) guard is essential for inputs like "abba": when the second 'a' arrives at index 3, 'a' was last seen at index 0, which already falls outside the current window starting at index 2.

At each step, end - start + 1 gives the active window length. Because both start and end advance monotonically, the algorithm runs in O(n) time. Iterating via chars().enumerate() counts Unicode scalar values rather than raw UTF-8 bytes, matching the problem specification.

3.9 Sort, then walk once: merging ranges

The problem. Given a list of closed intervals such as [1,3] [2,6] [8,10] [15,18], merge all overlapping intervals into disjoint ranges ([1,6] [8,10] [15,18]).

The strategy. Sort the intervals by their start coordinate, then perform a single linear pass. In sorted order, each interval either overlaps the most recently merged interval (extending its end coordinate) or starts a new disjoint interval (Figure 3.8).

The module implements three variations: one using a named Interval struct, one using raw tuples, and one operating in place. Listing 3.8 presents the Interval struct and the first implementation.

Listing 3.8 Merging ranges held in a struct (lines 6 to 28). src/problems/merge_intervals.rs

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Clone, Copy)]
pub struct Interval {
    start: i32,
    end: i32,
}
pub fn merge_intervals(mut intervals: Vec<Interval>) -> Vec<Interval> {
    if intervals.is_empty() {
        return intervals;
    }

    intervals.sort_unstable_by_key(|interval| interval.start);

    let mut merged: Vec<Interval> = Vec::with_capacity(intervals.len());
    for Interval { start, end } in intervals {
        match merged.last_mut() {
            Some(previous) if start <= previous.end => {
                previous.end = previous.end.max(end);
            }
            _ => merged.push(Interval { start, end }),
        }
    }
    merged
}

sort_unstable_by_key(|interval| interval.start) orders intervals by start coordinate; unstable sorting may reorder elements with identical start keys, which is inconsequential here and avoids auxiliary allocation.

The loop header for Interval { start, end } in intervals destructures each struct directly. Calling merged.last_mut() yields a mutable reference to the active tail interval (or None on the first element). When the guard if start <= previous.end holds, previous.end = previous.end.max(end) extends the tail interval in place while preserving containment when a shorter interval lies entirely inside the previous one. Otherwise, the fallback arm appends a new interval.

Listing 3.9 implements the same algorithm over (i32, i32) tuples, replacing named fields with positional .0 and .1 accessors.

Listing 3.9 The same merge over tuples (lines 30 to 48).

pub fn merge_intervals2(mut intervals: Vec<(i32, i32)>) -> Vec<(i32, i32)> {
    if intervals.is_empty() {
        return intervals;
    }

    intervals.sort_unstable_by_key(|(start, _)| *start);

    let mut merged: Vec<(i32, i32)> = Vec::with_capacity(intervals.len());

    for &(start, end) in &intervals {
        match merged.last_mut() {
            Some(previous) if start <= previous.1 => {
                previous.1 = previous.1.max(end);
            }
            _ => merged.push((start, end)),
        }
    }
    merged
}

While behaviorally identical, the named struct in Listing 3.8 improves readability by making previous.end self-documenting rather than requiring callers to remember field positions.

Listing 3.10 eliminates the output vector entirely by compacting merged intervals into the prefix of the input vector.

Listing 3.10 Merging in place (lines 50 to 72).

/// In place: `last` is the last merged interval at the front of the vector.
/// O(1) extra space.
pub fn merge_intervals_in_place(intervals: &mut Vec<Interval>) {
    if intervals.is_empty() {
        return;
    }

    intervals.sort_unstable_by_key(|interval| interval.start);

    let mut last = 0;
    for i in 1..intervals.len() {
        match (intervals[last], intervals[i]) {
            (previous, current) if current.start <= previous.end => {
                intervals[last].end = previous.end.max(current.end);
            }
            (_, current) => {
                last += 1;
                intervals[last] = current;
            }
        }
    }
    intervals.truncate(last + 1);
}

The write cursor last tracks the index of the latest merged interval. Each subsequent interval either extends intervals[last] or advances last by one and copies into the new slot. Calling intervals.truncate(last + 1) discards the uncompacted tail, achieving O(1) auxiliary space beyond sorting.

Matching on (intervals[last], intervals[i]) copies both Copy structs out of the vector before mutating intervals[last], avoiding simultaneous overlapping borrows of the vector.

Listing 3.11 The tests (lines 74 to 106).

    #[test]
    fn merges_overlapping_and_adjacent() {
        let input = [(1, 3), (2, 6), (8, 10), (15, 18)].map(|(start, end)| Interval { start, end });
        let expected = [(1, 6), (8, 10), (15, 18)].map(|(start, end)| Interval { start, end });
        assert_eq!(merge_intervals(input.into()), expected);

            .map(|(start, end)| Interval { start, end })

The test suite constructs Interval values from tuple arrays via .map(|(start, end)| Interval { start, end }), verifying overlapping ranges, empty inputs, disjoint ranges, and unsorted inputs for the in-place variant. Because the overlap predicate uses <=, adjacent intervals that share an endpoint (such as [1,3] and [3,5]) merge into a single range.

3.10 Halving the search: binary search

In a sorted array, locating a target does not require a linear scan. Comparing the target against the midpoint eliminates half of the remaining range on every step: values smaller than the midpoint can lie only in the left half, and larger values only in the right half. Figure 3.9 locates 23 among eight elements in three comparisons.

The implementation below represents the active candidate set as a half-open range low..high, where low is inclusive and high is exclusive; the search space is empty precisely when low == high.

3.10.1 Searching a rotated array

A harder variant searches a sorted array that has been rotated by moving a prefix to the back, such as [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], while maintaining O(log n) complexity.

The algorithm relies on a structural invariant: splitting a rotated sorted array at any midpoint mid guarantees that at least one of the two halves remains strictly sorted. Comparing endpoint values identifies which half is sorted:

  • If the left half is sorted and target falls within [nums[low], nums[mid]), narrow the search to the left half.
  • If the right half is sorted and target falls within (nums[mid], nums[high - 1]], narrow the search to the right half.
  • Otherwise, discard the sorted half and search the opposite half.

Listing 3.12 Search in a rotated sorted array. src/problems/binary_search.rs

//! Binary search on a rotated sorted array.
//!
//! O(log n). The code uses explicit range bounds and
//! sorted-half checks; no recursion or nested `if` chains are required.

pub fn search_rotated(nums: &[i32], target: i32) -> Option<usize> {
    let mut low = 0usize;
    let mut high = nums.len();

    while low < high {
        let mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if nums[mid] == target {
            return Some(mid);
        }

        let left_is_sorted = nums[low] <= nums[mid];
        if left_is_sorted {
            if nums[low] <= target && target < nums[mid] {
                high = mid;
            } else {
                low = mid + 1;
            }
        } else if nums[mid] < target && target <= nums[high - 1] {
            low = mid + 1;
        } else {
            high = mid;
        }
    }

    None
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn finds_target_in_rotated_array() {
        let nums = [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2];
        assert_eq!(search_rotated(&nums, 0), Some(4));
        assert_eq!(search_rotated(&nums, 3), None);
        assert_eq!(search_rotated(&nums, 5), Some(1));
    }

    #[test]
    fn handles_unrotated_and_single() {
        assert_eq!(search_rotated(&[1, 2, 3, 4], 3), Some(2));
        assert_eq!(search_rotated(&[1], 1), Some(0));
        assert_eq!(search_rotated(&[1], 2), None);
    }
}

Computing mid = low + (high - low) / 2 avoids integer overflow when low + high would exceed usize::MAX.

The condition nums[low] <= nums[mid] confirms that the left half is monotonically ordered, in which case nums[low] <= target && target < nums[mid] determines whether the target lies inside it. For the right half, the upper bound uses nums[high - 1] because high is exclusive.

3.11 Rotating a square grid in place

The problem. Rotate an n × n matrix 90 degrees clockwise in place, using O(1) extra memory.

The strategy. Decompose the rotation into two in-place passes (Figure 3.11): first transpose the matrix across its main diagonal by swapping (i, j) with (j, i), then reverse every row.

Listing 3.13 The complete program. src/bin/rotate_matrix.rs

fn rotate(m: &mut [Vec<i32>]) {
    let n = m.len();

    for i in 0..n {
        for j in i + 1..n {
            let tmp = m[i][j];
            m[i][j] = m[j][i];
            m[j][i] = tmp;
        }
    }

    for row in m.iter_mut() {
        row.reverse();
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut m = vec![vec![1, 2, 3], vec![4, 5, 6], vec![7, 8, 9]];

    rotate(&mut m);

    for row in &m {
        println!("{:?}", row);
    }
}

Because rotate modifies cell values without inserting or removing rows, it accepts &mut [Vec<i32>] (a mutable slice of rows). In the transpose pass, starting the inner loop at j = i + 1 visits only the upper triangle so each off-diagonal pair is swapped once; iterating from 0 would swap every pair twice and restore the original grid.

The exchange uses an explicit temporary variable tmp rather than std::mem::swap(&mut m[i][j], &mut m[j][i]). Because m[i] and m[j] are indexed through the same outer slice m, the borrow checker cannot prove statically that i != j and therefore rejects two simultaneous mutable borrows of m.

In the second pass, for row in m.iter_mut() yields a mutable reference to each row, which row.reverse() reverses in place.

$ cargo run --bin rotate_matrix
[7, 4, 1]
[8, 5, 2]
[9, 6, 3]

3.12 Finding text inside text

The problem. Locate the first byte index where a pattern string (the needle) occurs inside a target string (the haystack).

The baseline approach. Trying every starting offset in the haystack and comparing the needle character by character restarts from scratch on every mismatch. For a haystack of length n and needle of length m, worst-case complexity is O(n × m).

The linear-time approach. When a mismatch occurs after several matching characters, those matched characters are already known to equal a prefix of the needle. If a proper suffix of the matched portion also equals a prefix of the needle, matching can resume from that prefix length without backtracking in the haystack. The Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) algorithm exploits this structure to achieve O(n + m) worst-case time.

Figure 3.12 illustrates a KMP fallback jump.

To compute fallback offsets in O(1), KMP preprocesses the needle into a failure table lps (longest proper prefix that is also a suffix). For each prefix needle[0..=i], lps[i] records the length of its longest proper prefix (excluding the entire substring) that matches its suffix. For "aabaaac":

index0123456
needleaabaaac
lps0101220

For example, lps[4] = 2 because "aabaa" both starts and ends with "aa".

Listing 3.14 The search and the table (lines 1 to 58). src/bin/kmp_pattern_matching.rs

struct Solution {}
impl Solution {
    /// @param haystack the string to search in
    /// @param needle   the pattern to find
    /// @return         first index of needle in haystack, or -1
    pub fn str_str(haystack: String, needle: String) -> i32 {
        let (haystack, needle) = (haystack.as_bytes(), needle.as_bytes());
        if needle.is_empty() {
            return 0;
        }

        let lps = Self::build_lps(needle);
        // left walks the needle, and right walks the haystack.
        let (mut left, mut right) = (0, 0);

        while right < haystack.len() {
            if haystack[right] == needle[left] {
                left += 1;
                right += 1;
            } else if left > 0 {
                // Fall back, keeping the characters that still match.
                left = lps[left - 1];
            } else {
                // A mismatch at the start of the needle.
                right += 1;
            }

            if left == needle.len() {
                // The whole needle matched.
                return (right - left) as i32;
            }
        }
        -1
    }

    // LPS: longest proper prefix of needle[0..=right] that is also a suffix
    fn build_lps(needle: &[u8]) -> Vec<usize> {
        let mut lps = vec![0; needle.len()];
        let (mut left, mut right) = (0, 1);

        while right < needle.len() {
            if needle[right] == needle[left] {
                left += 1;
                lps[right] = left;
                right += 1;
            } else if left > 0 {
                left = lps[left - 1];
            } else {
                // lps[right] stays 0.
                right += 1;
            }
        }
        lps
    }
}

fn main() {
    let cases = [
    // ...
}

str_str operates directly on byte slices from as_bytes() for O(1) indexing. Here left tracks the number of matched needle bytes and right scans the haystack. Each iteration executes one of three branches:

  1. Matching bytes: advance both left and right.
  2. Mismatch with left > 0: fall back to left = lps[left - 1] without moving right.
  3. Mismatch with left == 0: advance right.

Once left reaches needle.len(), the match begins at right - left.

build_lps runs the identical three-branch state machine of the needle against itself. Because right advances monotonically and total fallbacks cannot exceed total increments of left, preprocessing and searching together run in O(n + m) time.

Listing 3.15 The complete program. src/bin/kmp_pattern_matching.rs

struct Solution {}
impl Solution {
    /// @param haystack the string to search in
    /// @param needle   the pattern to find
    /// @return         first index of needle in haystack, or -1
    pub fn str_str(haystack: String, needle: String) -> i32 {
        let (haystack, needle) = (haystack.as_bytes(), needle.as_bytes());
        if needle.is_empty() {
            return 0;
        }

        let lps = Self::build_lps(needle);
        // left walks the needle, and right walks the haystack.
        let (mut left, mut right) = (0, 0);

        while right < haystack.len() {
            if haystack[right] == needle[left] {
                left += 1;
                right += 1;
            } else if left > 0 {
                // Fall back, keeping the characters that still match.
                left = lps[left - 1];
            } else {
                // A mismatch at the start of the needle.
                right += 1;
            }

            if left == needle.len() {
                // The whole needle matched.
                return (right - left) as i32;
            }
        }
        -1
    }

    // LPS: longest proper prefix of needle[0..=right] that is also a suffix
    fn build_lps(needle: &[u8]) -> Vec<usize> {
        let mut lps = vec![0; needle.len()];
        let (mut left, mut right) = (0, 1);

        while right < needle.len() {
            if needle[right] == needle[left] {
                left += 1;
                lps[right] = left;
                right += 1;
            } else if left > 0 {
                left = lps[left - 1];
            } else {
                // lps[right] stays 0.
                right += 1;
            }
        }
        lps
    }
}

fn main() {
    let cases = [
        ("sadbutsad", "sad"),
        ("leetcode", "leeto"),
        ("aabaaabaaac", "aabaaac"),
        ("hello", ""),
    ];

    for (haystack, needle) in cases {
        let result = Solution::str_str(haystack.to_string(), needle.to_string());
        println!("str_str({haystack:?}, {needle:?}) = {result}\n");
    }
}
$ cargo run --bin kmp_pattern_matching
str_str("sadbutsad", "sad") = 0

str_str("leetcode", "leeto") = -1

str_str("aabaaabaaac", "aabaaac") = 4

str_str("hello", "") = 0

The -1 sentinel follows the classic interview specification; idiomatic Rust APIs return Option<usize> instead. For production string searching, str::find in the standard library also runs in linear time (using the Two-Way algorithm).

3.13 The complete files

Listing 3.16 reproduces merge_intervals.rs in full, combining the excerpts from Section 3.9.

Listing 3.16 Merging overlapping intervals, with its tests. src/problems/merge_intervals.rs

//! Merge Intervals: sort by start, then merge overlapping intervals in one pass.
//!
//! The `match out.last_mut()` pattern is intentionally clean: no deep nesting,
//! no confusing boolean flags.

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Clone, Copy)]
pub struct Interval {
    start: i32,
    end: i32,
}
pub fn merge_intervals(mut intervals: Vec<Interval>) -> Vec<Interval> {
    if intervals.is_empty() {
        return intervals;
    }

    intervals.sort_unstable_by_key(|interval| interval.start);

    let mut merged: Vec<Interval> = Vec::with_capacity(intervals.len());
    for Interval { start, end } in intervals {
        match merged.last_mut() {
            Some(previous) if start <= previous.end => {
                previous.end = previous.end.max(end);
            }
            _ => merged.push(Interval { start, end }),
        }
    }
    merged
}

pub fn merge_intervals2(mut intervals: Vec<(i32, i32)>) -> Vec<(i32, i32)> {
    if intervals.is_empty() {
        return intervals;
    }

    intervals.sort_unstable_by_key(|(start, _)| *start);

    let mut merged: Vec<(i32, i32)> = Vec::with_capacity(intervals.len());

    for &(start, end) in &intervals {
        match merged.last_mut() {
            Some(previous) if start <= previous.1 => {
                previous.1 = previous.1.max(end);
            }
            _ => merged.push((start, end)),
        }
    }
    merged
}

/// In place: `last` is the last merged interval at the front of the vector.
/// O(1) extra space.
pub fn merge_intervals_in_place(intervals: &mut Vec<Interval>) {
    if intervals.is_empty() {
        return;
    }

    intervals.sort_unstable_by_key(|interval| interval.start);

    let mut last = 0;
    for i in 1..intervals.len() {
        match (intervals[last], intervals[i]) {
            (previous, current) if current.start <= previous.end => {
                intervals[last].end = previous.end.max(current.end);
            }
            (_, current) => {
                last += 1;
                intervals[last] = current;
            }
        }
    }
    intervals.truncate(last + 1);
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn merges_overlapping_and_adjacent() {
        let input = [(1, 3), (2, 6), (8, 10), (15, 18)].map(|(start, end)| Interval { start, end });
        let expected = [(1, 6), (8, 10), (15, 18)].map(|(start, end)| Interval { start, end });
        assert_eq!(merge_intervals(input.into()), expected);
    }

    #[test]
    fn handles_empty_and_disjoint() {
        assert_eq!(merge_intervals(vec![]), vec![]);
        let input = [(1, 2), (3, 4)].map(|(start, end)| Interval { start, end });
        let expected = [(1, 2), (3, 4)].map(|(start, end)| Interval { start, end });
        assert_eq!(merge_intervals(input.into()), expected);
    }

    #[test]
    fn merges_in_place() {
        let mut intervals: Vec<Interval> = [(8, 10), (1, 3), (15, 18), (2, 6)]
            .map(|(start, end)| Interval { start, end })
            .into();
        merge_intervals_in_place(&mut intervals);
        let expected = [(1, 6), (8, 10), (15, 18)].map(|(start, end)| Interval { start, end });
        assert_eq!(intervals, expected);

        let mut empty = vec![];
        merge_intervals_in_place(&mut empty);
        assert!(empty.is_empty());
    }
}

Summary

  • Big-O notation characterizes asymptotic time and auxiliary space growth by retaining only the dominant term and omitting constant factors.
  • A Vec<T> stores elements contiguously in a heap-allocated buffer, providing O(1) random-access indexing and amortized O(1) push via geometric capacity growth.
  • A String enforces a UTF-8 encoding invariant over a Vec<u8>; len() reports byte length, whereas chars() decodes Unicode scalar values sequentially.
  • A HashMap<K, V> maps keys to buckets with a randomly seeded hasher to resist collision attacks, delivering O(1) expected get and insert.
  • Indexing visited elements in a HashMap reduces complement queries in Two Sum from O(n2) to O(n) expected time.
  • Using a Vec as a LIFO stack solves nested delimiter validation and O(1) minimum-element queries (MinStack).
  • Converging two-pointer traversals reverse ASCII buffers in place in O(1) auxiliary space and solve Three Sum in O(n2) time after sorting.
  • Sliding windows paired with a last-seen index map compute the longest substring without repeated characters in O(n) time.
  • Sorting intervals by start coordinate permits a single O(n) pass to merge overlapping ranges, either into an output vector or in place.
  • Binary search halves the candidate range per step in O(log n) time and extends to rotated sorted arrays by identifying which half preserves monotonic order.
  • Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) preprocesses a pattern’s prefix-suffix table (lps) to locate substrings in O(n + m) worst-case time without backtracking in the haystack.

Exercises

  1. Update two_sum to perform complement arithmetic in i64 so extreme values cannot overflow, and add a unit test exercising i32::MIN.
  2. Modify is_valid to reject non-bracket characters explicitly, and add a unit test for "a".
  3. Guard reverse_str against empty strings, then implement a safe variant that reverses Unicode scalar values for arbitrary UTF-8 strings including "café".
  4. Implement standard binary search over a sorted slice returning Option<usize>, testing slices of length 0, 1, and 2.
  5. Modify the matrix rotation to rotate 90 degrees counterclockwise using a transpose and one reversal pass.

Iterators and references

This chapter covers

  • The Iterator trait and how for loops desugar to next calls
  • The three collection traversal modes: shared reference, mutable reference, and by value
  • Chaining lazy adapters (filter, map) and driving execution with consumers (collect)
  • Why filter closures receive &&T, and how pattern destructuring (|&&x|) strips reference layers
  • Lifetimes: what they represent, why the compiler requires them across function boundaries, and how to read 'a
  • Indexing a slice with a HashMap of borrowed references without cloning elements

Zero-cost collection traversal in Rust rests on two interlocking abstractions: lazy pull-based iterators and statically verified borrowing lifetimes. Together, they enable composable data pipelines and zero-copy indexing structures without garbage collection or dangling pointers.

The first half of this treatment formalizes the Iterator trait, its desugaring from for loops, and how lazy adapters compose without allocating intermediate buffers. The second half formalizes references and lifetimes. A lifetime is the static program region over which a reference is guaranteed to refer to valid, initialized memory; explicit 'a annotations express borrowing contracts across function boundaries so the borrow checker can verify soundness compositionally.

Both mechanisms converge in a complete program that indexes a slice of User structs by identifier using a HashMap of borrowed references, eliminating struct cloning altogether.

4.1 What an iterator is

An iterator is a stateful value implementing the Iterator trait, which requires a single method, next. Each call to next yields Some(item) while elements remain and None once the sequence is exhausted.

Conceptually, a slice iterator behaves like a cursor positioned just before the first element. Each next call advances the cursor and yields a reference to the element it crosses (Figure 4.1).

Application code rarely calls next manually because Rust’s for loop desugars directly to it. The loop:

for x in [10, 20, 30].iter() {
    println!("{x}");
}

is equivalent to:

let mut it = [10, 20, 30].iter();
while let Some(x) = it.next() {
    println!("{x}");
}

The while let Some(x) = it.next() loop continues pulling items until next returns None. The argument parser in Section 2.8 used this explicit form so the loop body could call next a second time to consume flag values.

4.2 Three ways to walk a collection

A collection such as Vec<String> owns its elements. Iterating over it requires choosing how each element is accessed: by shared reference, by mutable reference, or by owned value. Each mode corresponds to a distinct method (Figure 4.2).

  • iter() yields &T (shared references), leaving the collection intact and usable afterward.
  • iter_mut() yields &mut T, permitting in-place mutation of each element.
  • into_iter() yields T by value, moving ownership out of the collection so the collection cannot be accessed afterward.

In a for loop, the expression following in selects the mode automatically: for x in &names calls names.iter(), for x in &mut names calls names.iter_mut(), and for x in names calls names.into_iter(), consuming names.

TIP: When an iterator item’s exact reference depth is unclear, inserting a deliberate type mismatch such as let () = x; inside the loop forces the compiler to print the inferred type of x in its diagnostic.

4.3 Chaining iterators

An iterator adapter wraps one iterator to produce another. filter retains only items for which a predicate closure returns true, while map transforms each item through a closure. By contrast, collect is a consumer: it drives the pipeline to completion and materializes the output into a target collection such as a Vec or HashMap.

Figure 4.3 traces three values flowing through a filter and map pipeline.

Rust iterator adapters are lazy. Evaluating iter().filter(...).map(...) constructs a nested state machine describing the pipeline without touching a single element. Execution begins only when a consumer such as collect or a for loop pulls items via next. Each element then traverses all stages sequentially before the next element is fetched, eliminating intermediate heap allocations.

Animation 4.1 traces functional_numbers_drill (Listing 4.1) on [10, 15, 20, 25, 30], showing demand propagating backward from collect and elements flowing forward one at a time.

WARNING: Because adapters are lazy, an iterator chain without a terminating consumer (collect, for, count, or for_each) performs no work at runtime. The compiler flags such dead pipelines with an unused_must_use warning (unused Map that must be used).

4.4 References to references

Inspecting the exact item types in Figure 4.3 clarifies a common point of confusion. Calling slice.iter() produces items of type &i32. Because filter must inspect each item without consuming it (so surviving items can be yielded downstream), filter passes a shared reference to the item (&Self::Item) into its predicate closure. Combining both layers gives the closure &&i32, a reference to a reference to an i32 (Figure 4.4).

Closure parameters accept irrefutable patterns identical to let bindings, where &x strips one layer of reference:

  • .filter(|&&x| x % 2 == 0) strips both reference layers, binding x directly as i32.
  • .map(|&x| x * 10) strips the single reference layer yielded by iter(), because map passes Self::Item by value rather than by reference.

Pattern dereferencing works for i32 because i32 implements Copy, so binding x copies the integer out of the reference. Non-Copy types such as String cannot be moved out of a shared reference; attempting |&s| fails to compile, and the closure must bind |s| as a reference instead.

4.5 The same work in two styles

Listing 4.1 defines a small User struct alongside two slice transformations written in functional and imperative styles.

Listing 4.1 The User type and two ways to transform a slice (lines 1 to 23). src/bin/lifetime_reference_drill.rs

use std::collections::HashMap;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct User {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
}

fn functional_numbers_drill(slice: &[i32]) -> Vec<i32> {
    slice
        .iter()
        .filter(|&&x| x % 2 == 0)
        .map(|&x| x * 10)
        .collect()
}

fn imperative_numbers_map(slice: &[i32]) -> HashMap<i32, i32> {
    let mut map = HashMap::new();
    for &num in slice {
        map.insert(num, num * 100);
    }
    map
}

functional_numbers_drill implements the pipeline from Figure 4.3. Type inference determines that collect() should construct a Vec<i32> from the function’s return signature; when inference is ambiguous, callers specify the target type explicitly via turbofish syntax (collect::<Vec<i32>>()).

imperative_numbers_map uses a for loop to populate a HashMap mapping each input number to num * 100. The pattern for &num in slice copies the i32 out of each yielded &i32.

Neither style carries an inherent runtime penalty; under optimization, LLVM compiles both forms to comparable machine code. Iterator pipelines express linear data transformations cleanly, whereas explicit loops suit bodies with multiple side effects or complex early-exit control flow.

Because iterator pipelines frequently yield borrowed references into backing storage, soundness depends on static lifetime verification.

4.6 Lifetimes

Every reference borrows data owned elsewhere. If the owner is dropped while a reference remains live, that reference becomes a dangling pointer referencing freed memory, leading to undefined behavior or crashes in unmanaged languages. Figure 4.5 illustrates the minimal case.

To prevent dangling references at compile time, the borrow checker tracks the lexical and control-flow span over which each reference is used and verifies that it never extends past the point where its referent is dropped. That valid span is the reference’s lifetime.

Within a single function body, the compiler infers all lifetimes automatically. Across function boundaries, however, the compiler checks each function strictly against its signature. Consider a function that takes and returns a string slice:

fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str { ... }

Callers must know how long the returned &str remains valid. Because only one input reference exists, the compiler applies its lifetime elision rules and infers that the output lifetime matches s.

When multiple input references exist, elision cannot determine which input the output borrows from, so the signature must declare explicit lifetime parameters. A lifetime parameter begins with an apostrophe (conventionally 'a), is declared in angle brackets after the function name, and attaches to the related references:

fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str { ... }

This signature states a contract: for some lifetime 'a, both inputs remain valid for at least 'a, and the returned reference is valid for 'a. At every call site, the compiler verifies that the returned reference is never used after either input’s backing data is dropped.

Lifetime annotations never alter runtime behavior or extend how long values live; they document borrowing relationships so the compiler can verify memory safety statically.

4.7 A map that points into a slice

These lifetime mechanics directly enable zero-copy indexing. To index a slice of User structs by ID, one option is cloning each User into a HashMap<u32, User>. A cheaper alternative stores only borrowed pointers in a HashMap<u32, &User>, leaving the original structs untouched (Figure 4.6).

Avoiding copies introduces a lifetime dependency: the original slice must remain alive and immutable for as long as the map is used. Listing 4.2 encodes this contract in the function signature.

Listing 4.2 A map whose values point into the slice (lines 27 to 33).

fn struct_slice_to_map<'a>(slice: &'a [User]) -> HashMap<u32, &'a User> {
    let mut map = HashMap::new();
    for user in slice {
        map.insert(user.id, user);
    }
    map
}

Applying the contract from Section 4.6, slice is valid for 'a, and every &'a User stored in the returned HashMap shares that lifetime 'a. Consequently, attempting to drop users while still reading from the map triggers the same compile-time error shown in Figure 4.5.

Inside the body, for user in slice yields &'a User references directly, inserting pointers into the map with zero User clones.

4.8 Two lifetimes in one type

Listing 4.3 generalizes the input from a slice of structs to a slice of struct references (&[&'a User]).

Listing 4.3 A map built from a slice of references (lines 35 to 41).

fn ref_slice_to_map<'a>(slice: &[&'a User]) -> HashMap<u32, &'a User> {
    let mut map = HashMap::new();
    for &user in slice {
        map.insert(user.id, user);
    }
    map
}

The parameter type &[&'a User] contains two distinct lifetimes:

  • The outer & borrows the temporary slice of pointers itself; its lifetime is elided because the return type does not depend on it.
  • The inner &'a User carries the lifetime 'a of the underlying User structs.

Because the returned HashMap<u32, &'a User> references only 'a, the map depends exclusively on the User values and not on the intermediate pointer slice. The pointer slice can be dropped immediately after the call returns while the map remains valid (Figure 4.7).

The loop pattern for &user in slice copies each &'a User pointer out of the slice. Shared references implement Copy and occupy a single machine word, making this copy a register-width move.

4.9 The complete program

Listing 4.4 The complete program. src/bin/lifetime_reference_drill.rs

use std::collections::HashMap;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct User {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
}

fn functional_numbers_drill(slice: &[i32]) -> Vec<i32> {
    slice
        .iter()
        .filter(|&&x| x % 2 == 0)
        .map(|&x| x * 10)
        .collect()
}

fn imperative_numbers_map(slice: &[i32]) -> HashMap<i32, i32> {
    let mut map = HashMap::new();
    for &num in slice {
        map.insert(num, num * 100);
    }
    map
}

// The lifetime could be elided. It is written out because section 4.7 reads it.
#[allow(clippy::needless_lifetimes)]
fn struct_slice_to_map<'a>(slice: &'a [User]) -> HashMap<u32, &'a User> {
    let mut map = HashMap::new();
    for user in slice {
        map.insert(user.id, user);
    }
    map
}

fn ref_slice_to_map<'a>(slice: &[&'a User]) -> HashMap<u32, &'a User> {
    let mut map = HashMap::new();
    for &user in slice {
        map.insert(user.id, user);
    }
    map
}

fn main() {
    let vv = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6];

    let filtered: Vec<i32> = vv
        .iter()
        .filter(|x| *x % 2 == 0)
        .copied()
        .collect();
    println!("Filtered : {:?}", filtered);

    println!("--- Ultra-Lean Inline Slice Drill ---\n");

    let processed_nums = functional_numbers_drill(&[10, 15, 20, 25, 30]);
    println!("1. Functional Numbers (Even * 10): {:?}", processed_nums);

    let num_map = imperative_numbers_map(&[10, 15, 20, 25, 30]);
    println!("2. Imperative Numbers Map: {:?}", num_map);

    // explicit reference binding holding the inline array literal
    let users: &[User] = &[
        User {
            id: 101,
            name: "Alice".to_string(),
        },
        User {
            id: 102,
            name: "Bob".to_string(),
        },
        User {
            id: 103,
            name: "Charlie".to_string(),
        },
    ];
    println!("\n3. Zero-Allocation Struct Map (From &[User]):");
    let struct_map = struct_slice_to_map(users);
    for (id, user_ref) in &struct_map {
        println!("   Key ID: {} -> Value Name: {}", id, user_ref.name);
    }

    // explicit reference binding holding the inline array of &User
    let user_refs: &[&User] = &[struct_map[&101], struct_map[&102]];
    println!("\n4. Zero-Allocation Ref Slice Map (From &[&User]):");
    let ref_slice_map = ref_slice_to_map(user_refs);
    for (id, user_ref) in &ref_slice_map {
        println!("   Key ID: {} -> Value Name: {}", id, user_ref.name);
    }

    println!("\n--- Drill Completed Successfully! ---");
}

At the start of main, an additional iterator chain demonstrates an alternative way to handle &&i32 in filter: binding |x| and writing *x % 2 explicitly dereferences one layer while % auto-dereferences the second. Chaining .copied() converts each &i32 to i32 before collect builds the Vec<i32>.

Two declarations in main rely on an important compiler rule:

let users: &[User] = &[ User { ... }, User { ... }, User { ... } ];

Here &[ ... ] takes a reference to an unnamed array literal. Normally, an unnamed temporary value is dropped at the end of its statement, which would leave users dangling. When a reference to a temporary is bound directly in a let statement, however, Rust applies temporary lifetime extension, extending the backing array’s lifetime to the end of the enclosing block so users and user_refs remain valid throughout main.

Executing the binary produces:

$ cargo run --bin lifetime_reference_drill
Filtered : [2, 4, 6]
--- Ultra-Lean Inline Slice Drill ---

1. Functional Numbers (Even * 10): [100, 200, 300]
2. Imperative Numbers Map: {20: 2000, 10: 1000, 25: 2500, 15: 1500, 30: 3000}

3. Zero-Allocation Struct Map (From &[User]):
   Key ID: 101 -> Value Name: Alice
   Key ID: 102 -> Value Name: Bob
   Key ID: 103 -> Value Name: Charlie

4. Zero-Allocation Ref Slice Map (From &[&User]):
   Key ID: 102 -> Value Name: Bob
   Key ID: 101 -> Value Name: Alice

--- Drill Completed Successfully! ---

Repeated runs print the map entries in different orders because HashMap uses a randomly seeded hasher (Section 3.4). When deterministic ordering is required, use BTreeMap to maintain keys in sorted order or sort the keys explicitly prior to output.

Summary

  • An iterator is a stateful cursor implementing Iterator::next, yielding Some(item) until exhausted and None thereafter; for loops desugar directly to next calls.
  • iter() yields shared references (&T), iter_mut() yields exclusive mutable references (&mut T), and into_iter() transfers ownership (T) while consuming the source collection.
  • Iterator adapters (filter, map) are lazy state machines; no element is processed until a consumer (collect, for) pulls items through the pipeline one by one.
  • Because filter borrows each yielded item without consuming it, iter().filter(...) supplies &&T to its predicate closure; irrefutable patterns such as |&&x| dereference Copy values directly.
  • A lifetime designates the static program span during which a reference remains valid; the borrow checker rejects any reference whose use outlives its referent’s drop point.
  • Explicit lifetime parameters such as 'a bind input and output reference lifetimes across function signatures without altering runtime storage durations.
  • Indexing slices with HashMap<u32, &'a User> eliminates element cloning while statically guaranteeing that the index never outlives the underlying slice.

Exercises

  1. Rewrite imperative_numbers_map as a single iterator chain terminating in collect::<HashMap<_, _>>().
  2. Implement fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str, then write a main function that intentionally violates its lifetime contract and inspect the resulting compiler diagnostic.
  3. Change struct_slice_to_map to return a BTreeMap and verify that output order becomes deterministic across runs.
  4. Write a function taking &mut [User] that uses iter_mut() to append " (admin)" to every user’s name.

Heaps

This chapter covers

  • Binary heap structure and how a complete tree maps onto a contiguous Vec
  • How push and pop restore the heap invariant in O(log n) steps
  • Rust’s BinaryHeap, and converting it into a min-heap using Reverse
  • Lexicographical tuple ordering and prioritizing heap entries by (count, value)
  • Finding the k most frequent items using both an unbounded max-heap and a k-bounded min-heap
  • Computing a running median over a data stream using two balanced heaps

Priority-driven workloads require continuous access to the extreme element of a dynamic multiset without paying the O(n) maintenance cost of keeping the entire collection sorted. A binary heap resolves this tradeoff by enforcing a partial ordering invariant over a complete binary tree packed contiguously in a vector, supporting O(1) extremum inspection and O(log n) insertions and deletions.

This priority-queue abstraction underpins top-k frequency selection, priority scheduling, and streaming order-statistic maintenance. The sections below formalize the implicit array representation, sift-up and sift-down invariant restoration, and Rust’s BinaryHeap API before developing three complete applications: unbounded top-k selection, k-bounded top-k word ranking, and dual-heap streaming median maintenance.

Four formal definitions establish the terminology:

  • A binary tree is a hierarchical structure in which every node has at most two children (left and right); the unique node without a parent is the root.
  • A max-heap is a complete binary tree satisfying the max-heap invariant: every parent key is greater than or equal to the keys of both children, placing the global maximum at the root.
  • A min-heap inverts this ordering invariant so every parent key is less than or equal to its children’s keys, placing the global minimum at the root.
  • The median of a finite multiset of real numbers is its middle element in sorted order when cardinality is odd, or the arithmetic mean of the two middle elements when cardinality is even.

5.1 A tree stored in a vector

Although conceptually a tree, a binary heap stores no child or parent pointers. Because a heap is always a complete binary tree (every level filled except possibly the last, which fills from left to right), its nodes pack densely into a Vec in level order: the root at index 0, its two children at indexes 1 and 2, their children at indexes 3 through 6, and so on. Figure 5.1 depicts a six-element max-heap alongside its backing vector.

Dense level-order packing replaces pointer chasing with index arithmetic. For any node at index i, its left child lies at 2i + 1, its right child at 2i + 2, and its parent at (i - 1) / 2 (using integer division). In Figure 5.1, node 7 at index 1 has children at indexes 3 and 4, holding 3 and 5.

The heap invariant constrains only parent-child relationships; sibling and cousin ordering is unconstrained (for example, 7 sits to the left of 8 in Figure 5.1). Maintaining this partial order is far cheaper than keeping the entire array sorted.

A complete binary tree of n nodes has height floor(log₂ n), so a heap of one million items is roughly 20 levels deep.

5.2 Adding and removing

5.2.1 Push

Inserting a new element appends it to the end of the vector, occupying the next free leaf slot on the bottom level. If the new value exceeds its parent, violating the max-heap invariant, it swaps upward with its parent repeatedly (sift-up) until either its parent is larger or it reaches the root. Figure 5.2 traces pushing 10.

Because each swap ascends one level in a tree of height O(log n), push completes in O(log n) worst-case time.

5.2.2 Pop

Removing the maximum element extracts the root at index 0. To preserve tree completeness, the final element of the vector moves into index 0 and the vector length shrinks by one. That displaced element typically violates the heap invariant, so it swaps downward with its larger child repeatedly (sift-down) until both children are smaller or it becomes a leaf. Figure 5.3 traces popping 10.

Swapping with the larger child is mandatory because the promoted child becomes the new parent of its sibling and must therefore be at least as large as that sibling. Like push, pop traverses at most the height of the tree in O(log n) time.

Inspecting the maximum element without removal (peek) reads index 0 directly in O(1) time.

5.3 Heaps in Rust

Rust’s standard library provides std::collections::BinaryHeap<T>, implemented as a max-heap over a Vec<T>. Its core API maps directly to the operations above:

MethodWhat it doesCost
push(x)adds xO(log n)
pop()removes and returns the largest item, as an OptionO(log n)
peek()returns a reference to the largest item, as an OptionO(1)
len()the number of itemsO(1)
into_sorted_vec()consumes the heap and returns its items in ascending orderO(n log n)

BinaryHeap<T> orders elements via the Ord trait, which is implemented by integer types, String, and tuples of Ord elements.

5.3.1 How tuples compare

Rust compares tuples lexicographically from left to right: the first elements determine the ordering, and subsequent elements act as tie-breakers only when earlier elements are equal. Thus (3, 1) > (2, 9) because 3 > 2, while (3, 1) < (3, 2) because 1 < 2.

Placing the priority key first in a tuple lets a BinaryHeap order arbitrary payloads without defining a custom wrapper type: a heap of (count, value) pairs prioritizes by count and breaks ties by value.

5.3.2 A min-heap with Reverse

Rather than offering a separate min-heap type, the standard library provides the zero-cost wrapper std::cmp::Reverse<T>, whose Ord implementation inverts T’s ordering (Reverse(3) > Reverse(5) because 3 < 5). Consequently, BinaryHeap<Reverse<i32>> behaves as a min-heap keeping the smallest value at the root.

Callers wrap values on insertion (heap.push(Reverse(x))) and destructure the wrapper on extraction (if let Some(Reverse(x)) = heap.pop()).

With the implicit array layout and BinaryHeap interface established, the following three sections apply heaps to frequency ranking and streaming order statistics.

5.4 The k most frequent numbers

The problem. Given a slice of integers and a count k, return the k most frequently occurring numbers. For [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3] and k = 2, the result is 1 and 2.

The strategy. Tally frequencies in a HashMap, build a max-heap of (count, number) pairs, and pop k elements.

Listing 5.1 Top k with a full heap. src/problems/top_k_frequent.rs

//! Top K Frequent Elements.
//!
//! Count occurrences with a HashMap, then use a max-heap (`BinaryHeap`) to pull
//! out the top k elements. O(n log n) worst case; acceptable and readable.

use std::collections::{BinaryHeap, HashMap};

pub fn top_k_frequent(nums: &[i32], k: usize) -> Vec<i32> {
    let mut counts: HashMap<i32, usize> = HashMap::with_capacity(nums.len());
    for &num in nums.iter() {
        *counts.entry(num).or_insert(0) += 1;
    }

    // BinaryHeap is a max-heap in Rust, so (count, num) keeps highest counts first.
    let mut heap: BinaryHeap<(usize, i32)> = counts
        .into_iter()
        .map(|(num, count)| (count, num))
        .collect();

    let mut result = Vec::with_capacity(k);
    while result.len() < k {
        match heap.pop() {
            Some((_, num)) => result.push(num),
            None => break,
        }
    }
    result
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn returns_top_two() {
        let nums = [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3];
        let mut result = top_k_frequent(&nums, 2);
        result.sort_unstable();
        assert_eq!(result, vec![1, 2]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn k_larger_than_unique_values_returns_all() {
        let result = top_k_frequent(&[1, 2, 3], 10);
        assert_eq!(result.len(), 3);
    }
}

The implementation proceeds in three stages:

  1. *counts.entry(num).or_insert(0) += 1; increments the count for num. entry(num) locates the bucket, or_insert(0) initializes absent keys to 0 and returns &mut usize, and *... += 1 increments the counter in place.
  2. counts.into_iter().map(|(num, count)| (count, num)).collect() swaps each pair so the frequency leads, then constructs the BinaryHeap directly via collect (using linear-time Floyd heapification).
  3. The while loop extracts up to k elements, terminating early if pop() yields None when fewer than k distinct values exist (covered by the second unit test).

For n input elements and u distinct values, counting takes O(n) time, heap construction takes O(u) time, and k pops take O(k log u) time.

In the first unit test, sorting the returned vector before comparison avoids brittleness: elements with tied frequencies can appear in different orders depending on the randomized HashMap seed.

5.5 The k most frequent words, with a heap of size k

Inserting every distinct element into the heap wastes memory when u is large and k is small (for example, finding the top 3 words across millions of distinct tokens). Bounding the heap to at most k + 1 entries reduces both memory and comparison work.

The strategy. Maintain a min-heap of (count, word) pairs. After pushing each entry, if the heap length exceeds k, pop the root. Because a min-heap places the smallest entry at the root, every eviction discards the least frequent candidate seen so far, guaranteeing that the k highest-frequency words remain (Figure 5.4).

The program tokenizes input text into normalized words, counts occurrences, and filters them through the bounded min-heap.

Listing 5.2 The function (lines 1 to 41). src/bin/top_k_frequent_words.rs

use std::{
    cmp::Reverse as Rev,
    collections::{BinaryHeap, HashMap},
};

/// Returns vec!<(word, frequency)>, most frequent first.
fn top_k_frequent(sentence: &str, k: usize) -> Vec<(String, u32)> {
    // Split string by white spaces. Map it and trim any non alphanumeric characters. Finally,
    // filter all the empty strings and map everything to lowercase characters.
    let words: Vec<String> = sentence
        .split_whitespace()
        .map(|w| w.trim_matches(|c: char| !c.is_alphanumeric()))
        .filter(|w| !w.is_empty())
        .map(str::to_lowercase)
        .collect();

    // Build the frequency map...
    let mut frequencies = HashMap::<&str, u32>::new();
    for word in &words {
        *frequencies
            .entry(word.as_str())
            .or_default() += 1;
    }

    // Keep a min heap of size k. Reverse flips the max heap, so the least
    // frequent word sits on top and gets popped once we go over k.
    let mut min_heap = BinaryHeap::<Rev<(u32, &str)>>::new();
    for (&word, &frequency) in &frequencies {
        min_heap.push(Rev((frequency, word)));
        if min_heap.len() > k {
            min_heap.pop();
        }
    }

    // Ascending order of Reverse means most frequent first.
    min_heap
        .into_sorted_vec()
        .into_iter()
        .map(|Rev((frequency, word))| (word.to_string(), frequency))
        .collect()
}

Four design choices keep the implementation concise and allocation-lean:

  • Tokenization: The iterator chain splits on whitespace, strips leading and trailing non-alphanumeric characters via trim_matches (turning "sentence." into "sentence"), filters out empty remnants left by standalone punctuation, and lowercases each token by passing str::to_lowercase directly to map.
  • Zero-copy counting: The frequency map has type HashMap<&str, u32>, borrowing slices from words rather than cloning strings for every token occurrence. or_default() inserts 0 for absent keys.
  • Bounded min-heap: Aliasing std::cmp::Reverse as Rev keeps the type concise. Pushing Rev((frequency, word)) places the lowest-frequency pair at the root; whenever heap.len() > k, a single pop() evicts it.
  • Ordered output: into_sorted_vec() drains the heap in ascending order of Rev, which corresponds to descending order of frequency. The final map unwraps each Rev and allocates an owned String for only the surviving k words, since the local words vector is dropped upon return.

Bounding the heap size to k + 1 caps each heap operation at O(log k), reducing heap work from O(u log u) to O(u log k) and heap memory from O(u) to O(k).

5.5.1 The complete program

Listing 5.3 The complete program, with its tests. src/bin/top_k_frequent_words.rs

use std::{
    cmp::Reverse as Rev,
    collections::{BinaryHeap, HashMap},
};

/// Returns vec!<(word, frequency)>, most frequent first.
fn top_k_frequent(sentence: &str, k: usize) -> Vec<(String, u32)> {
    // Split string by white spaces. Map it and trim any non alphanumeric characters. Finally,
    // filter all the empty strings and map everything to lowercase characters.
    let words: Vec<String> = sentence
        .split_whitespace()
        .map(|w| w.trim_matches(|c: char| !c.is_alphanumeric()))
        .filter(|w| !w.is_empty())
        .map(str::to_lowercase)
        .collect();

    // Build the frequency map...
    let mut frequencies = HashMap::<&str, u32>::new();
    for word in &words {
        *frequencies
            .entry(word.as_str())
            .or_default() += 1;
    }

    // Keep a min heap of size k. Reverse flips the max heap, so the least
    // frequent word sits on top and gets popped once we go over k.
    let mut min_heap = BinaryHeap::<Rev<(u32, &str)>>::new();
    for (&word, &frequency) in &frequencies {
        min_heap.push(Rev((frequency, word)));
        if min_heap.len() > k {
            min_heap.pop();
        }
    }

    // Ascending order of Reverse means most frequent first.
    min_heap
        .into_sorted_vec()
        .into_iter()
        .map(|Rev((frequency, word))| (word.to_string(), frequency))
        .collect()
}

fn main() {
    let sentence = r"This is a short sentence. We'll count words.
    Let us count words in this sentence
    ";

    let top_k = top_k_frequent(sentence, 3);
    println!("Top 3 frequency [(word, frequency)] : \n {:#?}", top_k);
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn picks_most_frequent() {
        let result = top_k_frequent("a a a b b c", 2);
        assert_eq!(result, vec![("a".to_string(), 3), ("b".to_string(), 2)]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn ignores_case_and_punctuation() {
        let result = top_k_frequent("Hello, hello! HELLO world.", 1);
        assert_eq!(result, vec![("hello".to_string(), 3)]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn k_larger_than_word_count() {
        assert_eq!(top_k_frequent("x y", 10).len(), 2);
    }

    #[test]
    fn empty_input() {
        assert!(top_k_frequent("", 3).is_empty());
    }
}

In main, the sample text uses a raw string literal (r"..."), which disables backslash escaping and spans multiple lines. The unit tests exercise standard ranking, case folding and punctuation stripping, k exceeding the vocabulary size, and empty input.

$ cargo run --bin top_k_frequent_words
Top 3 frequency [(word, frequency)] :
 [
    (
        "words",
        2,
    ),
    (
        "this",
        2,
    ),
    (
        "sentence",
        2,
    ),
]

Four words appear twice in the sample input ("this", "sentence", "count", and "words"), and "count" is evicted. When frequencies tie, lexicographical tuple comparison falls back to the word string; the min-heap therefore evicts the alphabetically smallest word, retaining the alphabetically latest words among ties.

TIP: To retain the alphabetically earliest words on frequency ties, push Rev((frequency, Reverse(word))). The inner Reverse inverts string ordering alone, causing the alphabetically latest word to sit at the min-heap root and be evicted first.

5.6 The median of a stream

The problem. Integers arrive incrementally in a stream. After each arrival, report the median of all values received so far.

The baseline approach. Maintaining a sorted Vec allows O(1) median reads, but inserting each new element into its sorted position shifts up to n elements, costing O(n) per arrival.

The two-heap approach. Partition the seen values across two complementary heaps (Figure 5.5):

  • low: a max-heap storing the smaller half of the values, exposing the largest element of the lower half at its root.
  • high: a min-heap storing the larger half of the values, exposing the smallest element of the upper half at its root.

Two invariants hold after every insertion: every element in low is less than or equal to every element in high, and low.len() is either equal to high.len() or high.len() + 1. Under these invariants, the median is always available in O(1) at the roots: the root of low when the total count is odd, or the mean of both roots when the count is even.

5.6.1 Adding a number

Listing 5.4 The structure and add_num (lines 1 to 27). src/bin/median_finder.rs

use std::{cmp::Reverse, collections::BinaryHeap};

#[derive(Default)]
pub struct MedianFinder {
    low: BinaryHeap<i32>,
    high: BinaryHeap<Reverse<i32>>,
}

impl MedianFinder {
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        Self::default()
    }

    pub fn add_num(&mut self, num: i32) {
        self.low.push(num);

        if let Some(val) = self.low.pop() {
            self.high.push(Reverse(val));
        }

        if self.high.len() > self.low.len()
            && let Some(Reverse(val)) = self.high.pop()
        {
            self.low.push(val);
        }
    }
    // ...
}

add_num preserves both invariants in three unconditional or size-checked heap moves without explicit value comparisons:

  1. Push the incoming value into low.
  2. Pop the maximum element from low and push it into high, restoring the ordering invariant so every element in high is at least as large as every element remaining in low.
  3. If high.len() > low.len(), pop the minimum element from high and push it back into low, restoring the size balance invariant.

Tracing the first three arrivals (6, 10, and 2):

AddAfter step 1 (low)After step 2 (low / high)After step 3 (low / high)Median
6{6}{} / {6}{6} / {}6
10{6, 10}{6} / {10}{6} / {10}(6 + 10) / 2 = 8
2{2, 6}{2} / {6, 10}{2, 6} / {10}6

Because each step performs a constant number of heap pushes and pops, add_num runs in O(log n) time.

5.6.2 Reading the median

Listing 5.5 find_median (lines 28 to 37).

impl MedianFinder {
    // ...
    pub fn find_median(&self) -> Option<f64> {
        let max_low = *self.low.peek()?;

        if self.low.len() > self.high.len() {
            Some(max_low as f64)
        } else {
            let Reverse(min_high) = *self.high.peek()?;
            Some((max_low as f64 + min_high as f64) / 2.0)
        }
    }
}

*self.low.peek()? inspects the root of low. The ? operator works on Option identically to Result: if no values have been inserted yet, peek() yields None and find_median returns None immediately. The return type is Option<f64> because the mean of two integers can be fractional.

In the even-count branch, let Reverse(min_high) = *self.high.peek()?; unwraps the Reverse wrapper directly in the let pattern.

5.6.3 The complete program

Listing 5.6 The complete program, with its tests. src/bin/median_finder.rs

use std::{cmp::Reverse, collections::BinaryHeap};

#[derive(Default)]
pub struct MedianFinder {
    low: BinaryHeap<i32>,
    high: BinaryHeap<Reverse<i32>>,
}

impl MedianFinder {
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        Self::default()
    }

    pub fn add_num(&mut self, num: i32) {
        self.low.push(num);

        if let Some(val) = self.low.pop() {
            self.high.push(Reverse(val));
        }

        if self.high.len() > self.low.len()
            && let Some(Reverse(val)) = self.high.pop()
        {
            self.low.push(val);
        }
    }

    pub fn find_median(&self) -> Option<f64> {
        let max_low = *self.low.peek()?;

        if self.low.len() > self.high.len() {
            Some(max_low as f64)
        } else {
            let Reverse(min_high) = *self.high.peek()?;
            Some((max_low as f64 + min_high as f64) / 2.0)
        }
    }
}

const SAMPLE: [i32; 11] = [6, 10, 2, 6, 5, 0, 6, 3, 1, 0, 0];

fn main() {
    let mut finder = MedianFinder::new();

    for value in SAMPLE {
        finder.add_num(value);
        match finder.find_median() {
            Some(median) => println!("after {value:>2}: median {median}"),
            None => println!("after {value:>2}: no median"),
        }
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    /// The median of a sorted slice, computed directly.
    fn median_of_sorted(values: &[i32]) -> f64 {
        let middle = values.len() / 2;
        if values.len() % 2 == 1 {
            values[middle] as f64
        } else {
            (values[middle - 1] as f64 + values[middle] as f64) / 2.0
        }
    }

    #[test]
    fn an_empty_finder_has_no_median() {
        assert_eq!(MedianFinder::new().find_median(), None);
    }

    #[test]
    fn one_value_is_the_median() {
        let mut finder = MedianFinder::new();
        finder.add_num(7);
        assert_eq!(finder.find_median(), Some(7.0));
    }

    #[test]
    fn an_even_count_averages_the_middle_two() {
        let mut finder = MedianFinder::new();
        finder.add_num(1);
        finder.add_num(2);
        assert_eq!(finder.find_median(), Some(1.5));
    }

    #[test]
    fn three_values_are_ordered() {
        let mut finder = MedianFinder::new();
        for (value, median) in [1, 2, 3]
            .into_iter()
            .zip([1.0, 1.5, 2.0])
        {
            finder.add_num(value);
            assert_eq!(finder.find_median(), Some(median));
        }
    }

    #[test]
    fn duplicates_are_kept() {
        let mut finder = MedianFinder::new();
        for value in [4, 4, 4, 4] {
            finder.add_num(value);
        }
        assert_eq!(finder.find_median(), Some(4.0));
    }

    #[test]
    fn the_stream_matches_a_sort_on_every_step() {
        let mut finder = MedianFinder::new();
        let mut seen = Vec::new();

        for value in SAMPLE {
            finder.add_num(value);
            seen.push(value);
            seen.sort_unstable();

            assert_eq!(finder.find_median(), Some(median_of_sorted(&seen)));
        }
    }

    #[test]
    fn the_two_heaps_never_differ_by_more_than_one() {
        let mut finder = MedianFinder::new();

        for value in SAMPLE {
            finder.add_num(value);
            assert!(
                finder
                    .low
                    .len()
                    .abs_diff(finder.high.len())
                    <= 1
            );
        }
    }
}

main feeds eleven sample integers into MedianFinder and prints the running median after each step:

$ cargo run --bin median_finder
after  6: median 6
after 10: median 8
after  2: median 6
after  6: median 6
after  5: median 6
after  0: median 5.5
after  6: median 6
after  3: median 5.5
after  1: median 5
after  0: median 4
after  0: median 3

The test the_stream_matches_a_sort_on_every_step validates the two-heap implementation against a simple reference routine: after each insertion, it sorts a copy of all values seen so far, computes the median via median_of_sorted, and asserts equality with find_median(). Verifying an optimized algorithm against a slower, obviously correct reference implementation is known as oracle testing, and reliably catches subtle invariant bugs missed by small hand-crafted examples.

The final test verifies the size-balance invariant directly, asserting that the two heap lengths differ by at most 1 after every insertion.

Summary

  • A binary heap embeds a complete binary tree level by level in a contiguous Vec, locating the children of index i at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2 and its parent at (i - 1) / 2.
  • In a max-heap, every parent key dominates its children, exposing the global maximum at index 0 for O(1) peek.
  • push appends to the tail and restores the invariant via sift-up; pop promotes the tail element to index 0 and restores the invariant via sift-down through the larger child. Both operations run in O(log n) worst-case time.
  • Rust’s BinaryHeap<T> implements a max-heap; wrapping elements in the zero-cost std::cmp::Reverse<T> adapter yields a min-heap.
  • Lexicographical tuple ordering enables (count, value) priority keys without custom comparator structs.
  • Bounding a min-heap to k + 1 entries during top-k selection reduces heap space from O(u) to O(k) and heap work from O(u log u) to O(u log k).
  • Partitioning a stream across a lower max-heap (low) and an upper min-heap (high) maintains the running median in O(log n) time per insertion and O(1) time per query.

Exercises

  1. Implement a standalone max-heap over Vec<i32> supporting push, pop, and peek using the index formulas from Section 5.1, and oracle-test it against BinaryHeap on random sequences.
  2. Modify top_k_frequent_words to retain alphabetically earliest words on frequency ties using the nested Reverse pattern from Section 5.5, and add a unit test confirming the tie-breaking order.
  3. Add a len(&self) -> usize method to MedianFinder returning the total number of elements inserted.
  4. Extend MedianFinder to support a sliding window of the most recent 100 values by implementing lazy deletion (recording expired values in a hash map and discarding them when they surface at either heap root).

Recursion and dynamic programming

This chapter covers

  • Recognizing a problem that can be built from answers to smaller versions of itself
  • Filling a table of answers from the smallest case upward
  • Listing every subset of a set by exploring a tree of choices
  • The longest increasing run hidden inside a list, in O(n log n)
  • Choosing jobs that do not overlap, to earn the most

Dynamic programming solves combinatorial optimization and counting problems by evaluating smaller subproblems once, tabulating their optimal solutions, and combining those results to solve larger instances. The paradigm applies whenever a problem exhibits two structural properties:

  1. Optimal substructure: An optimal solution to a problem instance can be constructed directly from optimal solutions to smaller subproblems.
