  2. Overlapping subproblems: A direct recursive decomposition revisits the same subproblem instances repeatedly, so tabulating intermediate results collapses exponential recursion trees into polynomial time.

Five problems develop these principles in progression. Minimum-coin change presents bottom-up tabulation in its canonical form. Subset enumeration contrasts dynamic programming with exhaustive backtracking, where every distinct combination must be emitted and no overlapping subproblems exist. Longest increasing subsequence, weighted interval scheduling, and resource-constrained GPU scheduling combine dynamic programming with sorting and binary search.

Every dynamic programming derivation below begins by stating, in a single precise sentence, the invariant represented by one table entry. That statement defines the subproblem; once specified, both the recurrence relation and its implementation follow directly.

6.1 Making change with the fewest coins

The problem. Given a set of coin denominations with an unlimited supply of each, determine the minimum number of coins that sum to a target amount. With denominations 1, 2, and 5, the amount 11 requires three coins (5 + 5 + 1). Some target amounts have no valid representation; with only a coin of value 2, the amount 3 is impossible.

6.1.1 Why the obvious approach fails

A natural initial strategy selects the largest denomination that fits at each step. This greedy approach succeeds for denominations 1, 2, and 5, but it fails for arbitrary coin sets (Figure 6.1).

Consequently, the algorithm must evaluate every denomination at each step. Exhaustively enumerating every combination takes exponential time, whereas dynamic programming reduces the work to polynomial time.

6.1.2 The subproblem

Begin by defining the meaning of a single table entry:

dp[t] is the minimum number of coins that sum to exactly t.

Consider the final coin placed in an optimal solution for t. If that coin has value c, the preceding coins must sum to t - c, and the fewest coins required for that remainder is dp[t - c]. Choosing coin c last therefore costs dp[t - c] + 1 coins. Because the optimal final coin is unknown in advance, the recurrence evaluates every valid denomination and retains the minimum:

dp[t] = the minimum of dp[t - c] + 1 over every coin c such that c <= t.

The base case is dp[0] = 0, since zero coins sum to zero.

Filling the table by hand for the denominations in Figure 6.1 (1, 3, and 4) up to amount 6 demonstrates how each row evaluates every fitting coin and retains the smallest count:

tcoins that fitoptions from each coindp[t]
11dp[0] + 1 = 11
21dp[1] + 1 = 22
31, 3dp[2] + 1 = 3, dp[0] + 1 = 11
41, 3, 4dp[3] + 1 = 2, dp[1] + 1 = 2, dp[0] + 1 = 11
51, 3, 4dp[4] + 1 = 2, dp[2] + 1 = 3, dp[1] + 1 = 22
61, 3, 4dp[5] + 1 = 3, dp[3] + 1 = 2, dp[2] + 1 = 32

The entry dp[6] evaluates to 2 (from 3 + 3). The greedy strategy required three coins for the same amount because it committed to 4 and never reconsidered earlier choices. Because the table records the optimal count for every smaller amount, each new entry reduces to a fixed number of lookups plus one.

Both structural properties are required for this recurrence to hold. Subproblems must overlap so that caching results avoids repeated work: both dp[6] and dp[5] read dp[1], and larger tables revisit each entry many times. Optimal substructure must also hold so that the best solution for t is composed from best solutions for smaller remainders t - c. If a better way to form t - c existed, dp[t - c] would hold that smaller count. When either property fails, the table produces an incorrect result.

Because dp[t] depends exclusively on entries for smaller amounts, the table can be populated from left to right. Figure 6.2 illustrates the completed table for denominations 1, 2, and 5, along with the dependencies used to compute dp[11].

6.1.3 The code

Listing 6.1 Coin change (lines 6 to 29). src/problems/dp.rs

pub fn coin_change(coins: &[i32], amount: i32) -> Option<i32> {
    if amount < 0 {
        return None;
    }

    let amount = amount as usize;
    let mut dp = vec![usize::MAX; amount + 1];
    dp[0] = 0;

    for total in 1..=amount {
        for &coin in coins {
            let coin = coin as usize;
            if coin > total || dp[total - coin] == usize::MAX {
                continue;
            }
            dp[total] = dp[total].min(dp[total - coin] + 1);
        }
    }

    match dp[amount] {
        usize::MAX => None,
        count => Some(count as i32),
    }
}

Comparing the implementation against the recurrence clarifies each step:

  • Negative amounts are rejected up front, ensuring that the cast amount as usize is always well defined.
  • vec![usize::MAX; amount + 1] allocates one entry per amount from 0 through amount, using usize::MAX as a sentinel meaning “currently unreachable”.
  • dp[0] = 0 establishes the base case.
  • The outer loop advances from 1 through amount, while the inner loop evaluates every coin denomination.
  • The continue guard skips any coin larger than total as well as any remainder total - coin that remains unreachable. That second check also prevents usize::MAX + 1, which would overflow.
  • dp[total].min(dp[total - coin] + 1) updates the entry with the smaller of the current best count and the new candidate.

WARNING The second condition in that continue statement is required for correctness rather than performance. Removing it breaks the function: when dp[total - coin] holds the sentinel, evaluating dp[total - coin] + 1 adds one to the maximum usize. In a debug build, the program panics with "attempt to add with overflow". In a release build, the addition wraps around to 0, and the final match interprets 0 as a valid count of zero coins, causing the table to report artificially small counts. Checking for the sentinel before adding is mandatory whenever usize::MAX represents an unreachable state.

At the end of the function, a match converts the final table entry into the return value. Matching usize::MAX produces None, while any other value yields Some(count). Returning Option<i32> ensures that callers cannot confuse an impossible amount with a valid coin count.

Because the table contains amount + 1 entries and each entry inspects every denomination, the algorithm runs in O(amount × coins) time and uses O(amount) memory.

Listing 6.2 The complete file. src/problems/dp.rs

//! Coin Change: minimum number of coins to make an amount.
//!
//! Classic dynamic programming. `Option<i32>` expresses "impossible" instead of
//! a magic `-1`.

pub fn coin_change(coins: &[i32], amount: i32) -> Option<i32> {
    if amount < 0 {
        return None;
    }

    let amount = amount as usize;
    let mut dp = vec![usize::MAX; amount + 1];
    dp[0] = 0;

    for total in 1..=amount {
        for &coin in coins {
            let coin = coin as usize;
            if coin > total || dp[total - coin] == usize::MAX {
                continue;
            }
            dp[total] = dp[total].min(dp[total - coin] + 1);
        }
    }

    match dp[amount] {
        usize::MAX => None,
        count => Some(count as i32),
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn computes_minimum_coins() {
        assert_eq!(coin_change(&[1, 2, 5], 11), Some(3)); // 5 + 5 + 1
        assert_eq!(coin_change(&[2], 3), None);
        assert_eq!(coin_change(&[1], 0), Some(0));
    }
}

Running cargo test --lib coin_change executes the test suite, which verifies the example from Section 6.1, an unreachable amount, and the base case of 0.

6.2 Listing every subset

Not every recursive problem requires a memoization table. When a problem demands every valid solution rather than a single optimum, recursion explores the entire decision space and there are no overlapping subproblems to cache.

The problem. Enumerate every subset of a set of distinct integers. A subset is any selection of elements, including the empty selection and the full set. The input [1, 2, 3] has eight subsets: [], [1], [2], [3], [1, 2], [1, 3], [2, 3], and [1, 2, 3].

The idea. Construct subsets one element at a time, starting from the empty subset. From any partial subset, append one additional element whose index is strictly greater than the indices of all elements already chosen. Enforcing this index order prevents duplicate permutations such as [2, 1] from appearing alongside [1, 2]. Figure 6.3 depicts these decisions as a tree in which every node corresponds to a distinct subset.

To enumerate every node, the algorithm traverses the tree depth first, descending along one branch as far as possible before exploring its siblings. Descending pushes an element onto the active selection, and ascending pops it back off. This systematic search pattern is called backtracking.

Listing 6.3 Subsets by backtracking. src/problems/backtracking.rs

//! Subsets: enumerate every subset of a set of distinct integers.
//!
//! Backtracking with clean `path.push(...)` + recursive exploration + `pop`.
//! `Vec<Vec<i32>>` is sorted in the tests to avoid order-dependent assertions.

pub fn subsets(nums: Vec<i32>) -> Vec<Vec<i32>> {
    let mut result = Vec::with_capacity(1 << nums.len());
    let mut path = Vec::new();

    fn backtrack(nums: &[i32], start: usize, path: &mut Vec<i32>, result: &mut Vec<Vec<i32>>) {
        result.push(path.clone());
        for idx in start..nums.len() {
            path.push(nums[idx]);
            backtrack(nums, idx + 1, path, result);
            path.pop();
        }
    }

    backtrack(&nums, 0, &mut path, &mut result);
    result
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn generates_all_subsets() {
        let mut subsets = subsets(vec![1, 2, 3]);
        subsets.sort_unstable();
        assert_eq!(subsets.len(), 8);
        assert!(subsets.contains(&vec![]));
        assert!(subsets.contains(&vec![1, 2, 3]));
    }

    #[test]
    fn empty_input_has_one_subset() {
        assert_eq!(subsets(vec![]), vec![vec![]]);
    }
}

The helper backtrack is scoped as a private nested function inside subsets and accepts four parameters:

  • nums: an immutable borrow of the input slice.
  • start: the first index eligible for selection at this level.
  • path: a single mutable vector holding the subset currently under construction, passed as &mut.
  • result: the mutable output vector accumulating completed subsets, also passed as &mut.

Upon entry, backtrack appends path.clone() to result, recording the subset represented by the current tree node. For each index from start onward, it pushes the element, recurses to explore the subtree below, and pops the element upon return. After the pop, path is restored to its exact prior state, ready for the next sibling branch.

Tracing the opening calls of subsets(vec![1, 2, 3]) illustrates this push-and-pop discipline:

Callpath on entryRecordsThen pushes
backtrack(start 0)[][]1
backtrack(start 1)[1][1]2
backtrack(start 2)[1, 2][1, 2]3
backtrack(start 3)[1, 2, 3][1, 2, 3]nothing: the loop is empty
back in start 2[1, 2] after popno more positions
back in start 1[1] after pop3

Calling Vec::with_capacity(1 << nums.len()) preallocates the exact output capacity. Shifting 1 left by n bits computes 2ⁿ, which is the exact number of subsets of an n-element set.

The total work is O(n · 2ⁿ): there are 2ⁿ subsets, and cloning each copies up to n elements. Because the output itself has size O(n · 2ⁿ), this bound is asymptotically optimal.

6.3 The longest increasing run inside a list

The problem. Given a sequence of integers, select elements in their original relative order such that each selected element is strictly greater than the previous one. The goal is to find the maximum length of such an increasing subsequence. In [10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18], the elements 2, 3, 7, 18 form an increasing subsequence of length 4.

Unlike a contiguous substring, a subsequence may omit intervening elements while preserving their original relative order.

The direct dynamic program. Define dp[i] as the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at index i. For each i, inspecting every earlier index j with nums[j] < nums[i] and taking the maximum dp[j] + 1 yields an O(n²) algorithm, because each position scans all preceding positions.

A faster formulation. Maintain a separate ordered structure called tails, whose entries satisfy the following invariant:

The k-th smallest entry in tails is the smallest possible ending value of an increasing subsequence of length k.

Minimizing the ending value is advantageous because a smaller tail leaves more room for subsequent elements to extend the subsequence. As each input element arrives, two cases apply:

  • If the element exceeds every existing entry, it extends the longest subsequence discovered so far and is inserted into tails.
  • Otherwise, the smallest entry greater than or equal to the element is replaced by the new element, recording a smaller tail for a subsequence of that length.

When the scan completes, the cardinality of tails equals the length of the longest increasing subsequence. Figure 6.4 traces the evolution of tails on the sample input.

In the final row of Figure 6.4, tails holds 2, 3, 7, 18, which happens to be a valid increasing subsequence for this input. That coincidence does not hold in general: tails can combine elements from distinct subsequences, so only its length is guaranteed to match the answer.

Because the entries of tails remain strictly sorted, locating the smallest entry at least as large as a given element can be performed logarithmically in an ordered collection. The implementation below stores tails in a BTreeSet.

Listing 6.4 The complete program. src/bin/longest_increasing_subsequence.rs

use std::collections::BTreeSet;

fn lis_len(nums: &[i32]) -> usize {
    let mut tails = BTreeSet::new();

    for &num in nums {
        if let Some(&ceiling) = tails.range(num..).next() {
            tails.remove(&ceiling);
        }
        tails.insert(num);
    }

    tails.len()
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", lis_len(&[10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18])); // 4
    println!("{}", lis_len(&[0, 1, 0, 3, 2, 3])); // 4
    println!("{}", lis_len(&[7, 7, 7, 7])); // 1
    println!("{}", lis_len(&[5, 4, 3, 2, 1])); // 1
    println!("{}", lis_len(&[1, 2, 3, 4, 5])); // 5
    println!("{}", lis_len(&[])); // 0
}

The call tails.range(num..) yields an iterator over all entries greater than or equal to num in ascending order, and .next() retrieves the smallest such entry. If one exists, the function removes it before inserting num, effectively replacing the old tail with the smaller value.

Including num in the lower-bounded range num.. also handles duplicate inputs correctly. For [7, 7, 7, 7], each subsequent 7 locates the existing 7, removes it, and inserts 7 again, leaving the length at 1 as required for a strictly increasing subsequence.

Because range, remove, and insert each run in O(log n) time on a BTreeSet, the complete algorithm runs in O(n log n) time.

$ cargo run --bin longest_increasing_subsequence
4
4
1
1
5
0

The six output lines match the expected values documented in main.

6.4 Choosing jobs that do not overlap

The problem. A single machine executes one job at a time. Each job specifies a start time, an end time, and a profit. The objective is to select a set of non-overlapping jobs that maximizes total profit. Figure 6.5 illustrates four sample jobs.

A job interval [s, e) runs from time s up to, but excluding, time e. Consequently, a job ending at time 3 and a job starting at time 3 do not overlap.

6.4.1 Building the subproblem

Sorting the jobs by end time ensures that any job eligible to precede job i in a valid schedule finishes earlier and therefore appears earlier in the sorted slice. The subproblem is defined as follows:

dp[i] is the maximum profit achievable using only the first i jobs in the sorted list.

For job i, two mutually exclusive choices exist:

  • Skip the job: The maximum profit remains dp[i], the best total achievable without job i.
  • Schedule the job: Only jobs finishing at or before job i’s start time may precede it. Because the slice is sorted by end time, those compatible jobs form a prefix of length prev, yielding a total profit of dp[prev] + job.profit.

Thus dp[i + 1] is the maximum of those two values, and the final table entry gives the optimal profit.

Locating prev reduces to binary search over the sorted prefix in O(log n) time. The Rust standard library exposes this operation directly via slice::partition_point, which accepts a monotonic predicate that holds on a prefix and fails thereafter, returning the length of that prefix.

6.4.2 The code

Each job is represented as a compact Copy struct storing its start time, end time, and profit.

#[derive(Debug, Default, Clone, Copy)]
struct Job {
    start: u32,
    end: u32,
    profit: u64,
}

Listing 6.5 The complete program. src/bin/job_scheduling_with_profit_and_deadline.rs

#[derive(Debug, Default, Clone, Copy)]
struct Job {
    start: u32,
    end: u32,
    profit: u64,
}

fn max_profit(mut jobs: Vec<Job>) -> u64 {
    // Sort by end time so every job that could come before
    // job `i` in a schedule sits somewhere in jobs[..i].
    jobs.sort_unstable_by_key(|job| job.end);

    // dp[i] = best profit achievable using only the first `i` jobs.
    let mut dp = vec![0; jobs.len() + 1];

    for (i, job) in jobs.iter().enumerate() {
        // Binary search for how many earlier jobs finish by the time
        // this one starts. Those are exactly the jobs compatible with it,
        // and since they form a prefix, dp[prev] is their best profit.
        let prev = jobs[..i].partition_point(|j| j.end <= job.start);

        // Either skip this job (keep dp[i]),
        // or take it on top of the best compatible prefix.
        dp[i + 1] = dp[i].max(dp[prev] + job.profit);
    }

    // After considering every job, the last entry holds the answer.
    dp[jobs.len()]
}

fn main() {
    let jobs = vec![
        Job {
            start: 1,
            end: 3,
            profit: 50,
        },
        Job {
            start: 2,
            end: 4,
            profit: 10,
        },
        Job {
            start: 3,
            end: 5,
            profit: 40,
        },
        Job {
            start: 3,
            end: 6,
            profit: 70,
        },
    ];

    println!("{}", max_profit(jobs)); // 120
}

The comments inside max_profit mirror the derivation in Section 6.4.1. Calling jobs[..i].partition_point(|j| j.end <= job.start) counts how many of the first i jobs finish by job.start; sorting by end time guarantees the monotonic prefix property that partition_point requires. Tracing the algorithm on the sorted jobs A, B, C, and D produces the following table:

ijobprevskip: dp[i]take: dp[prev] + profitdp[i + 1]
0A [1, 3) 50000 + 50 = 5050
1B [2, 4) 100500 + 10 = 1050
2C [3, 5) 4015050 + 40 = 9090
3D [3, 6) 7019050 + 70 = 120120

For jobs C and D, prev equals 1, because only job A finishes by time 3. Sorting requires O(n log n) time, and each of the n jobs performs one O(log n) binary search, yielding an overall runtime of O(n log n).

$ cargo run --bin job_scheduling_with_profit_and_deadline
120

6.5 Jobs that also need memory and cores

The problem. Consider a cluster containing several GPUs, each with a fixed memory capacity and core count. Every job specifies both a memory requirement and a core requirement and can execute only on a GPU that satisfies both constraints. As in Section 6.4, each GPU executes one job at a time.

The program below addresses a narrower question: which single GPU yields the highest-profit schedule? The capacity left unused by this single-GPU restriction is analyzed in Section 6.5.4.

The sample cluster comprises two GPUs and the four jobs from Section 6.4, augmented with memory and core requirements:

jobtimememorycoresprofit
A[1, 3)12 GB2050
B[2, 4)8 GB1010
C[3, 5)40 GB6040
D[3, 6)60 GB9070

GPU 0 provides 80 GB of memory and 108 cores, accommodating all four jobs. GPU 1 provides 16 GB and 40 cores, accommodating only jobs A and B.

6.5.1 The fit test, and the same table

The resource constraint introduces a single boolean predicate: a job fits on a GPU if and only if the GPU has at least the required memory and at least the required cores.

The remainder of the algorithm reuses the table structure from Section 6.4. After sorting the jobs by end time and precomputing each job’s compatible prefix prev, the loop populates dp with the maximum of skipping the job or scheduling it after dp[prev]. A job that fails the fit test is skipped unconditionally, copying the preceding entry dp[i] into dp[i + 1].

6.5.2 The code

Each Job stores its resource requirements alongside its time interval and profit, and each Gpu stores its capacities together with a fits predicate.

#[derive(Debug, Default, Clone, Copy)]
struct Gpu {
    mem_gb: u32,
    cores: u32,
}

#[derive(Debug, Default, Clone, Copy)]
struct Job {
    start: u32,
    end: u32,
    mem_gb: u32,
    cores: u32,
    profit: u64,
}

impl Gpu {
    /// A job fits when the GPU has at least its memory and at least its cores.
    fn fits(&self, job: &Job) -> bool {
        (0..=self.mem_gb).contains(&job.mem_gb) && (0..=self.cores).contains(&job.cores)
    }
}

Listing 6.6 The complete program. src/bin/gpu_job_schedule.rs

//! Choose non-overlapping jobs for a GPU, where each job needs memory and cores.
//!
//! A job runs only on a GPU with enough memory and enough cores. For one GPU the
//! task is weighted interval scheduling: sort by end time, then take or skip each
//! job. The same table is reused for every GPU, and the best GPU wins.

#[derive(Debug, Default, Clone, Copy)]
struct Gpu {
    mem_gb: u32,
    cores: u32,
}

#[derive(Debug, Default, Clone, Copy)]
struct Job {
    start: u32,
    end: u32,
    mem_gb: u32,
    cores: u32,
    profit: u64,
}

impl Gpu {
    /// A job fits when the GPU has at least its memory and at least its cores.
    fn fits(&self, job: &Job) -> bool {
        (0..=self.mem_gb).contains(&job.mem_gb) && (0..=self.cores).contains(&job.cores)
    }
}

/// The best profit from work that runs on one GPU.
///
/// Every job it picks runs on the same GPU. That is the right model when a workload
/// is pinned to one device. Spreading the jobs over several GPUs is a different
/// problem, and the chapter measures what it is worth on the sample data.
fn max_profit(gpus: &[Gpu], mut jobs: Vec<Job>) -> u64 {
    jobs.sort_unstable_by_key(|job| job.end);

    // prev[i] = how many jobs finish by the time job `i` starts. The end times
    // are sorted, so each count is the length of a prefix, found in one search.
    let prev: Vec<usize> = jobs
        .iter()
        .map(|job| jobs.partition_point(|earlier| earlier.end <= job.start))
        .collect();

    // dp[i] = best profit using only the first `i` jobs. Reused for every GPU.
    let mut dp = vec![0; jobs.len() + 1];

    let pick_jobs_dp = |gpu: &Gpu| {
        for index in 0..jobs.len() {
            let job = &jobs[index];
            dp[index + 1] = if gpu.fits(job) {
                dp[index].max(dp[prev[index]] + job.profit)
            } else {
                dp[index]
            };
        }
        dp[jobs.len()]
    };

    gpus.iter()
        .map(pick_jobs_dp)
        .max()
        .unwrap_or(0)
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    fn large() -> Gpu {
        Gpu {
            mem_gb: 80,
            cores: 108,
        }
    }

    fn small() -> Gpu {
        Gpu {
            mem_gb: 16,
            cores: 40,
        }
    }

    fn sample_jobs() -> Vec<Job> {
        vec![
            Job {
                start: 1,
                end: 3,
                mem_gb: 12,
                cores: 20,
                profit: 50,
            },
            Job {
                start: 2,
                end: 4,
                mem_gb: 8,
                cores: 10,
                profit: 10,
            },
            Job {
                start: 3,
                end: 5,
                mem_gb: 40,
                cores: 60,
                profit: 40,
            },
            Job {
                start: 3,
                end: 6,
                mem_gb: 60,
                cores: 90,
                profit: 70,
            },
        ]
    }

    #[test]
    fn the_large_gpu_runs_the_best_pair() {
        assert_eq!(max_profit(&[large()], sample_jobs()), 120);
    }

    #[test]
    fn the_small_gpu_skips_what_does_not_fit() {
        assert_eq!(max_profit(&[small()], sample_jobs()), 50);
    }

    #[test]
    fn the_best_gpu_wins() {
        assert_eq!(max_profit(&[large(), small()], sample_jobs()), 120);
    }

    #[test]
    fn no_gpu_or_no_job_earns_nothing() {
        assert_eq!(max_profit(&[], sample_jobs()), 0);
        assert_eq!(max_profit(&[large()], Vec::new()), 0);
    }

    #[test]
    fn cores_alone_can_disqualify_a_job() {
        let jobs = vec![Job {
            start: 0,
            end: 1,
            mem_gb: 1,
            cores: 200,
            profit: 9,
        }];
        assert_eq!(max_profit(&[large()], jobs), 0);
    }
}

fn main() {
    let gpus = vec![
        Gpu {
            mem_gb: 80,
            cores: 108,
        },
        Gpu {
            mem_gb: 16,
            cores: 40,
        },
    ];

    let jobs = vec![
        Job {
            start: 1,
            end: 3,
            mem_gb: 12,
            cores: 20,
            profit: 50,
        },
        Job {
            start: 2,
            end: 4,
            mem_gb: 8,
            cores: 10,
            profit: 10,
        },
        Job {
            start: 3,
            end: 5,
            mem_gb: 40,
            cores: 60,
            profit: 40,
        },
        Job {
            start: 3,
            end: 6,
            mem_gb: 60,
            cores: 90,
            profit: 70,
        },
    ];

    println!("{}", max_profit(&gpus, jobs)); // 120
}

The function max_profit precomputes prev once and reuses a single dp buffer across all GPUs. The closure pick_jobs_dp populates the table for one GPU and returns its final entry; gpus.iter().map(pick_jobs_dp) evaluates every GPU, and .max() selects the highest total.

Reusing dp across iterations is sound because each step writes dp[i + 1] using only dp[i] and dp[prev[i]]. Since both indices are at most i, every read accesses a value already computed in the current pass, while dp[0] remains 0.

Animation 6.3 begins with the jobs unsorted, reorders them by end time, and displays the recurrence arithmetic for each job beside the table.

6.5.3 Two tables

Because GPU 0 satisfies the resource requirements of every job, its table matches Section 6.4:

ijobfitsprevskip dp[i]take dp[prev] + profitdp[i+1]
0Ayes000 + 50 = 5050
1Byes0500 + 10 = 1050
2Cyes15050 + 40 = 9090
3Dyes19050 + 70 = 120120

GPU 1 fails the fit test for jobs C and D, so both are skipped and the optimal profit remains 50:

ijobfitsprevskip dp[i]takedp[i+1]
0Ayes000 + 50 = 5050
1Byes0500 + 10 = 1050
2Cno150no fit50
3Dno150no fit50

The answer is max(120, 50) = 120.

$ cargo run --bin gpu_job_schedule
120

Sorting and computing compatible prefixes via binary search take O(n log n) time. Evaluating each GPU then fills its table in O(n) time, and reusing a single dp buffer keeps auxiliary memory at O(n).

6.5.4 What one GPU at a time costs

Selecting the maximum across GPUs returns a schedule for only one device, leaving the remaining GPUs idle even when they have available capacity.

The per-GPU optima cannot be summed directly because the schedules overlap in job assignments. The optimal schedule for GPU 1 runs job A alone for a profit of 50, but job A is already included in GPU 0’s schedule of 120; summing the two totals would double-count job A.

Partitioning the jobs across devices achieves a higher total: assigning A and D to GPU 0 and B to GPU 1 avoids all time conflicts and yields a combined profit of 120 + 10 = 130.

Finding an optimal multi-device assignment is a fundamentally harder combinatorial problem because the scheduler must decide which GPU runs each job. Independent per-GPU tables cannot capture cross-device contention. As job and GPU counts scale, the search space grows rapidly, so production cluster schedulers rely on heuristics, bin-packing approximations, or integer linear programming.

Summary

  • Dynamic programming eliminates redundant recomputation on problems exhibiting optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems by tabulating subproblem solutions bottom up.
  • Every dynamic programming formulation begins with an explicit subproblem invariant defining the exact meaning of a single table entry; the recurrence relation and loop order follow directly from that invariant.
  • Minimum-coin change computes dp[t] from dp[t - c] + 1 across all denominations c <= t in O(amount × |coins|) time and O(amount) space.
  • Greedy heuristics fail on arbitrary coin systems: for denominations {1, 3, 4} and target 6, a greedy choice selects three coins (4 + 1 + 1), whereas the optimal solution uses two (3 + 3).
  • Backtracking traverses an implicit decision tree depth first with a single mutable path, pushing on descent and popping on ascent; enumerating all 2n subsets runs in output-optimal O(n · 2n) time.
  • Longest increasing subsequence maintains the minimal ending value for each subsequence length in an ordered BTreeSet, reducing runtime from O(n2) to O(n log n).
  • Weighted interval scheduling sorts jobs by finish time, locates the latest compatible predecessor via slice::partition_point, and tabulates optimal prefix profits in O(n log n) time.
  • Adding memory and core constraints gates each job transition with a single feasibility predicate while reusing one dp buffer across all candidate GPUs.
  • Optimizing each GPU independently underutilizes multi-device clusters: on the sample workload, partitioning jobs across two GPUs achieves profit 130, whereas the best single-GPU schedule achieves 120.

Exercises

  1. Change coin_change to also return the coins it used. Store the last coin chosen for each amount, then follow those choices back from amount.
  2. Write the O(n²) version of the longest increasing subsequence described in section 6.3, and check that it agrees with lis_len on random lists.
  3. Generate all subsets without recursion. Count a number mask from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1, and include element i when bit i of mask is set.
  4. Extend max_profit to return which jobs it chose, not only the total.
  5. Change max_profit so the jobs may be split across the GPUs. Work out the best total for the two GPUs and four jobs in section 6.5 by hand. Then explain why one table per GPU cannot find it.

Types that refuse bad input

This chapter covers

  • Traits: what they are, how to implement one, and what #[derive] generates automatically
  • A newtype: a struct around one number that can only hold valid values
  • Error types that say what went wrong, with Display and std::error::Error
  • Converting between types with From and TryFrom
  • Enums whose variants carry data, used for commands, for states, and for errors
  • A parser that turns a line of text into a typed command

Robust systems enforce domain invariants at compile time through algebraic data types rather than scattering defensive runtime checks across business logic. By restricting construction to validated boundaries, custom structs and enums make invalid program states unrepresentable.

The implementations below model a command-line control plane that manages compute jobs, termed workloads, on a remote cluster. Each workload requests between 1 and 64 GPUs and transitions through discrete lifecycle states such as Pending, Running, and Terminated. Users issue text commands such as create triton 4, requesting a workload named triton with 4 GPUs.

Input validation illustrates the core architectural invariant. A GPU count arrives as untrusted text, and inputs such as 0, 99, or many must be rejected before reaching scheduling logic. Revalidating raw integers in every downstream function is brittle because a single omitted guard permits corrupt state to propagate. Validating once at the ingress boundary and encapsulating the result in a private-field newtype guarantees that every downstream function receiving that type observes a valid count by construction.

7.1 Traits

A trait defines a set of methods that a type guarantees to provide. The standard library supplies many traits; for example, Display defines a single method, fmt, that formats a value as human-readable text. Any type implementing Display can be formatted with println!("{}", x).

A trait is implemented for a type via an impl block naming both the trait and the type:

impl fmt::Display for GpuCountError {
    fn fmt(&self, formatter: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        write!(formatter, "...")
    }
}

For common traits with mechanical implementations, the compiler can generate the code automatically. Placing #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)] above a struct generates Debug (formatting with {:?}), Clone (duplicating with .clone()), and PartialEq (comparing with ==), operating field by field.

Table 7.1 summarizes the traits used in this chapter.

TraitWhat it gives youHow you get it
Debugprinting with {:?}, for programmers#[derive(Debug)]
Displayprinting with {}, for userswrite impl Display yourself
Clone, Copy.clone(), and for Copy, copying by assignmentderive
PartialEq, Eq== and !=derive
PartialOrd, Ord<, >, and sortingderive
Hashuse as a HashMap keyderive
std::error::Erroruse as an error with ? and Box<dyn Error>write an empty impl once Debug and Display exist
From, TryFromconversions between typeswrite impl yourself

7.2 A GPU count that is always valid

A newtype is a single-field struct that wraps a primitive value in a distinct type. Here, a GpuCount wraps a u32.

The enforcement mechanism is field privacy. Struct fields in Rust are private by default, so code outside the defining module cannot read or modify the inner field directly, nor can it construct GpuCount(0). Callers can obtain a GpuCount exclusively through the module’s public constructors. Because those constructors validate the range, every GpuCount instance in the program is guaranteed valid, as illustrated in Figure 7.1.

The module opens with a documentation comment summarizing its design principles:

Listing 7.1 The module comment (lines 1 to 12). src/problems/adt_idioms.rs

//! Small algebraic-data-type idioms.
//!
//! These patterns are short and cannot represent invalid states.
//!
//! - A newtype gives a primitive a name and a single validating constructor, so
//!   an out-of-range value cannot exist.
//! - An enum with data models a closed set of alternatives, and `match` forces
//!   every alternative to be handled.
//! - Typed errors carry the reason instead of a string, so the caller can react.
//! - `TryFrom` puts the validation on the type boundary, where it belongs.
//! - An iterator chain states the intent in one pass and removes index
//!   bookkeeping.

Listing 7.2 defines the GpuCount type:

Listing 7.2 GpuCount (lines 14 to 36).

use std::fmt;

/// A GPU count that is validated at construction.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash)]
pub struct GpuCount(u32);

impl GpuCount {
    pub const MIN: u32 = 1;
    pub const MAX: u32 = 64;

    /// Validate a raw count.
    pub fn new(value: u32) -> Result<Self, GpuCountError> {
        if (Self::MIN..=Self::MAX).contains(&value) {
            Ok(Self(value))
        } else {
            Err(GpuCountError(value))
        }
    }

    pub fn get(self) -> u32 {
        self.0
    }
}
  • pub struct GpuCount(u32); is a tuple struct, a struct whose fields are addressed by position rather than name. The type itself is public, while its inner field remains private.
  • pub const MIN: u32 = 1; and MAX are associated constants belonging to the type, referenced as GpuCount::MIN externally or Self::MIN inside the impl block.
  • new acts as the validation gate. The inclusive range (Self::MIN..=Self::MAX) covers 1 through 64, and .contains(&value) tests membership. Valid values yield Ok(Self(value)), whereas out-of-range values yield Err(GpuCountError(value)), carrying the rejected input (defined in Section 7.3).
  • get extracts the inner u32. Taking self by value is inexpensive because GpuCount derives Copy.

The #[derive(...)] attribute equips GpuCount with the same standard capabilities as the underlying u32, allowing it to be formatted, copied, compared, ordered, and used as a hash map key.

7.3 An error that says what went wrong

When new rejects an out-of-range value, it returns a GpuCountError (Listing 7.3).

Listing 7.3 The error type (lines 38 to 54).

/// Why a raw GPU count was rejected.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct GpuCountError(pub u32);

impl fmt::Display for GpuCountError {
    fn fmt(&self, formatter: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        write!(
            formatter,
            "gpu count {} is outside {}..={}",
            self.0,
            GpuCount::MIN,
            GpuCount::MAX
        )
    }
}

impl std::error::Error for GpuCountError {}

GpuCountError(pub u32) preserves the rejected value in a public field so callers can inspect the exact invalid input.

The Display implementation formats a human-readable diagnostic message. Like format!, the write! macro formats arguments directly into the provided formatter, producing output such as gpu count 0 is outside 1..=64.

The impl std::error::Error for GpuCountError {} block has an empty body because every method on Error provides a default implementation, requiring only that the type implement Debug and Display. Implementing std::error::Error integrates GpuCountError with generic error-handling interfaces such as Box<dyn std::error::Error>, used in Section 7.5.

7.4 Converting with From and TryFrom

The standard library provides two traits for explicit type conversions:

  • From<A> for B models infallible conversions. Implementing it provides both B::from(a) and the reciprocal a.into() wherever a B is expected.
  • TryFrom<A> for B models fallible conversions, returning a Result. Implementing it provides both B::try_from(a) and a.try_into().

Listing 7.4 The two conversions (lines 56 to 68).

impl TryFrom<u32> for GpuCount {
    type Error = GpuCountError;

    fn try_from(value: u32) -> Result<Self, Self::Error> {
        Self::new(value)
    }
}

impl From<GpuCount> for u32 {
    fn from(count: GpuCount) -> u32 {
        count.0
    }
}

Converting from u32 to GpuCount can fail and therefore implements TryFrom. Its body delegates to new so the validation logic remains in one place, and type Error = GpuCountError; declares the associated error type.

Converting from GpuCount back to u32 is infallible and implements From, returning the inner field count.0.

TIP: Rust also provides the as cast operator (such as x as u32), which never reports failure: casting 300 to u8 with as wraps to 44 without warning. Prefer From for infallible conversions and TryFrom for fallible ones, reserving as for cases where intentional truncation or bit-level conversion is desired.

7.5 Commands: an enum that carries data

7.5.1 Why an enum

The CLI supports four commands: list takes no arguments, get and delete each take an identifier, and create takes a name and a GPU count. A struct-based design might collect all optional fields into a single type:

struct Command {
    verb: String,
    id: Option<String>,        // only for get and delete
    name: Option<String>,      // only for create
    gpus: Option<u32>,         // only for create
}

That struct permits invalid combinations, such as a get command without an identifier or a list command carrying a GPU count, forcing every downstream consumer to revalidate which fields apply to the verb. An enum whose variants carry variant-specific payloads eliminates those invalid states at compile time:

Listing 7.5 The command enum (lines 70 to 77).

/// A closed set of commands, each carrying exactly the data it needs.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum Command {
    List,
    Get { id: String },
    Create { name: String, gpus: GpuCount },
    Delete { id: String },
}

A Create variant is guaranteed to contain both a name and a validated GpuCount, because the compiler forbids constructing it otherwise, whereas List carries no fields. In memory, every Command value occupies the size of its largest variant, as illustrated in Figure 7.2.

7.5.2 The parser’s errors and helper

Before examining the parser itself, consider its error representation and helper function. Assigning each failure mode a distinct error variant allows callers to determine the exact cause of a malformed line.

Listing 7.6 CommandError and argument (lines 119 to 148).

/// A typed parse failure, so callers can distinguish the cases.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum CommandError {
    Empty,
    UnknownVerb(String),
    MissingArgument(&'static str),
    InvalidGpuCount(String),
}

impl fmt::Display for CommandError {
    fn fmt(&self, formatter: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        match self {
            Self::Empty => write!(formatter, "empty command"),
            Self::UnknownVerb(verb) => write!(formatter, "unknown verb {verb:?}"),
            Self::MissingArgument(name) => write!(formatter, "missing argument: {name}"),
            Self::InvalidGpuCount(raw) => write!(formatter, "invalid gpu count: {raw:?}"),
        }
    }
}

impl std::error::Error for CommandError {}

fn argument<'a>(
    parts: &mut impl Iterator<Item = &'a str>,
    name: &'static str,
) -> Result<&'a str, CommandError> {
    parts
        .next()
        .ok_or(CommandError::MissingArgument(name))
}

CommandError enumerates every parsing failure mode, and its Display implementation formats a message for each variant. Because errors are typed variants rather than opaque strings, callers can match on them directly, such as displaying usage help on MissingArgument or printing the valid range on InvalidGpuCount. With a plain String error, callers would have to parse the error text to distinguish failure cases.

The helper argument extracts the next whitespace-delimited token from the iterator or fails with the missing parameter’s name. Its first parameter, &mut impl Iterator<Item = &'a str>, mutably borrows the caller’s iterator so each call consumes one token. The explicit lifetime 'a binds the returned &str to the input line, deferring heap allocation until parse invokes to_string().

7.5.3 Parsing a line of text

Parsing translates a single line of text into either a validated Command or an error describing the syntax or domain violation.

Listing 7.7 Command::parse and verb (lines 79 to 117).

impl Command {
    /// Parse one command line.
    pub fn parse(line: &str) -> Result<Self, CommandError> {
        let mut parts = line.split_whitespace();
        let verb = parts
            .next()
            .ok_or(CommandError::Empty)?;

        match verb {
            "list" => Ok(Self::List),
            "get" => Ok(Self::Get {
                id: argument(&mut parts, "id")?.to_string(),
            }),
            "delete" => Ok(Self::Delete {
                id: argument(&mut parts, "id")?.to_string(),
            }),
            "create" => {
                let name = argument(&mut parts, "name")?.to_string();
                let raw = argument(&mut parts, "gpu count")?;
                let value: u32 = raw
                    .parse()
                    .map_err(|_| CommandError::InvalidGpuCount(raw.to_string()))?;
                let gpus = GpuCount::new(value)
                    .map_err(|_| CommandError::InvalidGpuCount(raw.to_string()))?;
                Ok(Self::Create { name, gpus })
            }
            other => Err(CommandError::UnknownVerb(other.to_string())),
        }
    }

    pub fn verb(&self) -> &'static str {
        match self {
            Self::List => "list",
            Self::Get { .. } => "get",
            Self::Create { .. } => "create",
            Self::Delete { .. } => "delete",
        }
    }
}

The parse method returns Result<Self, CommandError>, producing either a validated command or the specific reason the line failed. Tracing Command::parse("create triton 4") step by step yields:

StepCodeResult
1line.split_whitespace()an iterator over "create", "triton", "4"
2parts.next().ok_or(CommandError::Empty)?verb is "create"
3match verbruns the "create" arm
4argument(&mut parts, "name")?"triton", turned into a String
5argument(&mut parts, "gpu count")?raw is "4"
6raw.parse()the number 4
7GpuCount::new(value)GpuCount(4)
8Ok(Self::Create { name, gpus })the finished command

Malformed inputs fail at the exact stage where validation breaks down. An empty line fails at step 2 because no initial token exists; ok_or converts None into Err(CommandError::Empty), and ? returns it immediately. The input create triton many fails at step 6 because "many" cannot be parsed as an integer, whereas create triton 0 passes integer parsing at step 6 and is rejected at step 7 by GpuCount::new.

Animation 7.1 traces both the valid command and the three malformed inputs through these stages.

Although steps 6 and 7 fail for different underlying reasons, both map to the same domain error. Calling .map_err(|_| CommandError::InvalidGpuCount(raw.to_string())) converts either failure into InvalidGpuCount, preserving the original token so the diagnostic message echoes the user’s input.

The verb method performs the inverse mapping from a command variant to its static verb name. Patterns such as Self::Get { .. } match a variant while ignoring its payload fields.

7.5.4 Adding up without an index

The module includes one additional utility function:

Listing 7.8 summarize (lines 150 to 157).

/// Count and sum in one pass, without managing an index.
pub fn summarize(values: &[i32]) -> (usize, i64) {
    values
        .iter()
        .fold((0usize, 0i64), |(count, sum), value| {
            (count + 1, sum + i64::from(*value))
        })
}

The fold combinator traverses the slice in a single pass while threading an accumulator (count, sum) initialized to (0, 0). Widening each i32 via i64::from(*value) uses an infallible From conversion, guaranteeing no loss of precision.

7.5.5 The complete file

Listing 7.9 The complete file, with its tests. src/problems/adt_idioms.rs

//! Small algebraic-data-type idioms.
//!
//! These patterns are short and cannot represent invalid states.
//!
//! - A newtype gives a primitive a name and a single validating constructor, so
//!   an out-of-range value cannot exist.
//! - An enum with data models a closed set of alternatives, and `match` forces
//!   every alternative to be handled.
//! - Typed errors carry the reason instead of a string, so the caller can react.
//! - `TryFrom` puts the validation on the type boundary, where it belongs.
//! - An iterator chain states the intent in one pass and removes index
//!   bookkeeping.

use std::fmt;

/// A GPU count that is validated at construction.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash)]
pub struct GpuCount(u32);

impl GpuCount {
    pub const MIN: u32 = 1;
    pub const MAX: u32 = 64;

    /// Validate a raw count.
    pub fn new(value: u32) -> Result<Self, GpuCountError> {
        if (Self::MIN..=Self::MAX).contains(&value) {
            Ok(Self(value))
        } else {
            Err(GpuCountError(value))
        }
    }

    pub fn get(self) -> u32 {
        self.0
    }
}

/// Why a raw GPU count was rejected.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct GpuCountError(pub u32);

impl fmt::Display for GpuCountError {
    fn fmt(&self, formatter: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        write!(
            formatter,
            "gpu count {} is outside {}..={}",
            self.0,
            GpuCount::MIN,
            GpuCount::MAX
        )
    }
}

impl std::error::Error for GpuCountError {}

impl TryFrom<u32> for GpuCount {
    type Error = GpuCountError;

    fn try_from(value: u32) -> Result<Self, Self::Error> {
        Self::new(value)
    }
}

impl From<GpuCount> for u32 {
    fn from(count: GpuCount) -> u32 {
        count.0
    }
}

/// A closed set of commands, each carrying exactly the data it needs.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum Command {
    List,
    Get { id: String },
    Create { name: String, gpus: GpuCount },
    Delete { id: String },
}

impl Command {
    /// Parse one command line.
    pub fn parse(line: &str) -> Result<Self, CommandError> {
        let mut parts = line.split_whitespace();
        let verb = parts
            .next()
            .ok_or(CommandError::Empty)?;

        match verb {
            "list" => Ok(Self::List),
            "get" => Ok(Self::Get {
                id: argument(&mut parts, "id")?.to_string(),
            }),
            "delete" => Ok(Self::Delete {
                id: argument(&mut parts, "id")?.to_string(),
            }),
            "create" => {
                let name = argument(&mut parts, "name")?.to_string();
                let raw = argument(&mut parts, "gpu count")?;
                let value: u32 = raw
                    .parse()
                    .map_err(|_| CommandError::InvalidGpuCount(raw.to_string()))?;
                let gpus = GpuCount::new(value)
                    .map_err(|_| CommandError::InvalidGpuCount(raw.to_string()))?;
                Ok(Self::Create { name, gpus })
            }
            other => Err(CommandError::UnknownVerb(other.to_string())),
        }
    }

    pub fn verb(&self) -> &'static str {
        match self {
            Self::List => "list",
            Self::Get { .. } => "get",
            Self::Create { .. } => "create",
            Self::Delete { .. } => "delete",
        }
    }
}

/// A typed parse failure, so callers can distinguish the cases.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum CommandError {
    Empty,
    UnknownVerb(String),
    MissingArgument(&'static str),
    InvalidGpuCount(String),
}

impl fmt::Display for CommandError {
    fn fmt(&self, formatter: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        match self {
            Self::Empty => write!(formatter, "empty command"),
            Self::UnknownVerb(verb) => write!(formatter, "unknown verb {verb:?}"),
            Self::MissingArgument(name) => write!(formatter, "missing argument: {name}"),
            Self::InvalidGpuCount(raw) => write!(formatter, "invalid gpu count: {raw:?}"),
        }
    }
}

impl std::error::Error for CommandError {}

fn argument<'a>(
    parts: &mut impl Iterator<Item = &'a str>,
    name: &'static str,
) -> Result<&'a str, CommandError> {
    parts
        .next()
        .ok_or(CommandError::MissingArgument(name))
}

/// Count and sum in one pass, without managing an index.
pub fn summarize(values: &[i32]) -> (usize, i64) {
    values
        .iter()
        .fold((0usize, 0i64), |(count, sum), value| {
            (count + 1, sum + i64::from(*value))
        })
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn parses_each_command_variant() {
        assert_eq!(Command::parse("list"), Ok(Command::List));
        assert_eq!(
            Command::parse("get wl-7"),
            Ok(Command::Get { id: "wl-7".into() })
        );
        assert_eq!(
            Command::parse("create triton 4"),
            Ok(Command::Create {
                name: "triton".into(),
                gpus: GpuCount::new(4).expect("valid")
            })
        );
        assert_eq!(
            Command::parse("delete wl-7"),
            Ok(Command::Delete { id: "wl-7".into() })
        );
    }

    #[test]
    fn rejects_bad_input_with_typed_errors() {
        assert_eq!(Command::parse(""), Err(CommandError::Empty));
        assert_eq!(
            Command::parse("frobnicate"),
            Err(CommandError::UnknownVerb("frobnicate".into()))
        );
        assert_eq!(
            Command::parse("get"),
            Err(CommandError::MissingArgument("id"))
        );
        assert_eq!(
            Command::parse("create triton 0"),
            Err(CommandError::InvalidGpuCount("0".into()))
        );
        assert_eq!(
            Command::parse("create triton many"),
            Err(CommandError::InvalidGpuCount("many".into()))
        );
    }

    #[test]
    fn newtype_rejects_out_of_range_values() {
        assert!(GpuCount::new(1).is_ok());
        assert!(GpuCount::new(64).is_ok());
        assert!(GpuCount::new(0).is_err());
        assert!(GpuCount::new(65).is_err());
        assert_eq!(u32::from(GpuCount::try_from(8).expect("valid")), 8);
        assert!(GpuCount::try_from(0).is_err());
    }

    #[test]
    fn summarize_reports_count_and_sum() {
        assert_eq!(summarize(&[]), (0, 0));
        assert_eq!(summarize(&[1, 2, 3]), (3, 6));
        assert_eq!(summarize(&[-5, 5]), (2, 0));
    }

    #[test]
    fn errors_render_a_reason() {
        assert_eq!(
            Command::parse("create triton 0")
                .unwrap_err()
                .to_string(),
            "invalid gpu count: \"0\""
        );
        assert!(
            GpuCount::new(99)
                .unwrap_err()
                .to_string()
                .contains("outside")
        );
    }
}

The unit tests serve as an executable specification of the module. parses_each_command_variant verifies one valid input per variant, rejects_bad_input_with_typed_errors asserts exact error equality with assert_eq! (enabled by deriving PartialEq on CommandError), and newtype_rejects_out_of_range_values checks both boundary values (1 and 64) along with the adjacent out-of-range values.

Because Cargo executes unit tests concurrently, their reporting order may vary across runs:

$ cargo test --lib adt_idioms
running 5 tests
test problems::adt_idioms::tests::newtype_rejects_out_of_range_values ... ok
test problems::adt_idioms::tests::summarize_reports_count_and_sum ... ok
test problems::adt_idioms::tests::rejects_bad_input_with_typed_errors ... ok
test problems::adt_idioms::tests::parses_each_command_variant ... ok
test problems::adt_idioms::tests::errors_render_a_reason ... ok

test result: ok. 5 passed; 0 failed

Whereas Command models user requests, the next section applies enums to entities whose state evolves over time.

7.6 The states of a workload

A workload is accepted (Pending), receives compute resources (Provisioning), executes (Running), shuts down (Terminating), and completes (Terminated). Any active state may transition to Failed, and a failed workload may be retried. Modeling a finite set of states together with the permitted transitions between them defines a state machine (Figure 7.3).

Listing 7.10 The states (lines 1 to 18). src/problems/state_machine.rs

//! Algebraic data types / enum state machines.
//!
//! Cloud SDKs model workloads as finite state machines. Rust `enum` is
//! perfect for this: invalid states are unrepresentable and transitions are
//! explicit `match` arms, not nested `if` chains.

use std::time::Duration;

/// Lifecycle of a GPU cloud workload exposed through an SDK/API.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum WorkloadState {
    Pending,
    Provisioning,
    Running,
    Terminating,
    Terminated,
    Failed,
}

Each state is a unit variant carrying no payload. Rust represents this enum in a single byte and derives Copy, allowing states to be passed by value.

Listing 7.11 The allowed moves (lines 20 to 56).

impl WorkloadState {
    /// Returns an error string for impossible transitions, or `Ok(())`.
    pub fn can_transition_to(self, next: Self) -> Result<(), String> {
        match (self, next) {
            // Forward lifecycle.
            (Self::Pending, Self::Provisioning)
            | (Self::Pending, Self::Failed)
            | (Self::Provisioning, Self::Running)
            | (Self::Provisioning, Self::Failed)
            | (Self::Running, Self::Terminating)
            | (Self::Running, Self::Failed)
            | (Self::Terminating, Self::Terminated)
            | (Self::Terminating, Self::Failed) => Ok(()),

            // Retry loops allowed from failed states.
            (Self::Failed, Self::Pending) | (Self::Failed, Self::Provisioning) => Ok(()),

            // Everything else is invalid.
            _ => Err(format!("cannot transition from {self:?} to {next:?}")),
        }
    }

    pub fn is_terminal(self) -> bool {
        matches!(self, Self::Terminated | Self::Failed)
    }

    pub fn summary(self) -> &'static str {
        match self {
            Self::Pending => "workload accepted, waiting for scheduler",
            Self::Provisioning => "GPU resources being allocated",
            Self::Running => "workload is running",
            Self::Terminating => "cleanup in progress",
            Self::Terminated => "workload stopped and billing ended",
            Self::Failed => "workload failed; inspect logs",
        }
    }
}

can_transition_to validates a single transition from self to next by matching on the tuple (self, next), where each arm corresponds to edges in Figure 7.3. Joining patterns with | forms an or-pattern: the first arm enumerates all forward and failure transitions, the second enumerates retries, and the catch-all arm _ rejects every other pair.

That final catch-all establishes a deny-by-default policy. If a new state is added later, all transitions into or out of it are rejected until explicitly permitted, which is the safest default for a state machine.

is_terminal delegates to the matches! macro, returning true when the value matches the given pattern. Failed is classified as terminal despite permitting retries because it holds no active compute resources. Finally, summary returns a fixed description with type &'static str, indicating a string literal embedded in the binary that remains valid for the entire program lifetime.

7.7 Errors from a server

The same module models structured errors returned by a remote server, where each failure category carries distinct metadata.

Listing 7.12 ApiError and its methods (lines 58 to 91).

/// API error modeled as an enum with associated data.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum ApiError {
    InvalidRequest(String),
    Unauthorized,
    RateLimited { retry_after: Duration },
    NotFound { resource_id: String },
    Server { status: u16, message: String },
}

impl ApiError {
    pub fn is_retryable(&self) -> bool {
        matches!(
            self,
            Self::RateLimited { .. }
                | Self::Server {
                    status: 500..=599,
                    ..
                }
        )
    }

    pub fn user_message(&self) -> String {
        match self {
            Self::InvalidRequest(msg) => format!("invalid request: {msg}"),
            Self::Unauthorized => "authentication required or token expired".to_string(),
            Self::RateLimited { retry_after } => {
                format!("rate limited, retry in {}ms", retry_after.as_millis())
            }
            Self::NotFound { resource_id } => format!("resource not found: {resource_id}"),
            Self::Server { status, message } => format!("server error {status}: {message}"),
        }
    }
}

A rate-limit error specifies the required backoff duration, a not-found error identifies the missing resource, and a server error carries both an HTTP status code and a diagnostic message.

The is_retryable method answers a standard client decision: whether retrying the request can succeed. Rate limits expire and HTTP 5xx server errors are often transient, making both retryable, whereas a missing resource remains absent. A single pattern expresses this policy:

Self::RateLimited { .. } | Self::Server { status: 500..=599, .. }

Inside the struct pattern, status: 500..=599 matches any HTTP 5xx status code while .. ignores the remaining fields. A client retry policy can query this predicate directly to separate transient failures from permanent errors.

The user_message method formats each variant into a human-readable string, converting retry_after to milliseconds via retry_after.as_millis().

Listing 7.13 A small parser (lines 93 to 101).

/// Typical SDK helper: never expose nested `if let` soup to callers.
pub fn parse_gpu_count(raw: &str) -> Result<u32, ApiError> {
    match raw.trim() {
        "" => Err(ApiError::InvalidRequest("gpuCount is empty".into())),
        parsed => parsed.parse::<u32>().map_err(|_| {
            ApiError::InvalidRequest(format!("gpuCount must be a number, got {raw:?}"))
        }),
    }
}

The parse_gpu_count helper provides a compact variant of the validation gate from Section 7.2. It trims surrounding whitespace, handles empty strings explicitly, and maps the standard library’s integer parse error into ApiError::InvalidRequest. Formatting with {raw:?} quotes the input so empty or whitespace-padded strings remain visible in the diagnostic message.

Listing 7.14 The complete file, with its tests. src/problems/state_machine.rs

//! Algebraic data types / enum state machines.
//!
//! Cloud SDKs model workloads as finite state machines. Rust `enum` is
//! perfect for this: invalid states are unrepresentable and transitions are
//! explicit `match` arms, not nested `if` chains.

use std::time::Duration;

/// Lifecycle of a GPU cloud workload exposed through an SDK/API.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum WorkloadState {
    Pending,
    Provisioning,
    Running,
    Terminating,
    Terminated,
    Failed,
}

impl WorkloadState {
    /// Returns an error string for impossible transitions, or `Ok(())`.
    pub fn can_transition_to(self, next: Self) -> Result<(), String> {
        match (self, next) {
            // Forward lifecycle.
            (Self::Pending, Self::Provisioning)
            | (Self::Pending, Self::Failed)
            | (Self::Provisioning, Self::Running)
            | (Self::Provisioning, Self::Failed)
            | (Self::Running, Self::Terminating)
            | (Self::Running, Self::Failed)
            | (Self::Terminating, Self::Terminated)
            | (Self::Terminating, Self::Failed) => Ok(()),

            // Retry loops allowed from failed states.
            (Self::Failed, Self::Pending) | (Self::Failed, Self::Provisioning) => Ok(()),

            // Everything else is invalid.
            _ => Err(format!("cannot transition from {self:?} to {next:?}")),
        }
    }

    pub fn is_terminal(self) -> bool {
        matches!(self, Self::Terminated | Self::Failed)
    }

    pub fn summary(self) -> &'static str {
        match self {
            Self::Pending => "workload accepted, waiting for scheduler",
            Self::Provisioning => "GPU resources being allocated",
            Self::Running => "workload is running",
            Self::Terminating => "cleanup in progress",
            Self::Terminated => "workload stopped and billing ended",
            Self::Failed => "workload failed; inspect logs",
        }
    }
}

/// API error modeled as an enum with associated data.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum ApiError {
    InvalidRequest(String),
    Unauthorized,
    RateLimited { retry_after: Duration },
    NotFound { resource_id: String },
    Server { status: u16, message: String },
}

impl ApiError {
    pub fn is_retryable(&self) -> bool {
        matches!(
            self,
            Self::RateLimited { .. }
                | Self::Server {
                    status: 500..=599,
                    ..
                }
        )
    }

    pub fn user_message(&self) -> String {
        match self {
            Self::InvalidRequest(msg) => format!("invalid request: {msg}"),
            Self::Unauthorized => "authentication required or token expired".to_string(),
            Self::RateLimited { retry_after } => {
                format!("rate limited, retry in {}ms", retry_after.as_millis())
            }
            Self::NotFound { resource_id } => format!("resource not found: {resource_id}"),
            Self::Server { status, message } => format!("server error {status}: {message}"),

}

/// Typical SDK helper: never expose nested `if let` soup to callers.
pub fn parse_gpu_count(raw: &str) -> Result<u32, ApiError> {
    match raw.trim() {
