12.8.2 Kahn’s algorithm on named courses

The second version takes courses with names and lists of prerequisites, the way the data might arrive from a file.

A course has a name and a list of prerequisites, the names of the courses that must come before it:

use std::collections::{HashMap, VecDeque};

#[derive(Clone)]
struct Course {
    name: String,
    depends_on: Vec<String>,
}

Listing 12.15 The complete program. src/bin/dependency_resolutiom.rs

use std::collections::{HashMap, VecDeque};

#[derive(Clone)]
struct Course {
    name: String,
    depends_on: Vec<String>,
}

fn topo_sort(courses: &[Course]) -> Vec<String> {
    let mut adj: HashMap<String, Vec<String>> = HashMap::new();
    let mut indegree: HashMap<String, usize> = HashMap::new();

    for Course { name, depends_on } in courses {
        indegree.insert(name.clone(), depends_on.len());
        adj.entry(name.clone()).or_default();
        for dep in depends_on {
            adj.entry(dep.clone())
                .or_default()
                .push(name.clone());
            indegree.entry(dep.clone()).or_insert(0);
        }
    }

    let mut queue: VecDeque<_> = indegree
        .iter()
        .filter(|&(_, deg)| *deg == 0)
        .map(|(name, _)| name.clone())
        .collect();

    let mut order = Vec::new();
    while let Some(node) = queue.pop_front() {
        for next in &adj[&node] {
            let d = indegree.get_mut(next).unwrap();
            *d -= 1;
            if *d == 0 {
                queue.push_back(next.clone());
            }
        }
        order.push(node);
    }

    if order.len() == indegree.len() {
        order
    } else {
        Vec::new()
    }
}

fn main() {
    let courses = vec![
        Course {
            name: "algos".into(),
            depends_on: vec!["datastructs".into()],
        },
        Course {
            name: "compilers".into(),
            depends_on: vec!["algos".into(), "os".into()],
        },
        Course {
            name: "os".into(),
            depends_on: vec!["datastructs".into()],
        },
    ];

    println!("{:?}", topo_sort(&courses));
}

The input encodes dependencies in reverse orientation relative to Kahn’s traversal: each Course lists the prerequisites it depends on, whereas Kahn’s algorithm traverses forward from each prerequisite to its unlocked dependents. The setup loop inverts every edge, appending name to adj[dep] for each prerequisite dep.

A course’s initial indegree equals the cardinality of its depends_on list. Root prerequisites that never appear as standalone Course entries (such as "datastructs") still require an entry in indegree; calling indegree.entry(dep.clone()).or_insert(0) initializes absent prerequisites to 0 without overwriting existing counts.

Destructuring for Course { name, depends_on } in courses binds immutable field references directly in the loop header because courses is a shared slice reference.

When a cycle prevents full resolution, this variant returns an empty Vec. Returning Option<Vec<String>> (as in Listing 12.14) is preferable in production interfaces because it distinguishes an empty input graph from a cyclic dependency error.

$ cargo run --bin dependency_resolutiom
["datastructs", "algos", "os", "compilers"]

Because the initial frontier is populated by iterating over a HashMap, iteration order is randomized per process. This graph has a unique zero-indegree root, yielding deterministic output; graphs with multiple concurrent zero-indegree roots may produce different valid topological orderings across executions.

12.9 Shortest paths

In a weighted graph, the cost of a path is the sum of its constituent edge weights, and a shortest path between two vertices minimizes that total weight rather than edge cardinality.

Whereas unweighted BFS minimizes hop count, Dijkstra’s algorithm computes single-source shortest paths from a start vertex to all reachable vertices in any graph with non-negative edge weights.

12.9.1 How Dijkstra’s algorithm works

Dijkstra’s algorithm maintains two auxiliary structures:

  • dist, storing the best known upper-bound path cost from the source to each vertex (initialized to 0 for the source).
  • A min-priority queue of (cost, vertex) entries, implemented with BinaryHeap and Reverse, so that the minimum-cost unsettled frontier vertex is always extracted next.

On each iteration, the algorithm extracts the minimum-cost entry (d, u) from the heap. For every outgoing edge (u, v, w), it evaluates the candidate path cost d + w; if this candidate strictly improves upon dist[v], the algorithm updates dist[v] and pushes (d + w, v) onto the heap. Tightening a vertex’s distance upper bound in this manner is called an edge relaxation step.

When a vertex u is extracted with its current recorded cost d == dist[u], its shortest-path distance is permanently settled. Because all remaining heap entries have cost at least d and edge weights are non-negative, no future path can reach u with a strictly lower total cost.

Because std::collections::BinaryHeap does not support an in-place decrease-key operation, relaxing an edge to a vertex already in the heap pushes a second, lower-cost entry while leaving the earlier entry intact. When that superseded entry is eventually popped, its cost exceeds dist[u] and the algorithm discards it; such entries are termed stale (lazy deletion).

Figure 12.7 traces the distance table and heap state across a four-vertex weighted graph.

Tracing the table in Figure 12.7 row by row illustrates how stale entries arise. Settling A records B at cost 4 and C at cost 1. Settling C discovers a cheaper path to B at cost 1 + 2 = 3, which replaces 4 and pushes a new heap entry while leaving (4, B) stale. Settling B at cost 3 then relaxes D from 6 down to 4. When (4, B) and (6, D) are eventually popped, each is discarded because its cost exceeds the recorded best distance.

12.9.2 Two versions side by side

Listing 12.16 Dijkstra over the index form (lines 23 to 44). src/problems/graph_dijkstra.rs

use std::{
    cmp::Reverse,
    collections::{BinaryHeap, HashMap},
    hash::Hash,
};

use crate::problems::graph_bfs::GraphAdjList;

/// Shortest distances from `start_node` over an index-based adjacency list.
pub fn dijkstra_vec(graph: &[Vec<(usize, u32)>], start_node: usize) -> Vec<Option<u32>> {
    let mut distances = vec![None; graph.len()];
    let mut min_heap = BinaryHeap::from([Reverse((0, start_node))]);

    distances[start_node] = Some(0);

    while let Some(Reverse((current_cost, current_node))) = min_heap.pop() {
        // stale heap entry, a shorter path was already recorded
        if distances[current_node].is_some_and(|best| current_cost > best) {
            continue;
        }
        for &(neighbor, weight) in &graph[current_node] {
            let new_distance = current_cost + weight;
            if distances[neighbor].is_none_or(|best| new_distance < best) {
                distances[neighbor] = Some(new_distance);
                min_heap.push(Reverse((new_distance, neighbor)));
            }
        }
    }
    distances
}

Distance upper bounds are stored in Vec<Option<u32>>, where None represents infinity (no path discovered yet). Two Option combinators express the core invariants cleanly:

  • is_some_and(|best| current_cost > best) identifies stale heap entries whose popped cost exceeds the settled or improved distance in distances.
  • is_none_or(|best| new_distance < best) evaluates the relaxation predicate, returning true when the neighbor is unreached or when the candidate path strictly lowers its recorded distance.

The heap stores Reverse((cost, node)). Because BinaryHeap is a max-heap by default, wrapping tuples in Reverse inverts the ordering into a min-heap; Rust orders tuples lexicographically, prioritizing cost first and breaking ties deterministically by vertex index.

Listing 12.17 Dijkstra over the map form (lines 46 to 73).

/// Shortest distances from `start_node` over a `HashMap` adjacency list.
pub fn dijkstra<Node>(graph: &GraphAdjList<Node>, start_node: Node) -> HashMap<Node, u32>
where
    Node: Copy + Eq + Hash + Ord,
{
    let mut distances = HashMap::from([(start_node, 0)]);
    let mut min_heap = BinaryHeap::from([Reverse((0, start_node))]);

    while let Some(Reverse((current_cost, current_node))) = min_heap.pop() {
        // stale heap entry, a shorter path was already recorded
        if current_cost > distances[&current_node] {
            continue;
        }
        for &(neighbor, weight) in graph[&current_node] {
            let new_distance = current_cost + weight;

            if new_distance
                < *distances
                    .get(&neighbor)
                    .unwrap_or(&u32::MAX)
            {
                distances.insert(neighbor, new_distance);
                min_heap.push(Reverse((new_distance, neighbor)));
            }
        }
    }
    distances
}

In this map-backed formulation, distances is a HashMap populated lazily with reached vertices, and Node requires an Ord bound to support lexicographic tie-breaking inside the priority queue.

Indexing distances[&current_node] is guaranteed not to panic because every vertex is inserted into distances prior to being pushed onto the heap. Calling distances.get(&neighbor).unwrap_or(&u32::MAX) treats unreached vertices as having cost u32::MAX (infinity).

Because each edge relaxation pushes at most one entry onto a heap of size O(E) and each heap push or pop takes O(log E) time, the total time complexity is O((V + E) log E), which simplifies to O(E log V) for connected simple graphs.

WARNING: current_cost + weight panics on arithmetic overflow in debug builds and wraps around modulo 2^32 in release builds. With u32 weights, a long path of large weights can overflow; Listing 12.20 prevents this hazard using checked_add.

12.9.3 Edges as a struct

The next three implementations replace raw (neighbor, weight) tuples with a named Edge struct and widen path costs to u64. Together they form a progressive refinement: first cloning vertex labels, then borrowing vertex references with explicit lifetimes, and finally guarding against missing adjacency entries and integer overflow.

Edge<Node> pairs a target vertex with its u64 weight, and AdjMap<Node> aliases the adjacency map from each vertex to its outgoing edge vector:

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Edge<Node> {
    to: Node,
    weight: u64,
}

type AdjMap<Node> = HashMap<Node, Vec<Edge<Node>>>;

Listing 12.18 The complete program. src/bin/dijkstra.rs

use std::{
    cmp::Reverse,
    collections::{BinaryHeap, HashMap},
    hash::Hash,
};

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Edge<Node> {
    to: Node,
    weight: u64,
}

type AdjMap<Node> = HashMap<Node, Vec<Edge<Node>>>;

fn dijkstra_ssmd_shortest<Node>(graph: &AdjMap<Node>, start: Node) -> HashMap<Node, u64>
where
    Node: Clone + Hash + Ord,
{
    let mut dist = HashMap::from([(start.clone(), 0)]);
    let mut heap = BinaryHeap::from([Reverse((0, start))]);

    while let Some(Reverse((cost, node))) = heap.pop() {
        if cost > dist[&node] {
            continue; // stale entry
        }
        for edge in &graph[&node] {
            let new_cost = cost + edge.weight;
            if dist
                .get(&edge.to)
                .is_none_or(|&d| new_cost < d)
            {
                dist.insert(edge.to.clone(), new_cost);
                heap.push(Reverse((new_cost, edge.to.clone())));
            }
        }
    }
    dist
}

fn main() {
    let graph: AdjMap<&str> = HashMap::from([
        (
            "A",
            vec![Edge { to: "B", weight: 4 }, Edge { to: "C", weight: 1 }],
        ),
        ("B", vec![Edge { to: "D", weight: 1 }]),
        (
            "C",
            vec![Edge { to: "B", weight: 2 }, Edge { to: "D", weight: 5 }],
        ),
        ("D", vec![]),
    ]);

    println!("{:#?}", graph);
    let dist = dijkstra_ssmd_shortest(&graph, "A");
    println!("{:#?}", dist); // {"A": 0, "C": 1, "B": 3, "D": 4} (order varies)
}

Named fields (edge.to, edge.weight) improve readability over positional tuple indexing (.0, .1). Relaxing the bound from Copy to Clone accommodates heap-allocated vertex identifiers such as String, at the cost of cloning keys on each insertion into dist or the priority queue.

Direct indexing graph[&node] panics if a vertex lacks an explicit key in the map, so main registers sink vertex "D" with an empty edge vector.

Listing 12.19 The graph types, and borrowing nodes instead of cloning them (lines 1 to 47). src/bin/dijkstra_with_lifetime.rs

use std::{
    cmp::Reverse,
    collections::{BinaryHeap, HashMap},
    hash::Hash,
};

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Edge<Node> {
    to: Node,
    weight: u64,
}

type AdjMap<Node> = HashMap<Node, Vec<Edge<Node>>>;

fn dijkstra_ssmd_shortest<'a, Node>(
    graph: &'a AdjMap<Node>,
    start: &'a Node,
) -> HashMap<&'a Node, u64>
where
    Node: Hash + Ord,
{
    let mut dist = HashMap::from([(start, 0u64)]);
    let mut heap = BinaryHeap::from([Reverse((0u64, start))]);

    while let Some(Reverse((cost, node))) = heap.pop() {
        if cost > dist[node] {
            continue; // stale entry
        }
        let Some(edges) = graph.get(node) else {
            continue;
        };

        for edge in edges {
            let Some(new_cost) = cost.checked_add(edge.weight) else {
                continue;
            };
            if dist
                .get(&edge.to)
                .is_none_or(|&d| new_cost < d)
            {
                dist.insert(&edge.to, new_cost);
                heap.push(Reverse((new_cost, &edge.to)));
            }
        }
    }
    dist
}

Both Edge<Node> and AdjMap<Node> are generic over the vertex identifier type Node (such as &str, String, or u32).

To eliminate key cloning, this implementation stores borrowed references &'a Node inside dist and the priority queue, removing the Clone trait bound entirely and avoiding heap allocations when vertices are owned String values.

The explicit lifetime parameter 'a binds the input graph, the start vertex reference, and the keys of the returned distance map to a common borrow scope. Because every &edge.to reference pushed onto the heap borrows directly from graph, the borrow checker enforces statically that graph remains immutable and valid for as long as the returned distance map is accessed.

Two let ... else guards harden this implementation against runtime panics:

  • let Some(edges) = graph.get(node) else { continue }; tolerates sink vertices omitted from the adjacency map (such as "D" in main).
  • let Some(new_cost) = cost.checked_add(edge.weight) else { continue }; skips edges whose cumulative path cost would overflow u64::MAX, preventing both debug panics and release-mode wraparound.

use std::{
    cmp::Reverse,
    collections::{BinaryHeap, HashMap},
    hash::Hash,
};

struct Edge<Node> {
    to: Node,
    weight: u64,
}

type AdjMap<Node> = HashMap<Node, Vec<Edge<Node>>>;

fn dijkstra_ssmd_shortest<Node>(graph: &AdjMap<Node>, start: Node) -> HashMap<Node, u64>
where
    Node: Clone + Hash + Ord,
{
    let mut dist = HashMap::from([(start.clone(), 0)]);
    let mut heap = BinaryHeap::from([Reverse((0u64, start))]);

    while let Some(Reverse((cost, node))) = heap.pop() {
        if cost > dist[&node] {
            continue; // stale entry
        }
        let Some(edges) = graph.get(&node) else {
            continue;

        for edge in edges {
            let Some(new_cost) = cost.checked_add(edge.weight) else {
                continue;

            if dist
                .get(&edge.to)
                .is_none_or(|&d| new_cost < d)
            {
                dist.insert(edge.to.clone(), new_cost);
                heap.push(Reverse((new_cost, edge.to.clone())));
            }
        }
    }
    dist
}

12.10 Connecting every node at the lowest cost

The final graph problem operates on an undirected, weighted graph. Modeling buildings as nodes and cabling costs as edge weights, the objective is to connect every node directly or indirectly at the minimum total edge weight.

A subset of edges connecting all vertices of an undirected graph without cycles is a spanning tree; a spanning tree of minimum total edge weight is a minimum spanning tree (MST). Every spanning tree over |V| = n vertices contains exactly n − 1 edges: removing any edge disconnects the graph, and adding any edge introduces a cycle.

Kruskal’s algorithm constructs an MST greedily by examining edges in non-decreasing order of weight. An edge is accepted into the spanning forest if and only if its endpoints belong to distinct connected components; any edge whose endpoints are already connected is discarded because it would close a cycle.

12.10.1 Union-find

Kruskal’s algorithm requires dynamic connectivity queries and component merges. A disjoint-set union (DSU or union-find) data structure maintains a partition of vertices into disjoint sets with near-constant amortized cost.

Each connected component is represented as an inverted tree encoded in a flat parent array, where parent[i] stores the parent index of vertex i. A component’s canonical representative (its root) satisfies parent[r] == r; two vertices belong to the same connected component if and only if they share the same root.

The structure exposes two core operations:

  • find(x) traverses parent pointers from x to its component root.
  • union(x, y) resolves the roots of x and y; if they differ, it links one root under the other to merge the two components.

Listing 12.22 Union-find (lines 10 to 49). src/bin/kruskals_algorithm.rs

use std::cmp::Ordering::{Equal, Greater, Less};

struct DisjointSet {
    parent: Vec<usize>,
    rank: Vec<usize>,
}

impl DisjointSet {
    fn new(n: usize) -> Self {
        Self {
            parent: (0..n).collect(),
            rank: vec![0; n],
        }
    }

    fn find(&mut self, elem: usize) -> usize {
        if self.parent[elem] != elem {
            self.parent[elem] = self.find(self.parent[elem]);
        }

        self.parent[elem]
    }

    fn union(&mut self, x: usize, y: usize) -> bool {
        let (x, y) = (self.find(x), self.find(y));

        if x == y {
            return false;
        }

        match self.rank[x].cmp(&self.rank[y]) {
            Less => self.parent[x] = y,
            Greater => self.parent[y] = x,
            Equal => {
                self.parent[x] = y;
                self.rank[y] += 1;
            }
        }

        true
    }
}

new initializes n singleton components by setting parent to [0, 1, ..., n - 1] via (0..n).collect().

find resolves the root recursively and rewrites parent[elem] directly to the root on stack unwind, flattening the lookup path so subsequent queries resolve in a single hop. This optimization is path compression.

union returns false if both vertices already share a root. Otherwise it merges the two trees via union by rank, attaching the tree of smaller rank beneath the root of higher rank to keep tree height logarithmic; when both roots share equal rank, one becomes the parent and its rank increments by 1.

Combined, path compression and union by rank achieve an amortized time complexity of O(α(V)) per operation, where α is the inverse Ackermann function (effectively constant for all practical graph sizes).

12.10.2 Kruskal’s algorithm

Listing 12.23 The edge type and Kruskal's algorithm (lines 3 to 65).

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Edge {
    u: usize,
    v: usize,
    w: u32,
}

fn kruskals(n: usize, mut edges: Vec<Edge>) -> Vec<Edge> {
    // Kruskal's algorithm is greedy: it takes the cheapest edges first.
    edges.sort_by_key(|e| e.w);

    let mut uf = DisjointSet::new(n);
    let mut mst = Vec::new();

    for edge in edges {
        if uf.union(edge.u, edge.v) {
            mst.push(edge);
        }
    }

    mst
}

An Edge connects zero-indexed vertices u and v with weight w; because the graph is undirected, endpoint order is symmetric.

edges.sort_by_key(|e| e.w) orders all edges by non-decreasing weight. Each edge is then tested via uf.union(edge.u, edge.v): a true return value indicates that the endpoints belonged to disjoint components, so the edge is moved directly into mst without copying (for edge in edges consumes the vector by value).

Edge sorting dominates the asymptotic complexity, yielding O(E log E) total time.

Figure 12.8 traces the parent array state across every edge of the sample graph.

Because sort_by_key is a stable sort, equal-weight edges preserve their original input ordering (edge 1-3 precedes 3-4, and 0-1 precedes 2-3).

Listing 12.24 The complete program. src/bin/kruskals_algorithm.rs

use std::cmp::Ordering::{Equal, Greater, Less};

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Edge {
    u: usize,
    v: usize,
    w: u32,
}

struct DisjointSet {
    parent: Vec<usize>,
    rank: Vec<usize>,
}

impl DisjointSet {
    fn new(n: usize) -> Self {
        Self {
            parent: (0..n).collect(),
            rank: vec![0; n],
        }
    }

    fn find(&mut self, elem: usize) -> usize {
        if self.parent[elem] != elem {
            self.parent[elem] = self.find(self.parent[elem]);
        }

        self.parent[elem]
    }

    fn union(&mut self, x: usize, y: usize) -> bool {
        let (x, y) = (self.find(x), self.find(y));

        if x == y {
            return false;
        }

        match self.rank[x].cmp(&self.rank[y]) {
            Less => self.parent[x] = y,
            Greater => self.parent[y] = x,
            Equal => {
                self.parent[x] = y;
                self.rank[y] += 1;
            }
        }

        true
    }
}

fn kruskals(n: usize, mut edges: Vec<Edge>) -> Vec<Edge> {
    // Kruskal's algorithm is greedy: it takes the cheapest edges first.
    edges.sort_by_key(|e| e.w);

    let mut uf = DisjointSet::new(n);
    let mut mst = Vec::new();

    for edge in edges {
        if uf.union(edge.u, edge.v) {
            mst.push(edge);
        }
    }

    mst
}

fn main() {
    let edges = vec![
        Edge { u: 0, v: 1, w: 4 },
        Edge { u: 0, v: 2, w: 3 },
        Edge { u: 1, v: 2, w: 1 },
        Edge { u: 1, v: 3, w: 2 },
        Edge { u: 2, v: 3, w: 4 },
        Edge { u: 3, v: 4, w: 2 },
    ];

    let mst = kruskals(5, edges);
    let total: u32 = mst.iter().map(|e| e.w).sum();

    for e in &mst {
        println!("{} - {} ({})", e.u, e.v, e.w);
    }
    println!("total: {total}");
}

Listing 12.25 Breadth-first search, with its tests. src/problems/graph_bfs.rs

//! Breadth-first search.
//!
//! Two variants of the same algorithm:
//!
//! - `bfs_vec`: nodes are `usize` indices and the graph is `Vec<Vec<(usize, u32)>>`,
//!   so `visited` is a plain `Vec<bool>`. This is the version to write first.
//! - `bfs`: nodes are any `Copy + Eq + Hash` type and the graph is a `HashMap`
//!   from a node to a slice of `(neighbor, weight)` edges.

use std::{
    collections::{HashMap, HashSet, VecDeque},
    hash::Hash,
};

/// Adjacency list keyed by node: each node maps to its `(neighbor, weight)` edges.
pub type GraphAdjList<'a, Node> = HashMap<Node, &'a [(Node, u32)]>;

/// BFS over an index-based adjacency list. Returns nodes in visiting order.
pub fn bfs_vec(graph: &[Vec<(usize, u32)>], start_node: usize) -> Vec<usize> {
    let mut visited = vec![false; graph.len()];
    let mut queue = VecDeque::from([start_node]);
    let mut result = vec![];

    visited[start_node] = true;

    while let Some(current_node) = queue.pop_front() {
        result.push(current_node);
        for &(neighbor, _) in &graph[current_node] {
            if !visited[neighbor] {
                visited[neighbor] = true;
                queue.push_back(neighbor);
            }
        }
    }
    result
}

/// BFS over a `HashMap` adjacency list. Returns nodes in visiting order.
pub fn bfs<Node>(graph: &GraphAdjList<Node>, start_node: Node) -> Vec<Node>
where
    Node: Copy + Eq + Hash,
{
    let mut visited = HashSet::new();
    let mut queue = VecDeque::from([start_node]);
    let mut result = vec![];

    visited.insert(start_node);

    while let Some(current_node) = queue.pop_front() {
        result.push(current_node);
        // slice iter yields &(Node, u32); `&` destructures it
        for &(neighbor, _) in graph[&current_node] {
            if visited.insert(neighbor) {
                queue.push_back(neighbor);
            }
        }
    }
    result
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    /// A -> B (1), A -> C (4), B -> C (2), B -> D (5), C -> D (1)
    fn sample_vec() -> Vec<Vec<(usize, u32)>> {
        vec![
            vec![(1, 1), (2, 4)],
            vec![(2, 2), (3, 5)],
            vec![(3, 1)],
            vec![],
        ]
    }

    fn sample_map() -> HashMap<&'static str, &'static [(&'static str, u32)]> {
        HashMap::from([
            ("A", &[("B", 1), ("C", 4)][..]),
            ("B", &[("C", 2), ("D", 5)][..]),
            ("C", &[("D", 1)][..]),
            ("D", &[][..]),
        ])
    }

    #[test]
    fn vec_variant_visits_level_by_level() {
        assert_eq!(bfs_vec(&sample_vec(), 0), vec![0, 1, 2, 3]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn vec_variant_skips_unreachable_nodes() {
        let graph = vec![vec![(1, 1)], vec![], vec![(0, 1)]];
        assert_eq!(bfs_vec(&graph, 0), vec![0, 1]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn vec_variant_handles_cycles() {
        let graph = vec![vec![(1, 1)], vec![(0, 1)]];
        assert_eq!(bfs_vec(&graph, 0), vec![0, 1]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn map_variant_visits_level_by_level() {
        assert_eq!(bfs(&sample_map(), "A"), vec!["A", "B", "C", "D"]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn both_variants_agree() {
        let names = ["A", "B", "C", "D"];
        let from_vec: Vec<&str> = bfs_vec(&sample_vec(), 0)
            .into_iter()
            .map(|index| names[index])
            .collect();
        assert_eq!(from_vec, bfs(&sample_map(), "A"));
    }
}

Listing 12.26 Depth-first search, with its tests. src/problems/graph_dfs.rs

//! Iterative depth-first search with an explicit stack.
//!
//! Two variants of the same algorithm:
//!
//! - `dfs_vec`: nodes are `usize` indices and the graph is `Vec<Vec<(usize, u32)>>`.
//! - `dfs`: nodes are any `Copy + Eq + Hash` type and the graph is a `HashMap`.
//!
//! A node is marked visited when it is popped, not when it is pushed, so it may
//! sit on the stack more than once. Neighbors are pushed in order, which means the
//! last neighbor is explored first.

use std::{collections::HashSet, hash::Hash};

use crate::problems::graph_bfs::GraphAdjList;

/// DFS over an index-based adjacency list. Returns nodes in visiting order.
pub fn dfs_vec(graph: &[Vec<(usize, u32)>], start_node: usize) -> Vec<usize> {
    let mut visited = vec![false; graph.len()];
    let mut stack = vec![start_node];
    let mut result = vec![];

    while let Some(current_node) = stack.pop() {
        if visited[current_node] {
            continue;
        }
        visited[current_node] = true;
        result.push(current_node);
        for &(neighbor, _) in &graph[current_node] {
            stack.push(neighbor);
        }
    }
    result
}

/// DFS over a `HashMap` adjacency list. Returns nodes in visiting order.
pub fn dfs<Node>(graph: &GraphAdjList<Node>, start_node: Node) -> Vec<Node>
where
    Node: Copy + Eq + Hash,
{
    let mut visited = HashSet::new();
    let mut stack = vec![start_node];
    let mut result = vec![];

    while let Some(current_node) = stack.pop() {
        if !visited.insert(current_node) {
            continue;
        }
        result.push(current_node);
        for &(neighbor, _) in graph[&current_node] {
            stack.push(neighbor);
        }
    }
    result
}

#[cfg(test)]

Listing 12.27 Dijkstra's algorithm, with its tests. src/problems/graph_dijkstra.rs

//! Dijkstra's shortest paths with a binary min-heap.
//!
//! Two variants of the same algorithm:
//!
//! - `dijkstra_vec`: nodes are `usize` indices and distances are a
//!   `Vec<Option<u32>>`, where `None` means unreachable.
//! - `dijkstra`: nodes are any `Copy + Eq + Hash + Ord` type and distances are a
//!   `HashMap` containing only the reachable nodes.
//!
//! Edge weights must be non-negative, which `u32` guarantees. `BinaryHeap` is a
//! max-heap, so entries are wrapped in `Reverse` to pop the smallest cost first.
//! A node can be in the heap several times; an entry whose cost is larger than the
//! recorded distance is stale and skipped.

use std::{
    cmp::Reverse,
    collections::{BinaryHeap, HashMap},
    hash::Hash,
};

use crate::problems::graph_bfs::GraphAdjList;

/// Shortest distances from `start_node` over an index-based adjacency list.
pub fn dijkstra_vec(graph: &[Vec<(usize, u32)>], start_node: usize) -> Vec<Option<u32>> {
    let mut distances = vec![None; graph.len()];
    let mut min_heap = BinaryHeap::from([Reverse((0, start_node))]);

    distances[start_node] = Some(0);

    while let Some(Reverse((current_cost, current_node))) = min_heap.pop() {
        // stale heap entry, a shorter path was already recorded
        if distances[current_node].is_some_and(|best| current_cost > best) {
            continue;
        }
        for &(neighbor, weight) in &graph[current_node] {
            let new_distance = current_cost + weight;
            if distances[neighbor].is_none_or(|best| new_distance < best) {
                distances[neighbor] = Some(new_distance);
                min_heap.push(Reverse((new_distance, neighbor)));
            }
        }
    }
    distances
}

/// Shortest distances from `start_node` over a `HashMap` adjacency list.
pub fn dijkstra<Node>(graph: &GraphAdjList<Node>, start_node: Node) -> HashMap<Node, u32>
where
    Node: Copy + Eq + Hash + Ord,
{
    let mut distances = HashMap::from([(start_node, 0)]);
    let mut min_heap = BinaryHeap::from([Reverse((0, start_node))]);

    while let Some(Reverse((current_cost, current_node))) = min_heap.pop() {
        // stale heap entry, a shorter path was already recorded
        if current_cost > distances[&current_node] {
            continue;
        }
        for &(neighbor, weight) in graph[&current_node] {
            let new_distance = current_cost + weight;

            if new_distance
                < *distances
                    .get(&neighbor)
                    .unwrap_or(&u32::MAX)
            {
                distances.insert(neighbor, new_distance);
                min_heap.push(Reverse((new_distance, neighbor)));
            }
        }
    }
    distances
}

    fn sample_vec() -> Vec<Vec<(usize, u32)>> {

        HashMap::from([
            ("A", &[("B", 1), ("C", 4)][..]),

}

Summary

  • A graph G = (V, E) permits arbitrary vertex connectivity and cycles, requiring every traversal to maintain an explicit visitation state structure.
  • Adjacency lists represent sparse graphs cleanly: the dense index form (Vec<Vec<...>>) maximizes cache locality and throughput, whereas the map form (HashMap) accommodates arbitrary hashable vertex identifiers.
  • BFS uses a FIFO queue to explore vertices in non-decreasing hop distance, whereas DFS uses a LIFO stack to explore full branches before backtracking; both run in O(V + E) time.
  • Arena-style integer indexing (NodeId = usize) eliminates reference-cycle ownership hazards in Rust graphs.
  • Directed cycle detection requires a three-state visitation machine (Unvisited, Visiting, Done); an edge targeting a Visiting ancestor is a back edge that closes a cycle.
  • Two-dimensional grids form implicit graphs whose orthogonal edges are computed from coordinate offsets, enabling O(R × C) flood-fill connected-component counting.
  • Kahn’s algorithm computes a topological ordering in O(V + E) time by iteratively removing zero-indegree vertices; producing fewer than |V| vertices proves the presence of a directed cycle.
  • Dijkstra’s algorithm computes single-source shortest paths over non-negative edge weights in O(E log V) time using a min-heap with lazy stale-entry deletion, hardened by checked_add and let ... else guards.
  • Kruskal’s algorithm constructs a minimum spanning tree in O(E log E) time by sorting edges and querying disjoint-set union with path compression and union by rank.

  2. Extend dijkstra_vec to record each node’s predecessor on its shortest path. Then write a function that rebuilds the path from the start to a given node.
  3. Rewrite count_islands with a Vec<bool> for visited, and with a DFS stack instead of a BFS queue. Check that the tests still pass.
  4. Change topo_sort in listing 12.15 to return Option<Vec<String>>, and add a test with a cycle.
  5. Rewrite find in listing 12.22 with a loop instead of recursion, keeping path compression.

An LRU cache

This chapter covers

  • What a cache is, and the least-recently-used rule for deciding what to throw away
  • An LRU cache built from a map and a queue of stamped events
  • An LRU cache built from a doubly linked list stored in a Vec, with indices as links
  • The same list split into small operations with stated preconditions
  • A benchmark of the Vec version against a list of Rc<RefCell<_>> nodes

A cache retains a bounded working set of recently accessed entries in low-latency storage to avoid repeating expensive computation or I/O. Web browsers cache decoded assets, database engines cache disk pages in RAM, and processors cache main memory in small SRAM arrays adjacent to each core.

Because capacity is strictly bounded, inserting a new entry into a full cache requires evicting an existing entry according to an eviction policy. The least recently used (LRU) policy evicts the entry that has remained unaccessed for the longest duration, exploiting temporal locality to maximize hit rates.

Implementing an O(1) LRU cache combines hash-indexed key lookup with a recency-ordered doubly linked structure. This chapter develops four progressively refined implementations (a timestamped lazy-eviction queue, an arena-backed doubly linked list, a precondition-partitioned modular arena, and a reference-counted list) and benchmarks the arena representation directly against Rc<RefCell<_>>.

13.1 What an LRU cache does

An LRU cache exposes two core operations, both executing in O(1) time:

  • get(key) returns the cached value associated with key, or None on a miss. A cache hit promotes key to the most-recently-used position.
  • put(key, value) inserts or updates the mapping for key and promotes it to the most-recently-used position. When inserting a new key at full capacity, the least-recently-used entry is evicted first.

Figure 13.1 traces five operations against a two-entry cache.

The third call changes the outcome. Without get(A), A would be the least recent entry, and put(C, 3) would evict A. Because get(A) counted as a use, B is evicted instead.

13.1.1 What a cache saves

A cache pays off when a hit is much cheaper than the work it replaces. Suppose a lookup in the cache takes 100 ns, and a miss means a database query that takes 1 ms, ten thousand times longer. The average cost of a request is then set almost entirely by the misses:

Hit rateAverage cost of a request
0%1 ms
50%about 500 µs
90%about 100 µs
99%about 10 µs

Going from 90% to 99% makes the average ten times smaller. The hit rate depends on what stays in the cache, and the eviction policy decides that.

Consider an eight-request trace against a three-entry cache: A, B, A, C, A, D, A, B. A request for a cached key is a hit; any other request is a miss that fetches the value from the backing store and inserts it. The table below compares LRU against FIFO (first in, first out), which evicts the earliest-arriving entry regardless of subsequent reads. Entries are listed from most recent to least recent.

RequestLRU: entries afterLRUFIFO: entries afterFIFO
AAmissAmiss
BB AmissB Amiss
AA BhitB Ahit
CC A BmissC B Amiss
AA C BhitC B Ahit
DD A Cmiss, evicts BD C Bmiss, evicts A
AA D ChitA D Cmiss, evicts B
BB A Dmiss, evicts CB A Dmiss, evicts C

LRU achieves 3 hits compared with 2 for FIFO: because every access promotes A back to the head of the recency list, the hot key remains resident, whereas FIFO evicts A on the sixth request solely because it arrived first, causing an immediate miss on the seventh request.

Animation 13.1 plays the same trace, with a robot for the cache and one for the slow store behind it.

LRU excels under workloads exhibiting strong temporal locality, yet it degrades under sequential scans (one-time sweeps over more distinct keys than cache capacity), which flush the hot working set completely. Production storage engines mitigate scan pollution using multi-queue or frequency-aware admission policies (such as 2Q, LRU-K, or W-TinyLFU) that promote keys into the protected tier only upon a second access.

An O(1) LRU cache must satisfy two simultaneous indexing requirements:

  1. O(1) key-to-entry lookup, provided by a HashMap.
  2. O(1) recency promotion and tail eviction, requiring a dynamically reorderable sequence.

Maintaining recency order inside a Vec requires O(n) element shifts on every promotion. The four implementations below achieve O(1) recency updates through timestamped queues and index-linked or pointer-linked doubly linked lists.

13.2 Version 1: stamped events in a queue

The first design avoids a doubly linked list altogether by logging every access into a FIFO queue and deferring deduplication to eviction time (lazy deletion).

A monotonically increasing generation: u64 counter increments on every get hit or put. Each access stamps the target key in two structures (Figure 13.2):

  • map: HashMap<K, (V, u64)> stores each resident key’s value paired with its most recent generation stamp.
  • recency: VecDeque<(K, u64)> appends a (key, generation) event to the back of the queue.

The queue preserves chronological access order from oldest (front) to newest (back). Repeatedly accessed keys accumulate multiple entries in recency; only the entry whose stamp matches the key’s current stamp in map is authoritative, while earlier entries are stale (analogous to lazy deletion in Dijkstra’s priority queue).

During eviction, the cache dequeues events from the front, discarding stale records until it encounters an authoritative event, whose key is guaranteed to be the least recently used resident entry.

Listing 13.1 The type (lines 10 to 24). src/problems/lru_cache.rs

use std::{
    collections::{HashMap, VecDeque},
    hash::Hash,
};

pub struct LruCache<K, V>
where
    K: Eq + Hash + Clone,
    V: Clone,
{
    capacity: usize,
    map: HashMap<K, (V, u64)>,
    recency: VecDeque<(K, u64)>,
    generation: u64,
}

The key must be Clone, because a copy of it goes into the queue with every event. The value must be Clone, because get returns a copy of it.

Listing 13.2 get and put (lines 49 to 71).

impl<K, V> LruCache<K, V>
where
    K: Eq + Hash + Clone,
    V: Clone,
{
    // ...
    pub fn get(&mut self, key: &K) -> Option<V> {
        let (value, _) = self.map.get(key)?.clone();
        self.generation += 1;
        self.recency
            .push_back((key.clone(), self.generation));
        self.map
            .insert(key.clone(), (value.clone(), self.generation));
        Some(value)
    }

    pub fn put(&mut self, key: K, value: V) {
        self.generation += 1;
        let is_new = self
            .map
            .insert(key.clone(), (value, self.generation))
            .is_none();
        self.recency
            .push_back((key, self.generation));

        if is_new {
            self.evict_if_needed();
        }
    }
    // ...
}

get looks up the key and returns early with None if it is missing: self.map.get(key)?. Then it advances the generation, records an event, and stores the value again with the new stamp.

put stores the value with a new stamp, and records an event. HashMap::insert returns the old value if the key was already present, or None if it was new. Only a new key can make the map too large, so only a new key triggers eviction.

Listing 13.3 Eviction (lines 73 to 87).

impl<K, V> LruCache<K, V>
where
    K: Eq + Hash + Clone,
    V: Clone,
{
    // ...
    fn evict_if_needed(&mut self) {
        while self.map.len() > self.capacity {
            let Some((key, generation)) = self.recency.pop_front() else {
                break;
            };

            match self.map.get(&key) {
                Some((_, current)) if *current == generation => {
                    self.map.remove(&key);
                    break;
                }
                _ => {}
            }
        }
    }
}

The loop runs while the map holds more keys than the capacity. Each pass pops the oldest event. The match guard Some((_, current)) if *current == generation accepts the event only if its stamp matches the key’s stamp in the map. A match removes the key and ends the loop. A stale event matches the _ arm and is dropped.

Each event is pushed once and popped at most once. So the total work over many calls is proportional to the number of calls, and each call costs O(1) on average. A cost measured this way, averaged over a sequence of calls, is called amortized.

Animation 13.2 runs the four calls of figure 13.2 with a capacity of 2, then a run of hits.

WARNING: The queue appends one new event per call, yet removes events only during eviction. Under a hit-heavy workload, evictions occur rarely and the queue can grow far beyond cache capacity, making memory usage proportional to total request count rather than cached entry count. Exercise 1 addresses bounding this queue.

13.3 Version 2: a linked list inside a Vec

The canonical O(1) LRU architecture maintains resident entries in a doubly linked list ordered from most recently used (head) to least recently used (tail), paired with a HashMap mapping each key directly to its node location. Promoting an interior node, inserting at the head, and evicting from the tail each execute in O(1) worst-case time.

A doubly linked list built from Rc<RefCell<_>> nodes incurs significant runtime overhead in Rust: every node requires an independent heap allocation, reference-count updates, dynamic borrow checks, and Weak back-links to prevent cycles.

An arena layout eliminates these costs by storing all nodes contiguously inside a single Vec<Node<K, V>> and encoding prev and next pointers as integer Option<usize> indices (Figure 13.3).

Because usize indices are copyable scalars outside the borrow checker’s aliasing model, multiple nodes and the lookup table can reference the same slot without Rc or RefCell. The trade-off shifts responsibility for referential integrity from the compiler to the implementation’s link-maintenance invariants.

Listing 13.4 The node and the cache (lines 20 to 45). src/problems/lru_cache_easy.rs

use std::{collections::HashMap, hash::Hash};

/// A single cache entry, linked into the recency list by index.
struct Node<K, V> {
    /// Retained so we can delete the corresponding map entry when evicting.
    key: K,
    value: V,
    /// Neighbour closer to the MRU end (or `None` if this is `head`).
    prev: Option<usize>,
    /// Neighbour closer to the LRU end (or `None` if this is `tail`).
    next: Option<usize>,
}

/// Fixed-capacity LRU cache.
pub struct LruCache<K, V> {
    /// Maximum number of entries; `>= 1` (enforced by `new`).
    cap: usize,
    /// Key → arena index. The single source of truth for "is this key cached?".
    lookup_table: HashMap<K, usize>,
    /// Arena of nodes; indices are the "pointers" of the linked list.
    nodes: Vec<Node<K, V>>,
    /// Arena index of the most recently used entry.
    head: Option<usize>,
    /// Arena index of the least recently used entry (next to be evicted).
    tail: Option<usize>,
}

Each node stores its key as well as its value. When a node is evicted, the cache reads the key from the node to remove the key from lookup_table.

prev and next are Option<usize>, where None means “no neighbor on that side”. head is the index of the most recently used node, and tail is the index of the least recently used one.

13.3.1 Moving a node to the front

Every get and put ends by moving one node to the front of the list. The method touch does it in two steps (figure 13.4):

  1. Detach the node: make its two neighbors point at each other, so the list skips it.
  2. Push it to the front: make it point at the old head, and make it the new head.

Animation 13.3 traces touch on a four-entry list: the backing Vec remains stationary in memory while only the logical index links change, redirecting A’s next to D as C moves to the front.

Listing 13.5 new and touch (lines 51 to 101).

impl<K, V> LruCache<K, V>
where
    K: Hash + Eq + Clone,
{
    /// Create a cache holding at most `cap` entries.
    ///
    /// # Panics
    /// Panics if `cap == 0`, since a zero-capacity cache cannot store anything.
    pub fn new(cap: usize) -> Self {
        assert!(cap > 0, "capacity must be > 0");
        Self {
            cap,
            lookup_table: HashMap::new(),
            nodes: Vec::new(),
            head: None,
            tail: None,
        }
    }

    /// Promote node `i` to `head` (MRU).
    ///
    /// Handles both cases in one pass:
    /// * **Already linked** — detach from its current neighbours first.
    /// * **Brand new** — the node has `prev = next = None` and is not yet
    ///   referenced by `head`/`tail`, so the detach step is skipped.
    fn touch(&mut self, i: usize) {
        let (prev, next) = (self.nodes[i].prev, self.nodes[i].next);

        // A node is "linked" if any of its four references exist.
        let linked =
            prev.is_some() || next.is_some() || self.head == Some(i) || self.tail == Some(i);

        if linked {
            // Splice `i` out of the list.
            match prev {
                Some(p) => self.nodes[p].next = next,
                None => self.head = next,
            }
            match next {
                Some(n) => self.nodes[n].prev = prev,
                None => self.tail = prev,
            }
        }

        // Splice `i` in at the front.
        self.nodes[i].prev = None;
        self.nodes[i].next = self.head;
        if let Some(h) = self.head {
            self.nodes[h].prev = Some(i);
        }
        self.head = Some(i);
        if self.tail.is_none() {
            self.tail = Some(i);
        }
    }
    // ...
}

touch first copies the node’s prev and next into local variables. Option<usize> is Copy, so this reads the values without keeping a borrow of self.nodes.

A brand-new node is not in the list yet, so there is nothing to detach. touch tells the two cases apart with linked. A node is in the list if it has a neighbor, or if it is the head or the tail. A list with one node has no neighbors, so the head and tail checks are needed for that case.

The detach step handles the ends of the list. If the node has no prev, it was the head, so the head moves to its next. If it has no next, it was the tail, so the tail moves to its prev.

The push step sets the node’s links, points the old head back at it, and makes it the head. If the list was empty, the node is also the tail.

13.3.2 get and put

Listing 13.6 get and put (lines 103 to 147).

impl<K, V> LruCache<K, V>
where
    K: Hash + Eq + Clone,
{
    // ...
    /// Look up `key`, promoting it to MRU on a hit.
    ///
    /// Returns `None` if the key is not cached.
    pub fn get(&mut self, key: &K) -> Option<&V> {
        let i = *self.lookup_table.get(key)?;
        self.touch(i);
        Some(&self.nodes[i].value)
    }

    /// Insert or update `key`. Promotes it to MRU. Evicts the LRU entry if
    /// the cache is full.
    pub fn put(&mut self, key: K, value: V) {
        // Case 1: key already present → update value, promote.
        if let Some(&i) = self.lookup_table.get(&key) {
            self.nodes[i].value = value;
            self.touch(i);
            return;
        }

        // Case 2: room to grow → append a fresh node.
        if self.nodes.len() < self.cap {
            let i = self.nodes.len();
            self.nodes.push(Node {
                key: key.clone(),
                value,
                prev: None,
                next: None,
            });
            self.lookup_table.insert(key, i);
            self.touch(i);
            return;
        }

        // Case 3: at capacity → reuse the LRU slot.
        // `tail` is guaranteed to be `Some` here because `cap >= 1` and the
        // arena is full, but we still handle `None` gracefully.
        if let Some(i) = self.tail {
            let old_key = std::mem::replace(&mut self.nodes[i].key, key);
            self.nodes[i].value = value;
            self.lookup_table.remove(&old_key);
            self.lookup_table
                .insert(self.nodes[i].key.clone(), i);
            self.touch(i);
        }
    }
}

get looks up the slot index, promotes the node, and returns a shared reference to the value. Because get takes &mut self, the cache remains mutably borrowed for as long as the returned Option<&V> remains live.

put handles three cases:

  1. The key is present. Overwrite the stored value and promote the node.
  2. Capacity remains. Push a new node onto the Vec, record its index, and promote it.
  3. The cache is full. Reuse the tail node’s slot for the incoming entry.

The third case highlights the primary advantage of an arena: eviction performs no deallocation and insertion performs no heap allocation. Instead, the tail slot is overwritten with the new key and value, and touch promotes its index to the head.

std::mem::replace(&mut self.nodes[i].key, key) installs the incoming key and returns the evicted key in a single operation so the evicted key can be removed from lookup_table; the table then receives a clone of the new key.

Animation 13.4 plays the three cases in order. It fills the cache, updates an entry, and then evicts the tail by reusing its slot. The last run leaves out the remove of the old key.

The file src/bin/lru_cache_arena.rs has the same cache with a main function:

Listing 13.7 The main function (lines 150 to 165). src/bin/lru_cache_arena.rs

use std::{collections::HashMap, hash::Hash};

fn main() {
    let mut cache = LruCache::new(2);

    cache.put("A", 10);
    cache.put("B", 20);
    println!("get A = {:?}", cache.get(&"A")); // Some(10), A now MRU

    cache.put("C", 30); // evicts B (LRU)

    println!("get B = {:?}", cache.get(&"B")); // None
    println!("get A = {:?}", cache.get(&"A")); // Some(10)
    println!("get C = {:?}", cache.get(&"C")); // Some(30)

    cache.put("A", 99);
    println!("get A = {:?}", cache.get(&"A")); // Some(99)
}
$ cargo run --bin lru_cache_arena
get A = Some(10)
get B = None
get A = Some(10)
get C = Some(30)
get A = Some(99)

13.4 Version 3: one operation per method

In Version 2, touch combines two distinct responsibilities and must first determine whether the target node is already linked. Version 3 decomposes it into three single-purpose methods, each documented with an explicit precondition (an invariant that callers must satisfy upon entry). Because the compiler cannot verify index invariants statically, the doc comments state each contract explicitly.

This version also fixes the key and value types to i32. i32 is Copy, so the code never clones a key.

Listing 13.8 The link operations (lines 63 to 94). src/bin/lru_cache_modular.rs

use std::collections::HashMap;

impl LruCache {
    // ...
    /// Unlink node `i` from the list. `i` must currently be linked.
    fn detach(&mut self, i: usize) {
        let (prev, next) = (self.nodes[i].prev, self.nodes[i].next);
        match prev {
            Some(p) => self.nodes[p].next = next,
            None => self.head = next,
        }
        match next {
            Some(n) => self.nodes[n].prev = prev,
            None => self.tail = prev,
        }
    }

    /// Link node `i` in at the MRU end. `i` must currently be unlinked.
    fn push_front(&mut self, i: usize) {
        self.nodes[i].prev = None;
        self.nodes[i].next = self.head;
        match self.head {
            Some(h) => self.nodes[h].prev = Some(i),
            None => self.tail = Some(i), // list was empty
        }
        self.head = Some(i);
    }

    /// Promote an already-linked node to MRU.
    fn promote_to_front(&mut self, i: usize) {
        if self.head == Some(i) {
            return; // already MRU
        }
        self.detach(i);
        self.push_front(i);
    }
    // ...
}
  • detach unlinks a node. Its precondition is that the node is in the list.
  • push_front links a node at the head. Its precondition is that the node is not in the list.
  • promote_to_front combines them for a node that is in the list. If the node is already the head, it does nothing.

Each method now does one thing, with no linked check. put calls push_front for a new node and promote_to_front for an existing one, so each call satisfies its precondition.

$ cargo run --bin lru_cache_modular
get 1 = Some(10)
get 2 = None
get 1 = Some(10)
get 3 = Some(30)
get 1 = Some(99)

13.5 Version 4: measuring the arena against Rc<RefCell<_>>

Determining whether an arena-backed list outperforms an Rc<RefCell<_>> list, and by what margin, requires empirical measurement. Both cache implementations are placed behind a unified trait interface and driven with an identical deterministic request stream.

13.5.1 One trait, two caches

Listing 13.9 The trait. benchmarking_examples/cache/mod.rs

//! Two LRU caches of the same design, stored differently, so one benchmark loop
//! can cover both.
//!
//! [`arena`] keeps nodes in a `Vec` and links them by `usize` index.
//! [`rc_list`] allocates an `Rc<RefCell<_>>` per node and links them by pointer.

pub mod arena;
pub mod rc_list;

use std::hash::Hash;

/// The operations every cache supports.
pub trait Cache<K, V>
where
    K: Hash + Eq + Clone,
    V: Copy,
{
    /// A cache that holds at most `capacity` entries.
    ///
    /// # Panics
    /// Panics if `capacity == 0`, since a zero-capacity cache cannot store
    /// anything.
    fn new(capacity: usize) -> Self;

    /// Looks up `key`, promoting it to most recently used on a hit.
    fn get(&mut self, key: &K) -> Option<V>;

    /// Inserts or updates `key`, evicting the least recently used entry when
    /// the cache is full.
    fn put(&mut self, key: K, value: V);

    /// How many entries are cached.
    fn len(&self) -> usize;

    /// Whether the cache holds no entries.
    fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
        self.len() == 0
    }

    /// The variant's name, for benchmark output.
    fn variant() -> &'static str;
}

The trait Cache<K, V> lists what the benchmark needs. new is part of the trait, so generic code can create a cache with C::new(capacity) without knowing which type C is. variant has no self parameter. It is called on the type, and gives each cache a name for the output.

V: Copy lets get return the value itself, Option<V>, instead of a reference. The benchmark stores u64 values, which are Copy.

The arena cache is version 2, split into two impl blocks. touch stays in an ordinary impl, because it is not part of the trait. The trait methods go in impl<K, V> Cache<K, V> for LruCache<K, V>, and their bodies are the get and put of section 13.3.2:

Listing 13.10 The arena cache's trait methods (lines 91 to 154). benchmarking_examples/cache/arena.rs

impl<K, V> Cache<K, V> for LruCache<K, V>
where
    K: Hash + Eq + Clone,
    V: Copy,
{
    fn new(capacity: usize) -> Self {
        assert!(capacity > 0, "capacity must be > 0");
        Self {
            cap: capacity,
            lookup_table: HashMap::new(),
            nodes: Vec::new(),
            head: None,
            tail: None,
        }
    }

    fn get(&mut self, key: &K) -> Option<V> {
        let i = *self.lookup_table.get(key)?;
        self.touch(i);
        Some(self.nodes[i].value)
    }

    fn put(&mut self, key: K, value: V) {
        // Case 1: key already present, update the value and promote.
        if let Some(&i) = self.lookup_table.get(&key) {
            self.nodes[i].value = value;
            self.touch(i);
            return;
        }

        // Case 2: room to grow, append a fresh node.
        if self.nodes.len() < self.cap {
            let i = self.nodes.len();
            self.nodes.push(Node {
                key: key.clone(),
                value,
                prev: None,
                next: None,
            });
            self.lookup_table.insert(key, i);
            self.touch(i);
            return;
        }

        // Case 3: at capacity, reuse the LRU slot. `tail` is `Some` here because
        // `cap >= 1` and the arena is full, but handle `None` anyway.
        if let Some(i) = self.tail {
            let old_key = std::mem::replace(&mut self.nodes[i].key, key);
            self.nodes[i].value = value;
            self.lookup_table.remove(&old_key);
            self.lookup_table
                .insert(self.nodes[i].key.clone(), i);
            self.touch(i);
        }
    }

    fn len(&self) -> usize {
        self.lookup_table.len()
    }

    fn variant() -> &'static str {
        "arena (Vec + indices)"
    }
}

Listing 13.20, at the end of the chapter, has the whole file.

13.5.2 The Rc<RefCell<_>> list

Listing 13.11 The node and the cache (lines 10 to 33). benchmarking_examples/cache/rc_list.rs

use std::{
    cell::RefCell,
    collections::HashMap,
    hash::Hash,
    rc::{Rc, Weak},
};

use super::Cache;

type Link<K, V> = Option<Rc<RefCell<Node<K, V>>>>;

struct Node<K, V> {
    key: K,
    value: V,
    prev: Weak<RefCell<Node<K, V>>>,
    next: Link<K, V>,
}

pub struct LruCache<K, V> {
    cap: usize,
    map: HashMap<K, Rc<RefCell<Node<K, V>>>>,
    head: Link<K, V>,
    tail: Link<K, V>,
}

This is the doubly linked list of chapter 9. A node is Rc<RefCell<Node>>: Rc so several owners can hold it, and RefCell so it can be changed through those shared handles. next is a strong link, and prev is a Weak link, so two neighbors do not keep each other alive forever. The map holds one more Rc to every node.

Listing 13.12 detach and push_front (lines 35 to 69).

impl<K, V> LruCache<K, V>
where
    K: Hash + Eq + Clone,
    V: Copy,
{
    fn detach(&mut self, node: &Rc<RefCell<Node<K, V>>>) {
        let (prev, next) = {
            let entry = node.borrow();
            (entry.prev.clone(), entry.next.clone())
        };

        match prev.upgrade() {
            Some(previous) => previous.borrow_mut().next = next.clone(),
            None => self.head = next.clone(),
        }
        match &next {
            Some(following) => following.borrow_mut().prev = prev,
            None => self.tail = prev.upgrade(),
        }
    }

    fn push_front(&mut self, node: Rc<RefCell<Node<K, V>>>) {
        let head = self.head.clone();
        {
            let mut entry = node.borrow_mut();
            entry.prev = Weak::new();
            entry.next = head.clone();
        }
        match &head {
            Some(previous) => previous.borrow_mut().prev = Rc::downgrade(&node),
            None => self.tail = Some(node.clone()),
        }
        self.head = Some(node);
    }
}

The logic mirrors Listing 13.8 using reference-counted pointers rather than integer indices, at the cost of additional runtime bookkeeping at each step:

  • detach reads the node’s links inside a small block. node.borrow() returns a guard that holds a shared borrow of the RefCell. The block ends before any neighbor is changed, so the guard is dropped early. A RefCell panics if a borrow_mut happens while another borrow of the same cell is alive.
  • prev.upgrade() turns the Weak link into an Rc, if the node still exists.
  • Each .clone() of an Rc or a Weak increases a reference count, and each drop decreases one.

Listing 13.13 The trait methods and Drop (lines 71 to 139).

impl<K, V> Cache<K, V> for LruCache<K, V>
where
    K: Hash + Eq + Clone,
    V: Copy,
{
    fn new(capacity: usize) -> Self {
        assert!(capacity > 0, "capacity must be > 0");
        Self {
            cap: capacity,
            map: HashMap::new(),
            head: None,
            tail: None,
        }
    }

    fn get(&mut self, key: &K) -> Option<V> {
        let node = self.map.get(key)?.clone();
        self.detach(&node);
        self.push_front(node.clone());
        Some(node.borrow().value)
    }

    fn put(&mut self, key: K, value: V) {
        if let Some(node) = self.map.get(&key).cloned() {
            node.borrow_mut().value = value;
            self.detach(&node);
            self.push_front(node);
            return;
        }

        if self.map.len() >= self.cap
            && let Some(victim) = self.tail.clone()
        {
            let old_key = victim.borrow().key.clone();
            self.map.remove(&old_key);
            self.detach(&victim);
        }

        let node = Rc::new(RefCell::new(Node {
            key: key.clone(),
            value,
            prev: Weak::new(),
            next: None,
        }));
        self.map.insert(key, node.clone());
        self.push_front(node);
    }

    fn len(&self) -> usize {
        self.map.len()
    }

    fn variant() -> &'static str {
        "Rc<RefCell> list"
    }
}

impl<K, V> Drop for LruCache<K, V> {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        // Unlink iteratively: dropping a million-node chain recursively overflows
        // the stack.
        let mut current = self.head.take();
        while let Some(node) = current {
            let next = node.borrow_mut().next.take();
            node.borrow_mut().prev = Weak::new();
            current = next;
        }
    }
}

On a miss with a full cache, put removes the tail node from the map and detaches it. When victim goes out of scope, the last Rc to that node is dropped, and its memory is freed. Then Rc::new allocates a new node for the new key. So every eviction frees one heap block and allocates another.

The Drop implementation is the fix from chapter 9. Dropping a long chain of next links recursively uses one stack frame per node, and a large cache would overflow the stack. The loop breaks the links one node at a time. The map drops its Rc handles afterward, and each drop then frees a single node.

Figure 13.5 compares where the two caches keep their nodes.

Each arena node occupies 48 bytes (8 bytes each for u64 key and value, plus 16 bytes each for the two Option<usize> index links). By contrast, each Rc<RefCell<Node>> allocation occupies 56 bytes (the 32-byte node plus strong count, weak count, and RefCell borrow state). Although per-node byte footprints are comparable, the two designs differ fundamentally in allocator churn and spatial cache locality.

13.5.3 The benchmark

Listing 13.14 The request stream and the timed loop (lines 52 to 106). benchmarking_examples/benchmark.rs

use std::{
    hint::black_box,
    time::{Duration, Instant},
};

use systems_lab::{
    cache::{Cache, arena::LruCache as ArenaCache, rc_list::LruCache as RcCache},
    lists::{SinglyList, boxed, boxed_drop, enum_drop, enum_node},
};

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Cache: arena vs Rc<RefCell> linked list
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

/// Request stream with realistic locality: four requests in five come from a hot
/// set of 1% of the keys, the rest from the whole space.
fn key_at(state: u64) -> u64 {
    let mixed = state >> 17;
    if (state >> 33) % 100 < 80 {
        mixed % (KEY_SPACE / 100)
    } else {
        mixed % KEY_SPACE
    }
}

/// The fastest of `CACHE_RUNS` timed passes, with the hit count and final size
/// from the last one. Each pass starts from an empty cache, so the stream is the
/// same every time.
fn best_cache_run<C: Cache<u64, u64>>() -> (Duration, u64, usize) {
    let mut best = Duration::MAX;
    let mut hits = 0;
    let mut len = 0;

    for _ in 0..CACHE_RUNS {
        let mut cache = C::new(CACHE_CAPACITY);
        let (elapsed, run_hits) = cache_workload(&mut cache);
        best = best.min(elapsed);
        hits = run_hits;
        len = cache.len();
    }
    (best, hits, len)
}

/// The same request stream against any cache.
fn cache_workload<C: Cache<u64, u64>>(cache: &mut C) -> (Duration, u64) {
    let mut state = 0x9e37_79b9_7f4a_7c15u64;
    let mut hits = 0u64;

    let start = Instant::now();
    for _ in 0..OPERATIONS {
        state = state
            .wrapping_mul(6_364_136_223_846_793_005)
            .wrapping_add(1_442_695_040_888_963_407);
        let key = key_at(state);

        match cache.get(&key) {
            Some(value) => {
                hits += 1;
                black_box(value);
            }
            None => cache.put(key, key.rotate_left(17)),
        }
    }
    (start.elapsed(), hits)
}

A fair comparison needs both caches to see exactly the same requests. The program makes its own request stream from a number called state. Each step multiplies and adds two fixed constants, so the same starting state always produces the same sequence. A generator of this kind is called a linear congruential generator.

key_at shapes the stream to look like real traffic. Real caches see some keys far more often than others. Here, 80% of requests pick from a hot set of 1% of the keys, and the rest pick from all 131,072 keys. The capacity, 65,536, is half the key space.

Each request calls get. On a miss, it calls put, the way a program fills a cache after it computes a missing value. black_box tells the compiler to treat the value as used, so the optimizer cannot remove the work.

Listing 13.15 Running and checking both caches (lines 108 to 158).

fn cache_benchmark() {
    println!(
        "LRU cache: {} entries, {} requests over {} keys",
        with_thousands(CACHE_CAPACITY as u64),
        with_thousands(OPERATIONS),
        with_thousands(KEY_SPACE)
    );
    println!("A miss inserts and evicts the least recently used entry.");
    println!("Best of {CACHE_RUNS} runs per cache.\n");

    let (arena_time, arena_hits, arena_len) = best_cache_run::<ArenaCache<u64, u64>>();
    let (list_time, list_hits, list_len) = best_cache_run::<RcCache<u64, u64>>();

    // Same population and same hit count, or this compares nothing.
    assert_eq!(arena_len, list_len);
    assert_eq!(
        arena_hits, list_hits,
        "the two runs saw different request streams"
    );

    println!(
        "  hit rate: {:.1}%  ({} hits, {} inserts)\n",
        arena_hits as f64 * 100.0 / OPERATIONS as f64,
        with_thousands(arena_hits),
        with_thousands(OPERATIONS - arena_hits)
    );

    let per_request = |elapsed: Duration| elapsed.as_nanos() as f64 / OPERATIONS as f64;

    // `{:.2?}` uses Duration's own Debug format, rounded to two decimals.
    println!("  {:<22} {:>12} {:>13}", "storage", "total", "per request");
    println!("  {}", "-".repeat(48));
    for (name, elapsed) in [
        (
            <ArenaCache<u64, u64> as Cache<u64, u64>>::variant(),
            arena_time,
        ),
        (<RcCache<u64, u64> as Cache<u64, u64>>::variant(), list_time),
    ] {
        println!(
            "  {name:<22} {elapsed:>12.2?} {:>8.0} ns",
            per_request(elapsed)
        );
    }

    let speedup = list_time.as_secs_f64() / arena_time.as_secs_f64();
    println!(
        "\n  the arena is {speedup:.2}x faster on the same requests: {arena_time:.2?} against {list_time:.2?}"
    );
    println!("  the arena reuses the evicted slot; the list frees a node and allocates another");
}

best_cache_run::<ArenaCache<u64, u64>>() runs the generic function with the arena cache, and the next line runs it with the Rc cache. The ::<...> syntax, called the turbofish, names the type parameter explicitly.

Before printing any times, the function checks that both caches finished with the same size and the same number of hits. Two correct LRU caches given the same requests make the same decisions. If the counts differed, one cache would have a bug, and its time would mean nothing.

<ArenaCache<u64, u64> as Cache<u64, u64>>::variant() is the fully qualified way to call a trait function that has no self. It names both the type and the trait.

Listing 13.16 The complete benchmark program. benchmarking_examples/benchmark.rs

//! One main for every benchmark in the lab.
//!
//! Usage:
//!   cargo run --release --bin benchmark                    # cache, then lists
//!   cargo run --release --bin benchmark cache              # cache only
//!   cargo run --release --bin benchmark list               # all four variants
//!   cargo run --release --bin benchmark list enum 500000   # one variant, one size
//!
//! The recursive list variants abort with a stack overflow past roughly 265,000
//! nodes, so run them below that size or on their own.

use std::{
    hint::black_box,
    time::{Duration, Instant},
};

use systems_lab::{
    cache::{Cache, arena::LruCache as ArenaCache, rc_list::LruCache as RcCache},
    lists::{SinglyList, boxed, boxed_drop, enum_drop, enum_node},
};

const CACHE_CAPACITY: usize = 65_536;
const KEY_SPACE: u64 = 131_072;
const OPERATIONS: u64 = 10_000_000;
const DEFAULT_LIST_ELEMENTS: usize = 200_000;
/// Timed passes per cache; the fastest is reported, since a slow pass is noise.
const CACHE_RUNS: usize = 3;
/// Timed passes per list variant.
const LIST_RUNS: usize = 3;

fn main() {
    let arguments: Vec<String> = std::env::args().skip(1).collect();

    match arguments.first().map(String::as_str) {
        Some("cache") => cache_benchmark(),
        Some("list") => {
            let variant = arguments.get(1).map(String::as_str);
            let elements = arguments
                .get(2)
                .and_then(|value| value.parse().ok())
                .unwrap_or(DEFAULT_LIST_ELEMENTS);
            list_benchmark(variant, elements);
        }
        _ => {
            cache_benchmark();
            println!();
            list_benchmark(None, DEFAULT_LIST_ELEMENTS);
        }
    }
}
