16.5 A counting semaphore

Whereas a lock restricts a critical section to a single thread, a semaphore admits up to N concurrent threads. It maintains a bounded pool of permits: a thread acquires a permit before entering the protected region and returns it upon exit. When the permit count reaches zero, additional threads block until an active holder releases a permit (figure 16.6).

Semaphores bound concurrency around finite resources such as database connections, in-flight network requests, and open file descriptors.

16.5.1 Waiting without spinning

Because permits may be held for milliseconds or longer, waiting threads should sleep rather than spin. A condition variable (Condvar) suspends a thread until another thread signals a state change. It always operates in tandem with a Mutex protecting the predicate state:

  1. The waiting thread locks the mutex and evaluates the predicate.
  2. While the predicate is unsatisfied, it calls condvar.wait(guard), which atomically releases the mutex and puts the thread to sleep.
  3. Another thread locks the mutex, updates the state, and invokes notify_one().
  4. The sleeping thread wakes with the mutex re-acquired and re-evaluates the predicate.

Re-checking the predicate in step 4 is mandatory for two reasons: another thread may have acquired the newly released permit before the woken thread ran, and operating systems may deliver spurious wakeups with no corresponding notification. Condition-variable waits must therefore always execute inside a while loop rather than an if statement.

Listing 16.13 The state, the guard, and acquire_guard. src/problems/semaphore.rs

use std::{
    sync::{Condvar, Mutex},
    time::Duration,
};

struct State {
    available: usize,
}

/// A counting semaphore. Cloning is not provided; share one behind `Arc`.
pub struct Semaphore {
    state: Mutex<State>,
    released: Condvar,
}

/// Releases one permit when dropped.
pub struct SemaphoreGuard<'a> {
    semaphore: &'a Semaphore,
}

impl Drop for SemaphoreGuard<'_> {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        self.semaphore.release();
    }
}

impl Semaphore {
    /// Create a semaphore with `permits` permits available.
    pub fn new(permits: usize) -> Self {
        Self {
            state: Mutex::new(State { available: permits }),
            released: Condvar::new(),
        }
    }

    /// Block until a permit is available.
    pub fn acquire(&self) {
        let _guard = self.acquire_guard();
    }

    /// Block until a permit is available, returning a guard that releases it.
    pub fn acquire_guard(&self) -> SemaphoreGuard<'_> {
        let mut state = self
            .state
            .lock()
            .expect("semaphore mutex poisoned");
        while state.available == 0 {
            state = self
                .released
                .wait(state)
                .expect("semaphore mutex poisoned");
        }
        state.available -= 1;
        SemaphoreGuard { semaphore: self }
    }
    // ...
}

acquire_guard returns a SemaphoreGuard holding a reference to the semaphore; its Drop implementation calls release, applying the same RAII pattern from section 16.4 so that permits are returned even on early returns or panics.

Inside acquire_guard, self.released.wait(state) consumes the mutex guard, suspends the thread, and returns a re-acquired guard upon wakeup. Once the loop terminates, at least one permit is available while the thread holds the mutex, allowing it to decrement the available count safely.

Listing 16.14 The other ways to acquire, and release (lines 47 to 103).

impl Semaphore {
    // ...
    /// Take a permit only if one is free right now.
    pub fn try_acquire(&self) -> Option<SemaphoreGuard<'_>> {
        let mut state = self
            .state
            .lock()
            .expect("semaphore mutex poisoned");
        if state.available == 0 {
            None
        } else {
            state.available -= 1;
            Some(SemaphoreGuard { semaphore: self })
        }
    }

    /// Take a permit, waiting at most `timeout`.
    pub fn try_acquire_timeout(&self, timeout: Duration) -> Option<SemaphoreGuard<'_>> {
        let mut state = self
            .state
            .lock()
            .expect("semaphore mutex poisoned");
        if state.available > 0 {
            state.available -= 1;
            return Some(SemaphoreGuard { semaphore: self });
        }

        let (mut state, _timed_out) = self
            .released
            .wait_timeout(state, timeout)
            .expect("semaphore mutex poisoned");

        if state.available == 0 {
            None
        } else {
            state.available -= 1;
            Some(SemaphoreGuard { semaphore: self })
        }
    }

    /// Permits currently free. Useful for metrics, not for control flow.
    pub fn available_permits(&self) -> usize {
        self.state
            .lock()
            .expect("semaphore mutex poisoned")
            .available
    }

    fn release(&self) {
        let mut state = self
            .state
            .lock()
            .expect("semaphore mutex poisoned");
        state.available += 1;
        self.released.notify_one();
    }
}

/// Releases one permit when dropped.
pub struct SemaphoreGuard<'a> {
    semaphore: &'a Semaphore,
}

impl Drop for SemaphoreGuard<'_> {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        self.semaphore.release();
    }
}

The release method increments the permit count and wakes one waiting thread via notify_one. Keeping release private and invoking it solely from SemaphoreGuard::drop prevents callers from releasing permits they never acquired.

Two methods in this listing exhibit deliberate limitations:

  • acquire binds the result of acquire_guard to _guard, which drops immediately when acquire returns. The permit is released before the caller executes any work, making acquire_guard the only method that actually holds a permit.
  • try_acquire_timeout calls wait_timeout once without looping. If a spurious wakeup occurs or another thread claims the permit first, it returns None prematurely before the full timeout elapses. A complete implementation tracks the deadline and loops over the remaining duration (Exercise 4).

Listing 16.15 The complete file, with tests. src/problems/semaphore.rs

//! Counting semaphore built from `Mutex` + `Condvar`.
//!
//! A semaphore bounds how many callers may proceed at once without protecting any
//! data. It is the primitive behind connection pools, per-account limits, and
//! bounded fan-out in a client library or command-line tool.
//!
//! The RAII guard returns the permit on drop, so a panicking worker cannot leak a
//! permit and slowly deadlock the pool.

use std::{
    sync::{Condvar, Mutex},
    time::Duration,
};

struct State {
    available: usize,
}

/// A counting semaphore. Cloning is not provided; share one behind `Arc`.
pub struct Semaphore {
    state: Mutex<State>,
    released: Condvar,
}

impl Semaphore {
    /// Create a semaphore with `permits` permits available.
    pub fn new(permits: usize) -> Self {
        Self {
            state: Mutex::new(State { available: permits }),
            released: Condvar::new(),
        }
    }

    /// Block until a permit is available.
    pub fn acquire(&self) {
        let _guard = self.acquire_guard();
    }

    /// Block until a permit is available, returning a guard that releases it.
    pub fn acquire_guard(&self) -> SemaphoreGuard<'_> {
        let mut state = self
            .state
            .lock()
            .expect("semaphore mutex poisoned");
        while state.available == 0 {
            state = self
                .released
                .wait(state)
                .expect("semaphore mutex poisoned");
        }
        state.available -= 1;
        SemaphoreGuard { semaphore: self }
    }

    /// Take a permit only if one is free right now.
    pub fn try_acquire(&self) -> Option<SemaphoreGuard<'_>> {
        let mut state = self
            .state
            .lock()
            .expect("semaphore mutex poisoned");
        if state.available == 0 {
            None
        } else {
            state.available -= 1;
            Some(SemaphoreGuard { semaphore: self })
        }
    }

    /// Take a permit, waiting at most `timeout`.
    pub fn try_acquire_timeout(&self, timeout: Duration) -> Option<SemaphoreGuard<'_>> {
        let mut state = self
            .state
            .lock()
            .expect("semaphore mutex poisoned");
        if state.available > 0 {
            state.available -= 1;
            return Some(SemaphoreGuard { semaphore: self });
        }

        let (mut state, _timed_out) = self
            .released
            .wait_timeout(state, timeout)
            .expect("semaphore mutex poisoned");

        if state.available == 0 {
            None
        } else {
            state.available -= 1;
            Some(SemaphoreGuard { semaphore: self })
        }
    }

    /// Permits currently free. Useful for metrics, not for control flow.
    pub fn available_permits(&self) -> usize {
        self.state
            .lock()
            .expect("semaphore mutex poisoned")
            .available
    }

    fn release(&self) {
        let mut state = self
            .state
            .lock()
            .expect("semaphore mutex poisoned");
        state.available += 1;
        self.released.notify_one();
    }
}

/// Releases one permit when dropped.
pub struct SemaphoreGuard<'a> {
    semaphore: &'a Semaphore,
}

impl Drop for SemaphoreGuard<'_> {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        self.semaphore.release();
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use std::{
        sync::{
            Arc,
            atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering},
        },
        thread,
    };

    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn never_exceeds_the_permit_count() {
        let permits = 4;
        let semaphore = Arc::new(Semaphore::new(permits));
        let active = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
        let peak = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));

        let mut handles = Vec::new();
        for _ in 0..32 {
            let semaphore = Arc::clone(&semaphore);
            let active = Arc::clone(&active);
            let peak = Arc::clone(&peak);
            handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
                let _guard = semaphore.acquire_guard();
                let now = active.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst) + 1;
                peak.fetch_max(now, Ordering::SeqCst);
                thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(1));
                active.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
            }));
        }
        for handle in handles {
            handle.join().expect("worker panicked");
        }

        assert!(peak.load(Ordering::SeqCst) <= permits);
        assert_eq!(semaphore.available_permits(), permits);
    }

    #[test]
    fn guard_returns_the_permit_on_drop() {
        let semaphore = Semaphore::new(1);
        {
            let _guard = semaphore.acquire_guard();
            assert_eq!(semaphore.available_permits(), 0);
        }
        assert_eq!(semaphore.available_permits(), 1);
    }

    #[test]
    fn try_acquire_reports_contention() {
        let semaphore = Semaphore::new(1);
        let first = semaphore
            .try_acquire()
            .expect("first permit is free");
        assert!(semaphore.try_acquire().is_none());
        drop(first);
        assert!(semaphore.try_acquire().is_some());
    }

    #[test]
    fn timeout_gives_up_when_no_permit_arrives() {
        let semaphore = Semaphore::new(0);
        assert!(
            semaphore
                .try_acquire_timeout(Duration::from_millis(5))
                .is_none()
        );
    }
}

The never_exceeds_the_permit_count test spawns 32 threads competing for 4 permits. Each thread increments an active counter upon acquiring a permit, records the maximum observed concurrency in peak using fetch_max, and verifies that peak never exceeds 4.

16.6 When a lock holder panics

A lock protects multi-step invariants that are temporarily broken mid-update. During a bank transfer, for instance, debiting one account and crediting another leaves the combined balance inconsistent between the two writes; the lock hides that intermediate state from other threads.

If a thread panics mid-update, stack unwinding drops the MutexGuard and releases the lock while the protected data remains partially mutated. To prevent subsequent threads from unknowingly operating on broken invariants, std::sync::Mutex marks itself poisoned (figure 16.7), causing every future call to lock() to return Err(PoisonError) rather than Ok(guard).

Poisoning flags the anomaly without locking out recovery logic: PoisonError::into_inner() yields the underlying MutexGuard so that audit or repair code can inspect and restore the data.

Listing 16.16 The ledger and the recovery function. src/bin/mutex_poisoning.rs

use std::{
    error::Error,
    sync::{Arc, Mutex, MutexGuard, PoisonError},
    thread,
};

/// Shared ledger state. In a real system this would be behind a transactional
/// store; here it is plain in-memory state to illustrate lock poisoning.
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct Ledger {
    cash_on_hand: i64,
    stock_value: i64,
    transaction_id: u32,
    is_settled: bool,
}

/// Recovers from a poisoned mutex by taking ownership of the guard that the
/// panicked thread left behind.
///
/// `PoisonError::into_inner()` gives us the `MutexGuard`, which means we still
/// hold the lock while repairing state. The guard is dropped when this function
/// returns.
fn recover_ledger(poisoned: PoisonError<MutexGuard<'_, Ledger>>) -> Ledger {
    // into_inner() returns the MutexGuard. We own the lock exclusively even
    // though the previous holder panicked.
    let mut guard = poisoned.into_inner();

    println!("[Reconciliation] Physical audit reveals a cash discrepancy.");
    println!(
        "[Reconciliation] Digital cash: {} | Corrected cash: {}",
        guard.cash_on_hand,
        guard.cash_on_hand - 200
    );

    // Correct the data while we still hold the guard.
    guard.cash_on_hand -= 200;
    guard.is_settled = true;
    guard.transaction_id += 1;

    println!("[Reconciliation] Ledger corrected. Transaction marked failed and closed.");

    // Clone the inner data to return an owned value. The guard drops here and
    // releases the lock.
    guard.clone()
}

Ledger holds the shared accounting state: cash on hand, stock value, a transaction identifier, and a settlement flag. Panicking between field updates leaves the ledger out of balance.

recover_ledger consumes the PoisonError, extracts the guard with into_inner(), reconciles the fields while holding the lock, and returns a cloned copy of the repaired ledger before the guard drops at function exit.

Listing 16.17 The complete program. src/bin/mutex_poisoning.rs

// ============================================================================
// Mutex poisoning: failed transaction and audit recovery
//
// Ported from the Rust playground repo (`scam_transaction.rs`).
//
// Story:
//   A branch executes a financial transaction that mutates shared state under
//   a `Mutex`. Mid-transaction the thread panics. In Rust, a `Mutex` whose
//   guard was held during a panic becomes **poisoned**. Future `lock()` calls
//   return `Err(PoisonError)` instead of silently letting another thread
//   observe an inconsistent partial update.
//
// Where this appears in practice:
//   - Controllers/reconcilers mutate shared state; a panic while holding a lock
//     is a real failure mode in worker pools, caches, and rate limiters.
//   - Rust chooses fail-fast over data corruption: a poisoned mutex tells
//     callers that the protected invariant may be broken. The caller must
//     decide whether to abort, recover, or reset state.
//   - `PoisonError::into_inner()` returns the `MutexGuard`, so a recovery path
//     can inspect/correct the last known state without waiting for the lock to
//     be released by the panicked thread.
//
// Run:
//   cargo run --bin mutex_poisoning
// ============================================================================

use std::{
    error::Error,
    sync::{Arc, Mutex, MutexGuard, PoisonError},
    thread,
};

/// Shared ledger state. In a real system this would be behind a transactional
/// store; here it is plain in-memory state to illustrate lock poisoning.
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct Ledger {
    cash_on_hand: i64,
    stock_value: i64,
    transaction_id: u32,
    is_settled: bool,
}

impl Ledger {
    fn new() -> Self {
        Ledger {
            cash_on_hand: 10_000,
            stock_value: 5_000,
            transaction_id: 0,
            is_settled: false,
        }
    }
}

/// Recovers from a poisoned mutex by taking ownership of the guard that the
/// panicked thread left behind.
///
/// `PoisonError::into_inner()` gives us the `MutexGuard`, which means we still
/// hold the lock while repairing state. The guard is dropped when this function
/// returns.
fn recover_ledger(poisoned: PoisonError<MutexGuard<'_, Ledger>>) -> Ledger {
    // into_inner() returns the MutexGuard. We own the lock exclusively even
    // though the previous holder panicked.
    let mut guard = poisoned.into_inner();

    println!("[Reconciliation] Physical audit reveals a cash discrepancy.");
    println!(
        "[Reconciliation] Digital cash: {} | Corrected cash: {}",
        guard.cash_on_hand,
        guard.cash_on_hand - 200
    );

    // Correct the data while we still hold the guard.
    guard.cash_on_hand -= 200;
    guard.is_settled = true;
    guard.transaction_id += 1;

    println!("[Reconciliation] Ledger corrected. Transaction marked failed and closed.");

    // Clone the inner data to return an owned value. The guard drops here and
    // releases the lock.
    guard.clone()
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let ledger = Arc::new(Mutex::new(Ledger::new()));

    // Thread A: the faulty transaction. It mutates one side of the ledger and
    // then panics before marking the transaction settled.
    let ledger_a = Arc::clone(&ledger);
    let handle_a = thread::spawn(move || {
        // SAFETY-free normal code: if the mutex is already poisoned, unwrap()
        // panics; in a controlled demo this is the first lock so it is fine.
        let mut guard = ledger_a.lock().unwrap();

        println!(
            "[Branch A] Transaction {} commenced.",
            guard.transaction_id + 1
        );
        guard.stock_value -= 1_000;
        println!(
            "[Branch A] Stock deducted. New value: {}",
            guard.stock_value
        );
        guard.cash_on_hand += 1_200;
        println!(
            "[Branch A] Cash updated. New balance: {}",
            guard.cash_on_hand
        );

        // Panic while `guard` is still alive -> the Mutex becomes poisoned.
        panic!("[Branch A] Settlement failure: arithmetic overflow in reconciliation.");
    });

    // A panic in a spawned thread does not abort the process unless the panic
    // strategy is set to abort. `join()` returns Err, which is expected here.
    let _ = handle_a.join();

    // Thread B: the forensic audit. It sees Err(PoisonError), inspects the
    // recovered state, and repairs the ledger.
    let ledger_b = Arc::clone(&ledger);
    let handle_b = thread::spawn(move || {
        println!("\n[Audit] Attempting to access the ledger...");

        match ledger_b.lock() {
            Ok(guard) => {
                println!("[Audit] Ledger is not poisoned: {:?}", *guard);
            }
            Err(poisoned) => {
                println!("[Audit] Mutex is poisoned. Recovered state before correction:");
                println!("[Audit] {:?}", *poisoned.get_ref());

                let corrected = recover_ledger(poisoned);
                println!("[Audit] Corrected ledger: {:?}", corrected);
            }
        }
    });

    handle_b.join().unwrap();

    // Important: recovering the data does NOT clear the poison bit on the
    // Mutex itself. Subsequent lock() calls still return Err(PoisonError) so
    // callers can decide whether the repaired state is trustworthy.
    // Uncommenting the next lines would panic:
    //
    // let _guard = ledger.lock().unwrap();

    Ok(())
}

// ============================================================================
// Tests (cargo test --bin mutex_poisoning)
// ============================================================================
#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn ledger_starts_in_expected_state() {
        let ledger = Ledger::new();
        assert_eq!(ledger.cash_on_hand, 10_000);
        assert_eq!(ledger.stock_value, 5_000);
        assert!(!ledger.is_settled);
    }

    #[test]
    fn recovery_repairs_a_poisoned_ledger() {
        let ledger = Arc::new(Mutex::new(Ledger::new()));

        // Poison the mutex from a helper thread, exactly like the demo.
        let ledger_a = Arc::clone(&ledger);
        let handle = thread::spawn(move || {
            let _guard = ledger_a.lock().unwrap();
            panic!("boom");
        });
        let _ = handle.join();

        let lock_result = ledger.lock();
        assert!(lock_result.is_err(), "mutex should be poisoned");

        let recovered = recover_ledger(lock_result.unwrap_err());
        assert!(recovered.is_settled);
        assert_eq!(recovered.transaction_id, 1);
        assert_eq!(recovered.cash_on_hand, 10_000 - 200);
    }
}

In main, Branch A modifies stock and cash and then panics before marking the transaction settled. The panic terminates only Thread A; handle_a.join() returns Err, which main intentionally discards with let _ =.

Thread B subsequently attempts to lock the ledger, matching on the Result to branch into recovery. Calling poisoned.get_ref() inspects the inconsistent state before recover_ledger repairs it.

$ cargo run --bin mutex_poisoning
[Branch A] Transaction 1 commenced.
[Branch A] Stock deducted. New value: 4000
[Branch A] Cash updated. New balance: 11200

thread '<unnamed>' (5795284) panicked at src/bin/mutex_poisoning.rs:109:9:
[Branch A] Settlement failure: arithmetic overflow in reconciliation.
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace

[Audit] Attempting to access the ledger...
[Audit] Mutex is poisoned. Recovered state before correction:
[Audit] Ledger { cash_on_hand: 11200, stock_value: 4000, transaction_id: 0, is_settled: false }
[Reconciliation] Physical audit reveals a cash discrepancy.
[Reconciliation] Digital cash: 11200 | Corrected cash: 11000
[Reconciliation] Ledger corrected. Transaction marked failed and closed.
[Audit] Corrected ledger: Ledger { cash_on_hand: 11000, stock_value: 4000, transaction_id: 1, is_settled: true }

Because panic diagnostics are written to standard error, they may interleave with standard output depending on terminal buffering. The parenthesized identifier is the operating system thread ID and varies across runs.

Extracting the guard via into_inner() does not reset the poison flag; subsequent lock() calls continue returning Err unless the caller explicitly clears the flag with Mutex::clear_poison (introduced in Rust 1.77) after restoring the invariants.

16.7 Deadlock

A deadlock occurs when a set of threads waits cyclically for resources held by one another, preventing any thread in the cycle from making progress. In the canonical two-lock scenario, Thread 1 holds lock A while waiting for lock B, and Thread 2 holds lock B while waiting for lock A; neither thread can release its held lock.

Deadlock analysis models resource dependencies as a directed wait-for graph, where each node represents a thread and a directed edge T0 -> T1 denotes that T0 is blocked waiting on a lock currently held by T1. A deadlock exists if and only if the wait-for graph contains a directed cycle (figure 16.8), which can be detected using the three-state depth-first search from section 12.6.

has_deadlock accepts dependency edges as (waiter, holder) pairs and constructs an adjacency list:

/// Iterative-friendly depth-first search over a small adjacency list.
fn has_deadlock(waits_for: &[(usize, usize)]) -> bool {
    let Some(highest) = waits_for
        .iter()
        .flat_map(|(a, b)| [*a, *b])
        .max()
    else {
        return false;
    };

    let mut edges = vec![Vec::new(); highest + 1];
    for (waiter, holder) in waits_for {
        edges[*waiter].push(*holder);
    }
    // ...
}

A let ... else statement extracts the maximum thread identifier, returning false immediately when the edge slice is empty. The resulting adjacency list stores, for each thread, the list of holders it waits upon.

The cycle detector applies the three-state DFS from section 12.6, encoding node states as 0 (unvisited), 1 (active on the current recursion stack), and 2 (completely explored):

fn has_deadlock(waits_for: &[(usize, usize)]) -> bool {
    // ...
    // 1 = on the current path, 2 = fully explored.
    fn visit(node: usize, edges: &[Vec<usize>], state: &mut [u8]) -> bool {
        match state[node] {
            1 => return true,
            2 => return false,
            _ => state[node] = 1,
        }
        for &next in &edges[node] {
            if visit(next, edges, state) {
                return true;
            }
        }
        state[node] = 2;
        false
    }

    let mut state = vec![0u8; edges.len()];
    (0..edges.len()).any(|node| visit(node, &edges, &mut state))
}

Reaching any node in state 1 indicates a back-edge closing a cycle, causing visit to return true immediately. Nodes in state 2 have already been verified cycle-free and are skipped. Iterating with any across all nodes ensures disconnected cycles are detected even when no outside thread waits on them.

main evaluates three graphs, including the self-loop (0, 0), which models a thread attempting to re-acquire a non-reentrant Mutex it already holds.

Listing 16.18 The complete program. src/bin/concurrency_deadlock.rs

//! Deadlock detection: a deadlock exists exactly when the wait-for graph has a
//! cycle. Each edge `(waiter, holder)` means the first task is blocked on the
//! second.
//!
//! Run with: cargo run --bin concurrency_deadlock

/// Iterative-friendly depth-first search over a small adjacency list.
fn has_deadlock(waits_for: &[(usize, usize)]) -> bool {
    let Some(highest) = waits_for
        .iter()
        .flat_map(|(a, b)| [*a, *b])
        .max()
    else {
        return false;
    };

    let mut edges = vec![Vec::new(); highest + 1];
    for (waiter, holder) in waits_for {
        edges[*waiter].push(*holder);
    }

    // 1 = on the current path, 2 = fully explored.
    fn visit(node: usize, edges: &[Vec<usize>], state: &mut [u8]) -> bool {
        match state[node] {
            1 => return true,
            2 => return false,
            _ => state[node] = 1,
        }
        for &next in &edges[node] {
            if visit(next, edges, state) {
                return true;
            }
        }
        state[node] = 2;
        false
    }

    let mut state = vec![0u8; edges.len()];
    (0..edges.len()).any(|node| visit(node, &edges, &mut state))
}

fn main() {
    let acyclic = [(0, 1), (1, 2), (0, 2)];
    let cycle = [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 0)];
    let self_wait = [(0, 0)];

    for (label, graph) in [
        ("0->1, 1->2, 0->2", &acyclic[..]),
        ("0->1, 1->2, 2->0", &cycle[..]),
        ("0->0", &self_wait[..]),
    ] {
        println!("{label:<20} deadlock: {}", has_deadlock(graph));
    }

    // The four Coffman conditions must all hold for a deadlock; removing any one
    // of them prevents it.
    println!("\nCoffman conditions:");
    for condition in [
        "mutual exclusion",
        "hold and wait",
        "no preemption",
        "circular wait",
    ] {
        println!("  - {condition}");
    }

    assert!(!has_deadlock(&acyclic));
    assert!(has_deadlock(&cycle));
    assert!(has_deadlock(&self_wait));
    assert!(!has_deadlock(&[]));

    println!("\nall checks passed");
}
$ cargo run --bin concurrency_deadlock
0->1, 1->2, 0->2     deadlock: false
0->1, 1->2, 2->0     deadlock: true
0->0                 deadlock: true

Coffman conditions:
  - mutual exclusion
  - hold and wait
  - no preemption
  - circular wait

all checks passed

Deadlock requires all four Coffman conditions to hold simultaneously:

  1. Mutual exclusion: each lock can be held by at most one thread at a time.
  2. Hold and wait: a thread retains at least one lock while blocking to acquire another.
  3. No preemption: a held lock cannot be forcibly reclaimed from its owner.
  4. Circular wait: a closed chain of threads exists in which each waits for a lock held by the next.

Breaking any single condition eliminates deadlock. In practice, systems prevent deadlock most reliably by breaking circular wait: establishing a strict global lock ordering and requiring every thread to acquire locks in that order. When every thread acquires lock A before lock B, no thread can hold B while requesting A, making cycles impossible.

Summary

  • thread::spawn requires 'static closures that own their captured data, whereas thread::scope permits borrowing local stack data by joining all spawned threads before returning.
  • Collect join handles before calling join, because chaining .map(spawn).map(join) on a lazy iterator executes threads sequentially.
  • Send and Sync are auto traits that enforce thread safety at compile time; Rc and RefCell lack the required bounds, preventing unsynchronized sharing across threads.
  • Atomic operations perform read-modify-write transitions indivisibly. Relaxed suffices for independent counters, whereas Release and Acquire synchronize surrounding memory writes between threads.
  • Parallel summation of a billion i32 elements scaled by 3 to 4x on eight hardware threads, bounded by memory bandwidth and four physical cores. Amdahl’s law caps speedup at 1 / s for a serial fraction s.
  • A spin lock combines an atomic flag, a compare-exchange acquisition loop, and an RAII guard that releases on drop; its unsafe impl Sync relies on upholding mutual exclusion invariants.
  • A counting semaphore built from a Mutex and Condvar checks its predicate inside a while loop to handle contention and spurious wakeups.
  • Panicking while holding a MutexGuard poisons the mutex; recovery code can inspect and repair the state through PoisonError::into_inner.
  • Threads deadlock if and only if their wait-for graph contains a cycle; enforcing a global lock acquisition order eliminates circular wait.

Exercises

  1. Write a version of parallel_sum from listing 16.1 as a single lazy chain, .map(spawn).map(join).sum(), and time both on a large slice. Explain the difference.
  2. Make the three pairs of functions in parallel_sum.rs one generic function over T: Sum<T> + Copy + Send + Sync. Which extra bound does sum::<T>() over &T items need?
  3. Close the gap in SpinGuard. Add a field _marker: PhantomData<&'a mut T>, and explain why this makes the guard Sync only when T: Sync.
  4. Rewrite try_acquire_timeout to loop until a permit is free or the whole timeout has passed. Use Instant::now() to compute the time left for each wait.
  5. Write a program that deadlocks with two Mutex values and two threads. Then fix it by taking the locks in a fixed order.

Queues and bounded buffers

This chapter covers

  • Passing work between threads through a shared queue
  • Putting a waiting thread to sleep with a Condvar, and waking it again
  • A bounded buffer, where producers wait when the queue is full
  • Three ways to handle a poisoned lock inside a queue
  • Closing a queue so that every waiting thread wakes up and every loop ends
  • A ring buffer for one producer and one consumer, with no lock at all

Many concurrent systems decouple work generation from work execution across distinct thread roles: producer threads emit tasks (accepting network connections, parsing input streams, or receiving messages), while consumer threads process those tasks asynchronously. Because production and consumption rates fluctuate independently, the two cohorts require a synchronized intermediary to buffer in-flight work.

That intermediary is a queue, where producers enqueue elements at the tail and consumers dequeue them from the head. Elements emerge in strict arrival order, a scheduling discipline known as FIFO (first in, first out).

The sections below construct six progressive queue designs. Each iteration resolves a concrete synchronization, liveness, or memory-safety limitation of its predecessor, culminating in a lock-free single-producer, single-consumer ring buffer.

17.1 Why a queue needs a limit

When producers enqueue items faster than consumers can drain them, an unbounded queue grows continuously until the process exhausts available memory and is terminated by the operating system (figure 17.1).

A bounded queue enforces a fixed capacity. When the queue reaches capacity, push blocks until a consumer removes an item, throttling the producer to match the consumer’s throughput. Propagating congestion upstream to slow the source of work is known as backpressure, trading temporary latency for memory stability.

A bounded queue with blocking push and pop operations is commonly referred to as a bounded buffer.

17.2 A shared queue

The initial design is an unbounded queue that establishes the two core primitives used across the mutex-based implementations: a VecDeque guarded by a Mutex and a Condvar for blocking waits.

The standard library’s VecDeque provides O(1) amortized insertion at the back and removal from the front, while a Mutex serializes concurrent access across threads.

When a consumer finds the queue empty, it blocks on the Condvar. Following the condition-variable protocol from section 16.5, waiting atomically releases the mutex and suspends the thread; when a producer invokes notify_one, one sleeping consumer wakes with the mutex re-acquired.

Listing 17.1 The queue (lines 7 to 29). src/bin/thread_safe_queue.rs

use std::{
    collections::VecDeque,
    sync::{Arc, Condvar, Mutex},
    thread,
};

#[derive(Default)]
struct SyncQueue {
    items: Mutex<VecDeque<i32>>,
    not_empty: Condvar,
}

impl SyncQueue {
    fn push(&self, item: i32) {
        if let Ok(mut q) = self.items.lock() {
            q.push_back(item);
            self.not_empty.notify_one();
        }
    }

    fn pop(&self) -> Option<i32> {
        let q = self.items.lock().ok()?;
        let mut q = self
            .not_empty
            .wait_while(q, |q| q.is_empty())
            .ok()?;
        q.pop_front()
    }
}

In push, the producer locks the mutex, appends the item, and wakes one waiting consumer. Because if let Ok(mut q) ignores a poisoned lock, an item passed to a poisoned queue is dropped without notifying the caller; section 17.4 replaces this behavior with explicit error handling.

In pop, wait_while pairs the mutex guard with a predicate closure and sleeps for as long as the predicate holds:

let mut q = self.not_empty.wait_while(q, |q| q.is_empty()).ok()?;

wait_while encapsulates the manual while loop from section 16.5, re-evaluating q.is_empty() after every wakeup and returning the guard once an item is available. The trailing .ok()? maps a poisoned mutex to None.

Animation 17.1 traces an item moving from a producer to a consumer blocked in wait_while, then demonstrates the hang that occurs when notify_one is omitted.

Listing 17.2 main (lines 31 to 56). src/bin/thread_safe_queue.rs

fn main() {
    let q = Arc::new(SyncQueue::default());

    // producer
    let producer = {
        let q = Arc::clone(&q);
        thread::spawn(move || {
            for i in 0..5 {
                q.push(i);
                println!("Producer pushed {i}");
            }
        })
    };

    let consumer = {
        let q = Arc::clone(&q);
        thread::spawn(move || {
            for _ in 0..5 {
                println!("Cosnumer popped: {:?}", q.pop());
            }
        })
    };

    producer.join().unwrap();
    consumer.join().unwrap();
}

In main, the queue is shared via Arc. Each thread is spawned inside a short block that clones the Arc under the same local name:

let producer = {
    let q = Arc::clone(&q);
    thread::spawn(move || { ... })
};

Shadowing q inside the block keeps the identifier concise while leaving the outer Arc intact for subsequent threads.

$ cargo run --bin thread_safe_queue
Producer pushed 0
Producer pushed 1
Producer pushed 2
Producer pushed 3
Producer pushed 4
Cosnumer popped: Some(0)
Cosnumer popped: Some(1)
Cosnumer popped: Some(2)
Cosnumer popped: Some(3)
Cosnumer popped: Some(4)

In this execution, the producer completed before the consumer was scheduled; on other runs the output lines interleave. Regardless of scheduling, the consumer always receives values in strict FIFO order from 0 through 4.

17.3 A bounded buffer

Introducing a fixed capacity creates a second blocking condition: producers must wait whenever the queue is full. To distinguish the two waiter populations, the bounded buffer maintains two condition variables sharing a single mutex (figure 17.2):

  • not_empty: waited on by consumers when the queue is empty, and notified by producers after an insertion.
  • not_full: waited on by producers when the queue is full, and notified by consumers after a removal.

Using a single condition variable with notify_one can deadlock the queue: a producer waking another producer instead of a consumer leaves the woken producer blocked on a full buffer while runnable consumers remain asleep. Calling notify_all on one condition variable avoids deadlock at the cost of waking every waiting thread on every operation. Separate condition variables route each signal directly to a thread that can make progress.

Listing 17.3 The type and new (lines 19 to 38). src/bin/bounded_buffer.rs

use std::{
    collections::VecDeque,
    sync::{Arc, Condvar, Mutex},
    thread,
    time::Duration,
};

struct BoundedQueue<T> {
    inner: Mutex<VecDeque<T>>,
    capacity: usize,
    not_empty: Condvar,
    not_full: Condvar,
}

impl<T> BoundedQueue<T> {
    fn new(capacity: usize) -> Self {
        // Capacity 0 makes no sense: no producer could ever push,
        // and every pop would block forever.
        assert!(capacity > 0, "capacity must be > 0");

        Self {
            inner: Mutex::new(VecDeque::with_capacity(capacity)),
            capacity,
            not_empty: Condvar::new(),
            not_full: Condvar::new(),
        }
    }
    // ...
}

Pre-allocating with VecDeque::with_capacity(capacity) reserves the full buffer up front so that push operations never trigger heap reallocation. A zero capacity is rejected immediately, as no item could ever be enqueued.

Listing 17.4 push (lines 42 to 76).

impl<T> BoundedQueue<T> {
    // ...
    fn push(&self, item: T) {
        // Acquire the shelf lock. `guard` is our exclusive handle to the deque.
        let mut guard = self.inner.lock().unwrap();

        // Wait while the shelf is full.
        //
        // Why `while` and not `if`:
        //   1. Condvars are allowed to wake up for no reason (spurious wakeup).
        //   2. Even on a real wakeup, another producer may have raced us and
        //      taken the free slot before we reacquired the lock.
        // So we must re-check the condition every time we wake.
        //
        // Why `guard = ...wait(guard)`:
        //   `wait` consumes the guard (it releases the lock on our behalf),
        //   puts us to sleep, then re-locks and hands us a NEW guard.
        //   The reassignment just means "here's my fresh key to the shelf."
        //   The VecDeque inside is the same one — we're not replacing the queue.
        while guard.len() == self.capacity {
            guard = self.not_full.wait(guard).unwrap();
        }

        // We have room. Add the item to the back of the deque.
        guard.push_back(item);

        // Release the lock BEFORE ringing the bell.
        // This is an optimization, not a correctness requirement.
        // If we notify while still holding the lock, the thread we wake will
        // immediately block on `lock()` until we release it — a wasted wakeup.
        drop(guard);

        // Ring the "not empty" bell: one consumer can now make progress.
        // `notify_one` (not `notify_all`) because exactly ONE item was added,
        // so only ONE consumer can succeed. Waking all of them = stampede.
        self.not_empty.notify_one();
    }
    // ...
}

The inline comments in push document each invariant, and figure 17.3 traces the exact sequence of lock handoffs when a producer blocks on a full queue.

In guard = self.not_full.wait(guard).unwrap();, wait consumes guard by value to release the mutex before sleeping, then re-acquires the mutex on wakeup and returns a fresh guard, which is assigned back to the same binding.

After pushing the item, drop(guard) releases the mutex before notify_one() is called. Notifying while still holding the lock remains correct, yet it can cause the signaled consumer to resume, immediately contend on the still-held mutex, and re-block. Dropping the guard first avoids that redundant context switch.

Listing 17.5 pop (lines 78 to 102).

impl<T> BoundedQueue<T> {
    // ...
    fn pop(&self) -> T {
        // Acquire the shelf lock.
        let mut guard = self.inner.lock().unwrap();

        // Wait while the shelf is empty.
        // Same `while` reasoning as push: spurious wakeups + races with other
        // consumers who may have grabbed the item before we reacquired the lock.
        while guard.is_empty() {
            guard = self.not_empty.wait(guard).unwrap();
        }

        // Safe to unwrap: the `while` loop guarantees the deque is non-empty,
        // and we hold the lock so nobody can change that between the check
        // and this line.
        let item = guard.pop_front().unwrap();

        // Release before notifying (same optimization as in push).
        drop(guard);

        // Ring the "not full" bell: one producer can now make progress.
        // Exactly one slot opened, so wake exactly one producer.
        self.not_full.notify_one();

        item
    }
}

pop mirrors push: it waits on not_empty while the deque is empty, removes the front element, releases the mutex, and signals not_full. The unwrap() on pop_front() is guaranteed to succeed because the while loop exited only after verifying the deque was non-empty while holding the mutex continuously.

Listing 17.6 main (lines 105 to 150). src/bin/bounded_buffer.rs

fn main() {
    // Small capacity (3) so that with two slow consumers you can actually
    // SEE producers block: the queue fills up and push() sleeps in `not_full`.
    let queue = Arc::new(BoundedQueue::new(3));

    let mut handles = vec![];

    // ---- Producers ----
    // Two producers, each pushes 5 items. `Arc::clone` bumps the refcount so
    // each thread shares the same queue; ownership of the clone moves in.
    for p in 0..2 {
        let q = Arc::clone(&queue);
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            for i in 0..5 {
                let item = format!("p{}:item{}", p, i);
                println!("  [producer {}] pushing {}", p, item);
                q.push(item);
                // Slow down so we don't blast through the whole buffer instantly.
                thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(30));
            }
        }));
    }

    // ---- Consumers ----
    // Two consumers, each pops 5 items. Consumers are SLOWER than producers
    // here (60ms vs 30ms), so the queue fills up and you'll see producers
    // stall on `not_full.wait(...)`.
    for c in 0..2 {
        let q = Arc::clone(&queue);
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            for _ in 0..5 {
                let item = q.pop();
                println!("[consumer {}] got {}", c, item);
                thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(60));
            }
        }));
    }

    // Join everything. If our synchronization is wrong, this is where you'd
    // hang (a thread sleeping forever) or panic (unwrap on empty / on a
    // poisoned mutex after another thread panicked while holding it).
    for h in handles {
        h.join().unwrap();
    }
    println!("done");
}

In main, two producers and two consumers share a buffer of capacity 3. Producers sleep 30 ms between items while consumers sleep 60 ms, ensuring that producers outpace consumers and exercise backpressure.

[consumer 0] got p1:item0

  [producer 1] pushing p1:item1
  [producer 0] pushing p0:item2
  [producer 1] pushing p1:item2
[consumer 1] got p0:item1
[consumer 0] got p1:item1
  [producer 0] pushing p0:item3
  [producer 1] pushing p1:item3
[consumer 1] got p0:item2
[consumer 0] got p1:item2

Interleaving varies across runs, while items from any individual producer preserve their relative order. Because the diagnostic line is printed prior to calling push, the log does not display blocking durations directly; Exercise 1 adds wait-time instrumentation.

17.4 When the lock is poisoned

Because bounded_buffer.rs calls .unwrap() on every lock() and wait(), a panic by any thread holding the mutex poisons the lock (as seen in section 16.6) and cascades panics to every other thread using the queue. The next two implementations propagate poisoning as structured errors instead (figure 17.4).

17.4.1 A custom error type

Listing 17.7 The error and an extension trait (lines 9 to 31). src/bin/bounded_buffer_with_error_handling.rs

use std::{
    collections::VecDeque,
    fmt,
    sync::{Arc, Condvar, Mutex, PoisonError},
    thread,
    time::Duration,
};

#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct QueuePoisonedError;

impl fmt::Display for QueuePoisonedError {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        write!(
            f,
            "The queue's internal mutex was poisoned by a panicking thread"
        )
    }
}

impl std::error::Error for QueuePoisonedError {}

trait PoisonMap<T> {
    fn map_poison(self) -> Result<T, QueuePoisonedError>;
}

impl<T> PoisonMap<T> for Result<T, PoisonError<T>> {
    fn map_poison(self) -> Result<T, QueuePoisonedError> {
        self.map_err(|_| QueuePoisonedError)
    }
}

QueuePoisonedError is a zero-sized unit struct implementing Display and std::error::Error, enabling composition with ? and Box<dyn Error>.

PoisonMap is an extension trait: a locally defined trait implemented for a foreign type (here, the standard library’s Result<T, PoisonError<T>>). Implementing PoisonMap<T> attaches a map_poison method directly to lock and wait results, converting PoisonError<T> into QueuePoisonedError without repetitive map_err closures.

Listing 17.8 push and pop (lines 51 to 74).

impl<T> BoundedQueue<T> {
    // ...
    fn push(&self, item: T) -> Result<(), QueuePoisonedError> {
        let mut guard = self.inner.lock().map_poison()?;
        while guard.len() == self.capacity {
            guard = self.not_full.wait(guard).map_poison()?;
        }
        guard.push_back(item);
        drop(guard);
        self.not_empty.notify_one();
        Ok(())
    }

    fn pop(&self) -> Result<T, QueuePoisonedError> {
        let mut guard = self.inner.lock().map_poison()?;
        while guard.is_empty() {
            guard = self
                .not_empty
                .wait(guard)
                .map_poison()?;
        }
        let item = guard.pop_front().unwrap();
        drop(guard);
        self.not_full.notify_one();
        Ok(item)
    }
}

Appending .map_poison()? to each lock() and wait() preserves the exact control flow of listing 17.4 while changing both methods to return Result.

The complete source appears in listing 17.19 at the end of the chapter.

In main, worker threads log errors with dbg! and exit their loops via break rather than unwinding.

The second unit test intentionally poisons the queue by spawning a thread that acquires the private inner mutex (accessible to tests within the same module) and panics before releasing it. Both push and pop must subsequently return Err(QueuePoisonedError).

$ cargo test --bin bounded_buffer_with_error_handling
running 2 tests
test tests::test_zero_capacity_panics - should panic ... ok

test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out

17.4.2 A boxed error

The third implementation erases the error type behind a trait object:

use std::{
    collections::VecDeque,
    error::Error,
    sync::{Arc, Condvar, Mutex},
    thread,
    time::Duration,
};

type RuntimeError = Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>;

Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync> accommodates any error implementing Error. The Send + Sync bounds are required because each worker thread returns its Result across a thread boundary to main via join().

Listing 17.9 push (lines 29 to 46). src/bin/bounded_buffer_error_propagation.rs

impl<T> BoundedQueue<T> {
    // ...
    fn push(&self, item: T) -> Result<(), RuntimeError> {
        let mut guard = self
            .inner
            .lock()
            .map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;

        while guard.len() == self.capacity {
            guard = self
                .not_full
                .wait(guard)
                .map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
        }

        guard.push_back(item);
        drop(guard);
        self.not_empty.notify_one();
        Ok(())
    }
    // ...
}

Applying ? directly to PoisonError fails to compile because PoisonError<MutexGuard<'_, T>> borrows the mutex, whereas Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync> implicitly requires 'static. Calling .map_err(|e| e.to_string())? converts the borrowed error into an owned String, which the standard library’s From<String> implementation then boxes into the trait object.

Listing 17.10 main (lines 72 to 111). src/bin/bounded_buffer_error_propagation.rs

fn main() -> Result<(), RuntimeError> {
    let queue = Arc::new(BoundedQueue::new(3));

    let producers = (0..2).map(|p| {
        let q = Arc::clone(&queue);
        thread::spawn(move || -> Result<(), RuntimeError> {
            for i in 0..5 {
                let item = format!("p{}:item{}", p, i);
                println!("  [producer {}] pushing {}", p, item);
                q.push(item)?;
                thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(30));
            }
            Ok(())
        })
    });

    let consumers = (0..2).map(|c| {
        let q = Arc::clone(&queue);
        thread::spawn(move || -> Result<(), RuntimeError> {
            for _ in 0..5 {
                let item = q.pop()?;
                println!("[consumer {}] got {}", c, item);
                thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(60));
            }
            Ok(())
        })
    });

    let handles: Vec<_> = producers.chain(consumers).collect();

    for h in handles {
        match h.join() {
            Ok(r) => println!("Thread joined : {:#?}", r),
            Err(e) => eprintln!("Error occured : {:#?}", e),
        }
    }

    println!("done");
    Ok(())
}

In main, producers and consumers are lazy iterator adapters; no threads start until producers.chain(consumers).collect() materializes all four JoinHandles into a Vec, after which the loop joins them.

Annotating each thread closure as move || -> Result<(), RuntimeError> supplies the target error type needed by ? inside the body. Consequently, handle.join() yields Ok(r) where r is itself the thread’s Result.

17.5 Many producers and consumers with wait_while

The fourth implementation streamlines the bounded buffer by delegating both condition loops to wait_while and replaces Arc with scoped threads in main.

The struct layout matches section 17.3: a VecDeque behind a Mutex, a fixed capacity, and two condition variables (not_empty and not_full):

use std::{
    collections::VecDeque,
    sync::{Condvar, Mutex},
    thread,
};

pub struct BoundedBuffer<T> {
    queue: Mutex<VecDeque<T>>,
    capacity: usize,
    not_empty: Condvar,
    not_full: Condvar,
}

impl<T> BoundedBuffer<T> {
    pub fn new(capacity: usize) -> Self {
        assert!(capacity > 0, "capacity must be > 0");

        Self {
            queue: Mutex::new(VecDeque::with_capacity(capacity)),
            capacity,
            not_empty: Condvar::new(),
            not_full: Condvar::new(),
        }
    }
    // ...
}

In push, wait_while accepts the guard and a predicate closure, suspending the thread while the predicate evaluates to true and re-checking it after every wakeup. This provides the same protection against spurious wakeups and racing producers as the explicit while loop in section 17.3:

impl<T> BoundedBuffer<T> {
    // ...
    /// Blocks while the buffer is full.
    pub fn push(&self, item: T) {
        let cap = self.capacity;

        let mut queue = self.queue.lock().unwrap();
        queue = self
            .not_full
            .wait_while(queue, |q| q.len() >= cap)
            .unwrap();

        queue.push_back(item);
        drop(queue);

        self.not_empty.notify_one();
    }
    // ...
}

Copying self.capacity into a local cap before constructing |q| q.len() >= cap avoids borrowing self inside the closure. Calling drop(queue) before notify_one() releases the mutex before waking a consumer, avoiding immediate lock contention.

pop follows the symmetric sequence: waiting while empty, popping the front element, releasing the lock, and notifying not_full:

impl<T> BoundedBuffer<T> {
    // ...
    /// Blocks while the buffer is empty.
    pub fn pop(&self) -> T {
        let mut queue = self.queue.lock().unwrap();
        queue = self
            .not_empty
            .wait_while(queue, |q| q.is_empty())
            .unwrap();

        let item = queue.pop_front().unwrap();
        self.not_full.notify_one();
        item
    }
}

MPMC denotes multiple producers and multiple consumers. In main, four producers enqueue 10 items each while two consumers dequeue 20 items each:

fn main() {
    let buffer = BoundedBuffer::<(usize, usize)>::new(8);
    let buffer = &buffer;

    const PRODUCERS: usize = 4;
    const CONSUMERS: usize = 2;
    const PER_PRODUCER: usize = 10;
    const PER_CONSUMER: usize = PRODUCERS * PER_PRODUCER / CONSUMERS;

    thread::scope(|s| {
        for p in 0..PRODUCERS {
            s.spawn(move || {
                for i in 0..PER_PRODUCER {
                    buffer.push((p, i));
                }
            });
        }

        for c in 0..CONSUMERS {
            s.spawn(move || {
                for _ in 0..PER_CONSUMER {
                    let item = buffer.pop();
                    println!("consumer {c}: {item:?}");
                }
            });
        }
    });
}

Deriving PER_CONSUMER from the producer constants guarantees that total items popped equal total items pushed, allowing every thread to terminate cleanly.

The complete program is included in listing 17.21 at the end of the chapter.

Rebinding let buffer = &buffer; turns the local variable into a shared reference so that each move closure copies only the reference into its scoped thread, while thread::scope ensures buffer outlives all workers.

$ cargo run --bin mpmc_bounded_buffer

consumer 1: (2, 0)
consumer 0: (1, 0)
consumer 0: (3, 2)
consumer 0: (3, 3)
...
consumer 0: (3, 8)
consumer 0: (0, 9)
consumer 0: (2, 9)

The complete output comprises 40 (producer, index) pairs. Items originating from any single producer appear in monotonically increasing index order across the combined stream, while items from different producers interleave according to OS thread scheduling.

17.6 Closing a queue

Every implementation thus far lacks a termination protocol. The examples rely on hardcoded item counts, whereas production consumers rarely know the total volume of work in advance; without a shutdown signal, a consumer calling pop in a loop blocks indefinitely once all producers exit.

The library implementation in bounded_queue.rs resolves this by adding an explicit close operation (figure 17.5).

Listing 17.11 The state (lines 16 to 27). src/problems/bounded_queue.rs

use std::{
    collections::VecDeque,
    sync::{Condvar, Mutex},
};

struct State<T> {
    items: VecDeque<T>,
    capacity: usize,
    closed: bool,
}

/// A bounded MPMC queue. Share it behind `Arc`; all methods take `&self`.
pub struct BoundedQueue<T> {
    state: Mutex<State<T>>,
    not_empty: Condvar,
    not_full: Condvar,
}

The mutex now guards a dedicated State<T> struct combining the deque, capacity, and closed boolean. Keeping closed under the same mutex ensures that threads inspect the flag and queue length atomically, preventing lost wakeups during shutdown.

Listing 17.12 push and pop (lines 47 to 94).

impl<T> BoundedQueue<T> {
    // ...
    /// Push an item, blocking while the queue is full.
    ///
    /// Returns `Err(item)` if the queue is closed, so the caller keeps ownership
    /// instead of losing the value.
    pub fn push(&self, item: T) -> Result<(), T> {
        let mut state = self
            .state
            .lock()
            .expect("queue mutex poisoned");
        loop {
            if state.closed {
                return Err(item);
            }
            if state.items.len() < state.capacity {
                state.items.push_back(item);
                self.not_empty.notify_one();
                return Ok(());
            }
            state = self
                .not_full
                .wait(state)
                .expect("queue mutex poisoned");
        }
    }

    /// Pop an item, blocking while the queue is empty.
    ///
    /// Returns `None` once the queue is closed and drained, which is how a
    /// consumer loop terminates cleanly.
    pub fn pop(&self) -> Option<T> {
        let mut state = self
            .state
            .lock()
            .expect("queue mutex poisoned");
        loop {
            if let Some(item) = state.items.pop_front() {
                self.not_full.notify_one();
                return Some(item);
            }
            if state.closed {
                return None;
            }
            state = self
                .not_empty
                .wait(state)
                .expect("queue mutex poisoned");
        }
    }
    // ...
}

Both operations use an explicit loop that re-evaluates both the buffer state and the closed flag after every wakeup.

push returns Result<(), T>: if the queue is closed, it returns Err(item), transferring ownership back to the caller rather than discarding the value.

pop returns Option<T> and checks for queued items before inspecting closed. Draining buffered items before signaling closure ensures no already-enqueued work is abandoned; pop returns None only when the queue is both closed and empty, allowing consumers to terminate cleanly with while let Some(item) = queue.pop().

Listing 17.13 close (lines 109 to 122).

impl<T> BoundedQueue<T> {
    // ...
    /// Close the queue.
    ///
    /// Pending and future `pop` calls return `None` after the queue drains, and
    /// future `push` calls fail. Idempotent.
    pub fn close(&self) {
        let mut state = self
            .state
            .lock()
            .expect("queue mutex poisoned");
        state.closed = true;
        drop(state);
        self.not_empty.notify_all();
        self.not_full.notify_all();
    }
    // ...
}

close sets closed = true under the lock and invokes notify_all() on both not_empty and not_full, waking every blocked producer and consumer so they can observe the new state and return. Repeating close leaves the state unchanged, making the operation idempotent.

Animation 17.3 illustrates closing a full queue while a producer is blocked in push, followed by the hang caused when close omits notify_all.

The complete implementation and test suite appear in listing 17.22 at the end of the chapter.

The four unit tests verify the core contract:

  • preserves_order_across_threads enqueues 0 through 999 on one thread and verifies strict FIFO delivery and clean loop termination on another after close.
  • never_exceeds_capacity tracks the peak observed queue length against a slow consumer and asserts it never exceeds 4.
  • close_wakes_a_blocked_consumer blocks a consumer on an empty queue for 20 ms, calls close, and confirms pop returns None rather than hanging.
  • push_after_close_returns_the_item verifies that rejected items are returned intact inside Err.

17.7 A ring buffer without a lock

All previous queues acquire a mutex on every operation. When concurrency is restricted to exactly one producer thread and one consumer thread, an SPSC (single producer, single consumer) topology, the mutex can be eliminated entirely in favor of atomic indices.

17.7.1 The idea

A ring buffer maps a fixed-size array of N slots onto a circular index space (figure 17.6), tracked by two monotonically increasing counters:

  • head counts the total items removed; the consumer reads from slot head % N.
  • tail counts the total items inserted; the producer writes to slot tail % N.

The current occupancy is tail - head: the ring is empty when tail == head and full when tail - head == N.

Mutual exclusion is unnecessary because each counter has a single writer: only the producer mutates tail, and only the consumer mutates head, while each side performs read-only loads of the opposing counter.

Memory visibility relies on the Release/Acquire synchronization pattern from section 16.4. The producer writes the payload into its target slot before publishing the incremented tail with Release. The consumer loads tail with Acquire before reading the slot, guaranteeing that observing the updated tail makes the slot’s payload visible.

17.7.2 The type

Listing 17.14 The ring (lines 25 to 38). src/problems/ring_buffer.rs

use std::{
    cell::UnsafeCell,
    mem::MaybeUninit,
    sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering},
};

/// Ring buffer with capacity `N` (the maximum number of queued items).
pub struct SpscRing<T, const N: usize> {
    slots: [UnsafeCell<MaybeUninit<T>>; N],
    /// Next index to read. Written only by the consumer.
    head: AtomicUsize,
    /// Next index to write. Written only by the producer.
    tail: AtomicUsize,
}

// SAFETY: at most one thread mutates `head` and one mutates `tail`. A slot is
// initialized before `tail` is published with a release store, and the consumer
// performs an acquire load of `tail` before reading that slot, so there is no
// data race and no read of uninitialized memory under the SPSC discipline.
unsafe impl<T: Send, const N: usize> Sync for SpscRing<T, N> {}

The definition introduces three low-level Rust features:

  • const N: usize is a const generic parameter specifying the fixed array capacity at compile time, as in SpscRing<u64, 256>.
  • MaybeUninit<T> represents storage that may be uninitialized. Because empty ring slots hold no valid T and Rust forbids uninitialized values of type T, MaybeUninit makes the initialization state explicit; reading the value requires unsafe to assert that the slot is populated.
  • UnsafeCell permits mutating individual slots through &self, as in the spin lock of section 16.4.

The constructor initializes the fixed array with std::array::from_fn, invoking the closure once per slot index.

17.7.3 Push and pop

Listing 17.15 push and pop (lines 71 to 107).

impl<T, const N: usize> SpscRing<T, N> {
    // ...
    /// Enqueue a value, returning `Err(value)` when the ring is full.
    pub fn push(&self, value: T) -> Result<(), T> {
        let tail = self.tail.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
        let head = self.head.load(Ordering::Acquire);
        if tail.wrapping_sub(head) >= N {
            return Err(value);
        }

        let index = tail % N;
        // SAFETY: the slot at `index` is free because the ring is not full, and
        // only the producer writes it.
        unsafe { (*self.slots[index].get()).write(value) };

        // Publish the slot to the consumer.
        self.tail
            .store(tail.wrapping_add(1), Ordering::Release);
        Ok(())
    }

    /// Dequeue a value, or `None` when the ring is empty.
    pub fn pop(&self) -> Option<T> {
        let head = self.head.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
        let tail = self.tail.load(Ordering::Acquire);
        if head == tail {
            return None;
        }

        let index = head % N;
        // SAFETY: `head != tail`, so the producer has published this slot and
        // only the consumer reads it.
        let value = unsafe { (*self.slots[index].get()).assume_init_read() };

        // Publish the freed slot to the producer.
        self.head
            .store(head.wrapping_add(1), Ordering::Release);
        Some(value)
    }
}

In push, the producer loads its own tail with Relaxed (since no other thread modifies tail) and loads head with Acquire. That Acquire load synchronizes with the consumer’s Release store of head, ensuring the consumer has finished reading a recycled slot before the producer overwrites it.

When the ring is full, push returns Err(value) to preserve ownership. Otherwise, it writes the element via MaybeUninit::write and publishes the slot by storing tail.wrapping_add(1) with Release.

pop performs the symmetric sequence: loading tail with Acquire, moving the value out via assume_init_read, and publishing the freed slot by storing head.wrapping_add(1) with Release.

Using wrapping_add and wrapping_sub ensures that tail.wrapping_sub(head) remains exact even if the 64-bit counters wrap around zero after 2⁶⁴ operations.

Animation 17.4 traces an 8-slot ring as counters wrap past capacity and fill the buffer, then illustrates the data corruption that occurs when tail is published before writing the slot.

Listing 17.16 Drop (lines 116 to 121).

impl<T, const N: usize> Drop for SpscRing<T, N> {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        // Drop any items that were never popped.
        while self.pop().is_some() {}
    }
}

Because MaybeUninit<T> does not track initialization, it never runs destructors automatically. Implementing Drop for SpscRing drains all remaining initialized elements via pop(), allowing each returned T to drop normally. The dropped_ring_drops_queued_items test verifies that every queued element’s destructor executes.

WARNING: The soundness of SpscRing relies on an unchecked caller invariant: at most one thread may invoke push, and at most one thread may invoke pop. Because both methods accept &self and SpscRing implements Sync, safe code can share one instance across two producers and race on the same slot, causing undefined behavior. A sound public API splits the ring into non-clonable Producer and Consumer handles taking &mut self, enforcing the SPSC contract at compile time (Exercise 5).

The complete implementation and tests appear in listing 17.23 at the end of the chapter.

The concurrency test transfers 50,000 sequential integers across a 256-slot ring, calling thread::yield_now() whenever the producer encounters a full ring or the consumer encounters an empty ring. A sentinel value (u64::MAX) signals completion, and the consumer verifies that every integer arrives in exact order.
