22.7.3 The two clients side by side

The two implementations exhibit complementary failure-handling gaps: the asynchronous client inspects HTTP status codes yet propagates transport errors from send().await? immediately without retrying, whereas the blocking client retries transport errors yet ignores HTTP status codes. A complete client unifies both paths under a Retryable classification covering transient transport faults alongside 429 and 5xx responses.

Neither client applies full jitter or honors server Retry-After headers; both mechanisms are already formulated in the retry policy of Section 19.2.

22.7.4 Where the merged client belongs

The repository includes an empty rust-async-http-examples crate reserved for a unified client library. Extracting the asynchronous client from Section 22.7.2 into lib.rs with public retry and cache abstractions enables deterministic integration tests against the local HTTP server from Chapter 21 rather than an external echo service.

22.8 Questions that come up

“What happens when a future returns Pending?” The future guarantees that it has registered cx.waker() to be invoked once forward progress becomes possible. The executor suspends polling that task and schedules other runnable tasks; when the waker fires, the executor re-enqueues and polls the task again.

“Why does poll take Pin<&mut Self>?” A compiler-generated async state machine can store internal references pointing to its own fields across .await points. Pinning guarantees that the future remains at a fixed memory address from its first poll until Drop, keeping every self-reference valid.

“Why must spawned futures be Send in Tokio?” A multi-threaded work-stealing executor may resume a suspended task on a different worker thread after any .await point. Every value held live across a suspension point must therefore implement Send.

“Can blocking code be called inside an async task?” Only for negligible durations. A blocking system call stalls the underlying worker thread and starves every other task multiplexed onto that thread. Blocking CPU or I/O work must be offloaded via tokio::task::spawn_blocking, while network and timer waits use asynchronous primitives.

“Is a std::sync::Mutex allowed in async code?” Yes, provided the MutexGuard is dropped before any .await point. Holding a synchronous mutex guard across a suspension point can block the executor thread or induce deadlock; locks held across .await boundaries require an async-aware lock such as tokio::sync::Mutex.

Summary

  • The Future trait defines a single cooperative polling method, poll: Poll::Ready completes the task, whereas Poll::Pending obligates the future to arrange a Waker notification when progress becomes possible.
  • An executor re-polls tasks upon wake notifications without busy-spinning. Spurious wakeups are benign, whereas a dropped or uninvoked waker breaks liveness without raising an error.
  • block_on implements a minimal single-future executor: pin the future, construct a thread-unparking Waker, poll in a loop, and call thread::park() on Poll::Pending.
  • Leaf futures either re-arm their own waker immediately (YieldTimes, yield_now) or register the waker with an external event source (Delay, kernel sockets, timer wheels).
  • In a multi-task executor, waking a task and scheduling it are the same operation: Task implements Wake by pushing itself back onto the run queue.
  • An async block compiles into a state-machine enum with one variant per .await suspension point, storing only the local variables live across that point.
  • Future::poll requires Pin<&mut Self> so self-referential state machines cannot relocate in memory after their first poll, preserving internal borrows.
  • Spawned futures require Send because wakers and work-stealing executors may transfer a task across worker threads between polls.
  • Both HTTP clients compose caching, retry, and transport layers; unifying them requires classifying both transport errors and retryable HTTP status codes (429, 5xx), combined with jitter and Retry-After handling.

Exercises

  1. Add a poll counter to block_on and print it. Check that the count matches the number of wakes for Delay, and that a spurious wake adds one poll without breaking anything.
  2. Write a ReadyNow future that returns Ready on its first poll. Confirm that MiniExecutor::run completes it in one poll.
  3. Change MiniExecutor::run to return the number of tasks it completed. Test it with tasks that yield different numbers of times.
  4. Give Delay a Drop that sets a flag the timer thread checks, so a cancelled delay does not keep a thread asleep.
  5. Merge the two HTTP clients. Retry a retryable status and a transport error, add jitter to the delay, and honor Retry-After when the server sends it.
  6. Move the async client into rust-async-http-examples as a library, and test it against chapter 21’s local server.

Mapping files and copying less

This chapter covers

  • The kernel page cache: how file data resides in physical RAM and why read incurs a user-space copy
  • Demand-paged virtual memory mappings (mmap): page table population via minor and major page faults
  • Shared (MAP_SHARED) and private (MAP_PRIVATE) mappings, explicit writeback via msync, and copy-on-write isolation
  • Asynchronous error delivery (SIGBUS), cross-process aliasing hazards, and selection criteria between mmap and read
  • Kernel-space file-to-socket transfer via sendfile and scatter-gather DMA zero-copy transmission
  • The architectural boundary where user-space TLS encryption and dynamic compression preclude zero-copy I/O

Every conventional file transfer across the user-kernel boundary pays a memory bandwidth tax: the kernel copies file bytes from its internal page cache into a caller-allocated buffer, and a subsequent network transmission copies those same bytes back into a kernel socket buffer. Eliminating redundant copies requires either exposing page cache frames directly in a process’s virtual address space through demand-paged memory mappings (mmap) or delegating file-to-socket movement entirely to the kernel (sendfile). Both mechanisms shift the cost profile of I/O from linear byte copying to virtual memory management, page fault handling, and scatter-gather DMA descriptors.

Two reference programs quantify these mechanisms. mmap_file maps a 64-page file into virtual memory, records minor page faults across consecutive traversal passes, and contrasts write propagation under shared and private mappings. zero_copy transmits a 256 MiB file over a loopback TCP socket, measuring system call volume and wall-clock throughput for a conventional read/write loop against Linux sendfile.

23.1 Where a file’s bytes live

The operating system maintains recently accessed file blocks in physical memory inside the kernel page cache, indexed by file inode and page offset (page 0 spans bytes 0 to 4,095, page 1 spans bytes 4,096 to 8,191, and so forth). All buffered file I/O traverses this cache: reading an uncached page triggers a storage read into a newly allocated page frame, whereas subsequent reads of that page by any process are satisfied directly from RAM.

Because the page cache resides in kernel address space, the read system call cannot expose a cached physical frame directly to user space. Instead, the kernel copies the requested byte range from the page cache into a caller-supplied buffer. Upon return from read(fd, &mut buffer), the same data occupies physical memory twice: once in the kernel page cache and once in the process’s heap or stack buffer.

A demand-paged memory mapping eliminates this duplication. The mmap system call reserves a contiguous virtual address range within the process’s address space, associates it with a specified byte range of an open file descriptor, and returns the base virtual address. When the process dereferences an address within that range, the hardware memory management unit (MMU) translates the virtual address through the page table directly to the physical frame in the kernel page cache (Figure 23.1), granting direct in-place access without a copy.

As depicted in Figure 23.2, a file mapping constitutes a standard virtual memory area (VMA) within the process’s address space alongside the stack, heap, and executable text segments. Its page table entries resolve directly to the physical frames managed by the kernel page cache.

Invoking mmap transfers no file data and populates no page table entries; it records only the virtual memory area metadata in the kernel. The initial memory access to each mapped page triggers a hardware page fault (Section 15.5), trapping into the kernel. The page fault handler locates the target page in the page cache (or schedules a block I/O read if the page is absent), installs the corresponding page table entry, and resumes the faulting instruction. A fault satisfied from an already-resident page cache frame is a minor fault (costing microseconds), whereas a fault requiring block storage I/O is a major fault (dominated by storage latency).

For a 64-page mapping whose backing file is already resident in the page cache, fault accumulation proceeds in three distinct phases:

StepWhat the kernel doesFaults
mmap of 64 pagesreserves 64 pages of addresses, fills no entries0
first read of each pagefills that page’s entryone per page
second read of each pagenothing: the entries are already filled0

The remainder of this section encapsulates the mapping lifecycle in an RAII Rust wrapper and verifies this fault profile empirically.

23.1.1 A type that owns a mapping

Direct invocation of mmap requires FFI bindings through the libc crate. A live mapping consists of a base virtual address and a byte length that must be released via munmap exactly once. Encapsulating these invariants in an owning struct with a Drop implementation ensures deterministic unmapping:

use std::{
    fs::{self, File},
    io,
    os::fd::AsRawFd,
    path::Path,
    ptr::NonNull,
    slice,
};

/// A file mapped into this process's address space. Unmapped when dropped.
struct Mapping {
    ptr: NonNull<u8>,
    len: usize,
}

The NonNull<u8> pointer encodes the invariant that a constructed Mapping always holds a non-null virtual base address. The libc crate exposes POSIX C interfaces through unsafe extern "C" declarations parameterized by platform ABI types: c_int for C int, size_t for unsigned byte counts, off_t for file offsets, and *mut c_void for untyped pointers. The contract of mmap is specified as follows:

unsafe extern "C" {
    fn mmap(
        addr: *mut c_void, // where to map; null lets the kernel choose
        len: size_t,       // how many bytes to map
        prot: c_int,       // what is allowed: PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE
        flags: c_int,      // MAP_SHARED or MAP_PRIVATE (section 23.2)
        fd: c_int,         // the open file
        offset: off_t,     // where in the file; a multiple of the page size
    ) -> *mut c_void;      // the mapping's address, or MAP_FAILED
}

Invoking an extern "C" function requires an unsafe block because the Rust compiler cannot verify pointer validity, alignment, or lifetime invariants across the foreign function boundary. Mapping::new executes the system call and validates its return value:

impl Mapping {
    /// Map the first `len` bytes of `file` for reading and writing.
    ///
    /// `shared` chooses `MAP_SHARED`, whose writes reach the file, over
    /// `MAP_PRIVATE`, whose writes stay in this process.
    fn new(file: &File, len: usize, shared: bool) -> io::Result<Self> {
        let flags = if shared {
            libc::MAP_SHARED
        } else {
            libc::MAP_PRIVATE
        };

        // SAFETY: a null address lets the kernel choose where to place the
        // mapping, and the descriptor is open for reading and writing. The
        // result is checked against MAP_FAILED before it is used.
        let address = unsafe {
            libc::mmap(
                std::ptr::null_mut(),
                len,
                libc::PROT_READ | libc::PROT_WRITE,
                flags,
                file.as_raw_fd(),
                0,
            )
        };
        if address == libc::MAP_FAILED {
            return Err(io::Error::last_os_error());
        }

        let ptr = NonNull::new(address.cast::<u8>()).ok_or_else(io::Error::last_os_error)?;
        Ok(Self { ptr, len })
    }
    // ...
}

On failure, mmap returns the sentinel value MAP_FAILED ((void *)-1) rather than a null pointer; the constructor therefore compares the result against MAP_FAILED before reading errno via io::Error::last_os_error().

Safe byte-level access is exposed through shared and mutable slices constructed from the base pointer and length:

impl Mapping {
    // ...
    fn bytes(&self) -> &[u8] {
        // SAFETY: the mapping is `len` bytes long and stays valid until drop.
        unsafe { slice::from_raw_parts(self.ptr.as_ptr(), self.len) }
    }

    fn bytes_mut(&mut self) -> &mut [u8] {
        // SAFETY: as in `bytes`, and `&mut self` makes this the only borrow.
        unsafe { slice::from_raw_parts_mut(self.ptr.as_ptr(), self.len) }
    }
    // ...
}

Because bytes_mut requires &mut self, the borrow checker enforces exclusive mutable access within the current process, matching the aliasing discipline of Vec<u8>. Releasing the virtual address range in Drop invokes munmap with the original base address and length:

unsafe extern "C" {
    fn munmap(addr: *mut c_void, len: size_t) -> c_int; // 0, or -1 with errno set
}
impl Drop for Mapping {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        // SAFETY: the range is exactly the mapping created in `new`, and no
        // borrow of it can outlive `self`.
        unsafe {
            libc::munmap(self.ptr.as_ptr().cast(), self.len);
        }
    }
}

The lifetime of any slice returned by bytes or bytes_mut is bound to &self or &mut self, preventing a slice from outliving the Mapping instance. Without this compile-time lifetime tie, dereferencing a slice after munmap would access an unmapped virtual address and raise SIGSEGV.

23.1.2 Counting the faults

The kernel maintains per-process resource accounting counters, including minor and major page fault totals. getrusage populates a caller-supplied rusage structure with these counters, while sysconf queries runtime system parameters such as the hardware page size:

unsafe extern "C" {
    fn getrusage(
        who: c_int,          // RUSAGE_SELF: this process
        usage: *mut rusage,  // filled in; ru_minflt counts minor faults
    ) -> c_int;              // 0, or -1 with errno set
    fn sysconf(name: c_int) -> c_long; // _SC_PAGESIZE gives the page size
}

Sampling ru_minflt immediately before and after a traversal pass isolates the exact fault count incurred by that pass:

/// Minor page faults this process has taken so far: faults the kernel served
/// from memory, without reading the disk.
fn minor_faults() -> u64 {
    // SAFETY: `getrusage` fills the struct it is given and nothing else.
    let usage = unsafe {
        let mut usage = std::mem::zeroed::<libc::rusage>();
        libc::getrusage(libc::RUSAGE_SELF, &mut usage);
        usage
    };
    u64::try_from(usage.ru_minflt).expect("fault count is not negative")
}

/// Read one byte from every page, so each page is touched once.
fn touch_every_page(bytes: &[u8], page: usize) -> u64 {
    bytes
        .iter()
        .step_by(page)
        .map(|&byte| u64::from(byte))
        .sum()
}

touch_every_page reads one byte per page by advancing an iterator with step_by(page). Accumulating and returning the byte sum introduces a data dependency that prevents dead-code elimination from optimizing away the memory loads.

main creates a 64-page file, maps it with MAP_SHARED, and executes two consecutive traversal passes:

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    // ...
    let mut shared = Mapping::new(&file, len, true)?;

    let before = minor_faults();
    touch_every_page(shared.bytes(), page);
    let first = minor_faults() - before;

    let before = minor_faults();
    touch_every_page(shared.bytes(), page);
    let second = minor_faults() - before;

    println!("first pass over the mapping:  {first} minor faults");
    println!("second pass over the mapping: {second} minor faults\n");
    // ...
}

Animation 23.1 traces both traversal passes, the shared and private write behaviors of Section 23.2, and the truncation fault of Section 23.2.1.

On macOS, the measured fault counts match the theoretical single-page-per-fault model exactly:

$ cargo run --bin mmap_file
page size 4096 bytes, file 64 pages (262144 bytes)

first pass over the mapping:  64 minor faults
second pass over the mapping: 0 minor faults

Every fault is classified as minor because the preceding fs::write call already populated the kernel page cache with all 64 pages; no block device reads occur during traversal.

On Linux, the identical binary reports first pass over the mapping: 5 minor faults. During a read fault on a file-backed mapping, the Linux virtual memory subsystem performs fault-around: it speculatively installs page table entries for neighboring pages that are already resident in the page cache. With the default fault-around window of 64 KiB (16 pages of 4 KiB each), traversing 64 pages requires a minimum of 4 fault-around traps. On both operating systems, the second pass incurs zero faults because all 64 page table entries remain resident.

23.2 Shared and private mappings

The flags parameter passed to mmap determines how store instructions to mapped pages interact with the kernel page cache and backing file (Figure 23.3):

  • MAP_SHARED: page table entries map directly to the shared page cache frames with write permissions enabled. A store modifies the cached page in place, making the update immediately visible to every process mapping or reading the same file. The kernel flushes modified (dirty) pages to storage asynchronously during background writeback.
  • MAP_PRIVATE: page table entries initially map to the shared page cache frames, but the kernel marks those entries read-only in hardware. The first store to a page triggers a protection fault; the kernel allocates a fresh anonymous physical frame, copies the original page contents into it, updates the process’s page table entry to point to the private frame with write permission, and resumes the store. This copy-on-write (CoW) isolation ensures that modifications remain private to the process and never propagate to the backing file.

Background writeback operates on the kernel’s dirty-page flushing schedule (commonly bounded near 30 seconds). When durability requires flushing dirty pages at a deterministic boundary, the application invokes msync:

unsafe extern "C" {
    fn msync(
        addr: *mut c_void, // start of the range, as returned by mmap
        len: size_t,       // length of the range
        flags: c_int,      // MS_SYNC: return after the write completes
    ) -> c_int;            // 0, or -1 with errno set
}

Passing MS_SYNC blocks the calling thread until all dirty pages within the specified virtual range have been written to the underlying storage subsystem:

impl Mapping {
    // ...
    /// Write the changed pages of a shared mapping back to the file now.
    fn sync(&self) -> io::Result<()> {
        // SAFETY: the range is exactly the mapping created in `new`.
        let result = unsafe { libc::msync(self.ptr.as_ptr().cast(), self.len, libc::MS_SYNC) };
        if result == 0 {
            Ok(())
        } else {
            Err(io::Error::last_os_error())
        }
    }
}

main writes HELLO through the shared mapping and synchronizes it to disk, then creates a MAP_PRIVATE mapping of the same file and writes world:

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    // ...
    shared.bytes_mut()[..5].copy_from_slice(b"HELLO");
    shared.sync()?;
    drop(shared);
    println!(
        "after writing HELLO through MAP_SHARED, the file starts with {:?}",
        file_prefix(&path)?
    );

    let mut private = Mapping::new(&file, len, false)?;
    private.bytes_mut()[..5].copy_from_slice(b"world");
    println!(
        "after writing world through MAP_PRIVATE, the mapping holds {:?}",
        String::from_utf8_lossy(&private.bytes()[..5])
    );
    drop(private);
    println!("and the file still starts with {:?}", file_prefix(&path)?);
    // ...
}

file_prefix inspects the backing file via fs::read, querying the kernel page cache directly rather than the private mapping:

after writing HELLO through MAP_SHARED, the file starts with "HELLO"
after writing world through MAP_PRIVATE, the mapping holds "world"
and the file still starts with "HELLO"

POSIX fork relies on this same copy-on-write primitive at process granularity. The kernel duplicates the parent’s page tables for the child and marks all writable anonymous pages read-only in both processes; physical frame duplication is deferred until either process executes a store to a shared page.

23.2.1 What a mapping cannot report

A failing read system call returns -1 and sets errno, enabling synchronous error handling in user space. A load or store instruction targeting a memory-mapped address has no error return channel; consequently, the kernel must report I/O and bounds failures asynchronously via signals:

  • If another process truncates the backing file, physical pages beyond the new file length are invalidated. Dereferencing a virtual address in the truncated region raises SIGBUS, which terminates the process unless a signal handler is registered.
  • If the storage device returns a media or transport error while servicing a major page fault, the kernel likewise delivers SIGBUS to the faulting thread.

Furthermore, Rust’s borrow checker enforces aliasing invariants only within a single process. A &[u8] slice asserts that its referenced bytes remain immutable for the duration of the borrow, yet an external process can mutate a MAP_SHARED backing file concurrently. Mapping::bytes is therefore sound only under the external precondition that no concurrent writer modifies the file. For this reason, the ecosystem memmap2 crate marks Mmap::map as an unsafe fn, delegating that cross-process aliasing contract to the caller.

23.2.2 When to map, and when to read

Eliminating the kernel-to-user copy is not cost-free. A memory mapping incurs page fault trap overhead on first access to each page, consumes virtual address space, and requires a TLB shootdown upon munmap: the kernel must issue inter-processor interrupts (IPIs) to invalidate stale translation lookaside buffer entries across all CPU cores executing threads of the process.

Access patternBetter toolReason
Read a file once, front to backread into a reused bufferreadahead keeps the page cache ahead of the reader, and one buffer is cheap to copy into
Random reads over a large file, repeatedmmapeach page faults once, then reads cost what memory reads cost
Many processes reading the same large filemmap (shared, read-only)every process uses the page cache’s single copy
Files that other processes may truncatereada failed read returns an error instead of raising SIGBUS

Embedded storage engines such as LMDB map their B-tree data files to exploit zero-overhead repeated random reads and cross-process page cache sharing, whereas streaming log processors and file-copy utilities favor sequential read with a reused buffer to avoid page fault and TLB invalidation costs.

23.3 Sending a file to a socket

A static file server transmits file contents from disk to network sockets without inspecting or transforming the payload. A conventional implementation loops over read and write: read copies bytes from the kernel page cache into a user-space buffer, and write copies those bytes from the user-space buffer into the kernel’s socket send buffer (Figure 23.4). Each chunk requires two system calls, two context-switch boundaries, and two CPU-driven memory copies solely because the POSIX read/write interface routes data through a user-space buffer.

The sendfile system call transfers bytes directly from a file descriptor to a socket descriptor entirely inside the kernel. A single invocation specifies the destination socket, source file, starting offset, and byte count. On network interface cards (NICs) that support scatter-gather DMA (NETIF_F_SG), the kernel attaches references to the page cache frames directly to the socket buffer descriptors (sk_buff) and instructs the NIC to read payload bytes directly from physical memory via DMA. This zero-copy path eliminates both CPU payload copies and reduces system call overhead to a single transition per transfer segment.

23.3.1 Measuring both

Because Linux sendfile accepts a socket as out_fd with a distinct signature from BSD and macOS, zero_copy isolates its implementation inside a Linux-conditional module. connected_pair establishes a loopback TCP connection and spawns a consumer thread that drains the receiving socket to verify complete delivery:

#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]
mod linux {
    use std::{
        fs::{self, File},
        io::{self, Read, Write},
        net::{TcpListener, TcpStream},
        os::fd::AsRawFd,
        thread,
        time::{Duration, Instant},
    };

    /// What one transfer cost.
    pub struct Transfer {
        pub bytes: u64,
        pub syscalls: u64,
        pub elapsed: Duration,
    }

    /// A connected socket pair over loopback, with a thread on the far end
    /// that reads and discards everything until the sender closes.
    fn connected_pair() -> io::Result<(TcpStream, thread::JoinHandle<u64>)> {
        let listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0")?;
        let address = listener.local_addr()?;
        let sink = thread::spawn(move || {
            let (mut stream, _) = listener.accept().expect("accept");
            let mut buffer = vec![0u8; 1 << 20];
            let mut total = 0u64;
            loop {
                match stream.read(&mut buffer) {
                    Ok(0) | Err(_) => return total,
                    Ok(read) => total += read as u64,
                }
            }
        });
        Ok((TcpStream::connect(address)?, sink))
    }
    // ...
}

The Transfer struct records elapsed duration and system call count for each benchmark pass. Joining the receiver thread returns the total byte count observed on the peer socket, verifying that no bytes were dropped or truncated.

The baseline copy_loop reads up to buffer_size bytes per iteration and transmits them via write_all, incrementing the system call counter on each operation:

mod linux {
    // ...
    /// Send `file` with `read` into a buffer and `write` out of it.
    pub fn copy_loop(path: &str, buffer_size: usize) -> io::Result<Transfer> {
        let mut file = File::open(path)?;
        let (mut socket, sink) = connected_pair()?;
        let mut buffer = vec![0u8; buffer_size];
        let mut syscalls = 0;

        let start = Instant::now();
        loop {
            let read = file.read(&mut buffer)?;
            syscalls += 1;
            if read == 0 {
                break;
            }
            socket.write_all(&buffer[..read])?;
            syscalls += 1;
        }
        drop(socket);
        let bytes = sink.join().expect("sink thread");
        Ok(Transfer {
            bytes,
            syscalls,
            elapsed: start.elapsed(),
        })
    }
    // ...
}

Because write_all may issue multiple underlying write calls whenever the socket send buffer fills, counting one call per write_all yields a conservative lower bound on total system calls.

The sendfile implementation allocates no user-space transfer buffer and invokes the kernel transfer interface directly:

unsafe extern "C" {
    fn sendfile(
        out_fd: c_int,       // where the bytes go: the socket
        in_fd: c_int,        // where they come from: the file
        offset: *mut off_t,  // where to start reading; advanced by the kernel
        count: size_t,       // at most this many bytes
    ) -> ssize_t;            // bytes sent, or -1 with errno set
}

The transfer loop invokes sendfile repeatedly until offset reaches the file length:

mod linux {
    // ...
    /// Send `file` with `sendfile`, which moves the bytes inside the kernel.
    pub fn send_file(path: &str) -> io::Result<Transfer> {
        let file = File::open(path)?;
        let length = file.metadata()?.len();
        let (socket, sink) = connected_pair()?;
        let mut offset: libc::off_t = 0;
        let mut syscalls = 0;

        let start = Instant::now();
        while (offset as u64) < length {
            let remaining = (length - offset as u64) as usize;
            // SAFETY: both descriptors are open for the whole call, and the
            // kernel advances `offset` by the number of bytes it sent.
            let sent = unsafe {
                libc::sendfile(socket.as_raw_fd(), file.as_raw_fd(), &mut offset, remaining)
            };
            syscalls += 1;
            if sent < 0 {
                return Err(io::Error::last_os_error());
            }
        }
        drop(socket);
        let bytes = sink.join().expect("sink thread");
        Ok(Transfer {
            bytes,
            syscalls,
            elapsed: start.elapsed(),
        })
    }
    // ...
}

On each call, the kernel advances *offset by the number of bytes transferred. Linux caps a single sendfile call at 0x7ffff000 (2,147,479,552) bytes, and signal delivery can cause a short transfer; looping until completion handles both cases, though a 256 MiB loopback transfer completes in a single call.

main creates a 256 MiB file and performs an untimed warm-up transfer so that both timed runs operate against a hot page cache. Executed in release mode inside a Linux container:

$ cargo run --release --bin zero_copy
method                        MiB   syscalls         ms        MiB/s
read/write, 64 KiB            256       8193      316.4          809
sendfile                      256          1      194.3         1318

Transferring 256 MiB in 64 KiB chunks requires 4,096 read calls, 4,096 write calls, and one terminal read returning 0 (EOF), totaling 8,193 system calls. sendfile completed the identical transfer in 1 system call, reducing elapsed time by approximately 39%. Both runs share the fixed overhead of loopback TCP segmentation and the local receiver thread copying bytes into its own buffer; over a physical NIC to a remote host, eliminating sender-side copies represents a substantially larger fraction of total CPU cost.

23.3.2 Where zero-copy stops

sendfile requires that bytes leave the kernel unmodified relative to their representation in the page cache. Any payload transformation forces the CPU to read and rewrite every byte:

  • TLS encryption. User-space TLS implementations such as rustls encrypt records inside the application process. Serving a file over HTTPS requires reading plaintext into user space, encrypting it into ciphertext buffers, and writing the ciphertext to the socket. Linux kernel TLS (kTLS) restores zero-copy transmission by allowing the user-space library to perform the handshake and then install the symmetric session keys into the kernel socket via setsockopt(SOL_TLS). With kTLS active, sendfile transfers page cache frames directly while the kernel (or a kTLS-capable NIC) encrypts records inline.
  • On-the-fly compression. Dynamic response compression (gzip, brotli, zstd) requires reading every plaintext byte into CPU registers. Pre-compressing static assets on disk restores eligibility for sendfile by allowing the kernel to transmit the compressed representation directly.

23.4 The complete programs

Listing 23.1 Shared and private mappings, and the faults that load them. src/bin/mmap_file.rs

//! Mapping a file into memory with `mmap`.
//!
//! A mapping makes a file's bytes addressable like a slice. The kernel loads a
//! page the first time it is touched, which shows up as a page fault. The flags
//! decide where writes go: through a `MAP_SHARED` mapping they reach the file,
//! and through a `MAP_PRIVATE` mapping they stay in a private copy of the page.
//!
//! Run with: cargo run --bin mmap_file

use std::{
    fs::{self, File},
    io,
    os::fd::AsRawFd,
    path::Path,
    ptr::NonNull,
    slice,
};

/// A file mapped into this process's address space. Unmapped when dropped.
struct Mapping {
    ptr: NonNull<u8>,
    len: usize,
}

impl Mapping {
    /// Map the first `len` bytes of `file` for reading and writing.
    ///
    /// `shared` chooses `MAP_SHARED`, whose writes reach the file, over
    /// `MAP_PRIVATE`, whose writes stay in this process.
    fn new(file: &File, len: usize, shared: bool) -> io::Result<Self> {
        let flags = if shared {
            libc::MAP_SHARED
        } else {
            libc::MAP_PRIVATE
        };

        // SAFETY: a null address lets the kernel choose where to place the
        // mapping, and the descriptor is open for reading and writing. The
        // result is checked against MAP_FAILED before it is used.
        let address = unsafe {
            libc::mmap(
                std::ptr::null_mut(),
                len,
                libc::PROT_READ | libc::PROT_WRITE,
                flags,
                file.as_raw_fd(),
                0,
            )
        };
        if address == libc::MAP_FAILED {
            return Err(io::Error::last_os_error());
        }

        let ptr = NonNull::new(address.cast::<u8>()).ok_or_else(io::Error::last_os_error)?;
        Ok(Self { ptr, len })
    }

    fn bytes(&self) -> &[u8] {
        // SAFETY: the mapping is `len` bytes long and stays valid until drop.
        unsafe { slice::from_raw_parts(self.ptr.as_ptr(), self.len) }
    }

    fn bytes_mut(&mut self) -> &mut [u8] {
        // SAFETY: as in `bytes`, and `&mut self` makes this the only borrow.
        unsafe { slice::from_raw_parts_mut(self.ptr.as_ptr(), self.len) }
    }

    /// Write the changed pages of a shared mapping back to the file now.
    fn sync(&self) -> io::Result<()> {
        // SAFETY: the range is exactly the mapping created in `new`.
        let result = unsafe { libc::msync(self.ptr.as_ptr().cast(), self.len, libc::MS_SYNC) };
        if result == 0 {
            Ok(())
        } else {
            Err(io::Error::last_os_error())
        }
    }
}

impl Drop for Mapping {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        // SAFETY: the range is exactly the mapping created in `new`, and no
        // borrow of it can outlive `self`.
        unsafe {
            libc::munmap(self.ptr.as_ptr().cast(), self.len);
        }
    }
}

/// The size of one page of memory on this machine.
fn page_size() -> usize {
    // SAFETY: `sysconf` reads a system constant and has no side effects.
    let size = unsafe { libc::sysconf(libc::_SC_PAGESIZE) };
    usize::try_from(size).expect("page size is positive")
}

/// Minor page faults this process has taken so far: faults the kernel served
/// from memory, without reading the disk.
fn minor_faults() -> u64 {
    // SAFETY: `getrusage` fills the struct it is given and nothing else.
    let usage = unsafe {
        let mut usage = std::mem::zeroed::<libc::rusage>();
        libc::getrusage(libc::RUSAGE_SELF, &mut usage);
        usage
    };
    u64::try_from(usage.ru_minflt).expect("fault count is not negative")
}

/// Read one byte from every page, so each page is touched once.
fn touch_every_page(bytes: &[u8], page: usize) -> u64 {
    bytes
        .iter()
        .step_by(page)
        .map(|&byte| u64::from(byte))
        .sum()
}

/// The first five bytes of the file at `path`, as text.
fn file_prefix(path: &Path) -> io::Result<String> {
    let bytes = fs::read(path)?;
    Ok(String::from_utf8_lossy(&bytes[..5]).into_owned())
}

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    const PAGES: usize = 64;

    let page = page_size();
    let len = PAGES * page;
    let path = std::env::temp_dir().join("mmap_file_demo.bin");
    fs::write(&path, vec![b'a'; len])?;
    let file = File::options()
        .read(true)
        .write(true)
        .open(&path)?;

    println!("page size {page} bytes, file {PAGES} pages ({len} bytes)\n");

    let mut shared = Mapping::new(&file, len, true)?;

    let before = minor_faults();
    touch_every_page(shared.bytes(), page);
    let first = minor_faults() - before;

    let before = minor_faults();
    touch_every_page(shared.bytes(), page);
    let second = minor_faults() - before;

    println!("first pass over the mapping:  {first} minor faults");
    println!("second pass over the mapping: {second} minor faults\n");

    shared.bytes_mut()[..5].copy_from_slice(b"HELLO");
    shared.sync()?;
    drop(shared);
    println!(
        "after writing HELLO through MAP_SHARED, the file starts with {:?}",
        file_prefix(&path)?
    );

    let mut private = Mapping::new(&file, len, false)?;
    private.bytes_mut()[..5].copy_from_slice(b"world");
    println!(
        "after writing world through MAP_PRIVATE, the mapping holds {:?}",
        String::from_utf8_lossy(&private.bytes()[..5])
    );
    drop(private);
    println!("and the file still starts with {:?}", file_prefix(&path)?);

    fs::remove_file(&path)
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    /// A scratch file of `pages` pages of `b'a'`, unique to one test.
    fn scratch(name: &str, pages: usize) -> (std::path::PathBuf, File, usize) {
        let len = pages * page_size();
        let path = std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("mmap_file_test_{name}.bin"));
        fs::write(&path, vec![b'a'; len]).expect("write scratch file");
        let file = File::options()
            .read(true)
            .write(true)
            .open(&path)
            .expect("open scratch file");
        (path, file, len)
    }

    #[test]
    fn shared_writes_reach_the_file() {
        let (path, file, len) = scratch("shared", 2);
        let mut mapping = Mapping::new(&file, len, true).expect("map");
        mapping.bytes_mut()[..5].copy_from_slice(b"HELLO");
        mapping.sync().expect("msync");
        drop(mapping);
        assert_eq!(file_prefix(&path).expect("read"), "HELLO");
        fs::remove_file(path).expect("remove");
    }

    #[test]
    fn private_writes_stay_in_the_process() {
        let (path, file, len) = scratch("private", 2);
        let mut mapping = Mapping::new(&file, len, false).expect("map");
        mapping.bytes_mut()[..5].copy_from_slice(b"world");
        assert_eq!(&mapping.bytes()[..5], b"world");
        drop(mapping);
        assert_eq!(file_prefix(&path).expect("read"), "aaaaa");
        fs::remove_file(path).expect("remove");
    }
}

page size 4096 bytes, file 64 pages (262144 bytes)

first pass over the mapping:  64 minor faults
second pass over the mapping: 0 minor faults

Listing 23.2 A file sent over a socket with a read/write loop and with sendfile. src/bin/zero_copy.rs

//! Sending a file over a socket two ways: a read/write loop, and `sendfile`.
//!
//! The loop moves every byte through a buffer in this process: the kernel
//! copies it into the buffer on `read`, and copies it out again on `write`.
//! `sendfile` asks the kernel to move the bytes from the file to the socket
//! itself, so they never enter user space.
//!
//! Linux only. Run with: cargo run --release --bin zero_copy

#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]
mod linux {
    use std::{
        fs::{self, File},
        io::{self, Read, Write},
        net::{TcpListener, TcpStream},
        os::fd::AsRawFd,
        thread,
        time::{Duration, Instant},
    };

    /// What one transfer cost.
    pub struct Transfer {
        pub bytes: u64,
        pub syscalls: u64,
        pub elapsed: Duration,
    }

    /// A connected socket pair over loopback, with a thread on the far end
    /// that reads and discards everything until the sender closes.
    fn connected_pair() -> io::Result<(TcpStream, thread::JoinHandle<u64>)> {
        let listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0")?;
        let address = listener.local_addr()?;
        let sink = thread::spawn(move || {
            let (mut stream, _) = listener.accept().expect("accept");
            let mut buffer = vec![0u8; 1 << 20];
            let mut total = 0u64;
            loop {
                match stream.read(&mut buffer) {
                    Ok(0) | Err(_) => return total,
                    Ok(read) => total += read as u64,
                }
            }
        });
        Ok((TcpStream::connect(address)?, sink))
    }

    /// Send `file` with `read` into a buffer and `write` out of it.
    pub fn copy_loop(path: &str, buffer_size: usize) -> io::Result<Transfer> {
        let mut file = File::open(path)?;
        let (mut socket, sink) = connected_pair()?;
        let mut buffer = vec![0u8; buffer_size];
        let mut syscalls = 0;

        let start = Instant::now();
        loop {
            let read = file.read(&mut buffer)?;
            syscalls += 1;
            if read == 0 {
                break;
            }
            socket.write_all(&buffer[..read])?;
            syscalls += 1;
        }
        drop(socket);
        let bytes = sink.join().expect("sink thread");
        Ok(Transfer {
            bytes,
            syscalls,
            elapsed: start.elapsed(),
        })
    }

    /// Send `file` with `sendfile`, which moves the bytes inside the kernel.
    pub fn send_file(path: &str) -> io::Result<Transfer> {
        let file = File::open(path)?;
        let length = file.metadata()?.len();
        let (socket, sink) = connected_pair()?;
        let mut offset: libc::off_t = 0;
        let mut syscalls = 0;

        let start = Instant::now();
        while (offset as u64) < length {
            let remaining = (length - offset as u64) as usize;
            // SAFETY: both descriptors are open for the whole call, and the
            // kernel advances `offset` by the number of bytes it sent.
            let sent = unsafe {
                libc::sendfile(socket.as_raw_fd(), file.as_raw_fd(), &mut offset, remaining)
            };
            syscalls += 1;
            if sent < 0 {
                return Err(io::Error::last_os_error());
            }
        }
        drop(socket);
        let bytes = sink.join().expect("sink thread");
        Ok(Transfer {
            bytes,
            syscalls,
            elapsed: start.elapsed(),
        })
    }

    /// Write a scratch file of `size` bytes and return its path.
    pub fn scratch_file(size: usize) -> io::Result<String> {
        let path = std::env::temp_dir().join("zero_copy_demo.bin");
        fs::write(&path, vec![b'z'; size])?;
        Ok(path.to_string_lossy().into_owned())
    }
}

#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]
fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    const SIZE: usize = 256 << 20;

    let path = linux::scratch_file(SIZE)?;
    // One untimed pass, so the file is in the page cache for both runs.
    linux::copy_loop(&path, 64 << 10)?;

    println!(
        "{:<22} {:>10} {:>10} {:>10} {:>12}",
        "method", "MiB", "syscalls", "ms", "MiB/s"
    );
    let runs = [
        ("read/write, 64 KiB", linux::copy_loop(&path, 64 << 10)?),
        ("sendfile", linux::send_file(&path)?),
    ];
    for (name, run) in runs {
        let mib = run.bytes as f64 / (1 << 20) as f64;
        let ms = run.elapsed.as_secs_f64() * 1000.0;
        println!(
            "{name:<22} {mib:>10.0} {:>10} {ms:>10.1} {:>12.0}",
            run.syscalls,
            mib / run.elapsed.as_secs_f64()
        );
    }

    std::fs::remove_file(&path)
}

#[cfg(not(target_os = "linux"))]
fn main() {
    eprintln!("zero_copy uses Linux sendfile; run it on Linux");
}

#[cfg(all(test, target_os = "linux"))]
mod tests {
    use super::linux;

    #[test]
    fn both_methods_deliver_every_byte() {
        let path = linux::scratch_file(3 << 20).expect("scratch file");
        assert_eq!(
            linux::copy_loop(&path, 64 << 10)
                .expect("loop")
                .bytes,
            3 << 20
        );
        assert_eq!(
            linux::send_file(&path)
                .expect("sendfile")
                .bytes,
            3 << 20
        );
    }
}

23.5 Questions that come up

“Is a mapped file faster than read?” For repeated random access over a large file, mmap is typically faster: each page faults once, and subsequent accesses execute at memory-load speed without system call transitions. For a single sequential scan, read into a reused buffer is competitive or faster because kernel readahead keeps the page cache populated without incurring per-page fault traps or TLB shootdowns on teardown.

“What happens when two processes map the same file with MAP_SHARED?” Both processes’ page tables map to the identical physical frames in the kernel page cache. A store executed by one process is immediately visible to the other through cache coherence, prior to any disk writeback. POSIX shared memory (shm_open paired with mmap) uses this exact mechanism.

“Does msync make a write durable?” msync with MS_SYNC blocks until the kernel flushes all dirty pages in the range to the storage device. Physical durability beyond power loss still depends on the storage controller’s volatile write cache and flush barriers, matching the semantics of fsync.

“Why does a file server stop using sendfile when it turns on TLS?” User-space TLS libraries must read plaintext into process memory to encrypt each record before writing ciphertext to the socket. Offloading symmetric record encryption to the kernel via kTLS restores sendfile compatibility.

“What does fault-around change?” Fault-around reduces the minor page fault count during sequential access to a memory-mapped file by speculatively populating page table entries for neighboring pages already resident in the page cache. It does not alter observable memory semantics and issues no additional block I/O.

Summary

  • The kernel page cache stores recently accessed file pages in kernel memory; read copies bytes from the page cache into a caller-owned user-space buffer.
  • mmap reserves a virtual address range backed by a file without preloading data; the first access to each page triggers a hardware page fault that populates its page table entry.
  • A minor page fault resolves from an already-resident page cache frame; a major page fault requires a blocking read from storage.
  • Stores through MAP_SHARED mutate the page cache frame in place and propagate to disk via writeback or msync(MS_SYNC). Stores through MAP_PRIVATE trigger copy-on-write isolation into a private anonymous frame.
  • I/O errors or external file truncation on a mapped range deliver SIGBUS asynchronously rather than returning an error code. Exposing a MAP_SHARED region as &[u8] is sound only when no external process mutates the file concurrently.
  • sendfile transfers file data to a socket inside the kernel without user-space copies, reducing a 256 MiB loopback transfer from 8,193 system calls to 1.
  • User-space TLS encryption and dynamic compression require CPU access to payload bytes, precluding sendfile unless encryption is offloaded to kTLS or assets are pre-compressed.

Exercises

  1. Change PAGES to 4,096 and run mmap_file again. Drop the page cache (on Linux as root: echo 1 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches) between writing the file and mapping it, and record both ru_majflt and ru_minflt. Which faults become major?
  2. Map the file read-only with PROT_READ alone, and attempt a write through a raw pointer inside an unsafe block. Identify the resulting signal and classify the fault using Section 15.5.
  3. In copy_loop, benchmark buffer sizes of 4 KiB, 64 KiB, and 1 MiB. Account for the changes in system call count and elapsed wall-clock time.
  4. Add a third benchmark method to zero_copy that maps the entire file via mmap and passes the slice to write_all. Compare its system call count and throughput against copy_loop and sendfile.
  5. Write a test that truncates the backing file to one page while a two-page Mapping remains live. Verify that page 0 remains readable, explain why dereferencing page 1 is omitted from the test, and state the signal that accessing page 1 would raise.

File descriptors, fork, and pipes

This chapter covers

  • The three-level kernel descriptor architecture: per-process descriptor tables, open file descriptions, and the lowest-free-descriptor allocation rule
  • Descriptor inheritance across fork and exec, and async-signal-safety constraints in multithreaded processes
  • Kernel pipes: ring-buffer semantics, blocking rules, SIGPIPE/EPIPE, and end-of-file termination conditions
  • Constructing a two-stage shell pipeline (ls | wc -l) directly via pipe, fork, dup2, and execvp
  • Descriptor leaks that leave a pipe write end open and induce indefinite reader blocking
  • Close-on-exec (FD_CLOEXEC / O_CLOEXEC) semantics and atomic descriptor creation flags

Every POSIX process interacts with files, sockets, and pipes through a kernel-managed indirection layer: small non-negative integers called file descriptors index a per-process table whose entries reference shared kernel-level open file descriptions. Process creation (fork) duplicates that table by reference rather than by value, while program replacement (exec) preserves every entry not marked close-on-exec. Unix pipelines exploit the narrow window between fork and exec to rewire standard input and standard output onto kernel pipe descriptors, making descriptor lifecycle management critical to both process termination and security isolation.

The reference program fd_table exercises these kernel invariants directly through libc bindings: verifying lowest-free-descriptor allocation, constructing ls | wc -l without a shell, reproducing the indefinite hang caused by an unclosed pipe write end, and testing close-on-exec propagation across execvp.

24.1 The descriptor table

Each process owns a file descriptor table managed by the kernel, mapping non-negative integer indices to kernel I/O objects. By convention, process initialization populates the first three slots: 0 for standard input (stdin), 1 for standard output (stdout), and 2 for standard error (stderr).

A descriptor table entry does not reference an inode directly. Instead, it points to an open file description (a kernel struct file on Linux) allocated by a single open, pipe, or socket system call. The open file description stores per-opening state, including the current byte offset, access mode (O_RDONLY, O_WRONLY, O_RDWR), and file status flags such as O_APPEND or O_NONBLOCK. That kernel object in turn references the underlying inode or socket endpoint (Figure 24.1).

Three fundamental POSIX invariants follow directly from this three-level indirection:

  • Independent open calls allocate distinct open file descriptions. Each description maintains an independent file offset; advancing the offset through descriptor 3 has no effect on descriptor 4.
  • Duplicated descriptors alias the same open file description. dup, dup2, and fcntl(..., F_DUPFD, ...) install a new descriptor table entry referencing an existing open file description. Any read, write, or lseek through either descriptor advances the shared offset.
  • Allocation follows the lowest-free-number invariant. open and dup always assign the smallest non-negative integer not currently active in the process’s descriptor table. Closing descriptor 3 makes 3 the immediate return value of the next allocation.

An open file description is reference-counted across all descriptor tables in the system. Calling close removes a single descriptor table entry and decrements the description’s reference count; the kernel deallocates the description (and tears down the underlying pipe endpoint or network socket) only when that reference count reaches zero.

The per-process descriptor table size is bounded by the RLIMIT_NOFILE resource limit. A process that leaks descriptors eventually exhausts this table, causing subsequent open, accept, or socket calls to fail with EMFILE (“Too many open files”). In Rust, RAII wrappers such as std::fs::File, std::net::TcpStream, and std::os::fd::OwnedFd invoke close deterministically inside Drop, eliminating most accidental descriptor leaks.

24.1.1 Watching the numbers

On Linux and macOS, the pseudo-directory /dev/fd enumerates the calling process’s currently active descriptor numbers. open_fds reads and parses these entries:

use std::{
    ffi::CString,
    fs::{self, File},
    io::{self, Read, Write},
    os::fd::{AsRawFd, FromRawFd, OwnedFd, RawFd},
    path::Path,
    thread,
    time::Duration,
};

/// The descriptors open in this process, read from `/dev/fd`.
///
/// Reading the directory opens one more descriptor, which is in the list.
fn open_fds() -> io::Result<Vec<RawFd>> {
    let mut fds: Vec<RawFd> = fs::read_dir("/dev/fd")?
        .filter_map(Result::ok)
        .filter_map(|entry| entry.file_name().to_str()?.parse().ok())
        .collect();
    fds.sort_unstable();
    Ok(fds)
}

Each entry name corresponds to an integer descriptor index. The second filter_map retains entries that parse as i32. Because enumerating /dev/fd itself requires opening a directory descriptor, that transient descriptor appears in the returned list.

main opens a file twice, closes the lower-numbered descriptor, and opens the file a third time to verify slot reuse:

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    // ...
    println!("open at start: {:?}", open_fds()?);
    let first = File::open(&path)?;
    let second = File::open(&path)?;
    println!(
        "opened two files: fd {} and fd {}",
        first.as_raw_fd(),
        second.as_raw_fd()
    );
    let freed = first.as_raw_fd();
    drop(first);
    let third = File::open(&path)?;
    println!(
        "closed fd {freed}, opened another: fd {}\n",
        third.as_raw_fd()
    );
    // ...
}

The observed output confirms both allocation invariants:

open at start: [0, 1, 2, 3]
opened two files: fd 3 and fd 4
closed fd 3, opened another: fd 3

At startup, descriptors 0, 1, and 2 refer to the standard streams and descriptor 3 is the directory descriptor opened by fs::read_dir. Dropping the directory iterator closes descriptor 3, allowing the first File::open to acquire 3 and the second to acquire 4. Dropping the first File frees slot 3, which the third File::open immediately reclaims.

24.2 fork and exec

Unix separates process creation from executable loading into two orthogonal primitives:

  1. fork clones the calling process, producing a child process with a copy-on-write duplicate of the parent’s virtual address space (Section 23.2) and a shallow copy of the parent’s descriptor table. fork returns twice: in the parent it returns the child’s process identifier (pid_t), and in the child it returns 0.
  2. exec replaces the calling process’s address space with a new executable image while preserving its process identifier and descriptor table. Every descriptor entry whose per-descriptor close-on-exec (FD_CLOEXEC) flag is clear remains open in the new program; entries with FD_CLOEXEC set are closed atomically by the kernel during image replacement.

Because fork performs a shallow copy of the descriptor table (Figure 24.2), corresponding entries in parent and child reference the identical open file descriptions and increment their kernel reference counts. Parent and child therefore share file offsets on inherited descriptors. After exec, the replacement program inherits standard streams at indices 0, 1, and 2 solely because those entries were positioned there prior to exec.

Command shells construct I/O redirections and pipelines in the interval between fork and exec. Within the child process, the shell binds pipe endpoints or redirected files onto descriptors 0 and 1 via dup2, then invokes exec. The newly loaded executable reads descriptor 0 and writes descriptor 1 transparently, decoupled from whether those indices reference a terminal, regular file, or kernel pipe.

24.2.1 What the child may do before exec

In a multithreaded process, fork duplicates only the single thread that invoked it. All other threads vanish instantaneously in the child’s address space, leaving any mutexes they held (such as the global heap allocator lock) permanently locked with no owning thread to release them. Calling a lock-acquiring library function such as malloc inside the child before exec can therefore deadlock immediately.

POSIX restricts a multithreaded process’s post-fork, pre-exec child strictly to async-signal-safe system calls: primitives that acquire no user-space locks, including dup2, close, execvp, and _exit. Because Rust’s test harness executes tests concurrently across a thread pool, fd_table adheres strictly to this invariant by performing all heap allocations prior to fork.

The Program helper constructs null-terminated C strings in advance:

/// A program name and its arguments, as C strings.
struct Program(Vec<CString>);

impl Program {
    fn new(args: &[&str]) -> Self {
        Self(
            args.iter()
                .map(|arg| CString::new(*arg).expect("no NUL byte in an argument"))
                .collect(),
        )
    }

    /// The null-terminated pointer array `execvp` takes. It borrows `self`.
    fn argv(&self) -> Vec<*const libc::c_char> {
        self.0
            .iter()
            .map(|arg| arg.as_ptr())
            .chain(std::iter::once(std::ptr::null()))
            .collect()
    }
}

execvp expects a null-terminated array of *const c_char pointers. argv builds this pointer vector from the owned CString buffers; the pointers remain valid for the lifetime of Program.

The process-spawning primitive binds three POSIX calls:

unsafe extern "C" {
    fn fork() -> pid_t;                      // child's id in the parent, 0 in the child, -1 on error
    fn dup2(src: c_int, dst: c_int) -> c_int; // make dst refer to src's open file
    fn execvp(
        file: *const c_char,                  // program name, searched in PATH
        argv: *const *const c_char,           // arguments, ending with a null pointer
    ) -> c_int;                               // returns only on failure
}

spawn constructs argv before calling fork, then redirects standard streams and replaces the child image:

/// Start `program` in a child process. `stdin` and `stdout`, when given,
/// become the child's descriptors 0 and 1. Returns the child's process id.
fn spawn(
    program: &Program,
    stdin: Option<RawFd>,
    stdout: Option<RawFd>,
) -> io::Result<libc::pid_t> {
    // Allocate before `fork`: the child may only make async-signal-safe calls.
    let argv = program.argv();

    // SAFETY: the child below calls only dup2, execvp, and _exit.
    let pid = check(unsafe { libc::fork() })?;
    if pid > 0 {
        return Ok(pid);
    }

    // SAFETY: this is the child, a copy of the parent with one thread. dup2 copies
    // a descriptor without its close-on-exec flag; execvp replaces the program.
    unsafe {
        if let Some(fd) = stdin {
            libc::dup2(fd, 0);
        }
        if let Some(fd) = stdout {
            libc::dup2(fd, 1);
        }
        libc::execvp(argv[0], argv.as_ptr());
        libc::_exit(127)
    }
}

Because argv is allocated before fork, the child executes zero heap allocations. Inside the child, dup2(fd, 1) atomically closes any existing descriptor at slot 1 and points slot 1 at the open file description of fd. execvp searches PATH and does not return on success. On failure, the child terminates immediately via _exit(127) (the conventional shell exit code for “command not found”), bypassing user-space atexit handlers and preventing the child from returning into parent control flow.

The parent reaps terminated children with waitpid:

unsafe extern "C" {
    fn waitpid(
        pid: pid_t,          // the child to wait for
        status: *mut c_int,  // filled in; WEXITSTATUS(status) is the exit code
        options: c_int,      // 0 to wait, WNOHANG to return at once
    ) -> pid_t;              // the child's id, 0 if WNOHANG and still running, or -1
}
/// Wait for the child `pid` to exit, and return its exit status.
fn wait(pid: libc::pid_t) -> io::Result<i32> {
    let mut status = 0;
    // SAFETY: `waitpid` writes the status into the integer it is given.
    check(unsafe { libc::waitpid(pid, &mut status, 0) })?;
    Ok(libc::WEXITSTATUS(status))
}

/// Whether the child `pid` has exited, without waiting for it.
fn has_exited(pid: libc::pid_t) -> io::Result<bool> {
    let mut status = 0;
    // SAFETY: as in `wait`; WNOHANG returns 0 at once if the child is running.
    let result = check(unsafe { libc::waitpid(pid, &mut status, libc::WNOHANG) })?;
    Ok(result == pid)
}

An exited child remains in the kernel process table as a zombie holding its exit status until its parent reaps it via waitpid. Passing WNOHANG performs a non-blocking poll, returning 0 if the child is still executing.

24.3 Pipes

A pipe is a unidirectional, in-kernel FIFO ring buffer exposed through a pair of descriptors: a read end and a write end. Bytes written to the write end are delivered in strict FIFO order from the read end. On Linux, the default pipe buffer capacity is 64 KiB (16 memory pages).

Pipeline flow control and termination are governed by four kernel blocking and error semantics:

  • read on an empty pipe blocks until at least one byte is written or all write ends close.
  • read returns 0 (end-of-file) if and only if the pipe buffer is empty and the kernel reference count for the write-end open file description has reached zero across all processes.
  • write to a full pipe blocks until a reader drains sufficient buffer space.
  • write to a pipe whose read-end reference count is zero fails immediately: the kernel delivers SIGPIPE to the writing process, or returns -1 with errno == EPIPE if SIGPIPE is ignored or masked.

A shell executes ls | wc -l through a five-step descriptor protocol (Figure 24.3):

  1. Invoke pipe to allocate the read and write descriptors in the parent’s descriptor table.
  2. Invoke fork; in the first child, redirect stdout (descriptor 1) to the pipe write end with dup2 and invoke execvp("ls", ...).
  3. Invoke fork; in the second child, redirect stdin (descriptor 0) to the pipe read end with dup2 and invoke execvp("wc", ...).
  4. Close both the read and write pipe descriptors in the parent process.
  5. Reap both child processes with waitpid.

Step 4 establishes the termination invariant: once the parent closes its pipe descriptors, ls’s descriptor 1 is the sole remaining reference to the pipe’s write end. When ls exits, the kernel closes its descriptor table, dropping the write-end reference count to zero; wc -l then observes read() == 0, prints its line count, and exits.

24.3.1 Building the pipeline

The low-level pipe and descriptor control interfaces operate on raw integer descriptors:

unsafe extern "C" {
    fn pipe(fds: *mut c_int) -> c_int;            // fills [read end, write end]; 0 or -1
    fn fcntl(fd: c_int, cmd: c_int, ...) -> c_int; // F_SETFD sets flags; F_DUPFD copies
}

pipe writes [read_fd, write_fd] into a two-element array, while fcntl is a variadic system call accepting a command code and optional argument. Wrapping both descriptors in OwnedFd ensures deterministic closure on drop, and setting FD_CLOEXEC prevents accidental inheritance:

/// Turn a C return value into an `io::Result`: -1 means `errno` holds the error.
fn check(result: libc::c_int) -> io::Result<libc::c_int> {
    if result == -1 {
        Err(io::Error::last_os_error())
    } else {
        Ok(result)
    }
}

/// Set close-on-exec on `fd`, so a program started with `exec` does not get it.
fn set_cloexec(fd: RawFd) -> io::Result<()> {
    // SAFETY: F_SETFD changes only the descriptor's flags.
    check(unsafe { libc::fcntl(fd, libc::F_SETFD, libc::FD_CLOEXEC) })?;
    Ok(())
}

/// A pipe as (read end, write end). Both ends are close-on-exec.
fn pipe() -> io::Result<(OwnedFd, OwnedFd)> {
    let mut ends = [0; 2];
    // SAFETY: `pipe` writes two new descriptors into the array.
    check(unsafe { libc::pipe(ends.as_mut_ptr()) })?;
    // SAFETY: both descriptors were just created, and nothing else owns them.
    let (read_end, write_end) =
        unsafe { (OwnedFd::from_raw_fd(ends[0]), OwnedFd::from_raw_fd(ends[1])) };
    set_cloexec(read_end.as_raw_fd())?;
    set_cloexec(write_end.as_raw_fd())?;
    Ok((read_end, write_end))
}

check converts the POSIX -1/errno convention into io::Result. Marking the original pipe descriptors with FD_CLOEXEC eliminates explicit close calls in each child prior to exec: because dup2 clears FD_CLOEXEC on the target slot, descriptors 0 and 1 survive execvp while the original pipe descriptors close automatically upon image replacement.

ls_wc implements the five-step pipeline directly:

/// `ls dir | wc -l`, built the way a shell builds it. `wc` writes to this
/// process's standard output.
fn ls_wc(dir: &Path) -> io::Result<()> {
    let ls = Program::new(&["ls", dir.to_str().expect("UTF-8 path")]);
    let wc = Program::new(&["wc", "-l"]);

    let (read_end, write_end) = pipe()?;
    let writer = spawn(&ls, None, Some(write_end.as_raw_fd()))?;
    let reader = spawn(&wc, Some(read_end.as_raw_fd()), None)?;
    drop(read_end);
    drop(write_end);

    wait(writer)?;
    wait(reader)?;
    Ok(())
}

The explicit drop calls execute step 4 in the parent before waiting. Against a directory containing three files, the pipeline outputs:

ls fd_table_demo | wc -l
       3

On Linux, GNU wc formats the count as 3 without leading whitespace.

24.3.2 A write end left open

Animation 24.1 contrasts the properly closed pipeline with a defective run that omits step 4.

reader_waits_for_the_write_end reproduces this liveness failure by spawning wc -l, writing two lines to the pipe, and delaying closure of the parent’s write descriptor for one second:

/// Start `wc -l` on a pipe, write two lines into it, and keep the write end
/// open for `hold`. Returns whether `wc` was still running when `hold` ended.
fn reader_waits_for_the_write_end(hold: Duration) -> io::Result<bool> {
    let wc = Program::new(&["wc", "-l"]);
    let (read_end, write_end) = pipe()?;
    let reader = spawn(&wc, Some(read_end.as_raw_fd()), None)?;
    drop(read_end);

    let mut writer = File::from(write_end);
    writer.write_all(b"one\ntwo\n")?;
    thread::sleep(hold);
    let still_running = !has_exited(reader)?;

    drop(writer);
    wait(reader)?;
    Ok(still_running)
}
parent writes two lines to wc -l and holds the write end for 1 s:
       2
wc still running after 1 s: true

Although wc -l consumed both lines within microseconds, its read system call remained blocked for the entire second because the parent’s open descriptor held the write-end reference count at 1. wc -l emitted 2 and exited only after drop(writer) reduced the reference count to zero. In production software, omitting that drop causes a silent deadlock consuming zero CPU cycles and producing no error diagnostic.

An analogous failure occurs with TCP sockets: if a server forks a long-lived child process that inherits an accepted client socket without FD_CLOEXEC, closing the socket in the parent does not decrement the kernel reference count to zero. Consequently, the kernel does not transmit a TCP FIN, leaving the client connection hung indefinitely.

24.4 Close-on-exec

Every descriptor lacking the FD_CLOEXEC flag survives exec into the child process, creating three distinct classes of operational defects:

  • Port retention: A listening socket inherited by a long-lived child keeps the TCP port bound even after the parent server exits, causing a restarted parent to fail with EADDRINUSE.
  • Pipeline stalls: An inherited pipe write end prevents downstream readers from observing EOF (Section 24.3.2).
  • Privilege leakage: Sensitive file descriptors (credential stores, database sockets, configuration files) remain accessible to untrusted child executables.

Rust’s standard library sets FD_CLOEXEC on every file, socket, and pipe descriptor it allocates. Descriptor leaks in Rust binaries therefore originate from raw libc calls or linked C libraries. duplicate demonstrates both behaviors using fcntl:

/// A copy of `file`'s descriptor, numbered 100 or above, with or without
/// close-on-exec.
fn duplicate(file: &File, cloexec: bool) -> io::Result<OwnedFd> {
    let command = if cloexec {
        libc::F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC
    } else {
        libc::F_DUPFD
    };
    // SAFETY: F_DUPFD and F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC create a new descriptor and nothing else.
    let fd = check(unsafe { libc::fcntl(file.as_raw_fd(), command, 100) })?;
    // SAFETY: `fcntl` just created this descriptor, and nothing else owns it.
    Ok(unsafe { OwnedFd::from_raw_fd(fd) })
}

F_DUPFD duplicates a descriptor without setting FD_CLOEXEC, whereas F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC sets the flag atomically during duplication. Requesting the lowest free slot at or above 100 isolates the test descriptors from low-numbered descriptors allocated by the child executable itself.

child_has inspects the child’s inherited descriptor table by executing ls /dev/fd and capturing its standard output through a pipe:

/// Run `program` with its standard output on a pipe, and return what it wrote.
fn output(program: &Program) -> io::Result<String> {
    let (read_end, write_end) = pipe()?;
    let child = spawn(program, None, Some(write_end.as_raw_fd()))?;
    drop(write_end);

    let mut text = String::new();
    File::from(read_end).read_to_string(&mut text)?;
    wait(child)?;
    Ok(text)
}

output drops the parent’s write_end immediately after spawn so that read_to_string observes EOF once the child exits.

/// Whether a child started with `exec` has descriptor `fd` open.
fn child_has(fd: &OwnedFd) -> io::Result<bool> {
    let listing = output(&Program::new(&["ls", "/dev/fd"]))?;
    let number = fd.as_raw_fd().to_string();
    Ok(listing
        .split_whitespace()
        .any(|name| name == number))
}
fd 100 without close-on-exec, open in the child: true
fd 101 with close-on-exec,    open in the child: false

Setting FD_CLOEXEC via a separate fcntl call after pipe introduces a concurrency window: in a multithreaded process, another thread executing fork and exec between pipe and fcntl leaks both pipe ends into its child. Linux eliminates this race with atomic creation flags: pipe2(fds, O_CLOEXEC), open(..., O_CLOEXEC), socket(..., SOCK_CLOEXEC, ...), and accept4(..., SOCK_CLOEXEC). Rust’s standard library uses these atomic variants wherever the target kernel provides them.

24.5 The complete program

Listing 24.1 The descriptor table, ls | wc -l by hand, and close-on-exec. src/bin/fd_table.rs

//! The file descriptor table: how a process numbers its open files, what a
//! child inherits across `fork` and `exec`, and how a shell joins two programs
//! with a pipe.
//!
//! Run with: cargo run --bin fd_table

use std::{
    ffi::CString,
    fs::{self, File},
    io::{self, Read, Write},
    os::fd::{AsRawFd, FromRawFd, OwnedFd, RawFd},
    path::Path,
    thread,
    time::Duration,
};

/// The descriptors open in this process, read from `/dev/fd`.
///
/// Reading the directory opens one more descriptor, which is in the list.
fn open_fds() -> io::Result<Vec<RawFd>> {
    let mut fds: Vec<RawFd> = fs::read_dir("/dev/fd")?
        .filter_map(Result::ok)
        .filter_map(|entry| entry.file_name().to_str()?.parse().ok())
        .collect();
    fds.sort_unstable();
    Ok(fds)
}

/// Turn a C return value into an `io::Result`: -1 means `errno` holds the error.
fn check(result: libc::c_int) -> io::Result<libc::c_int> {
    if result == -1 {
        Err(io::Error::last_os_error())
    } else {
        Ok(result)
    }
}

/// Set close-on-exec on `fd`, so a program started with `exec` does not get it.
fn set_cloexec(fd: RawFd) -> io::Result<()> {
    // SAFETY: F_SETFD changes only the descriptor's flags.
    check(unsafe { libc::fcntl(fd, libc::F_SETFD, libc::FD_CLOEXEC) })?;
    Ok(())
}

/// A pipe as (read end, write end). Both ends are close-on-exec.
fn pipe() -> io::Result<(OwnedFd, OwnedFd)> {
    let mut ends = [0; 2];
    // SAFETY: `pipe` writes two new descriptors into the array.
    check(unsafe { libc::pipe(ends.as_mut_ptr()) })?;
    // SAFETY: both descriptors were just created, and nothing else owns them.
    let (read_end, write_end) =
        unsafe { (OwnedFd::from_raw_fd(ends[0]), OwnedFd::from_raw_fd(ends[1])) };
    set_cloexec(read_end.as_raw_fd())?;
    set_cloexec(write_end.as_raw_fd())?;
    Ok((read_end, write_end))
}

/// A copy of `file`'s descriptor, numbered 100 or above, with or without
/// close-on-exec.
fn duplicate(file: &File, cloexec: bool) -> io::Result<OwnedFd> {
    let command = if cloexec {
        libc::F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC
    } else {
        libc::F_DUPFD
    };
    // SAFETY: F_DUPFD and F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC create a new descriptor and nothing else.
    let fd = check(unsafe { libc::fcntl(file.as_raw_fd(), command, 100) })?;
    // SAFETY: `fcntl` just created this descriptor, and nothing else owns it.
    Ok(unsafe { OwnedFd::from_raw_fd(fd) })
}

/// A program name and its arguments, as C strings.
struct Program(Vec<CString>);

impl Program {
    fn new(args: &[&str]) -> Self {
        Self(
            args.iter()
                .map(|arg| CString::new(*arg).expect("no NUL byte in an argument"))
                .collect(),
        )
    }

    /// The null-terminated pointer array `execvp` takes. It borrows `self`.
    fn argv(&self) -> Vec<*const libc::c_char> {
        self.0
            .iter()
            .map(|arg| arg.as_ptr())
            .chain(std::iter::once(std::ptr::null()))
            .collect()
    }
}

/// Start `program` in a child process. `stdin` and `stdout`, when given,
/// become the child's descriptors 0 and 1. Returns the child's process id.
fn spawn(
    program: &Program,
    stdin: Option<RawFd>,
    stdout: Option<RawFd>,
) -> io::Result<libc::pid_t> {
    // Allocate before `fork`: the child may only make async-signal-safe calls.
    let argv = program.argv();

    // SAFETY: the child below calls only dup2, execvp, and _exit.
    let pid = check(unsafe { libc::fork() })?;
    if pid > 0 {
        return Ok(pid);
    }

    // SAFETY: this is the child, a copy of the parent with one thread. dup2 copies
    // a descriptor without its close-on-exec flag; execvp replaces the program.
    unsafe {
        if let Some(fd) = stdin {
            libc::dup2(fd, 0);
        }
        if let Some(fd) = stdout {
            libc::dup2(fd, 1);
        }
        libc::execvp(argv[0], argv.as_ptr());
        libc::_exit(127)
    }
}

/// Wait for the child `pid` to exit, and return its exit status.
fn wait(pid: libc::pid_t) -> io::Result<i32> {
    let mut status = 0;
    // SAFETY: `waitpid` writes the status into the integer it is given.
    check(unsafe { libc::waitpid(pid, &mut status, 0) })?;
    Ok(libc::WEXITSTATUS(status))
}

/// Whether the child `pid` has exited, without waiting for it.
fn has_exited(pid: libc::pid_t) -> io::Result<bool> {
    let mut status = 0;
    // SAFETY: as in `wait`; WNOHANG returns 0 at once if the child is running.
    let result = check(unsafe { libc::waitpid(pid, &mut status, libc::WNOHANG) })?;
    Ok(result == pid)
}

/// Run `program` with its standard output on a pipe, and return what it wrote.
fn output(program: &Program) -> io::Result<String> {
    let (read_end, write_end) = pipe()?;
    let child = spawn(program, None, Some(write_end.as_raw_fd()))?;
    drop(write_end);

    let mut text = String::new();
    File::from(read_end).read_to_string(&mut text)?;
    wait(child)?;
    Ok(text)
}

/// `ls dir | wc -l`, built the way a shell builds it. `wc` writes to this
/// process's standard output.
fn ls_wc(dir: &Path) -> io::Result<()> {
    let ls = Program::new(&["ls", dir.to_str().expect("UTF-8 path")]);
    let wc = Program::new(&["wc", "-l"]);

    let (read_end, write_end) = pipe()?;
    let writer = spawn(&ls, None, Some(write_end.as_raw_fd()))?;
    let reader = spawn(&wc, Some(read_end.as_raw_fd()), None)?;
    drop(read_end);
    drop(write_end);

    wait(writer)?;
    wait(reader)?;
    Ok(())
}

/// Start `wc -l` on a pipe, write two lines into it, and keep the write end
/// open for `hold`. Returns whether `wc` was still running when `hold` ended.
fn reader_waits_for_the_write_end(hold: Duration) -> io::Result<bool> {
    let wc = Program::new(&["wc", "-l"]);
    let (read_end, write_end) = pipe()?;
    let reader = spawn(&wc, Some(read_end.as_raw_fd()), None)?;
    drop(read_end);

    let mut writer = File::from(write_end);
    writer.write_all(b"one\ntwo\n")?;
    thread::sleep(hold);
    let still_running = !has_exited(reader)?;

    drop(writer);
    wait(reader)?;
    Ok(still_running)
}

/// Whether a child started with `exec` has descriptor `fd` open.
fn child_has(fd: &OwnedFd) -> io::Result<bool> {
    let listing = output(&Program::new(&["ls", "/dev/fd"]))?;
    let number = fd.as_raw_fd().to_string();
    Ok(listing
        .split_whitespace()
        .any(|name| name == number))
}

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    let dir = std::env::temp_dir().join("fd_table_demo");
    fs::create_dir_all(&dir)?;
    for name in ["a.txt", "b.txt", "c.txt"] {
        fs::write(dir.join(name), name)?;
    }
    let path = dir.join("a.txt");

    println!("open at start: {:?}", open_fds()?);
    let first = File::open(&path)?;
    let second = File::open(&path)?;
    println!(
        "opened two files: fd {} and fd {}",
        first.as_raw_fd(),
        second.as_raw_fd()
    );
    let freed = first.as_raw_fd();
    drop(first);
    let third = File::open(&path)?;
    println!(
        "closed fd {freed}, opened another: fd {}\n",
        third.as_raw_fd()
    );

    println!("ls fd_table_demo | wc -l");
    ls_wc(&dir)?;

    println!("\nparent writes two lines to wc -l and holds the write end for 1 s:");
    let still_running = reader_waits_for_the_write_end(Duration::from_secs(1))?;
    println!("wc still running after 1 s: {still_running}\n");

    let leaked = duplicate(&third, false)?;
    let kept = duplicate(&third, true)?;
    println!(
        "fd {} without close-on-exec, open in the child: {}",
        leaked.as_raw_fd(),
        child_has(&leaked)?
    );
    println!(
        "fd {} with close-on-exec,    open in the child: {}",
        kept.as_raw_fd(),
        child_has(&kept)?
    );

    fs::remove_dir_all(&dir)
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn a_child_writes_through_a_pipe() {
        let text = output(&Program::new(&["echo", "through the pipe"])).expect("run echo");
        assert_eq!(text, "through the pipe\n");
    }

    #[test]
    fn close_on_exec_decides_what_a_child_inherits() {
        let file = File::open("/dev/null").expect("open /dev/null");
        let leaked = duplicate(&file, false).expect("dup");
        let kept = duplicate(&file, true).expect("dup");
        assert!(child_has(&leaked).expect("ls"));
        assert!(!child_has(&kept).expect("ls"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn a_reader_waits_while_any_write_end_is_open() {
        let still_running = reader_waits_for_the_write_end(Duration::from_millis(200)).expect("wc");
        assert!(still_running);
    }
}
