24.6 Questions that come up

“What does 2>&1 do?” In the child process between fork and exec, the shell executes dup2(1, 2). Descriptor 2 then references the same open file description as descriptor 1, routing standard error to the same destination and shared offset as standard output.

“Why does yes | head -1 stop?” After reading one line, head exits and the kernel closes its descriptor table, dropping the pipe read-end reference count to zero. The next write by yes triggers SIGPIPE, terminating yes. Because the Rust runtime ignores SIGPIPE by default, a Rust writer instead receives io::ErrorKind::BrokenPipe (EPIPE).

“Why is fork slow for a large process, and what replaces it?” Although fork shares physical pages via copy-on-write, it must still duplicate the parent’s page table hierarchy. For a process with tens of gigabytes mapped, copying page tables takes milliseconds and temporarily degrades memory throughput via CoW faults. posix_spawn and vfork launch a child executable without duplicating the parent’s page tables; std::process::Command selects posix_spawn or vfork where the platform supports them.

“A server restarted and failed with EADDRINUSE. The old process is gone. What holds the port?” A surviving child process may have inherited the listening socket because FD_CLOEXEC was omitted; lsof -i :PORT or ss -tulpn identifies the owning PID. Alternatively, residual connections in TIME_WAIT may occupy the port unless the new listener enables SO_REUSEADDR.

“What does Too many open files mean?” The process has exhausted its RLIMIT_NOFILE descriptor table limit (EMFILE). Inspecting /proc/PID/fd on Linux reveals the leaked descriptor class, typically unclosed network sockets or files opened inside a loop without proper RAII cleanup.

Summary

  • A file descriptor indexes a per-process table whose entries reference kernel open file descriptions; each description stores the current file offset and status flags and points to the underlying inode or socket.
  • open allocates the lowest free descriptor index; dup2 binds a target index to an existing open file description, sharing its offset.
  • fork performs a shallow copy of the descriptor table, incrementing reference counts on all shared open file descriptions; exec preserves all entries except those marked FD_CLOEXEC.
  • Between fork and exec, a child of a multithreaded process may invoke only async-signal-safe system calls to avoid deadlocking on locks held by vanished threads.
  • A pipe reader observes EOF only when the buffer is empty and every write-end descriptor across all processes is closed; a leaked write end causes an indefinite read block.
  • Rust’s standard library sets FD_CLOEXEC on all descriptors it creates. Raw libc descriptors must set the flag explicitly, preferring atomic creation flags (O_CLOEXEC, SOCK_CLOEXEC, pipe2) to prevent multithreaded inheritance races.

Exercises

  1. Execute fd_table with standard input closed: cargo run --bin fd_table <&-. Which descriptor index does the first File::open return, and which allocation rule explains the result?
  2. Read a prefix of bytes from a file, then invoke spawn to run cat with that file’s descriptor bound to standard input. Does cat emit the entire file or only the unread remainder? Justify the behavior using Figure 24.2.
  3. Remove drop(write_end) from output and run the test suite. Identify which test hangs and which system call blocks indefinitely.
  4. Generalize ls_wc into a pipeline builder accepting an arbitrary slice of commands (such as ls | sort | wc -l). For n commands, how many pipes are created and how many pipe descriptors must the parent close?
  5. Replace pipe plus fcntl with pipe2(..., O_CLOEXEC) under #[cfg(target_os = "linux")], retaining the two-call implementation for non-Linux targets.

Edge-triggered epoll

This chapter covers

  • Readiness semantics as a persistent level versus a state-transition edge, and their implementation on the epoll ready list
  • Quantitative comparison of three socket handlers: single-read level-triggered, single-read edge-triggered, and drain-to-EAGAIN edge-triggered
  • The edge-triggered stall condition: unread kernel buffer data with no future readiness notification
  • Write-readiness efficiency under EPOLLET and bounded drain quotas to prevent single-connection starvation
  • Serializing per-socket dispatch across shared-instance worker threads with EPOLLONESHOT
  • Mitigating the accept thundering herd across per-thread event loops with EPOLLEXCLUSIVE and SO_REUSEPORT

An I/O multiplexer reports socket readiness under one of two semantic contracts: level-triggered notification, which reports a descriptor on every epoll_wait invocation while its readiness predicate remains true, or edge-triggered notification (EPOLLET), which reports a descriptor once per arrival transition. Edge-triggered mode reduces kernel re-evaluation overhead and permits persistent EPOLLOUT registration, but it imposes a strict non-blocking drain invariant: every handler must consume readiness until EAGAIN, or residual bytes remain stranded in the kernel receive buffer with no subsequent wakeup.

Because epoll is a Linux kernel subsystem, the accompanying epoll_edge benchmark runs inside a Linux container. It injects 10,000 bytes into a socket pair to measure exact event and byte counts across three handler designs, then verifies the concurrency guarantees of EPOLLONESHOT and EPOLLEXCLUSIVE.

25.1 Levels and edges

A socket satisfies the readable predicate whenever its kernel receive buffer contains at least one unread byte (or an EOF/error condition is pending). This predicate is a persistent state, or level: it remains asserted until read calls empty the buffer. The arrival of new bytes from the peer or network stack constitutes a state transition, or edge.

Level-triggered epoll reports the level: each call to epoll_wait returns the descriptor as long as unread bytes remain. Edge-triggered epoll reports only the edge: a single notification fires upon arrival, and no further event is delivered until additional bytes arrive.

This divergence arises directly from how the kernel maintains the epoll ready list introduced in Section 20.4 (Figure 25.1). When data arrives on a monitored socket, a kernel wait-queue callback enqueues the descriptor onto the epoll instance’s ready list. epoll_wait dequeues ready entries and copies them to user space. For a level-triggered entry, the kernel reinserts the descriptor onto the ready list before returning, causing the subsequent epoll_wait to re-poll the socket’s readiness predicate and report it again if unread bytes remain. For an edge-triggered entry, the kernel does not reinsert the descriptor; only a future arrival callback can enqueue it again.

The table below traces event delivery when 10,000 bytes arrive in a single burst and a handler reads at most 4,096 bytes per notification:

StepBytes in the bufferLevel-triggeredEdge-triggered
10,000 bytes arrive10,000eventevent
handler reads 4,0965,904event: still readablenothing
handler reads 4,0961,808event: still readablen/a
handler reads 1,8080nothingn/a

Under edge-triggered mode, 5,904 bytes remain unread in the receive buffer after the first event, yet the descriptor is absent from the ready list. If the peer is awaiting a protocol response to those 10,000 bytes before transmitting again, both endpoints block indefinitely in a classic liveness stall. Correctness under EPOLLET therefore requires a non-blocking socket drained in a loop until read returns EAGAIN, proving that the receive buffer is empty.

25.2 Three handlers, measured

The Linux epoll interface comprises three system calls and the epoll_event descriptor structure, which carries interest flags into epoll_ctl and triggered events out of epoll_wait:

struct epoll_event {
    events: u32, // EPOLLIN, EPOLLOUT, EPOLLET, ... combined with |
    u64: u64,    // data the caller chooses; the program stores the fd
}

unsafe extern "C" {
    fn epoll_create1(flags: c_int) -> c_int; // a new instance's fd; EPOLL_CLOEXEC
    fn epoll_ctl(
        epfd: c_int,                // the instance
        op: c_int,                  // EPOLL_CTL_ADD, EPOLL_CTL_MOD, or EPOLL_CTL_DEL
        fd: c_int,                  // the descriptor to watch
        event: *mut epoll_event,    // its flags
    ) -> c_int;                     // 0, or -1 with errno set
    fn epoll_wait(
        epfd: c_int,
        events: *mut epoll_event,   // an array the kernel fills
        maxevents: c_int,           // its length
        timeout: c_int,             // milliseconds; -1 waits forever
    ) -> c_int;                     // how many entries were filled, or -1
}

The Epoll wrapper owns the epoll file descriptor and closes it deterministically on drop:

#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]
mod linux {
    use std::{
        io::{self, Read, Write},
        net::{TcpListener, TcpStream},
        os::{
            fd::{AsRawFd, FromRawFd, OwnedFd, RawFd},
            unix::net::UnixStream,
        },
        sync::{Arc, Barrier},
        thread,
        time::Duration,
    };

    /// How long `epoll_wait` waits before the program decides no event is coming.
    const QUIET_MS: i32 = 100;

    /// An epoll instance. Closed when dropped.
    pub struct Epoll(OwnedFd);

    impl Epoll {
        pub fn new() -> io::Result<Self> {
            // SAFETY: epoll_create1 takes no pointers, and the result is checked.
            let fd = unsafe { libc::epoll_create1(libc::EPOLL_CLOEXEC) };
            if fd < 0 {
                return Err(io::Error::last_os_error());
            }
            // SAFETY: the descriptor was just created, and nothing else owns it.
            Ok(Self(unsafe { OwnedFd::from_raw_fd(fd) }))
        }

        fn control(&self, op: libc::c_int, fd: RawFd, flags: u32) -> io::Result<()> {
            let mut event = libc::epoll_event {
                events: flags,
                u64: fd as u64,
            };
            // SAFETY: `event` is a valid epoll_event that outlives the call.
            let result = unsafe { libc::epoll_ctl(self.0.as_raw_fd(), op, fd, &mut event) };
            if result < 0 {
                return Err(io::Error::last_os_error());
            }
            Ok(())
        }

        /// Add `fd` to the interest list.
        pub fn add(&self, fd: RawFd, flags: u32) -> io::Result<()> {
            self.control(libc::EPOLL_CTL_ADD, fd, flags)
        }

        /// Change the flags of `fd`. This also re-arms an `EPOLLONESHOT` descriptor.
        pub fn modify(&self, fd: RawFd, flags: u32) -> io::Result<()> {
            self.control(libc::EPOLL_CTL_MOD, fd, flags)
        }

        /// Wait up to `timeout_ms` and return the number of events.
        pub fn wait(&self, timeout_ms: i32) -> io::Result<usize> {
            let mut events = [libc::epoll_event { events: 0, u64: 0 }; 8];
            // SAFETY: `events` is a writable buffer of 8 entries.
            let ready =
                unsafe { libc::epoll_wait(self.0.as_raw_fd(), events.as_mut_ptr(), 8, timeout_ms) };
            if ready < 0 {
                return Err(io::Error::last_os_error());
            }
            Ok(ready as usize)
        }
    }
    // ...
}

epoll_create1(EPOLL_CLOEXEC) allocates the instance with close-on-exec set atomically (Section 24.4). control populates an epoll_event with the requested flag bitmask and descriptor identifier before invoking epoll_ctl. Because each benchmark monitors a single descriptor, wait returns only the event count.

The two read handlers differ solely by the presence of the drain loop:

mod linux {
    // ...
    /// Read once, at most 4,096 bytes, and return how many arrived.
    pub fn read_once(socket: &mut UnixStream) -> io::Result<usize> {
        let mut buffer = [0; 4096];
        socket.read(&mut buffer)
    }

    /// Read until the socket has nothing left (`EAGAIN`), and return the total.
    pub fn read_until_eagain(socket: &mut UnixStream) -> io::Result<usize> {
        let mut buffer = [0; 4096];
        let mut total = 0;
        loop {
            match socket.read(&mut buffer) {
                Ok(0) => return Ok(total),
                Ok(read) => total += read,
                Err(error) if error.kind() == io::ErrorKind::WouldBlock => return Ok(total),
                Err(error) => return Err(error),
            }
        }
    }
    // ...
}

read_once issues a single 4,096-byte read, whereas read_until_eagain loops until the non-blocking socket returns EAGAIN, surfaced in Rust as io::ErrorKind::WouldBlock.

run allocates a connected Unix domain socket pair, writes the 10,000-byte payload into one endpoint, and dispatches readiness events on the non-blocking peer until a 100 ms epoll_wait timeout expires:

mod linux {
    // ...
    /// Write `sent` bytes into one end of a socket pair. Then wait on the other
    /// end with `flags`, and call `handler` once per event, until no event comes.
    /// Returns the bytes `handler` read at each event.
    pub fn run(
        flags: u32,
        sent: usize,
        handler: fn(&mut UnixStream) -> io::Result<usize>,
    ) -> io::Result<Vec<usize>> {
        let (mut writer, mut reader) = UnixStream::pair()?;
        reader.set_nonblocking(true)?;
        let epoll = Epoll::new()?;
        epoll.add(reader.as_raw_fd(), flags)?;
        writer.write_all(&vec![b'x'; sent])?;

        let mut per_event = Vec::new();
        while epoll.wait(QUIET_MS)? > 0 {
            per_event.push(handler(&mut reader)?);
        }
        Ok(per_event)
    }
    // ...
}

UnixStream::pair isolates kernel socket-buffer semantics from network timing jitter. Setting the reading endpoint to non-blocking mode satisfies the precondition for read_until_eagain, and parameterizing run by a function pointer allows identical harness execution across all three configurations.

Animation 25.1 visualizes the three runs side by side.

The container execution reproduces the analytical table from Section 25.1 exactly:

10000 bytes written into a socket; one handler call per epoll event

level-triggered, read once  events 3, bytes per event [4096, 4096, 1808], left unread 0
edge-triggered,  read once  events 1, bytes per event [4096], left unread 5904
edge-triggered,  to EAGAIN  events 1, bytes per event [10000], left unread 0

Level-triggered single-read delivery required three epoll_wait cycles to drain all 10,000 bytes. Edge-triggered single-read delivery stalled with 5,904 bytes stranded in the kernel buffer, whereas draining to EAGAIN consumed all 10,000 bytes in a single event notification.

25.2.1 Why use edge-triggered mode

Edge-triggered notification eliminates redundant kernel work in two hot paths:

  • Elimination of ready-list re-polling. Under level-triggered mode, every partially drained descriptor is reinserted onto the ready list and re-polled by the kernel on each epoll_wait invocation. Under EPOLLET, each arrival transition produces exactly one notification.
  • Persistent EPOLLOUT registration. A TCP socket’s send buffer almost always has available capacity, meaning the socket is continuously writable. Under level-triggered mode (Section 20.4), an event loop must dynamically add EPOLLOUT via epoll_ctl when a write blocks and remove it once flushed, otherwise epoll_wait returns immediately on every iteration in a busy spin. Under edge-triggered mode, the loop registers EPOLLIN | EPOLLOUT | EPOLLET once at connection setup; a write-readiness edge fires only after a write returns EAGAIN and the kernel subsequently drains space in the send buffer.

For these reasons, the mio I/O abstraction layer underlying the Tokio runtime registers Linux sockets in edge-triggered mode by default.

Unbounded draining to EAGAIN introduces a fairness hazard: a high-rate peer transmitting faster than the event loop can consume keeps the handler trapped inside its read loop, starving every other socket on the same thread. Production event loops therefore enforce a per-event byte quota (Figure 25.2). When a handler reaches its quota without observing EAGAIN, it yields the socket onto an internal user-space continuation queue, services the remaining ready descriptors from epoll_wait, and revisits the continuation queue on the next cycle. Tokio applies this same cooperative budgeting mechanism across asynchronous tasks, forcing a task to yield after consuming its per-poll work budget even when its socket remains readable.

25.3 Several threads on one epoll: EPOLLONESHOT

When a pool of worker threads invokes epoll_wait concurrently on a single shared epoll instance, edge-triggered mode permits a race condition that dispatches the same socket to two threads simultaneously:

  1. Data arrives on a socket; Thread A returns from epoll_wait with that descriptor and begins reading.
  2. While Thread A is still servicing the socket, a second packet arrives, generating a new readiness edge and re-enqueuing the descriptor on the ready list.
  3. Thread B returns from epoll_wait with the identical descriptor and invokes read concurrently. The two threads interleave chunks of the same byte stream, corrupting framing and message ordering.

The EPOLLONESHOT flag prevents concurrent per-socket dispatch by atomically disabling the descriptor in the epoll interest list immediately after delivering a single event. The descriptor remains registered, but the kernel suppresses all subsequent notifications until the owning thread finishes processing and explicitly re-arms it with epoll_ctl(..., EPOLL_CTL_MOD, ...). Exclusivity is thereby guaranteed between event delivery and re-arming.

mod linux {
    // ...
    /// Events seen with `EPOLLONESHOT`: after the first write, after a second
    /// write, and after re-arming the descriptor.
    pub fn oneshot() -> io::Result<[usize; 3]> {
        let (mut writer, mut reader) = UnixStream::pair()?;
        reader.set_nonblocking(true)?;
        let epoll = Epoll::new()?;
        let flags = (libc::EPOLLIN | libc::EPOLLET | libc::EPOLLONESHOT) as u32;
        epoll.add(reader.as_raw_fd(), flags)?;

        writer.write_all(b"first")?;
        let first = epoll.wait(QUIET_MS)?;
        read_until_eagain(&mut reader)?;

        writer.write_all(b"second")?;
        let before_rearm = epoll.wait(QUIET_MS)?;
        epoll.modify(reader.as_raw_fd(), flags)?;
        let after_rearm = epoll.wait(QUIET_MS)?;
        Ok([first, before_rearm, after_rearm])
    }
    // ...
}
EPOLLONESHOT: first write 1 event, second write 0 events, after re-arming 1 event

The second write arrived while the descriptor was disarmed, causing epoll_wait to time out with zero events. Upon re-arming via EPOLL_CTL_MOD, the kernel detected the pending readable data and delivered the event immediately. Disarming a descriptor never discards incoming data; bytes remain buffered in the kernel receive queue until the descriptor is re-armed and drained.

25.4 Many waiters on one listener: EPOLLEXCLUSIVE

An alternative multithreaded server architecture assigns each worker thread a private epoll instance and registers the shared listening socket on every instance. When an incoming TCP connection completes the three-way handshake, the listener’s wait-queue callback notifies every registered epoll instance, waking all worker threads simultaneously. One thread succeeds in accept; the remaining threads receive EAGAIN and return to sleep. On a 64-core server, a single incoming connection triggers 64 thread wakeups and 63 wasted accept system calls, a contention pathology known as the thundering herd.

Introduced in Linux 4.5, EPOLLEXCLUSIVE (permitted only with EPOLL_CTL_ADD) registers an epoll instance as an exclusive waiter on the underlying file wait queue. When a connection arrives on the listener, the kernel wakes a single exclusive waiter (or a small bounded subset) rather than broadcasting to every sleeping thread (Figure 25.3).

woken_by_one_connection spawns four worker threads, synchronizes their epoll_ctl registrations with a Barrier, initiates one client connection, and tallies how many threads return from epoll_wait:

mod linux {
    // ...
    /// Start `waiters` threads, each blocked in `epoll_wait` on its own epoll
    /// instance that watches one shared listener. Connect one client, and
    /// return how many threads woke.
    pub fn woken_by_one_connection(waiters: usize, exclusive: bool) -> io::Result<usize> {
        let listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0")?;
        listener.set_nonblocking(true)?;
        let fd = listener.as_raw_fd();
        let flags = if exclusive {
            (libc::EPOLLIN | libc::EPOLLEXCLUSIVE) as u32
        } else {
            libc::EPOLLIN as u32
        };

        let registered = Arc::new(Barrier::new(waiters + 1));
        let threads: Vec<_> = (0..waiters)
            .map(|_| {
                let registered = Arc::clone(&registered);
                thread::spawn(move || -> io::Result<bool> {
                    let epoll = Epoll::new()?;
                    epoll.add(fd, flags)?;
                    registered.wait();
                    Ok(epoll.wait(500)? > 0)
                })
            })
            .collect();

        registered.wait();
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(50));
        let _client = TcpStream::connect(listener.local_addr()?)?;

        let mut woken = 0;
        for thread in threads {
            if thread.join().expect("waiter thread")? {
                woken += 1;
            }
        }
        Ok(woken)
    }
}

The Barrier guarantees that all workers have registered the listener prior to client connection, and the 50 ms delay allows each worker to block inside epoll_wait before the SYN arrives.

4 threads wait on one listener, and one client connects:
  without EPOLLEXCLUSIVE: 4 threads woke
  with EPOLLEXCLUSIVE:    1 thread woke

An orthogonal kernel-level solution is SO_REUSEPORT: each worker thread opens an independent listening socket bound to the identical IP address and port with SO_REUSEPORT enabled prior to bind. The kernel hashes the incoming packet’s four-tuple to route each new connection directly to one listener’s accept queue. Because no two threads share a listening descriptor, cross-thread wakeup contention is eliminated entirely.

25.5 The complete program

Listing 25.1 Level- and edge-triggered handlers, EPOLLONESHOT, and EPOLLEXCLUSIVE. src/bin/epoll_edge.rs

//! Edge-triggered epoll: what it reports, and the handler it needs.
//!
//! Level-triggered epoll reports a socket for as long as it has data.
//! Edge-triggered epoll reports it once per arrival, so a handler that leaves
//! data behind never hears about it again. The program also shows
//! `EPOLLONESHOT`, which disables a descriptor after one event, and
//! `EPOLLEXCLUSIVE`, which wakes one waiter instead of all of them.
//!
//! Linux only. Run with: cargo run --bin epoll_edge

#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]
mod linux {
    use std::{
        io::{self, Read, Write},
        net::{TcpListener, TcpStream},
        os::{
            fd::{AsRawFd, FromRawFd, OwnedFd, RawFd},
            unix::net::UnixStream,
        },
        sync::{Arc, Barrier},
        thread,
        time::Duration,
    };

    /// How long `epoll_wait` waits before the program decides no event is coming.
    const QUIET_MS: i32 = 100;

    /// An epoll instance. Closed when dropped.
    pub struct Epoll(OwnedFd);

    impl Epoll {
        pub fn new() -> io::Result<Self> {
            // SAFETY: epoll_create1 takes no pointers, and the result is checked.
            let fd = unsafe { libc::epoll_create1(libc::EPOLL_CLOEXEC) };
            if fd < 0 {
                return Err(io::Error::last_os_error());
            }
            // SAFETY: the descriptor was just created, and nothing else owns it.
            Ok(Self(unsafe { OwnedFd::from_raw_fd(fd) }))
        }

        fn control(&self, op: libc::c_int, fd: RawFd, flags: u32) -> io::Result<()> {
            let mut event = libc::epoll_event {
                events: flags,
                u64: fd as u64,
            };
            // SAFETY: `event` is a valid epoll_event that outlives the call.
            let result = unsafe { libc::epoll_ctl(self.0.as_raw_fd(), op, fd, &mut event) };
            if result < 0 {
                return Err(io::Error::last_os_error());
            }
            Ok(())
        }

        /// Add `fd` to the interest list.
        pub fn add(&self, fd: RawFd, flags: u32) -> io::Result<()> {
            self.control(libc::EPOLL_CTL_ADD, fd, flags)
        }

        /// Change the flags of `fd`. This also re-arms an `EPOLLONESHOT` descriptor.
        pub fn modify(&self, fd: RawFd, flags: u32) -> io::Result<()> {
            self.control(libc::EPOLL_CTL_MOD, fd, flags)
        }

        /// Wait up to `timeout_ms` and return the number of events.
        pub fn wait(&self, timeout_ms: i32) -> io::Result<usize> {
            let mut events = [libc::epoll_event { events: 0, u64: 0 }; 8];
            // SAFETY: `events` is a writable buffer of 8 entries.
            let ready =
                unsafe { libc::epoll_wait(self.0.as_raw_fd(), events.as_mut_ptr(), 8, timeout_ms) };
            if ready < 0 {
                return Err(io::Error::last_os_error());
            }
            Ok(ready as usize)
        }
    }

    /// Read once, at most 4,096 bytes, and return how many arrived.
    pub fn read_once(socket: &mut UnixStream) -> io::Result<usize> {
        let mut buffer = [0; 4096];
        socket.read(&mut buffer)
    }

    /// Read until the socket has nothing left (`EAGAIN`), and return the total.
    pub fn read_until_eagain(socket: &mut UnixStream) -> io::Result<usize> {
        let mut buffer = [0; 4096];
        let mut total = 0;
        loop {
            match socket.read(&mut buffer) {
                Ok(0) => return Ok(total),
                Ok(read) => total += read,
                Err(error) if error.kind() == io::ErrorKind::WouldBlock => return Ok(total),
                Err(error) => return Err(error),
            }
        }
    }

    /// Write `sent` bytes into one end of a socket pair. Then wait on the other
    /// end with `flags`, and call `handler` once per event, until no event comes.
    /// Returns the bytes `handler` read at each event.
    pub fn run(
        flags: u32,
        sent: usize,
        handler: fn(&mut UnixStream) -> io::Result<usize>,
    ) -> io::Result<Vec<usize>> {
        let (mut writer, mut reader) = UnixStream::pair()?;
        reader.set_nonblocking(true)?;
        let epoll = Epoll::new()?;
        epoll.add(reader.as_raw_fd(), flags)?;
        writer.write_all(&vec![b'x'; sent])?;

        let mut per_event = Vec::new();
        while epoll.wait(QUIET_MS)? > 0 {
            per_event.push(handler(&mut reader)?);
        }
        Ok(per_event)
    }

    /// Events seen with `EPOLLONESHOT`: after the first write, after a second
    /// write, and after re-arming the descriptor.
    pub fn oneshot() -> io::Result<[usize; 3]> {
        let (mut writer, mut reader) = UnixStream::pair()?;
        reader.set_nonblocking(true)?;
        let epoll = Epoll::new()?;
        let flags = (libc::EPOLLIN | libc::EPOLLET | libc::EPOLLONESHOT) as u32;
        epoll.add(reader.as_raw_fd(), flags)?;

        writer.write_all(b"first")?;
        let first = epoll.wait(QUIET_MS)?;
        read_until_eagain(&mut reader)?;

        writer.write_all(b"second")?;
        let before_rearm = epoll.wait(QUIET_MS)?;
        epoll.modify(reader.as_raw_fd(), flags)?;
        let after_rearm = epoll.wait(QUIET_MS)?;
        Ok([first, before_rearm, after_rearm])
    }

    /// Start `waiters` threads, each blocked in `epoll_wait` on its own epoll
    /// instance that watches one shared listener. Connect one client, and
    /// return how many threads woke.
    pub fn woken_by_one_connection(waiters: usize, exclusive: bool) -> io::Result<usize> {
        let listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0")?;
        listener.set_nonblocking(true)?;
        let fd = listener.as_raw_fd();
        let flags = if exclusive {
            (libc::EPOLLIN | libc::EPOLLEXCLUSIVE) as u32
        } else {
            libc::EPOLLIN as u32
        };

        let registered = Arc::new(Barrier::new(waiters + 1));
        let threads: Vec<_> = (0..waiters)
            .map(|_| {
                let registered = Arc::clone(&registered);
                thread::spawn(move || -> io::Result<bool> {
                    let epoll = Epoll::new()?;
                    epoll.add(fd, flags)?;
                    registered.wait();
                    Ok(epoll.wait(500)? > 0)
                })
            })
            .collect();

        registered.wait();
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(50));
        let _client = TcpStream::connect(listener.local_addr()?)?;

        let mut woken = 0;
        for thread in threads {
            if thread.join().expect("waiter thread")? {
                woken += 1;
            }
        }
        Ok(woken)
    }
}

#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]
fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    use linux::{read_once, read_until_eagain, run};

    const SENT: usize = 10_000;
    let level = libc::EPOLLIN as u32;
    let edge = (libc::EPOLLIN | libc::EPOLLET) as u32;

    println!("{SENT} bytes written into a socket; one handler call per epoll event\n");
    let runs = [
        ("level-triggered, read once ", run(level, SENT, read_once)?),
        ("edge-triggered,  read once ", run(edge, SENT, read_once)?),
        (
            "edge-triggered,  to EAGAIN ",
            run(edge, SENT, read_until_eagain)?,
        ),
    ];
    for (name, per_event) in runs {
        let left = SENT - per_event.iter().sum::<usize>();
        println!(
            "{name} events {}, bytes per event {per_event:?}, left unread {left}",
            per_event.len()
        );
    }

    let [first, before, after] = linux::oneshot()?;
    println!(
        "\nEPOLLONESHOT: first write {first} event, second write {before} events, \
         after re-arming {after} event"
    );

    println!("\n4 threads wait on one listener, and one client connects:");
    println!(
        "  without EPOLLEXCLUSIVE: {} threads woke",
        linux::woken_by_one_connection(4, false)?
    );
    println!(
        "  with EPOLLEXCLUSIVE:    {} thread woke",
        linux::woken_by_one_connection(4, true)?
    );
    Ok(())
}

#[cfg(not(target_os = "linux"))]
fn main() {
    eprintln!("epoll_edge uses Linux epoll; run it on Linux");
}

#[cfg(all(test, target_os = "linux"))]
mod tests {
    use super::linux::*;

    const LEVEL: u32 = libc::EPOLLIN as u32;
    const EDGE: u32 = (libc::EPOLLIN | libc::EPOLLET) as u32;

    #[test]
    fn level_triggered_reports_until_the_data_is_gone() {
        assert_eq!(
            run(LEVEL, 10_000, read_once).expect("run"),
            [4096, 4096, 1808]
        );
    }

    #[test]
    fn edge_triggered_with_one_read_leaves_data_behind() {
        assert_eq!(run(EDGE, 10_000, read_once).expect("run"), [4096]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn edge_triggered_drained_to_eagain_reads_everything() {
        assert_eq!(run(EDGE, 10_000, read_until_eagain).expect("run"), [10_000]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn oneshot_waits_for_a_rearm() {
        assert_eq!(oneshot().expect("oneshot"), [1, 0, 1]);
    }
}
$ cargo run --bin epoll_edge
10000 bytes written into a socket; one handler call per epoll event

level-triggered, read once  events 3, bytes per event [4096, 4096, 1808], left unread 0
edge-triggered,  read once  events 1, bytes per event [4096], left unread 5904
edge-triggered,  to EAGAIN  events 1, bytes per event [10000], left unread 0

EPOLLONESHOT: first write 1 event, second write 0 events, after re-arming 1 event

4 threads wait on one listener, and one client connects:
  without EPOLLEXCLUSIVE: 4 threads woke
  with EPOLLEXCLUSIVE:    1 thread woke

25.6 Questions that come up

“A server under edge-triggered epoll sometimes stops answering one client, while CPU use is zero. What should be checked first?” Audit every read and accept handler to confirm that it loops until EAGAIN (or re-enqueues the descriptor on an application-level continuation list when hitting a drain cap). Terminating a read handler after a fixed buffer fill leaves unread bytes stranded in the kernel receive buffer with no future edge event to trigger dispatch.

“Does edge-triggered mode apply to accept?” Yes. If multiple connections arrive simultaneously in the listen backlog, an edge-triggered listener may fire a single EPOLLIN notification; the handler must therefore call accept in a loop until EAGAIN, matching accept_ready in Section 20.4.

“What happens to an edge-triggered socket when the peer closes it?” Receiving a TCP FIN constitutes a readiness transition. epoll delivers EPOLLIN (along with EPOLLRDHUP if registered), and the subsequent drain loop consumes any remaining buffered bytes before observing read() == 0.

“Is kqueue edge-triggered?” BSD and macOS kqueue supports both semantics per filter registration: EV_CLEAR resets the event state after delivery to provide edge-triggered behavior, and EV_DISPATCH disables the event after delivery to provide EPOLLONESHOT semantics.

“Why not have every thread call accept on one blocking listener?” Modern Linux kernels use exclusive wakeups (WQ_FLAG_EXCLUSIVE) for threads blocked directly inside accept, waking only one thread per connection. The thundering herd re-emerges when multiple private epoll instances register the same listener, because each epoll instance attaches a non-exclusive wait-queue callback unless EPOLLEXCLUSIVE is specified.

Summary

  • Socket readability is a persistent level (non-empty receive buffer); data arrival is a state-transition edge.
  • Level-triggered epoll reinserts reported descriptors onto the ready list and re-polls them on every epoll_wait. Edge-triggered epoll (EPOLLET) delivers one event per arrival transition and does not re-notify until new bytes arrive.
  • Edge-triggered handlers must drain non-blocking sockets until EAGAIN. Reading a single 4,096-byte chunk from a 10,000-byte arrival stranded 5,904 bytes unread with no subsequent notification.
  • EPOLLET eliminates ready-list re-polling and allows persistent EPOLLOUT registration, but requires per-event byte quotas and user-space continuation queues to prevent busy sockets from starving peers.
  • EPOLLONESHOT disarms a descriptor after a single event until re-armed via EPOLL_CTL_MOD, enforcing single-thread ownership in shared-epoll worker pools.
  • EPOLLEXCLUSIVE suppresses the accept thundering herd across per-thread epoll instances (waking 1 of 4 threads rather than all 4); SO_REUSEPORT eliminates shared listeners altogether by hashing connections across per-thread listening sockets.

Exercises

  1. Modify run so that after the edge-triggered single-read stall completes, the writer injects one additional byte, and record the resulting event and byte counts. How many bytes does read_once return on the second event, and why?
  2. Register EPOLLOUT | EPOLLET on a socket in run and count events while no writes occur. Fill the send buffer until write returns WouldBlock, drain bytes from the peer, and verify that a single writable edge fires.
  3. Cap read_until_eagain at 8,192 bytes per invocation and return a boolean indicating whether the cap was reached prior to EAGAIN. Implement a continuation queue in the event loop that services capped descriptors after processing each epoll_wait batch.
  4. Execute woken_by_one_connection with 16 worker threads and 10 sequential connections. Compare total thread wakeups with and without EPOLLEXCLUSIVE.
  5. Reimplement woken_by_one_connection using SO_REUSEPORT (via the socket2 crate before bind) and measure how 10 incoming connections distribute across the worker threads.

Futexes and memory ordering

This chapter covers

  • The Linux futex: a kernel wait queue keyed by the virtual or physical address of a user-space atomic word
  • A three-state sleeping mutex whose uncontended fast path executes entirely in user space without system calls
  • Atomic value verification inside futex_wait and elimination of the lost-wakeup race
  • Empirical system-call and throughput comparison against std::sync::Mutex under single- and multi-threaded contention
  • Hardware store buffers and store-load memory reordering under x86 total store order (TSO)
  • Million-iteration litmus tests for store buffering and message passing across Relaxed, Release/Acquire, and SeqCst

A user-space spin lock (Chapter 16) minimizes latency for nanosecond-scale critical sections, but wastes CPU cycles and degrades scheduling throughput whenever a lock is held across blocking I/O or preempted by the scheduler. Scalable mutual exclusion requires a hybrid design: an uncontended user-space fast path that acquires and releases the lock via single atomic instructions, paired with a kernel-assisted slow path that deschedules contending threads onto a wait queue until release. On Linux, this boundary is implemented by the futex (fast user-space mutex) system call, whose correctness rests directly on the underlying hardware memory model.

Two reference programs examine both layers of synchronization. futex_mutex constructs a three-state sleeping mutex over raw SYS_futex calls, counting exact futex_wait and futex_wake invocations against std::sync::Mutex. litmus executes one million synchronized rounds each of the store-buffering and message-passing litmus tests, measuring hardware memory reordering rates across atomic orderings.

26.1 Sleeping on a word

A futex is a kernel wait queue hashed by the address of a 32-bit atomic word residing in user-space memory. The kernel assigns no semantic meaning to the integer’s value; user space defines the state machine, while the kernel provides two wait-queue primitives:

  • futex_wait(addr, expected): atomically verifies that the 32-bit word at addr still equals expected; if so, it enqueues the calling thread on the kernel wait queue for addr and deschedules it. If the word holds any other value, the call returns immediately with EAGAIN.
  • futex_wake(addr, n): dequeues and wakes up to n threads currently sleeping on the wait queue associated with addr.

Because the lock state word resides in user space (Figure 26.1), acquiring an uncontended lock requires a single atomic compare-and-swap instruction with zero kernel transitions. A thread invokes futex_wait only upon contention, and unlock invokes futex_wake only when the state word indicates that sleeping waiters may exist.

26.1.1 Why the kernel checks the word

futex_wait performs the comparison *addr == expected and wait-queue insertion under the kernel’s internal hash-bucket spinlock. Without that atomic verification, the following interleaving produces a permanent deadlock:

  1. Thread B reads the lock word, observes it held, and decides to sleep.
  2. Thread A releases the lock, updates the word to unlocked, and invokes futex_wake. Because Thread B has not yet entered the wait queue, futex_wake wakes zero threads.
  3. Thread B enters the kernel wait queue and sleeps indefinitely with no future waker.

With the atomic check in place, step 3 detects that *addr != expected, aborts the sleep, and returns immediately so Thread B can retry acquisition. This race is the classic lost wake-up hazard, identical in structure to the reason POSIX condition variables (Condvar, Chapter 16) require an associated mutex.

26.2 A mutex with three states

A minimal sleeping mutex encodes three states in its 32-bit atomic word (Figure 26.2):

  • 0 (UNLOCKED): the lock is free.
  • 1 (LOCKED): the lock is held, with no known contending waiters.
  • 2 (CONTENDED): the lock is held, and one or more threads may be sleeping in futex_wait.

Distinguishing states 1 and 2 enables unlock to elide futex_wake on the uncontended path: transitioning from 1 to 0 requires a single atomic instruction, whereas transitioning from 2 to 0 additionally invokes futex_wake.

26.2.1 The system calls

Because libc exposes no typed wrapper for futex, the program invokes SYS_futex through the generic variadic syscall interface:

unsafe extern "C" {
    fn syscall(number: c_long, ...) -> c_long;
}

// The futex call, as the kernel defines its arguments:
// syscall(SYS_futex, uaddr: *const u32, op: c_int, val: u32, timeout: *const timespec)
//   FUTEX_WAIT: sleep if *uaddr == val, until woken or until the timeout (null: none)
//   FUTEX_WAKE: wake up to val threads sleeping on uaddr; timeout is unused

The wait and wake wrappers encapsulate the raw system calls:

#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]
mod linux {
    use std::{
        cell::UnsafeCell,
        ops::{Deref, DerefMut},
        sync::atomic::{
            AtomicU32,
            AtomicU64,
            Ordering::{Acquire, Relaxed, Release},
        },
    };

    const UNLOCKED: u32 = 0;
    const LOCKED: u32 = 1;
    const CONTENDED: u32 = 2;

    /// Sleep while `word` holds `expected`. The kernel checks the value and
    /// queues the thread as one step, so a wake that happens first is not lost.
    fn futex_wait(word: &AtomicU32, expected: u32) {
        // SAFETY: `word` is a valid, aligned u32 for the whole call, and a null
        // timeout means wait without a time limit.
        unsafe {
            libc::syscall(
                libc::SYS_futex,
                word.as_ptr(),
                libc::FUTEX_WAIT | libc::FUTEX_PRIVATE_FLAG,
                expected,
                std::ptr::null::<libc::timespec>(),
            );
        }
    }

    /// Wake one thread sleeping on `word`, if there is one.
    fn futex_wake_one(word: &AtomicU32) {
        // SAFETY: `word` is a valid, aligned u32 for the whole call.
        unsafe {
            libc::syscall(
                libc::SYS_futex,
                word.as_ptr(),
                libc::FUTEX_WAKE | libc::FUTEX_PRIVATE_FLAG,
                1,
            );
        }
    }
    // ...
}

Passing FUTEX_PRIVATE_FLAG informs the kernel that the futex word is not shared across process address spaces, allowing the kernel to hash the wait queue by virtual address without inspecting shared-memory page tables. AtomicU32::as_ptr yields the stable address of the underlying 32-bit word. futex_wait ignores its return code because callers must already tolerate spurious wakeups (such as EINTR from signal delivery) by re-evaluating the lock word in a loop.

26.2.2 lock and unlock

FutexMutex<T> bundles the 32-bit state word, atomic telemetry counters for wait and wake system calls, and the UnsafeCell<T> holding the protected payload:

mod linux {
    // ...
    /// A mutual-exclusion lock that sleeps in the kernel while it waits.
    pub struct FutexMutex<T> {
        state: AtomicU32,
        waits: AtomicU64,
        wakes: AtomicU64,
        value: UnsafeCell<T>,
    }

    // SAFETY: the lock gives one thread at a time access to `value`, so sharing
    // the mutex is safe whenever `T` may move between threads.
    unsafe impl<T: Send> Sync for FutexMutex<T> {}

    impl<T> FutexMutex<T> {
        pub const fn new(value: T) -> Self {
            Self {
                state: AtomicU32::new(UNLOCKED),
                waits: AtomicU64::new(0),
                wakes: AtomicU64::new(0),
                value: UnsafeCell::new(value),
            }
        }
        // ...
}

As with the spin lock in Chapter 16, unsafe impl Sync upholds the soundness invariant that at most one thread holds a mutable reference to value at any instant. lock returns an RAII Guard that releases the mutex on drop. Acquisition attempts the uncontended fast path before falling back to lock_contended:

mod linux {
    // ...
    impl<T> FutexMutex<T> {
        // ...
        pub fn lock(&self) -> Guard<'_, T> {
            if self
                .state
                .compare_exchange(UNLOCKED, LOCKED, Acquire, Relaxed)
                .is_err()
            {
                self.lock_contended();
            }
            Guard { mutex: self }
        }

        /// The slow path: mark the lock contended, and sleep until it is free.
        fn lock_contended(&self) {
            while self.state.swap(CONTENDED, Acquire) != UNLOCKED {
                self.waits.fetch_add(1, Relaxed);
                futex_wait(&self.state, CONTENDED);
            }
        }

        fn unlock(&self) {
            if self.state.swap(UNLOCKED, Release) == CONTENDED {
                self.wakes.fetch_add(1, Relaxed);
                futex_wake_one(&self.state);
            }
        }
        // ...
    }
    // ...
}

compare_exchange(UNLOCKED, LOCKED, Acquire, Relaxed) claims an uncontended lock in one atomic instruction. On failure, lock_contended executes swap(CONTENDED, Acquire): if the previous state was UNLOCKED (0), the caller has acquired the lock; otherwise, the caller sleeps via futex_wait(CONTENDED) and loops upon wakeup.

A thread acquiring the lock via lock_contended deliberately leaves the state word at CONTENDED (2) even if no other threads remain asleep. Because user space cannot observe the kernel wait queue’s length atomically, preserving state 2 prevents a lost wakeup at the cost of an occasional redundant futex_wake on an empty queue.

unlock executes swap(UNLOCKED, Release), establishing a happens-before relationship that publishes all critical-section writes to the next acquiring thread (Section 16.4.3). If the prior state was CONTENDED, unlock invokes futex_wake(&self.state, 1) to wake a single waiter.

The Guard implementation provides Deref, DerefMut, and automatic unlock in Drop:

mod linux {
    // ...
    /// Access to the value while the lock is held. Unlocks when dropped.
    pub struct Guard<'a, T> {
        mutex: &'a FutexMutex<T>,
    }

    impl<T> Deref for Guard<'_, T> {
        type Target = T;

        fn deref(&self) -> &T {
            // SAFETY: the guard exists only while this thread holds the lock.
            unsafe { &*self.mutex.value.get() }
        }
    }

    impl<T> DerefMut for Guard<'_, T> {
        fn deref_mut(&mut self) -> &mut T {
            // SAFETY: as in `deref`, and `&mut self` makes this the only borrow.
            unsafe { &mut *self.mutex.value.get() }
        }
    }

    impl<T> Drop for Guard<'_, T> {
        fn drop(&mut self) {
            self.mutex.unlock();
        }
    }
}

Animation 26.1 traces two threads across all three states and illustrates the lost-wakeup deadlock when the atomic word check is omitted.

26.2.3 Measured

main executes one million counter increments under both FutexMutex and std::sync::Mutex, partitioned across 1, 2, and 4 threads inside a two-vCPU Linux container:

$ cargo run --release --bin futex_mutex
threads     total    waits    wakes     futex ms       std ms
      1   1000000        0        0         30.8         25.1
      2   1000000    23712    59752         64.4         56.2
      4   1000000    28006    71826         71.0         56.1

At one thread, one million lock-unlock cycles executed with zero kernel transitions, averaging approximately 30 ns per cycle. At two threads, roughly 2.4% of acquisitions entered futex_wait, while futex_wake executed 2.5 times as frequently as futex_wait due to the conservative CONTENDED state preservation in lock_contended.

Although std::sync::Mutex on Linux implements the identical three-state futex protocol, it achieved lower wall-clock latency under contention by performing a brief adaptive spin (up to 100 iterations of relaxed loads) before invoking futex_wait. When critical sections last only a few nanoseconds, short-duration spinning absorbs transient contention without incurring two system calls and a context switch. Because container scheduling introduces 10% or greater variance in wall-clock duration across runs (one four-thread std::sync::Mutex run measured 214 ms), the deterministic waits and wakes counters provide the primary behavioral signal.

26.3 What the hardware reorders

Section 16.2.3 defined the Rust/C++ memory model contracts: Relaxed enforces atomicity without ordering constraints on surrounding memory accesses, Release/Acquire establishes pairwise happens-before edges, and SeqCst enforces a single total modification order across all sequentially consistent operations. Those abstract rules exist because physical processors reorder memory operations to hide cache-coherence latency.

26.3.1 Store buffers

Committing a store directly to a coherent L1 cache stalls the pipeline whenever the target cache line resides exclusively in another core’s cache. To mask this coherence latency, modern superscalar cores enqueue outgoing stores in a private FIFO store buffer and immediately retire subsequent instructions while the store drains asynchronously to cache. A core’s own loads perform store-to-load forwarding from its local store buffer (preserving single-thread program semantics), whereas remote cores observe a store only after it drains into the coherent cache hierarchy.

Consequently, a load to address y that follows a store to address x in program order can execute and read from cache before the earlier store to x becomes globally visible. Figure 26.3 depicts two cores executing this symmetric pattern concurrently: both loads observe the stale value 0 from memory while both stores remain queued in their private store buffers.

Animation 26.2 contrasts one round of store-buffer reordering under Relaxed against the drained serialization enforced by SeqCst.

x86-64 processors implement total store order (TSO): hardware preserves store-store, load-load, and load-store order, permitting only store-load reordering via store buffers. Weakly ordered architectures such as ARM64 (Apple Silicon, AWS Graviton) permit store-store and load-load reordering as well. Independently of hardware strength, optimizing compilers may freely reorder Relaxed memory accesses on any target architecture.

26.3.2 The litmus tests

A litmus test is a minimal two-thread concurrent program designed to detect whether a specific non-sequentially-consistent outcome occurs on target hardware. Each harness allocates fresh atomic variables per round to eliminate reset synchronization and aligns both threads at a spin barrier before every iteration so their memory instructions overlap in time:

use std::{
    sync::atomic::{
        AtomicU32,
        AtomicUsize,
        Ordering::{self, Acquire, Relaxed, Release, SeqCst},
    },
    thread,
};

const ROUNDS: usize = 1_000_000;

/// A fresh, zeroed atomic for every round, so no round needs a reset.
fn zeroed(rounds: usize) -> Vec<AtomicU32> {
    (0..rounds)
        .map(|_| AtomicU32::new(0))
        .collect()
}

/// Wait until both threads have reached `round`. Keeps the two threads on the
/// same round, so their operations overlap in time.
fn meet(arrived: &AtomicUsize, round: usize) {
    arrived.fetch_add(1, SeqCst);
    while arrived.load(SeqCst) < 2 * (round + 1) {
        std::hint::spin_loop();
    }
}

meet implements a single-counter spin barrier: each thread increments the shared counter and spins until the count reaches the threshold for the current round.

The store-buffering (SB) litmus test implements Figure 26.3 directly, counting rounds in which both threads observe 0:

/// Store buffering. Thread 1 stores x and loads y; thread 2 stores y and loads
/// x. Returns the rounds in which both loads read 0.
fn store_buffering(store: Ordering, load: Ordering) -> usize {
    let (x, y) = (zeroed(ROUNDS), zeroed(ROUNDS));
    let (r1, r2) = (zeroed(ROUNDS), zeroed(ROUNDS));
    let arrived = AtomicUsize::new(0);

    thread::scope(|scope| {
        scope.spawn(|| {
            for i in 0..ROUNDS {
                meet(&arrived, i);
                x[i].store(1, store);
                r1[i].store(y[i].load(load), Relaxed);
            }
        });
        scope.spawn(|| {
            for i in 0..ROUNDS {
                meet(&arrived, i);
                y[i].store(1, store);
                r2[i].store(x[i].load(load), Relaxed);
            }
        });
    });

    (0..ROUNDS)
        .filter(|&i| r1[i].load(Relaxed) == 0 && r2[i].load(Relaxed) == 0)
        .count()
}

The message-passing (MP) litmus test publishes a payload word followed by a readiness flag, counting rounds in which the consumer observes the flag set (1) alongside stale payload data (0):

/// Message passing. Thread 1 writes data, then sets a flag; thread 2 reads the
/// flag, then the data. Returns the rounds in which thread 2 saw the flag set
/// but the data still 0.
fn message_passing(store: Ordering, load: Ordering) -> usize {
    let (data, flag) = (zeroed(ROUNDS), zeroed(ROUNDS));
    let (seen_flag, seen_data) = (zeroed(ROUNDS), zeroed(ROUNDS));
    let arrived = AtomicUsize::new(0);

    thread::scope(|scope| {
        scope.spawn(|| {
            for i in 0..ROUNDS {
                meet(&arrived, i);
                data[i].store(42, Relaxed);
                flag[i].store(1, store);
            }
        });
        scope.spawn(|| {
            for i in 0..ROUNDS {
                meet(&arrived, i);
                seen_flag[i].store(flag[i].load(load), Relaxed);
                seen_data[i].store(data[i].load(Relaxed), Relaxed);
            }
        });
    });

    (0..ROUNDS)
        .filter(|&i| seen_flag[i].load(Relaxed) == 1 && seen_data[i].load(Relaxed) == 0)
        .count()
}

Message passing is the foundational synchronization idiom behind locks, channels, and publication queues, relying on a Release store paired with an Acquire load (Section 16.4.3).

Executed on an Intel x86-64 processor:

$ cargo run --release --bin litmus
store buffering, 1000000 rounds: both loads read 0
  Relaxed               14472
  Release / Acquire     15019
  SeqCst                    0

message passing, 1000000 rounds: flag read as 1, data read as 0
  Relaxed                   0
  Release / Acquire         0
  SeqCst                    0

A Linux container on the same host recorded 6,342 and 5,045 store-buffering reorderings, with zero anomalies elsewhere. These measurements confirm three architectural properties:

  • Store-load reordering is empirically frequent. Approximately 1.5% of rounds observed r1 == 0 && r2 == 0 under Relaxed. Upgrading to Release/Acquire produced the same reordering rate: Release prevents prior accesses from moving after a store and Acquire prevents subsequent accesses from moving before a load, but neither prevents a subsequent load from bypassing a prior store.
  • SeqCst eliminates store-load reordering. On x86-64, a SeqCst store compiles to a locked instruction (xchg) or mov followed by mfence, draining the core’s store buffer before subsequent loads issue. Every SeqCst access then participates in a global total order, guaranteeing that at least one store precedes the opposing load.
  • Passing tests on x86-64 do not prove memory-ordering soundness. Message passing recorded zero failures under Relaxed solely because x86-64 TSO forbids hardware store-store and load-load reordering. The Relaxed implementation remains formally incorrect: it fails empirically on ARM64 hardware and permits compiler reordering on all architectures.

26.4 The complete programs

Listing 26.1 A mutex on the futex system call. src/bin/futex_mutex.rs

//! A mutex built on the futex system call.
//!
//! The lock is one 32-bit word with three states: 0 unlocked, 1 locked, and
//! 2 locked with threads that may be asleep waiting for it. Taking a free lock
//! and releasing a lock nobody waits for are single atomic instructions. Only a
//! thread that has to wait, and an unlock that has to wake it, enter the kernel.
//!
//! Linux only. Run with: cargo run --release --bin futex_mutex

#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]
mod linux {
    use std::{
        cell::UnsafeCell,
        ops::{Deref, DerefMut},
        sync::atomic::{
            AtomicU32,
            AtomicU64,
            Ordering::{Acquire, Relaxed, Release},
        },
    };

    const UNLOCKED: u32 = 0;
    const LOCKED: u32 = 1;
    const CONTENDED: u32 = 2;

    /// Sleep while `word` holds `expected`. The kernel checks the value and
    /// queues the thread as one step, so a wake that happens first is not lost.
    fn futex_wait(word: &AtomicU32, expected: u32) {
        // SAFETY: `word` is a valid, aligned u32 for the whole call, and a null
        // timeout means wait without a time limit.
        unsafe {
            libc::syscall(
                libc::SYS_futex,
                word.as_ptr(),
                libc::FUTEX_WAIT | libc::FUTEX_PRIVATE_FLAG,
                expected,
                std::ptr::null::<libc::timespec>(),
            );
        }
    }

    /// Wake one thread sleeping on `word`, if there is one.
    fn futex_wake_one(word: &AtomicU32) {
        // SAFETY: `word` is a valid, aligned u32 for the whole call.
        unsafe {
            libc::syscall(
                libc::SYS_futex,
                word.as_ptr(),
                libc::FUTEX_WAKE | libc::FUTEX_PRIVATE_FLAG,
                1,
            );
        }
    }

    /// A mutual-exclusion lock that sleeps in the kernel while it waits.
    pub struct FutexMutex<T> {
        state: AtomicU32,
        waits: AtomicU64,
        wakes: AtomicU64,
        value: UnsafeCell<T>,
    }

    // SAFETY: the lock gives one thread at a time access to `value`, so sharing
    // the mutex is safe whenever `T` may move between threads.
    unsafe impl<T: Send> Sync for FutexMutex<T> {}

    impl<T> FutexMutex<T> {
        pub const fn new(value: T) -> Self {
            Self {
                state: AtomicU32::new(UNLOCKED),
                waits: AtomicU64::new(0),
                wakes: AtomicU64::new(0),
                value: UnsafeCell::new(value),
            }
        }

        pub fn lock(&self) -> Guard<'_, T> {
            if self
                .state
                .compare_exchange(UNLOCKED, LOCKED, Acquire, Relaxed)
                .is_err()
            {
                self.lock_contended();
            }
            Guard { mutex: self }
        }

        /// The slow path: mark the lock contended, and sleep until it is free.
        fn lock_contended(&self) {
            while self.state.swap(CONTENDED, Acquire) != UNLOCKED {
                self.waits.fetch_add(1, Relaxed);
                futex_wait(&self.state, CONTENDED);
            }
        }

        fn unlock(&self) {
            if self.state.swap(UNLOCKED, Release) == CONTENDED {
                self.wakes.fetch_add(1, Relaxed);
                futex_wake_one(&self.state);
            }
        }

        /// The number of `futex` wait and wake calls this mutex has made.
        pub fn syscalls(&self) -> (u64, u64) {
            (self.waits.load(Relaxed), self.wakes.load(Relaxed))
        }

        pub fn into_inner(self) -> T {
            self.value.into_inner()
        }
    }

    /// Access to the value while the lock is held. Unlocks when dropped.
    pub struct Guard<'a, T> {
        mutex: &'a FutexMutex<T>,
    }

    impl<T> Deref for Guard<'_, T> {
        type Target = T;

        fn deref(&self) -> &T {
            // SAFETY: the guard exists only while this thread holds the lock.
            unsafe { &*self.mutex.value.get() }
        }
    }

    impl<T> DerefMut for Guard<'_, T> {
        fn deref_mut(&mut self) -> &mut T {
            // SAFETY: as in `deref`, and `&mut self` makes this the only borrow.
            unsafe { &mut *self.mutex.value.get() }
        }
    }

    impl<T> Drop for Guard<'_, T> {
        fn drop(&mut self) {
            self.mutex.unlock();
        }
    }
}

#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]
fn main() {
    use std::{
        sync::Mutex,
        thread,
        time::{Duration, Instant},
    };

    use linux::FutexMutex;

    const INCREMENTS: u64 = 1_000_000;

    /// Run `add` INCREMENTS times in total, split across `threads`.
    fn timed(threads: u64, add: &(dyn Fn() + Sync)) -> Duration {
        let start = Instant::now();
        thread::scope(|scope| {
            for _ in 0..threads {
                scope.spawn(|| (0..INCREMENTS / threads).for_each(|_| add()));
            }
        });
        start.elapsed()
    }

    // One untimed pass of each, so neither pays for a cold start in the table.
    let warm = FutexMutex::new(0u64);
    timed(1, &|| *warm.lock() += 1);
    let warm = Mutex::new(0u64);
    timed(1, &|| *warm.lock().unwrap() += 1);

    println!(
        "{:>7} {:>9} {:>8} {:>8} {:>12} {:>12}",
        "threads", "total", "waits", "wakes", "futex ms", "std ms"
    );
    for threads in [1, 2, 4] {
        let futex = FutexMutex::new(0u64);
        let futex_time = timed(threads, &|| *futex.lock() += 1);
        let (waits, wakes) = futex.syscalls();

        let std = Mutex::new(0u64);
        let std_time = timed(threads, &|| *std.lock().unwrap() += 1);
        assert_eq!(std.into_inner().unwrap(), INCREMENTS);

        println!(
            "{threads:>7} {:>9} {waits:>8} {wakes:>8} {:>12.1} {:>12.1}",
            futex.into_inner(),
            futex_time.as_secs_f64() * 1000.0,
            std_time.as_secs_f64() * 1000.0
        );
    }
}

#[cfg(not(target_os = "linux"))]
fn main() {
    eprintln!("futex_mutex uses the Linux futex system call; run it on Linux");
}

#[cfg(all(test, target_os = "linux"))]
mod tests {
    use std::thread;

    use super::linux::FutexMutex;

    #[test]
    fn an_uncontended_lock_makes_no_system_calls() {
        let mutex = FutexMutex::new(0);
        for _ in 0..1000 {
            *mutex.lock() += 1;
        }
        assert_eq!(mutex.syscalls(), (0, 0));
        assert_eq!(mutex.into_inner(), 1000);
    }

    #[test]
    fn contended_increments_are_not_lost() {
        let mutex = FutexMutex::new(0);
        thread::scope(|scope| {
            for _ in 0..8 {
                scope.spawn(|| {
                    for _ in 0..10_000 {
                        *mutex.lock() += 1;
                    }
                });
            }
        });
        assert_eq!(mutex.into_inner(), 80_000);
    }
}

Listing 26.2 Store buffering and message passing, a million rounds each. src/bin/litmus.rs

//! Memory-ordering litmus tests, run many times on real hardware.
//!
//! A litmus test is two short threads and a question: can this combination
//! of results happen? Each test runs a million rounds and counts the rounds
//! that ended with the result in question.
//!
//! Run with: cargo run --release --bin litmus

use std::{
    sync::atomic::{
        AtomicU32,
        AtomicUsize,
        Ordering::{self, Acquire, Relaxed, Release, SeqCst},
    },
    thread,
};

const ROUNDS: usize = 1_000_000;

/// A fresh, zeroed atomic for every round, so no round needs a reset.
fn zeroed(rounds: usize) -> Vec<AtomicU32> {
    (0..rounds)
        .map(|_| AtomicU32::new(0))
        .collect()
}

/// Wait until both threads have reached `round`. Keeps the two threads on the
/// same round, so their operations overlap in time.
fn meet(arrived: &AtomicUsize, round: usize) {
    arrived.fetch_add(1, SeqCst);
    while arrived.load(SeqCst) < 2 * (round + 1) {
        std::hint::spin_loop();
    }
}

/// Store buffering. Thread 1 stores x and loads y; thread 2 stores y and loads
/// x. Returns the rounds in which both loads read 0.
fn store_buffering(store: Ordering, load: Ordering) -> usize {
    let (x, y) = (zeroed(ROUNDS), zeroed(ROUNDS));
    let (r1, r2) = (zeroed(ROUNDS), zeroed(ROUNDS));
    let arrived = AtomicUsize::new(0);

    thread::scope(|scope| {
        scope.spawn(|| {
            for i in 0..ROUNDS {
                meet(&arrived, i);
                x[i].store(1, store);
                r1[i].store(y[i].load(load), Relaxed);
            }
        });
        scope.spawn(|| {
            for i in 0..ROUNDS {
                meet(&arrived, i);
                y[i].store(1, store);
                r2[i].store(x[i].load(load), Relaxed);
            }
        });
    });

    (0..ROUNDS)
        .filter(|&i| r1[i].load(Relaxed) == 0 && r2[i].load(Relaxed) == 0)
        .count()
}

/// Message passing. Thread 1 writes data, then sets a flag; thread 2 reads the
/// flag, then the data. Returns the rounds in which thread 2 saw the flag set
/// but the data still 0.
fn message_passing(store: Ordering, load: Ordering) -> usize {
    let (data, flag) = (zeroed(ROUNDS), zeroed(ROUNDS));
    let (seen_flag, seen_data) = (zeroed(ROUNDS), zeroed(ROUNDS));
    let arrived = AtomicUsize::new(0);

    thread::scope(|scope| {
        scope.spawn(|| {
            for i in 0..ROUNDS {
                meet(&arrived, i);
                data[i].store(42, Relaxed);
                flag[i].store(1, store);
            }
        });
        scope.spawn(|| {
            for i in 0..ROUNDS {
                meet(&arrived, i);
                seen_flag[i].store(flag[i].load(load), Relaxed);
                seen_data[i].store(data[i].load(Relaxed), Relaxed);
            }
        });
    });

    (0..ROUNDS)
        .filter(|&i| seen_flag[i].load(Relaxed) == 1 && seen_data[i].load(Relaxed) == 0)
        .count()
}

fn main() {
    let orderings = [
        ("Relaxed", Relaxed, Relaxed),
        ("Release / Acquire", Release, Acquire),
        ("SeqCst", SeqCst, SeqCst),
    ];

    println!("store buffering, {ROUNDS} rounds: both loads read 0");
    for (name, store, load) in orderings {
        println!("  {name:<18} {:>8}", store_buffering(store, load));
    }

    println!("\nmessage passing, {ROUNDS} rounds: flag read as 1, data read as 0");
    for (name, store, load) in orderings {
        println!("  {name:<18} {:>8}", message_passing(store, load));
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]

    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn seq_cst_forbids_both_loads_reading_zero() {
        assert_eq!(store_buffering(SeqCst, SeqCst), 0);
