26.5 Questions that come up

“Why not always spin, or always sleep?” Pure spinning burns CPU cycles for the entire duration of a hold and starves other runnable threads when a lock holder is preempted. Pure sleeping incurs two system calls and a context switch (microseconds) even when the lock is released nanoseconds later. Adaptive hybrid locks (brief user-space spinning followed by a futex_wait sleep, as implemented in std::sync::Mutex) optimize for both regimes.

“What is priority inversion, and does a futex help?” Priority inversion occurs when a high-priority thread blocks on a lock held by a low-priority thread while a medium-priority thread preempts the low-priority holder indefinitely. Linux provides priority-inheritance futexes (FUTEX_LOCK_PI), which temporarily elevate the lock holder’s scheduling priority to match the highest-priority waiter until release.

“Can a futex be shared between processes?” Yes. Placing the atomic 32-bit word in a shared memory region (such as a MAP_SHARED mapping from Section 23.2) and omitting FUTEX_PRIVATE_FLAG instructs the kernel to key the wait queue by physical page and offset rather than process-local virtual address.

“When is Relaxed correct?” Relaxed is sound when no other memory access depends on the ordering of the atomic operation (for example, monotonic telemetry counters or unique identifier generation via fetch_add). Whenever an atomic value signals that accompanying memory is initialized or ready, Release/Acquire synchronization is mandatory.

“When is SeqCst needed?” SeqCst is required when correctness depends on a single global total order across distinct atomic variables, as in Dekker’s mutual-exclusion algorithm or work-stealing deque synchronization (the store-buffering pattern). Code structured around mutexes, channels, and pairwise Release/Acquire publication rarely requires SeqCst.

Summary

  • A futex is a kernel wait queue keyed by the address of a 32-bit user-space atomic word. futex_wait atomically verifies the word’s value before descheduling the caller, preventing lost wake-ups.
  • A three-state mutex (UNLOCKED, LOCKED, CONTENDED) executes uncontended acquisition and release with a single atomic instruction each, entering the kernel only to block or wake waiters.
  • One million single-threaded increments incurred zero system calls; under contention, conservative retention of the CONTENDED state produced more futex_wake calls than futex_wait calls.
  • std::sync::Mutex reduces contention overhead relative to a purely sleeping futex by spinning briefly before entering the kernel.
  • Processor store buffers allow a subsequent load to execute before an earlier store drains to coherent cache; x86-64 TSO permits this single reordering, whereas ARM64 permits store-store and load-load reordering as well.
  • Store buffering observed both loads reading 0 in roughly 1.5% of a million rounds under Relaxed and Release/Acquire, and zero times under SeqCst. Message passing recorded zero failures on x86-64 due to TSO, which does not make Relaxed sound.

Exercises

  1. Add an adaptive spin loop to lock_contended (up to 100 Relaxed loads terminating early upon observing UNLOCKED) before executing the first swap. Compare the resulting waits, wakes, and wall-clock timings against the table in Section 26.2.3.
  2. Insert a 50-microsecond busy loop inside the critical section and execute four threads. Compare FutexMutex against the Chapter 16 spin lock in both wall-clock duration and total CPU time (/usr/bin/time -v).
  3. Defeat the expected verification by passing a constant mismatch value (such as 7) to futex_wait. Explain why CPU utilization spikes to 100% per thread.
  4. Change the message-passing test to Relaxed for both threads and execute it on an aarch64 processor. Record the number of reordered rounds.
  5. Implement the load-buffering (LB) litmus test: Thread 1 loads x then stores y = 1, while Thread 2 loads y then stores x = 1. Determine whether r1 == 1 && r2 == 1 is possible under Relaxed on x86-64 and justify the observed result.

Closing TCP connections

This chapter covers

  • Independent full-duplex teardown via TCP’s four-way FIN/ACK handshake
  • Kernel state transitions for active close (FIN_WAIT1, FIN_WAIT2, TIME_WAIT) and passive close (CLOSE_WAIT, LAST_ACK), inspected via /proc/net/tcp
  • TIME_WAIT protocol invariants, the 60-second Linux 2 MSL duration, and ephemeral port exhaustion on high-rate clients
  • SO_REUSEADDR semantics for rebinding a listening port occupied by TIME_WAIT entries
  • CLOSE_WAIT descriptor accumulation caused by servers that fail to close peer-terminated sockets
  • Abrupt termination via TCP RST when closing a socket with unread receive-buffer data or SO_LINGER

A TCP connection is a full-duplex byte stream whose teardown is asymmetric and outlives user-space descriptor closure. When an application calls shutdown or close, the kernel transitions the underlying transmission control block (TCB) through a deterministic state machine that can persist for 60 seconds after the process drops the socket (TIME_WAIT), or indefinitely if a server neglects to close a peer-terminated descriptor (CLOSE_WAIT). Failing to account for these kernel states manifests in production as ephemeral port exhaustion (EADDRNOTAVAIL), restart failures (EADDRINUSE), descriptor exhaustion (EMFILE), and unexpected connection resets (ECONNRESET).

The reference program tcp_close exercises these kernel transitions directly inside a Linux container by parsing /proc/net/tcp after each protocol step, reproducing CLOSE_WAIT leaks, TIME_WAIT bind conflicts, and unread-buffer resets.

27.1 Two directions, two FINs

Because TCP carries two independent, full-duplex byte streams, each direction terminates separately. An endpoint with no further payload to transmit emits a FIN segment, which the peer acknowledges with an ACK; data may continue flowing in the reverse direction (a half-closed connection) until the peer transmits its own FIN and receives the final ACK. Orderly teardown therefore requires four segments: FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK.

The endpoint transmitting the first FIN executes the active close; its peer executes the passive close. The two endpoints traverse disjoint subsets of the TCP state machine (Figure 27.1):

SideStateWaiting for
activeFIN_WAIT1the ACK of its FIN
activeFIN_WAIT2the peer’s FIN
activeTIME_WAITa fixed time, 60 seconds on Linux, before the connection is forgotten
passiveCLOSE_WAITits own program to close the socket
passiveLAST_ACKthe ACK of its FIN

Two of these states depend on local events rather than network arrivals: CLOSE_WAIT persists until the local application closes its socket descriptor, and TIME_WAIT persists until a kernel timer expires. Sections 27.2 and 27.3 analyze both states and their operational failure modes.

27.1.1 Reading the states

Linux exposes active IPv4 TCP control blocks through /proc/net/tcp, emitting one line per socket. The second and third columns encode the local and remote endpoints in hexadecimal (for example, 0100007F:1F90 for 127.0.0.1:8080), and the fourth column encodes the TCP state as a hexadecimal enumeration from 01 (ESTABLISHED) through 0B (CLOSING).

The parser helpers extract endpoint port pairs and map hexadecimal state codes to canonical TCP state names:

#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]
mod linux {
    use std::{
        collections::BTreeMap,
        fs,
        io::{self, Read, Write},
        mem,
        net::{SocketAddr, SocketAddrV4, TcpListener, TcpStream},
        os::fd::{FromRawFd, OwnedFd},
        thread,
        time::Duration,
    };

    /// Long enough for loopback segments to be sent, received, and acknowledged.
    pub const SETTLE: Duration = Duration::from_millis(50);

    /// One line of /proc/net/tcp: local port, remote port, and state.
    struct Entry {
        local: u16,
        remote: u16,
        state: &'static str,
    }

    /// The name of a TCP state, from the number Linux prints for it.
    fn state_name(code: u8) -> &'static str {
        match code {
            0x01 => "ESTABLISHED",
            0x02 => "SYN_SENT",
            0x03 => "SYN_RECV",
            0x04 => "FIN_WAIT1",
            0x05 => "FIN_WAIT2",
            0x06 => "TIME_WAIT",
            0x07 => "CLOSE",
            0x08 => "CLOSE_WAIT",
            0x09 => "LAST_ACK",
            0x0A => "LISTEN",
            0x0B => "CLOSING",
            _ => "UNKNOWN",
        }
    }

    /// The port in an address written as `0100007F:1F90`.
    fn port_of(field: &str) -> Option<u16> {
        let (_, port) = field.split_once(':')?;
        u16::from_str_radix(port, 16).ok()
    }

    /// Every IPv4 TCP socket the kernel knows about.
    fn entries() -> io::Result<Vec<Entry>> {
        let table = fs::read_to_string("/proc/net/tcp")?;
        Ok(table
            .lines()
            .skip(1)
            .filter_map(|line| {
                let fields: Vec<&str> = line.split_whitespace().collect();
                Some(Entry {
                    local: port_of(fields.get(1)?)?,
                    remote: port_of(fields.get(2)?)?,
                    state: state_name(u8::from_str_radix(fields.get(3)?, 16).ok()?),
                })
            })
            .collect())
    }
    // ...
}

entries skips the header row, tokenizes each record on whitespace, and extracts the three target columns; the ? operator inside filter_map discards malformed lines. Because all test traffic traverses 127.0.0.1, the (local_port, remote_port) pair uniquely identifies each socket endpoint.

state queries a single endpoint’s state, and census aggregates state counts across all sockets associated with a server port:

mod linux {
    // ...
    /// The state of the socket whose local and remote ports are `local` and
    /// `remote`, or "gone" if the kernel has forgotten it.
    pub fn state(local: SocketAddr, remote: SocketAddr) -> io::Result<&'static str> {
        Ok(entries()?
            .into_iter()
            .find(|entry| entry.local == local.port() && entry.remote == remote.port())
            .map_or("gone", |entry| entry.state))
    }

    /// How many sockets on the server's `port` are in each state, counting
    /// both the server's side and the clients' side of each connection.
    pub fn census(port: u16) -> io::Result<BTreeMap<&'static str, usize>> {
        let mut counts = BTreeMap::new();
        for entry in entries()? {
            if entry.state != "LISTEN" && (entry.local == port || entry.remote == port) {
                *counts.entry(entry.state).or_insert(0) += 1;
            }
        }
        Ok(counts)
    }

    /// A connected pair over loopback: (client, server's accepted socket).
    pub fn connected(listener: &TcpListener) -> io::Result<(TcpStream, TcpStream)> {
        let client = TcpStream::connect(listener.local_addr()?)?;
        let (server, _) = listener.accept()?;
        Ok((client, server))
    }
    // ...
}

Once the kernel reclaims a TCB, its entry disappears from /proc/net/tcp and state reports gone. connected returns both ends of a loopback TCP pair so a single process can drive and inspect both endpoints deterministically.

27.1.2 A close, step by step

The first scenario executes an orderly half-close sequence: the client closes its write half via shutdown(Write), the server drains until EOF and transmits a reply, and both endpoints drop their descriptors. A 50 ms delay after each step ensures loopback segment delivery completes before /proc/net/tcp is sampled:

1. An orderly close, client first, with a half-close

  step                                   client       server
  connected                              ESTABLISHED  ESTABLISHED
  client shutdown(Write): FIN sent       FIN_WAIT2    CLOSE_WAIT
  server read to end, wrote a reply      FIN_WAIT2    CLOSE_WAIT
  server dropped its socket: FIN sent    TIME_WAIT    gone
  client read the reply, dropped         TIME_WAIT    gone

FIN_WAIT1 is transient on loopback because the peer’s ACK arrives within microseconds, advancing the client TCB directly into FIN_WAIT2 before the poll executes; over a wide-area link with non-trivial round-trip latency, FIN_WAIT1 is directly observable.

Row three demonstrates half-closed duplex operation: the client’s transmit direction is closed while the server’s remains open to deliver the response. When the server drops its socket, the server TCB transmits FIN, transitions through LAST_ACK, and is reclaimed upon receiving the client’s final ACK. The client TCB enters TIME_WAIT and persists in kernel memory even after the client drops its descriptor, demonstrating that TIME_WAIT is owned strictly by the kernel network stack rather than the application process.

Animation 27.1 traces this orderly teardown followed by a server that leaks descriptors in CLOSE_WAIT.

27.2 TIME_WAIT

The active-closing endpoint retains its TCB in TIME_WAIT before releasing the connection’s four-tuple. This mandatory holding interval enforces two transport-layer safety invariants:

  • Reliable delivery of the final ACK. If the final ACK is lost in transit, the passive peer remains in LAST_ACK and retransmits its FIN. An active endpoint still in TIME_WAIT recognizes the retransmitted FIN and re-emits the ACK. Had it purged the TCB immediately, it would reply with RST, causing the peer to observe an error on an orderly close.
  • Isolation from delayed duplicate segments. Packets delayed in the network can arrive after connection teardown. If a new connection immediately reused the identical four-tuple (local IP, local port, remote IP, remote port), stale segments from the previous incarnation could pass sequence checks and corrupt the new byte stream. TIME_WAIT quarantines the four-tuple until delayed segments expire.

RFC 9293 specifies TIME_WAIT as twice the maximum segment lifetime (2 MSL); Linux hardcodes TCP_TIMEWAIT_LEN to 60 seconds.

27.2.1 The cost: ports on a busy client

A TIME_WAIT control block occupies only a few hundred bytes of kernel memory. The constraining resource is four-tuple cardinality. For every outbound connection to a fixed (remote IP, remote port), the client kernel selects a local port from the ephemeral port range (net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range, defaulting to 32,768 through 60,999 on Linux, yielding 28,232 ports). When the client performs the active close, each port remains pinned in TIME_WAIT for 60 seconds, bounding sustained connection churn to roughly 28,232 / 60 ≈ 470 new connections per second per destination endpoint (Figure 27.2). Exceeding this rate exhausts the ephemeral pool and causes connect to fail with EADDRNOTAVAIL.

Three architectural mitigations address client-side ephemeral port exhaustion:

  • Connection reuse. Persistent HTTP keep-alive connections or a bounded client connection pool (Chapter 29) amortize connection setup and eliminate per-request TIME_WAIT churn.
  • Server-initiated active close. Shifting active close onto the server places TIME_WAIT entries on the server side, where all connections share a single listening port and are distinguished by distinct client endpoints.
  • net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse. Enabling this Linux sysctl permits outbound connect calls to reclaim a TIME_WAIT four-tuple safely after one second when TCP timestamps (RFC 7323) guarantee monotonically increasing timestamps relative to the closed incarnation.

27.2.2 Binding a port with connections in TIME_WAIT

When a server initiates active close and subsequently restarts within 60 seconds, residual TIME_WAIT entries still occupy its listening port. By default, bind rejects a new listening socket on that port with EADDRINUSE. Setting SO_REUSEADDR instructs the kernel to permit bind whenever no active LISTEN socket holds the identical (IP, port) pair. Because Rust’s TcpListener::bind enables SO_REUSEADDR automatically on Unix, tcp_close invokes raw libc socket primitives to contrast both configurations:

unsafe extern "C" {
    fn socket(domain: c_int, ty: c_int, protocol: c_int) -> c_int; // AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0
    fn setsockopt(
        fd: c_int,
        level: c_int,          // SOL_SOCKET
        name: c_int,           // SO_REUSEADDR
        value: *const c_void,  // points at the option's value, a c_int here
        len: socklen_t,        // its size in bytes
    ) -> c_int;
    fn bind(fd: c_int, addr: *const sockaddr, len: socklen_t) -> c_int;
}

sockaddr serves as the polymorphic C address header; an IPv4 endpoint is populated in sockaddr_in and passed as a *const sockaddr pointer alongside its byte length:

mod linux {
    // ...
    /// Bind a listening socket to `port` on loopback with raw calls, setting
    /// `SO_REUSEADDR` only if `reuse` is true. `TcpListener::bind` always sets it.
    pub fn bind_raw(port: u16, reuse: bool) -> io::Result<OwnedFd> {
        // SAFETY: socket takes no pointers, and the result is checked.
        let fd = unsafe { libc::socket(libc::AF_INET, libc::SOCK_STREAM | libc::SOCK_CLOEXEC, 0) };
        if fd < 0 {
            return Err(io::Error::last_os_error());
        }
        // SAFETY: the descriptor was just created, and nothing else owns it.
        let socket = unsafe { OwnedFd::from_raw_fd(fd) };

        let enable: libc::c_int = 1;
        let address = SocketAddrV4::new([127, 0, 0, 1].into(), port);
        // SAFETY: sockaddr_in is plain data, and all zeros is a valid value.
        let mut raw: libc::sockaddr_in = unsafe { mem::zeroed() };
        raw.sin_family = libc::AF_INET as libc::sa_family_t;
        raw.sin_port = address.port().to_be();
        raw.sin_addr.s_addr = u32::from_ne_bytes(address.ip().octets());

        // SAFETY: the option value and the address are valid for the lengths
        // passed, and outlive both calls.
        let result = unsafe {
            if reuse {
                libc::setsockopt(
                    fd,
                    libc::SOL_SOCKET,
                    libc::SO_REUSEADDR,
                    (&enable as *const libc::c_int).cast(),
                    mem::size_of::<libc::c_int>() as libc::socklen_t,
                );
            }
            libc::bind(
                fd,
                (&raw as *const libc::sockaddr_in).cast(),
                mem::size_of::<libc::sockaddr_in>() as libc::socklen_t,
            )
        };
        if result < 0 {
            return Err(io::Error::last_os_error());
        }
        Ok(socket)
    }
    // ...
}

The third scenario closes a connection server-first, drops the listener, and attempts to rebind the port with SO_REUSEADDR disabled and enabled:

3. TIME_WAIT on the server's port, and binding it again

  server closed first, then the client: {"TIME_WAIT": 1}
  bind port again, SO_REUSEADDR false: Address already in use (os error 98)
  bind port again, SO_REUSEADDR true : bound

A single residual TIME_WAIT entry suffices to block an unconfigured bind call.

27.3 CLOSE_WAIT

Upon receiving a peer’s FIN, the passive endpoint transitions to CLOSE_WAIT and remains there indefinitely until its owning process invokes close (or shutdown(Write)). The kernel cannot unilaterally exit CLOSE_WAIT, because only the application knows whether it still intends to transmit response bytes before closing its half of the stream.

A server that neglects to drop accepted sockets after clients disconnect accumulates CLOSE_WAIT sockets for the lifetime of the process, pinning one file descriptor per leaked connection. Common root causes include read handlers that ignore a 0-byte EOF return, connection maps that omit eviction on error paths, and reference-counting cycles (Rc/Arc) that retain socket owners indefinitely.

leaky_server reproduces this pathology by retaining five accepted sockets in a Vec while all five clients connect and immediately close:

mod linux {
    // ...
    /// A server that accepts `clients` connections and never closes them,
    /// while each client connects and closes at once. Returns the listener's
    /// port and the accepted sockets, still open.
    pub fn leaky_server(clients: usize) -> io::Result<(u16, Vec<TcpStream>)> {
        let listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0")?;
        let port = listener.local_addr()?.port();
        let mut kept = Vec::new();
        for _ in 0..clients {
            let (client, server) = connected(&listener)?;
            drop(client);
            kept.push(server);
        }
        thread::sleep(SETTLE);
        Ok((port, kept))
    }
    // ...
}
2. A server that never closes what clients closed

  while the server keeps 5 sockets: {"CLOSE_WAIT": 5, "FIN_WAIT2": 5}
  after the server drops them:      {"TIME_WAIT": 5}

All five connections stalled mid-teardown: the clients remained in FIN_WAIT2 awaiting the server’s FIN, while the server held five sockets in CLOSE_WAIT. Dropping the server’s Vec transmitted five FIN segments and transitioned the client endpoints into TIME_WAIT. Because the clients had already closed their local descriptors, Linux would otherwise bound such orphaned FIN_WAIT2 sockets with net.ipv4.tcp_fin_timeout (defaulting to 60 seconds) before reclaiming them.

In production diagnostics, ss -tan state close-wait enumerates all CLOSE_WAIT sockets across the host. A monotonically increasing CLOSE_WAIT count indicates a descriptor leak in the owning server process that will eventually terminate new connections with EMFILE (Section 24.1).

27.4 Reset instead of FIN

When a process closes a TCP socket whose kernel receive buffer still holds unread bytes, the kernel aborts orderly teardown and transmits a reset (RST) segment instead of a FIN, signaling data loss to the peer. The peer’s subsequent read fails with ECONNRESET (“Connection reset by peer”), and any unread bytes queued in the peer’s receive buffer are discarded:

mod linux {
    // ...
    /// The client writes bytes the server never reads, then the server closes.
    /// Returns what the client's next read reports.
    pub fn close_with_unread_data() -> io::Result<io::Result<usize>> {
        let listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0")?;
        let (mut client, server) = connected(&listener)?;
        client.write_all(b"a request the server never reads")?;
        thread::sleep(SETTLE);
        drop(server);
        thread::sleep(SETTLE);
        Ok(client.read(&mut [0; 64]))
    }
}
4. Closing with unread data

  client read failed: Connection reset by peer (os error 104)

This mechanism causes a subtle failure mode in HTTP servers. If a server rejects an oversized request by writing an HTTP 413 response and immediately calling close while unread request-body bytes remain in the kernel receive buffer, the resulting RST can overtake or flush the response on the client, causing the client to report ECONNRESET instead of reading the HTTP error status. Production servers prevent this race via a lingering close: after writing the error response, the server invokes shutdown(Write) to transmit FIN, drains and discards incoming request bytes for a bounded interval, and only then closes the descriptor.

An application can also trigger an immediate RST explicitly by enabling SO_LINGER with l_onoff = 1 and l_linger = 0 before closing. This bypasses TIME_WAIT and forces ECONNRESET on the peer; although edge proxies occasionally use it to shed abusive connections rapidly, it discards unsent data in the send buffer and violates orderly transport semantics.

27.5 The complete program

Listing 27.1 The states of a closing connection, read from /proc/net/tcp. src/bin/tcp_close.rs

//! Closing a TCP connection: the states each side passes through, `TIME_WAIT`
//! on the side that closes first, the `CLOSE_WAIT` sockets a server keeps when
//! it never closes, and the reset that replaces `FIN` when data goes unread.
//!
//! Linux only: the states are read from /proc/net/tcp.
//! Run with: cargo run --bin tcp_close

#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]
mod linux {
    use std::{
        collections::BTreeMap,
        fs,
        io::{self, Read, Write},
        mem,
        net::{SocketAddr, SocketAddrV4, TcpListener, TcpStream},
        os::fd::{FromRawFd, OwnedFd},
        thread,
        time::Duration,
    };

    /// Long enough for loopback segments to be sent, received, and acknowledged.
    pub const SETTLE: Duration = Duration::from_millis(50);

    /// One line of /proc/net/tcp: local port, remote port, and state.
    struct Entry {
        local: u16,
        remote: u16,
        state: &'static str,
    }

    /// The name of a TCP state, from the number Linux prints for it.
    fn state_name(code: u8) -> &'static str {
        match code {
            0x01 => "ESTABLISHED",
            0x02 => "SYN_SENT",
            0x03 => "SYN_RECV",
            0x04 => "FIN_WAIT1",
            0x05 => "FIN_WAIT2",
            0x06 => "TIME_WAIT",
            0x07 => "CLOSE",
            0x08 => "CLOSE_WAIT",
            0x09 => "LAST_ACK",
            0x0A => "LISTEN",
            0x0B => "CLOSING",
            _ => "UNKNOWN",
        }
    }

    /// The port in an address written as `0100007F:1F90`.
    fn port_of(field: &str) -> Option<u16> {
        let (_, port) = field.split_once(':')?;
        u16::from_str_radix(port, 16).ok()
    }

    /// Every IPv4 TCP socket the kernel knows about.
    fn entries() -> io::Result<Vec<Entry>> {
        let table = fs::read_to_string("/proc/net/tcp")?;
        Ok(table
            .lines()
            .skip(1)
            .filter_map(|line| {
                let fields: Vec<&str> = line.split_whitespace().collect();
                Some(Entry {
                    local: port_of(fields.get(1)?)?,
                    remote: port_of(fields.get(2)?)?,
                    state: state_name(u8::from_str_radix(fields.get(3)?, 16).ok()?),
                })
            })
            .collect())
    }

    /// The state of the socket whose local and remote ports are `local` and
    /// `remote`, or "gone" if the kernel has forgotten it.
    pub fn state(local: SocketAddr, remote: SocketAddr) -> io::Result<&'static str> {
        Ok(entries()?
            .into_iter()
            .find(|entry| entry.local == local.port() && entry.remote == remote.port())
            .map_or("gone", |entry| entry.state))
    }

    /// How many sockets on the server's `port` are in each state, counting
    /// both the server's side and the clients' side of each connection.
    pub fn census(port: u16) -> io::Result<BTreeMap<&'static str, usize>> {
        let mut counts = BTreeMap::new();
        for entry in entries()? {
            if entry.state != "LISTEN" && (entry.local == port || entry.remote == port) {
                *counts.entry(entry.state).or_insert(0) += 1;
            }
        }
        Ok(counts)
    }

    /// A connected pair over loopback: (client, server's accepted socket).
    pub fn connected(listener: &TcpListener) -> io::Result<(TcpStream, TcpStream)> {
        let client = TcpStream::connect(listener.local_addr()?)?;
        let (server, _) = listener.accept()?;
        Ok((client, server))
    }

    /// Bind a listening socket to `port` on loopback with raw calls, setting
    /// `SO_REUSEADDR` only if `reuse` is true. `TcpListener::bind` always sets it.
    pub fn bind_raw(port: u16, reuse: bool) -> io::Result<OwnedFd> {
        // SAFETY: socket takes no pointers, and the result is checked.
        let fd = unsafe { libc::socket(libc::AF_INET, libc::SOCK_STREAM | libc::SOCK_CLOEXEC, 0) };
        if fd < 0 {
            return Err(io::Error::last_os_error());
        }
        // SAFETY: the descriptor was just created, and nothing else owns it.
        let socket = unsafe { OwnedFd::from_raw_fd(fd) };

        let enable: libc::c_int = 1;
        let address = SocketAddrV4::new([127, 0, 0, 1].into(), port);
        // SAFETY: sockaddr_in is plain data, and all zeros is a valid value.
        let mut raw: libc::sockaddr_in = unsafe { mem::zeroed() };
        raw.sin_family = libc::AF_INET as libc::sa_family_t;
        raw.sin_port = address.port().to_be();
        raw.sin_addr.s_addr = u32::from_ne_bytes(address.ip().octets());

        // SAFETY: the option value and the address are valid for the lengths
        // passed, and outlive both calls.
        let result = unsafe {
            if reuse {
                libc::setsockopt(
                    fd,
                    libc::SOL_SOCKET,
                    libc::SO_REUSEADDR,
                    (&enable as *const libc::c_int).cast(),
                    mem::size_of::<libc::c_int>() as libc::socklen_t,
                );
            }
            libc::bind(
                fd,
                (&raw as *const libc::sockaddr_in).cast(),
                mem::size_of::<libc::sockaddr_in>() as libc::socklen_t,
            )
        };
        if result < 0 {
            return Err(io::Error::last_os_error());
        }
        Ok(socket)
    }

    /// A server that accepts `clients` connections and never closes them,
    /// while each client connects and closes at once. Returns the listener's
    /// port and the accepted sockets, still open.
    pub fn leaky_server(clients: usize) -> io::Result<(u16, Vec<TcpStream>)> {
        let listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0")?;
        let port = listener.local_addr()?.port();
        let mut kept = Vec::new();
        for _ in 0..clients {
            let (client, server) = connected(&listener)?;
            drop(client);
            kept.push(server);
        }
        thread::sleep(SETTLE);
        Ok((port, kept))
    }

    /// The client writes bytes the server never reads, then the server closes.
    /// Returns what the client's next read reports.
    pub fn close_with_unread_data() -> io::Result<io::Result<usize>> {
        let listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0")?;
        let (mut client, server) = connected(&listener)?;
        client.write_all(b"a request the server never reads")?;
        thread::sleep(SETTLE);
        drop(server);
        thread::sleep(SETTLE);
        Ok(client.read(&mut [0; 64]))
    }
}

#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]
fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    use std::{
        io::{Read, Write},
        net::{Shutdown, TcpListener},
        thread,
    };

    use linux::{SETTLE, census, connected, state};

    println!("1. An orderly close, client first, with a half-close\n");
    let listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0")?;
    let (mut client, mut server) = connected(&listener)?;
    let (c, s) = (client.local_addr()?, server.local_addr()?);
    let show = |step: &str| -> std::io::Result<()> {
        thread::sleep(SETTLE);
        println!("  {step:<38} {:<12} {}", state(c, s)?, state(s, c)?);
        Ok(())
    };
    println!("  {:<38} {:<12} server", "step", "client");
    show("connected")?;
    client.shutdown(Shutdown::Write)?;
    show("client shutdown(Write): FIN sent")?;
    let mut request = Vec::new();
    server.read_to_end(&mut request)?;
    server.write_all(b"reply")?;
    show("server read to end, wrote a reply")?;
    drop(server);
    show("server dropped its socket: FIN sent")?;
    let mut reply = String::new();
    client.read_to_string(&mut reply)?;
    drop(client);
    show("client read the reply, dropped")?;

    println!("\n2. A server that never closes what clients closed\n");
    let (port, kept) = linux::leaky_server(5)?;
    println!("  while the server keeps 5 sockets: {:?}", census(port)?);
    drop(kept);
    thread::sleep(SETTLE);
    println!("  after the server drops them:      {:?}", census(port)?);

    println!("\n3. TIME_WAIT on the server's port, and binding it again\n");
    let listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0")?;
    let port = listener.local_addr()?.port();
    let (client, server) = connected(&listener)?;
    drop(server);
    thread::sleep(SETTLE);
    drop(client);
    drop(listener);
    thread::sleep(SETTLE);
    println!(
        "  server closed first, then the client: {:?}",
        census(port)?
    );
    for reuse in [false, true] {
        let outcome = match linux::bind_raw(port, reuse) {
            Ok(_) => "bound".to_string(),
            Err(error) => error.to_string(),
        };
        println!("  bind port again, SO_REUSEADDR {reuse:<5}: {outcome}");
    }

    println!("\n4. Closing with unread data\n");
    match linux::close_with_unread_data()? {
        Ok(read) => println!("  client read returned {read}"),
        Err(error) => println!("  client read failed: {error}"),
    }
    Ok(())
}

#[cfg(not(target_os = "linux"))]
fn main() {
    eprintln!("tcp_close reads TCP states from Linux's /proc/net/tcp; run it on Linux");
}

#[cfg(all(test, target_os = "linux"))]
mod tests {
    use std::{io::ErrorKind, net::TcpListener, thread};

    use super::linux::*;

    #[test]
    fn the_side_that_closes_first_holds_time_wait() {
        let listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0").expect("bind");
        let (client, server) = connected(&listener).expect("connect");
        let (c, s) = (client.local_addr().unwrap(), server.local_addr().unwrap());
        drop(server);
        thread::sleep(SETTLE);
        drop(client);
        thread::sleep(SETTLE);
        assert_eq!(state(s, c).expect("state"), "TIME_WAIT");
        assert_eq!(state(c, s).expect("state"), "gone");
    }

    #[test]
    fn a_server_that_never_closes_holds_close_wait() {
        let (port, _kept) = leaky_server(3).expect("server");
        assert_eq!(
            census(port)
                .expect("census")
                .get("CLOSE_WAIT"),
            Some(&3)
        );
    }

    #[test]
    fn unread_data_turns_close_into_reset() {
        let error = close_with_unread_data()
            .expect("setup")
            .expect_err("read should fail");
        assert_eq!(error.kind(), ErrorKind::ConnectionReset);
    }
}

  server read to end, wrote a reply      FIN_WAIT2    CLOSE_WAIT
  server dropped its socket: FIN sent    TIME_WAIT    gone
  client read the reply, dropped         TIME_WAIT    gone

2. A server that never closes what clients closed

  while the server keeps 5 sockets: {"CLOSE_WAIT": 5, "FIN_WAIT2": 5}
  after the server drops them:      {"TIME_WAIT": 5}

  server closed first, then the client: {"TIME_WAIT": 1}
  bind port again, SO_REUSEADDR false: Address already in use (os error 98)
  bind port again, SO_REUSEADDR true : bound

4. Closing with unread data

  client read failed: Connection reset by peer (os error 104)

27.6 Questions that come up

“A server has 30,000 sockets in TIME_WAIT. Is that a problem?” Rarely on a server. Each TIME_WAIT entry occupies a few hundred bytes of kernel memory and all share the server’s listening port without consuming ephemeral ports. The same count on a client targeting a single upstream endpoint exhausts the 28,232-port ephemeral range and causes EADDRNOTAVAIL.

“A server has 3,000 sockets in CLOSE_WAIT and the number keeps rising. What happened?” Remote peers closed their write directions, and the server process failed to close its descriptors. Audit read loops for ignored 0-byte EOF returns, connection registries that omit cleanup on error paths, and reference cycles retaining TcpStream instances.

“Why not shorten TIME_WAIT?” Linux fixes TCP_TIMEWAIT_LEN at 60 seconds as a compile-time kernel constant to uphold RFC 9293’s 2 MSL guarantee. Eliminating client-side TIME_WAIT churn is properly addressed through persistent connection pooling or net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse with TCP timestamps enabled.

“What is the difference between shutdown(Write) and close?” shutdown(Write) transmits a FIN to close the outbound byte stream while keeping the descriptor open for reading (and affects all duplicated descriptors referencing that socket). close removes a single descriptor table entry; the kernel transmits FIN (or RST if unread data remains) only when the open file description’s reference count reaches zero.

“Both sides send FIN at the same moment. What happens?” Both endpoints transition from FIN_WAIT1 into the simultaneous-close state CLOSING upon receiving the peer’s FIN, and then into TIME_WAIT upon receiving the peer’s ACK.

Summary

  • Each direction of a full-duplex TCP connection terminates independently via FIN and ACK, requiring four segments for complete teardown.
  • Active close traverses FIN_WAIT1, FIN_WAIT2, and TIME_WAIT; passive close traverses CLOSE_WAIT and LAST_ACK.
  • TIME_WAIT lasts 60 seconds on Linux (2 MSL) to retransmit lost final ACKs and prevent delayed duplicate segments from corrupting a reused four-tuple.
  • On a high-rate client, TIME_WAIT pins ephemeral ports, capping throughput at roughly 470 new connections per second per destination unless connections are reused.
  • SO_REUSEADDR permits a restarting server to bind a port still referenced by TIME_WAIT entries; TcpListener::bind enables it automatically on Unix.
  • CLOSE_WAIT persists until the local application closes the socket; unbounded CLOSE_WAIT growth signals a descriptor leak culminating in EMFILE.
  • Closing a socket with unread receive-buffer bytes (or SO_LINGER with a zero timeout) transmits RST instead of FIN, surfacing as ECONNRESET on the peer.

Exercises

  1. Insert thread::sleep(Duration::from_secs(61)) at the end of scenario 1 and re-query the client’s /proc/net/tcp state. Confirm that the TIME_WAIT entry has been reclaimed.
  2. Invert leaky_server so the server performs active close while clients retain their descriptors open. Identify which side enters FIN_WAIT2, which enters CLOSE_WAIT, and which transitions to TIME_WAIT upon client drop.
  3. Open and close 1,000 loopback connections sequentially from the client side and print census; repeat with the server closing first and compare the resulting state distributions.
  4. In close_with_unread_data, drain the client’s bytes on the server prior to dropping the server socket. Record the new return value of the client’s read.
  5. Configure SO_LINGER with { l_onoff: 1, l_linger: 0 } via libc::setsockopt on the server socket in scenario 1 before dropping it. Identify which TCP states vanish and what error the client’s read reports.

TLS and mutual TLS

This chapter covers

  • Transport Layer Security (TLS) guarantees over TCP: confidentiality, authenticated integrity, and cryptographic peer authentication
  • X.509 certificates, certificate authorities (CAs), trust stores, and the three mandatory verification checks
  • The single-round-trip TLS 1.3 handshake and wire-level record framing inspected byte by byte
  • Configuring a rustls client and server with ephemeral X.509 certificates generated via rcgen
  • Handshake failure diagnostics for hostname mismatch and untrusted issuer chains
  • Mutual TLS (mTLS) client authentication, CertificateRequired alerts, and certificate rotation lifecycles

Unencrypted TCP transmits payloads in plaintext across every intermediate router and network link, providing neither confidentiality against passive eavesdropping nor integrity against active tampering or endpoint impersonation. Transport Layer Security (TLS) inserts a cryptographic record and handshake layer directly above TCP, providing three formal security guarantees: confidentiality via symmetric authenticated encryption (AEAD), integrity via per-record authentication tags that detect modification or truncation, and endpoint authentication via X.509 public-key certificates.

The reference program tls_mtls constructs a self-contained public-key infrastructure (PKI) in memory using rcgen and executes five TLS 1.3 scenarios over loopback with rustls: standard server-authenticated TLS, hostname-mismatch rejection, untrusted-CA rejection, mutual TLS rejection of an unauthenticated client, and mutual TLS with a verified client certificate.

28.1 Certificates and trust

TLS establishes cryptographic identity using asymmetric (public-key) cryptography. An endpoint generates a key pair comprising a confidential private key and a publicly distributed public key. A digital signature computed with the private key can be verified by any party holding the corresponding public key, yet cannot be forged without possessing the private key.

An X.509 certificate is a digitally signed assertion binding a subject’s identity (such as a DNS name) and validity window (not_before to not_after) to a public key. The signing entity is a certificate authority (CA), and each verifying party maintains a trust store of trusted root CA certificates. Upon receiving a server’s certificate chain during a handshake, the client enforces three mandatory verification invariants (Figure 28.1):

  1. Signature chain validation. Every certificate in the chain carries a valid signature from its issuer, terminating at a root CA present in the client’s trust store.
  2. Temporal validity. The current wall-clock time falls within every certificate’s [not_before, not_after] interval.
  3. Subject identity match. At least one Subject Alternative Name (SAN) in the leaf certificate matches the target hostname requested by the client.

Because certificates are transmitted publicly, presenting a valid certificate alone does not prove ownership. During the handshake, the server additionally signs a cryptographic hash of the entire handshake transcript with its private key (CertificateVerify), proving live possession of the private key bound to the certificate’s public key.

On the public internet, operating systems and browsers ship trust stores containing hundreds of commercial root CAs. Within private infrastructure and service meshes, organizations operate internal CAs that issue short-lived certificates exclusively for internal service-to-service traffic, mirroring the structure of tls_mtls.

28.1.1 Making the certificates

The rcgen crate generates asymmetric key pairs and X.509 certificates programmatically. Pki synthesizes a self-signed root CA and uses it to sign distinct leaf certificates for the server (localhost) and the client (billing):

use std::{
    io::{self, Read, Write},
    net::{TcpListener, TcpStream},
    sync::{Arc, Mutex},
    thread,
};

use rcgen::{BasicConstraints, CertificateParams, DnType, IsCa, KeyPair};
use rustls::{
    ClientConfig,
    ClientConnection,
    RootCertStore,
    ServerConfig,
    ServerConnection,
    StreamOwned,
    crypto::{CryptoProvider, ring},
    pki_types::{CertificateDer, PrivateKeyDer, PrivatePkcs8KeyDer, ServerName},
    server::WebPkiClientVerifier,
};

type Error = Box<dyn std::error::Error + Send + Sync>;

/// A certificate and the private key that goes with it.
struct Identity {
    cert: CertificateDer<'static>,
    key: PrivatePkcs8KeyDer<'static>,
}

impl Identity {
    fn key(&self) -> PrivateKeyDer<'static> {
        PrivateKeyDer::Pkcs8(self.key.clone_key())
    }
}

/// A certificate authority, and certificates it signed for a server and a client.
struct Pki {
    ca: CertificateDer<'static>,
    server: Identity,
    client: Identity,
}

impl Pki {
    fn new() -> Result<Self, Error> {
        let ca_key = KeyPair::generate()?;
        let mut ca_params = CertificateParams::new(Vec::<String>::new())?;
        ca_params.is_ca = IsCa::Ca(BasicConstraints::Unconstrained);
        ca_params
            .distinguished_name
            .push(DnType::CommonName, "lab CA");
        let ca = ca_params.self_signed(&ca_key)?;

        let issue = |name: &str| -> Result<Identity, Error> {
            let key = KeyPair::generate()?;
            let mut params = CertificateParams::new(vec![name.to_string()])?;
            params
                .distinguished_name
                .push(DnType::CommonName, name);
            let cert = params.signed_by(&key, &ca, &ca_key)?;
            Ok(Identity {
                cert: cert.der().clone(),
                key: PrivatePkcs8KeyDer::from(key.serialize_der()),
            })
        };
        let server = issue("localhost")?;
        let client = issue("billing")?;
        Ok(Self {
            ca: ca.der().clone(),
            server,
            client,
        })
    }

    /// A trust store holding only this CA.
    fn roots(&self) -> Result<RootCertStore, Error> {
        let mut roots = RootCertStore::empty();
        roots.add(self.ca.clone())?;
        Ok(roots)
    }
}

Setting IsCa::Ca authorizes the root certificate to sign subordinate certificates, and self_signed signs the root with its own private key; clients trust a root CA strictly by explicit inclusion in their trust store. CertificateParams::new populates the SAN entries for each leaf certificate, and signed_by certifies the leaf public key using the CA’s signing key. roots constructs a RootCertStore trusting solely this local CA.

28.2 The TLS 1.3 handshake

Before transmitting application data, the endpoints execute a handshake to negotiate cipher suites, derive shared symmetric keys, and authenticate identities. TLS 1.3 completes this protocol in a single network round trip (1-RTT):

StepFromMessagesEncrypted
1clientClientHello: cipher suites, a key share, and the server’s name (SNI)no
2serverServerHello: the chosen suite and the server’s key shareno
3serverCertificate, CertificateVerify (the signature), Finishedyes
4clientFinishedyes

Following step 2, both endpoints combine their local ephemeral private value with the peer’s public key share via elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE) to derive identical symmetric handshake keys with forward secrecy; a passive observer recording the wire cannot compute these keys. Every handshake message subsequent to ServerHello (including the server’s certificate) is encrypted under those keys. The client validates the certificate chain, CertificateVerify signature, and Finished MAC in step 3 before transmitting its own Finished message and initial application payload in step 4.

TLS encapsulates all handshake messages, alerts, and application payloads into records. Each record begins with an unencrypted 5-byte header: a 1-byte content type (22 for handshake, 23 for application data), a 2-byte legacy protocol version (0x0303), and a 2-byte big-endian payload length.

28.2.1 Watching the wire

To inspect wire-level framing without external packet capture, Tap wraps the client’s TcpStream and records a copy of every outbound byte. records parses the captured stream header by header:

/// A TCP stream that keeps a copy of every byte it sends.
struct Tap {
    stream: TcpStream,
    sent: Arc<Mutex<Vec<u8>>>,
}

impl Read for Tap {
    fn read(&mut self, buffer: &mut [u8]) -> io::Result<usize> {
        self.stream.read(buffer)
    }
}

impl Write for Tap {
    fn write(&mut self, buffer: &[u8]) -> io::Result<usize> {
        let written = self.stream.write(buffer)?;
        self.sent
            .lock()
            .expect("tap lock")
            .extend_from_slice(&buffer[..written]);
        Ok(written)
    }

    fn flush(&mut self) -> io::Result<()> {
        self.stream.flush()
    }
}

/// The TLS records in a byte stream, as (content type, length) pairs.
fn records(mut bytes: &[u8]) -> Vec<(&'static str, usize)> {
    let mut found = Vec::new();
    while let [kind, _, _, high, low, rest @ ..] = bytes {
        let length = usize::from(*high) << 8 | usize::from(*low);
        let name = match kind {
            20 => "change_cipher_spec",
            21 => "alert",
            22 => "handshake",
            23 => "application_data",
            _ => "unknown",
        };
        found.push((name, length));
        bytes = rest.get(length..).unwrap_or_default();
    }
    found
}

The slice pattern [kind, _, _, high, low, rest @ ..] matches while at least five header bytes remain, extracting the record type and big-endian length. rest.get(length..) advances past the record body and returns None if the buffer terminates mid-record.

28.2.2 A client and a server

rustls decouples cryptographic state machines (ClientConnection and ServerConnection) from transport I/O. StreamOwned composes a TLS state machine with any type implementing std::io::Read and std::io::Write, driving the handshake automatically on the first I/O call.

Builder methods assemble immutable ServerConfig and ClientConfig structures, explicitly selecting the ring cryptographic provider:

fn main() -> Result<(), Error> {
    let pki = Pki::new()?;
    let server_only = || -> Result<ServerConfig, Error> {
        Ok(ServerConfig::builder_with_provider(provider())
            .with_safe_default_protocol_versions()?
            .with_no_client_auth()
            .with_single_cert(vec![pki.server.cert.clone()], pki.server.key())?)
    };
    let client_trusting = |roots: RootCertStore| -> Result<ClientConfig, Error> {
        Ok(ClientConfig::builder_with_provider(provider())
            .with_safe_default_protocol_versions()?
            .with_root_certificates(roots)
            .with_no_client_auth())
    };
    // ...
}

with_safe_default_protocol_versions enables TLS 1.3 and TLS 1.2 while excluding deprecated protocol versions. with_no_client_auth configures unidirectional authentication: the server authenticates to the client, and no client certificate is requested.

The server accepts a single connection, uppercases one message, and performs an authenticated shutdown:

/// Accept one connection, and answer one message in capitals. Returns what
/// the server learned about the client, or the error that ended the handshake.
fn serve_once(listener: TcpListener, config: Arc<ServerConfig>) -> thread::JoinHandle<String> {
    thread::spawn(move || {
        let outcome = || -> Result<String, Error> {
            let (stream, _) = listener.accept()?;
            let mut tls = StreamOwned::new(ServerConnection::new(config)?, stream);
            let mut message = [0; 64];
            let read = tls.read(&mut message)?;
            tls.write_all(&message[..read].to_ascii_uppercase())?;
            tls.conn.send_close_notify();
            tls.flush()?;
            Ok(match tls.conn.peer_certificates() {
                Some(chain) => format!("client presented {} verified certificate", chain.len()),
                None => "client presented no certificate".to_string(),
            })
        };
        outcome().unwrap_or_else(|error| format!("handshake failed: {error}"))
    })
}

Invoking send_close_notify transmits a cryptographically authenticated close_notify alert prior to closing the TCP socket. Without this alert, an active attacker could inject a forged TCP FIN to truncate a response prematurely; rustls therefore surfaces an unauthenticated EOF as an unexpected end-of-file error.

The client connects through Tap, transmits hello over tls, and reads the server’s reply:

/// What one client connection saw.
struct Session {
    version: String,
    suite: String,
    reply: String,
    sent: Vec<u8>,
}

/// Connect to `listener` with `config`, expecting the server to be `name`,
/// send one message, and read the reply.
fn connect(listener: &TcpListener, config: ClientConfig, name: &str) -> Result<Session, Error> {
    let sent = Arc::new(Mutex::new(Vec::new()));
    let tap = Tap {
        stream: TcpStream::connect(listener.local_addr()?)?,
        sent: Arc::clone(&sent),
    };
    let name = ServerName::try_from(name.to_string())?;
    let mut tls = StreamOwned::new(ClientConnection::new(Arc::new(config), name)?, tap);

    tls.write_all(b"hello over tls")?;
    let mut reply = String::new();
    tls.read_to_string(&mut reply)?;

    Ok(Session {
        version: format!(
            "{:?}",
            tls.conn
                .protocol_version()
                .ok_or("no version")?
        ),
        suite: format!(
            "{:?}",
            tls.conn
                .negotiated_cipher_suite()
                .ok_or("no suite")?
                .suite()
        ),
        reply,
        sent: sent.lock().expect("tap lock").clone(),
    })
}

ServerName serves two roles: rustls transmits it in the ClientHello Server Name Indication (SNI) extension and verifies it against the SANs in the server’s certificate.

Animation 28.1 traces this standard TLS 1.3 exchange followed by the mutual TLS scenarios of Section 28.4.

Scenario 1 verifies normal TLS 1.3 negotiation and wire-level encryption:

1. The client checks the server's certificate
  client: TLSv1_3 TLS13_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, reply "HELLO OVER TLS"
  client sent records: [("handshake", 231), ("change_cipher_spec", 1), ("application_data", 69), ("application_data", 31)]
  "hello" readable on the wire: false
  server: client presented no certificate

The client transmitted four records:

  • handshake (231 bytes): the unencrypted ClientHello record containing cipher suites, key share, and SNI.
  • change_cipher_spec (1 byte): a compatibility dummy record retained by RFC 8446 so legacy middleboxes expecting TLS 1.2 state machines do not drop the connection.
  • application_data (69 bytes): the client’s encrypted Finished message; TLS 1.3 wraps all post-ServerHello handshake records in outer type 23 (application_data) to obscure record boundaries from passive observers.
  • application_data (31 bytes): the 14-byte plaintext hello over tls, plus 1 byte encoding the inner content type and a 16-byte AES-256-GCM authentication tag (Figure 28.2).

Scanning the captured byte stream confirms that the plaintext substring "hello" never appears on the wire.

28.3 When the check fails

Scenarios 2 and 3 violate the hostname-identity check and the trusted-CA chain check, respectively:

2. The client expects a different name
  client: invalid peer certificate: certificate not valid for name "billing.example"; certificate is only valid for DnsName("localhost")
  server: handshake failed: unexpected end of file

3. The client does not trust the CA
  client: invalid peer certificate: UnknownIssuer
  server: handshake failed: unexpected end of file

In both cases, the client aborts the handshake at step 3 prior to transmitting any application data and closes the socket, causing the server to observe an unexpected EOF. Although the server’s certificate is structurally well-formed in both runs, rejecting a mismatched hostname or an untrusted issuer prevents man-in-the-middle impersonation.

Encrypting a channel to an unauthenticated peer provides confidentiality against passive observers while remaining completely vulnerable to active interception. Accordingly, rustls provides no boolean toggle to disable verification; bypassing certificate validation requires implementing a custom ServerCertVerifier explicitly gated behind the danger API namespace.

28.4 Mutual TLS

Standard TLS authenticates only the server at the transport layer; clients remain anonymous until they present application-level credentials (such as bearer tokens or passwords) inside the encrypted channel. In mutual TLS (mTLS), the server transmits a CertificateRequest during the handshake, requiring the client to present an X.509 certificate signed by a CA in the server’s trust store alongside a CertificateVerify signature proving possession of the client’s private key.

Internal microservice architectures use mTLS to bind cryptographic caller identities directly to transport connections: once verified, the subject name in the client certificate (billing) serves as an unforgeable principal for authorization policies.

Enabling mTLS on the server attaches a WebPkiClientVerifier configured with the shared CA trust store:

fn main() -> Result<(), Error> {
    // ...
    let verifier =
        WebPkiClientVerifier::builder_with_provider(Arc::new(pki.roots()?), provider()).build()?;
    let mutual = || -> Result<ServerConfig, Error> {
        Ok(ServerConfig::builder_with_provider(provider())
            .with_safe_default_protocol_versions()?
            .with_client_cert_verifier(verifier.clone())
            .with_single_cert(vec![pki.server.cert.clone()], pki.server.key())?)
    };

    println!("\n4. Mutual TLS, client without a certificate");
    run(mutual()?, client_trusting(pki.roots()?)?, "localhost")?;

    println!("\n5. Mutual TLS, client with the billing certificate");
    let client = ClientConfig::builder_with_provider(provider())
        .with_safe_default_protocol_versions()?
        .with_root_certificates(pki.roots()?)
        .with_client_auth_cert(vec![pki.client.cert.clone()], pki.client.key())?;
    run(mutual()?, client, "localhost")
}
4. Mutual TLS, client without a certificate
  client: received fatal alert: CertificateRequired
  server: handshake failed: peer sent no certificates

5. Mutual TLS, client with the billing certificate
  client: TLSv1_3 TLS13_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, reply "HELLO OVER TLS"
  client sent records: [("handshake", 231), ("change_cipher_spec", 1), ("application_data", 481), ("application_data", 31)]
  "hello" readable on the wire: false
  server: client presented 1 verified certificate

In scenario 4, the client lacking a certificate receives a fatal CertificateRequired TLS alert. In scenario 5, presenting the billing certificate expands the client’s encrypted handshake record from 69 bytes to 481 bytes; the additional 412 bytes encode the client’s X.509 certificate and CertificateVerify signature.

Because every X.509 certificate carries a finite validity window, production mTLS deployments automate short-lived certificate issuance and rotation (typically hours or days, as in SPIFFE/SPIRE). Short validity periods bound the blast radius of a compromised private key without requiring global revocation checks on every handshake.

28.4.1 What TLS costs

  • Handshake latency. Establishing a fresh TLS 1.3 connection requires one round trip for the TCP three-way handshake plus one round trip for the TLS handshake (2 RTT total) before the first request departs, exceeding 100 ms across continental regions. Session resumption (pre-shared key tickets) avoids full certificate verification on repeat connections, and persistent connection pools (Chapter 29) amortize handshake latency across thousands of requests.
  • CPU overhead. Asymmetric ECDHE key exchange and digital signatures consume tens to hundreds of microseconds per handshake, whereas hardware-accelerated symmetric AEAD encryption (AES-GCM via AES-NI or ARMv8 Crypto) sustains multi-gigabyte-per-second throughput per core.
  • User-space copies. Because rustls encrypts records in user space, static file servers cannot invoke sendfile directly on a rustls stream without copying payload bytes through user space, unless symmetric encryption is offloaded to kernel TLS (Section 23.3.2).

28.5 The complete program

Listing 28.1 TLS and mutual TLS with rustls, on certificates made by rcgen. src/bin/tls_mtls.rs

//! TLS with rustls: a client that checks the server's certificate, the errors
//! it reports when the check fails, and mutual TLS, where the server checks a
//! certificate from the client as well.
//!
//! The certificates are made at startup with rcgen: one certificate authority,
//! a server certificate for "localhost", and a client certificate for a
//! service called "billing". Nothing secret is stored on disk.
//!
//! Run with: cargo run --bin tls_mtls

use std::{
    io::{self, Read, Write},
    net::{TcpListener, TcpStream},
    sync::{Arc, Mutex},
    thread,
};

use rcgen::{BasicConstraints, CertificateParams, DnType, IsCa, KeyPair};
use rustls::{
    ClientConfig,
    ClientConnection,
    RootCertStore,
    ServerConfig,
    ServerConnection,
    StreamOwned,
    crypto::{CryptoProvider, ring},
    pki_types::{CertificateDer, PrivateKeyDer, PrivatePkcs8KeyDer, ServerName},
    server::WebPkiClientVerifier,
};

type Error = Box<dyn std::error::Error + Send + Sync>;

/// A certificate and the private key that goes with it.
struct Identity {
    cert: CertificateDer<'static>,
    key: PrivatePkcs8KeyDer<'static>,
}

impl Identity {
    fn key(&self) -> PrivateKeyDer<'static> {
        PrivateKeyDer::Pkcs8(self.key.clone_key())
    }
}

/// A certificate authority, and certificates it signed for a server and a client.
struct Pki {
    ca: CertificateDer<'static>,
    server: Identity,
    client: Identity,
}

impl Pki {
    fn new() -> Result<Self, Error> {
        let ca_key = KeyPair::generate()?;
        let mut ca_params = CertificateParams::new(Vec::<String>::new())?;
        ca_params.is_ca = IsCa::Ca(BasicConstraints::Unconstrained);
        ca_params
            .distinguished_name
            .push(DnType::CommonName, "lab CA");
        let ca = ca_params.self_signed(&ca_key)?;

        let issue = |name: &str| -> Result<Identity, Error> {
            let key = KeyPair::generate()?;
            let mut params = CertificateParams::new(vec![name.to_string()])?;
            params
                .distinguished_name
                .push(DnType::CommonName, name);
            let cert = params.signed_by(&key, &ca, &ca_key)?;
            Ok(Identity {
                cert: cert.der().clone(),
                key: PrivatePkcs8KeyDer::from(key.serialize_der()),
            })
        };
        let server = issue("localhost")?;
        let client = issue("billing")?;
        Ok(Self {
            ca: ca.der().clone(),
            server,
            client,
        })
    }

    /// A trust store holding only this CA.
    fn roots(&self) -> Result<RootCertStore, Error> {
        let mut roots = RootCertStore::empty();
        roots.add(self.ca.clone())?;
        Ok(roots)
    }
}

/// The ring crypto provider, named explicitly so the program does not depend
/// on which provider other crates enable.
fn provider() -> Arc<CryptoProvider> {
    Arc::new(ring::default_provider())
}

/// A TCP stream that keeps a copy of every byte it sends.
struct Tap {
    stream: TcpStream,
    sent: Arc<Mutex<Vec<u8>>>,
}

impl Read for Tap {
    fn read(&mut self, buffer: &mut [u8]) -> io::Result<usize> {
        self.stream.read(buffer)
    }
}

impl Write for Tap {
    fn write(&mut self, buffer: &[u8]) -> io::Result<usize> {
        let written = self.stream.write(buffer)?;
        self.sent
            .lock()
            .expect("tap lock")
            .extend_from_slice(&buffer[..written]);
        Ok(written)
    }

    fn flush(&mut self) -> io::Result<()> {
        self.stream.flush()
    }
}

/// The TLS records in a byte stream, as (content type, length) pairs.
fn records(mut bytes: &[u8]) -> Vec<(&'static str, usize)> {
    let mut found = Vec::new();
    while let [kind, _, _, high, low, rest @ ..] = bytes {
        let length = usize::from(*high) << 8 | usize::from(*low);
        let name = match kind {
            20 => "change_cipher_spec",
            21 => "alert",
            22 => "handshake",
            23 => "application_data",
            _ => "unknown",
        };
        found.push((name, length));
        bytes = rest.get(length..).unwrap_or_default();
    }
    found
}

/// Accept one connection, and answer one message in capitals. Returns what
/// the server learned about the client, or the error that ended the handshake.
fn serve_once(listener: TcpListener, config: Arc<ServerConfig>) -> thread::JoinHandle<String> {
    thread::spawn(move || {
        let outcome = || -> Result<String, Error> {
            let (stream, _) = listener.accept()?;
            let mut tls = StreamOwned::new(ServerConnection::new(config)?, stream);
            let mut message = [0; 64];
            let read = tls.read(&mut message)?;
            tls.write_all(&message[..read].to_ascii_uppercase())?;
            tls.conn.send_close_notify();
            tls.flush()?;
            Ok(match tls.conn.peer_certificates() {
                Some(chain) => format!("client presented {} verified certificate", chain.len()),
                None => "client presented no certificate".to_string(),
            })
        };
        outcome().unwrap_or_else(|error| format!("handshake failed: {error}"))
    })
}

/// What one client connection saw.
struct Session {
    version: String,
    suite: String,
    reply: String,
    sent: Vec<u8>,
}

/// Connect to `listener` with `config`, expecting the server to be `name`,
/// send one message, and read the reply.
fn connect(listener: &TcpListener, config: ClientConfig, name: &str) -> Result<Session, Error> {
    let sent = Arc::new(Mutex::new(Vec::new()));
    let tap = Tap {
        stream: TcpStream::connect(listener.local_addr()?)?,
        sent: Arc::clone(&sent),
    };
    let name = ServerName::try_from(name.to_string())?;
    let mut tls = StreamOwned::new(ClientConnection::new(Arc::new(config), name)?, tap);

    tls.write_all(b"hello over tls")?;
    let mut reply = String::new();
    tls.read_to_string(&mut reply)?;

    Ok(Session {
        version: format!(
            "{:?}",
            tls.conn
                .protocol_version()
                .ok_or("no version")?
        ),
        suite: format!(
            "{:?}",
            tls.conn
                .negotiated_cipher_suite()
                .ok_or("no suite")?
                .suite()
        ),
        reply,
        sent: sent.lock().expect("tap lock").clone(),
    })
}

/// Run one client against one server, and print what each side reported.
fn run(server: ServerConfig, client: ClientConfig, name: &str) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0")?;
    let server = serve_once(listener.try_clone()?, Arc::new(server));
    match connect(&listener, client, name) {
        Ok(session) => {
            println!(
                "  client: {} {}, reply {:?}",
                session.version, session.suite, session.reply
            );
            println!("  client sent records: {:?}", records(&session.sent));
            let visible = session
                .sent
                .windows(5)
                .any(|window| window == b"hello");
            println!("  \"hello\" readable on the wire: {visible}");
        }
        Err(error) => println!("  client: {error}"),
    }
    println!("  server: {}", server.join().expect("server thread"));
    Ok(())
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Error> {
    let pki = Pki::new()?;
    let server_only = || -> Result<ServerConfig, Error> {
        Ok(ServerConfig::builder_with_provider(provider())
            .with_safe_default_protocol_versions()?
            .with_no_client_auth()
            .with_single_cert(vec![pki.server.cert.clone()], pki.server.key())?)
    };
    let client_trusting = |roots: RootCertStore| -> Result<ClientConfig, Error> {
        Ok(ClientConfig::builder_with_provider(provider())
            .with_safe_default_protocol_versions()?
            .with_root_certificates(roots)
            .with_no_client_auth())
    };

    println!("1. The client checks the server's certificate");
    run(server_only()?, client_trusting(pki.roots()?)?, "localhost")?;

    println!("\n2. The client expects a different name");
    run(
        server_only()?,
        client_trusting(pki.roots()?)?,
        "billing.example",
    )?;

    println!("\n3. The client does not trust the CA");
    run(
        server_only()?,
        client_trusting(RootCertStore::empty())?,
        "localhost",
    )?;

    let verifier =
        WebPkiClientVerifier::builder_with_provider(Arc::new(pki.roots()?), provider()).build()?;
    let mutual = || -> Result<ServerConfig, Error> {
        Ok(ServerConfig::builder_with_provider(provider())
            .with_safe_default_protocol_versions()?
            .with_client_cert_verifier(verifier.clone())
            .with_single_cert(vec![pki.server.cert.clone()], pki.server.key())?)
    };

    println!("\n4. Mutual TLS, client without a certificate");
    run(mutual()?, client_trusting(pki.roots()?)?, "localhost")?;

    println!("\n5. Mutual TLS, client with the billing certificate");
    let client = ClientConfig::builder_with_provider(provider())
        .with_safe_default_protocol_versions()?
        .with_root_certificates(pki.roots()?)
        .with_client_auth_cert(vec![pki.client.cert.clone()], pki.client.key())?;
    run(mutual()?, client, "localhost")
}
