28.6 Questions that come up

“What does SNI do, and is it encrypted?” Server Name Indication (SNI) transmits the target hostname inside ClientHello, enabling a single IP address to host distinct certificates for multiple virtual domains. Standard SNI travels in plaintext; Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) encrypts the inner ClientHello (including SNI) when both client and server support it.

“Where should TLS end in a system?” Terminating TLS at an edge load balancer leaves backend traffic in plaintext, which is acceptable only inside a strictly isolated network perimeter. End-to-end mutual TLS between internal services preserves confidentiality and cryptographic service authentication across every network hop.

“A client fails with UnknownIssuer against a server that works in a browser. Why?” The server is typically transmitting only its leaf certificate while omitting the intermediate CA certificate required to chain to a trusted root. Web browsers often succeed via cached intermediates or AIA fetching, whereas minimal TLS clients reject incomplete chains. The server must transmit the full leaf-to-intermediate chain.

“What does 0-RTT mean?” TLS 1.3 zero-round-trip resumption allows a client with a cached session ticket to transmit encrypted application data alongside ClientHello before the handshake finishes. Because 0-RTT payloads lack single-use replay protection, servers must restrict 0-RTT strictly to idempotent operations (Chapter 19).

“How does a server revoke a client’s certificate before it expires?” The server can attach Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) to WebPkiClientVerifier so revoked serial numbers are rejected during handshake verification. Many internal systems supplement or replace CRLs with short-lived certificates (hours in duration) that expire naturally when renewal is halted.

Summary

  • TLS layers confidentiality (AEAD encryption), tamper and truncation detection (authentication tags and close_notify), and X.509 certificate authentication over TCP.
  • An X.509 certificate binds a public key to a subject identity and validity window, signed by a CA; verifying clients check the signature chain to a trusted root, validity dates, and hostname SAN match.
  • CertificateVerify proves live possession of the private key corresponding to the presented certificate.
  • TLS 1.3 establishes forward-secret keys via ECDHE in one round trip and encrypts all handshake messages after ServerHello; a 14-byte payload expands into a 31-byte encrypted record (1-byte inner type plus 16-byte AEAD tag).
  • Hostname mismatches and untrusted CAs abort the handshake before any application payload is transmitted.
  • Mutual TLS requires the client to present a verified certificate and signature; omitting one terminates the handshake with a fatal CertificateRequired alert.
  • Per-connection TLS overhead (one extra round trip and asymmetric cryptography) is amortized by session resumption and connection pooling.

Exercises

  1. Print the DER-encoded byte lengths of the server and client certificates in tls_mtls. Compare the client certificate size against the 412-byte increase in the mutual TLS encrypted handshake record and account for the remaining bytes.
  2. Issue the server certificate with both localhost and api.internal in CertificateParams::new, and verify successful TLS connections targeting each hostname.
  3. Set the server certificate’s not_after timestamp to yesterday via rcgen::date_time_ymd and record the exact verification error returned by rustls.
  4. Introduce an intermediate CA signed by the root CA and sign the server leaf certificate with that intermediate. Observe the client error when the server sends only its leaf certificate, then verify success when the full chain [leaf, intermediate] is sent.
  5. Restrict the server to TLS 1.2 via with_protocol_versions(&[&rustls::version::TLS12]) and compare the client’s captured wire records against the TLS 1.3 trace.

A client connection pool

This chapter covers

  • Amortizing per-connection overhead (TCP/TLS handshakes, congestion-window slow start, and TIME_WAIT port consumption) via persistent reuse
  • Bounded concurrency control: enforcing a hard cap on open sockets and a wait deadline for saturated callers
  • RAII borrowing via a guard type that returns healthy sockets on drop and discards broken sockets after I/O errors
  • LIFO idle-stack reuse and idle-timeout eviction to shrink pool footprint under light load
  • Detecting half-closed stale connections via non-blocking peek before lending
  • Empirical comparison of 2,000 concurrent requests with and without pooling

Establishing a new TCP connection for every outbound RPC imposes four compounding costs: a TCP three-way handshake (plus a TLS handshake when encrypted), TCP congestion-window slow start, server-side accept and descriptor allocation overhead, and a 60-second TIME_WAIT entry that rapidly exhausts client ephemeral ports (Chapter 27). A bounded client connection pool amortizes these setup and teardown costs by maintaining a capped set of persistent connections, lending them exclusively to calling threads via RAII guards, and reclaiming or evicting them deterministically.

The reference program conn_pool implements a thread-safe bounded pool using only the Rust standard library (Mutex, Condvar, and Drop), then benchmarks 2,000 multithreaded requests and verifies capacity limits, idle eviction, and stale-connection detection against a local line-oriented server.

29.1 What a new connection costs

Each freshly dialed connection incurs four distinct performance and resource penalties:

  • Handshake latency: one round trip for the TCP three-way handshake, plus a second round trip for TLS 1.3 (Chapter 28).
  • TCP slow start: a new connection begins with a minimal initial congestion window and requires multiple round trips to probe link capacity (Section 20.2), whereas a warm persistent connection retains its expanded window.
  • Server-side setup overhead: accept, descriptor allocation, and per-connection worker dispatch.
  • TIME_WAIT port pinning: active closure pins an ephemeral client port for 60 seconds (Section 27.2.1).

Across a 50 ms RTT link, connection handshakes alone add 100 ms to an RPC whose actual application latency is 5 ms.

Unbounded connection retention introduces an opposing hazard: every open socket consumes file descriptors and kernel socket buffers on both client and server, risking EMFILE or server overload. A production connection pool therefore enforces four invariants (Figure 29.1):

  1. Bounded capacity: total open sockets (in-use plus idle) never exceed max.
  2. Deterministic return: dropping a borrowed guard returns the socket to the idle pool unless explicitly marked broken via discard.
  3. LIFO reuse: the most recently returned idle socket is lent first, allowing surplus sockets to age out under low load.
  4. Staleness eviction: sockets idle beyond idle_timeout or closed asynchronously by the server are destroyed rather than lent.

29.2 The pool’s state

Config specifies the pool’s operational bounds, and Stats tracks cumulative connects, reuses, evictions, and stale discards:

use std::{
    io::{self, BufRead, BufReader, ErrorKind, Write},
    net::{SocketAddr, TcpListener, TcpStream},
    ops::{Deref, DerefMut},
    sync::{
        Arc,
        Condvar,
        Mutex,
        atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering::Relaxed},
    },
    thread,
    time::{Duration, Instant},
};

/// The limits a pool enforces.
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
struct Config {
    /// The most connections open at once, lent out or idle.
    max: usize,
    /// How long `get` waits for a connection before it gives up.
    wait_timeout: Duration,
    /// How long a connection may sit idle before the pool closes it.
    idle_timeout: Duration,
    /// Whether to check that an idle connection is still open before lending it.
    check_alive: bool,
}

/// What the pool has done, for the demonstration.
#[derive(Default)]
struct Stats {
    connects: AtomicUsize,
    reuses: AtomicUsize,
    evicted: AtomicUsize,
    stale: AtomicUsize,
}

Idle sockets reside in a Vec operated as a LIFO stack, paired with their return timestamps. The open counter tracks the total number of sockets currently owned by the pool (both idle and checked out):

struct Idle {
    stream: TcpStream,
    since: Instant,
}

/// The connections the pool owns: the idle ones, and a count of all open ones.
struct State {
    idle: Vec<Idle>,
    open: usize,
}

struct Pool {
    address: SocketAddr,
    config: Config,
    state: Mutex<State>,
    returned: Condvar,
    stats: Stats,
}

/// A connection lent out by the pool. Dropping it gives it back.
struct Pooled<'a> {
    pool: &'a Pool,
    stream: Option<TcpStream>,
    broken: bool,
}

The pool maintains the structural invariant open == idle.len() + checked_out. Because every mutation of open occurs while holding the internal Mutex, get can decide atomically whether capacity permits dialing a new connection.

Pooled<'a> wraps a checked-out TcpStream inside an Option alongside a shared reference &'a Pool. The lifetime parameter 'a prevents any borrowed handle from outliving the pool at compile time, while Option allows Drop to move ownership of the stream back into the idle stack.

29.3 Borrowing a connection

get executes a lock-protected state-machine loop until it acquires a usable socket or exhausts its deadline:

impl Pool {
    fn new(address: SocketAddr, config: Config) -> Self {
        Self {
            address,
            config,
            state: Mutex::new(State {
                idle: Vec::new(),
                open: 0,
            }),
            returned: Condvar::new(),
            stats: Stats::default(),
        }
    }

    /// Lend a connection: an idle one if there is one, a new one if the pool
    /// is below `max`, or the next one returned, waiting up to `wait_timeout`.
    fn get(&self) -> io::Result<Pooled<'_>> {
        let deadline = Instant::now() + self.config.wait_timeout;
        let mut state = self.state.lock().expect("pool lock");
        loop {
            if let Some(stream) = self.take_idle(&mut state) {
                self.stats.reuses.fetch_add(1, Relaxed);
                return Ok(self.lend(stream));
            }
            if state.open < self.config.max {
                state.open += 1;
                drop(state);
                return self.connect();
            }
            let now = Instant::now();
            if now >= deadline {
                return Err(io::Error::new(ErrorKind::TimedOut, "pool exhausted"));
            }
            state = self
                .returned
                .wait_timeout(state, deadline - now)
                .expect("pool lock")
                .0;
        }
    }
    // ...
}

Each iteration evaluates three branches in priority order:

  • Reuse an idle socket: take_idle pops the most recent healthy socket from the idle stack, or returns None.
  • Dial a new socket outside the lock: if open < max, get reserves a capacity slot by incrementing open under the mutex, releases the mutex immediately, and performs TcpStream::connect without holding the lock. Performing blocking network I/O while holding the mutex would serialize all pool operations, preventing concurrent threads from returning healthy sockets. Pre-incrementing open guarantees that concurrent callers never violate the max bound.
  • Wait with a bounded deadline: when open == max, the caller blocks on Condvar::wait_timeout until another thread returns or discards a socket, or until the deadline expires. Because wait_timeout atomically releases the mutex while sleeping (Section 16.5) and may return spuriously, the enclosing loop re-evaluates pool state on every wakeup.

If the deadline expires before a slot opens, get returns io::ErrorKind::TimedOut. Bounding wait time transforms downstream saturation into explicit backpressure rather than unbounded thread starvation (Chapter 17).

If TcpStream::connect fails after reserving a slot, connect decrements open under the mutex and notifies one waiting thread so the reserved capacity is not leaked:

impl Pool {
    // ...
    /// Open a new connection. The slot was reserved under the lock, and the
    /// connect runs outside it, so other callers are not held up.
    fn connect(&self) -> io::Result<Pooled<'_>> {
        match TcpStream::connect(self.address) {
            Ok(stream) => {
                self.stats
                    .connects
                    .fetch_add(1, Relaxed);
                Ok(self.lend(stream))
            }
            Err(error) => {
                self.release_slot();
                Err(error)
            }
        }
    }

    fn lend(&self, stream: TcpStream) -> Pooled<'_> {
        Pooled {
            pool: self,
            stream: Some(stream),
            broken: false,
        }
    }
    // ...
}

29.4 Giving it back

Implementing Drop on Pooled guarantees that every borrowed connection returns to the pool automatically across normal returns, early ? propagation, and stack unwinding:

impl Pool {
    // ...
    /// Take back a connection. A broken one is closed, and its slot is freed.
    fn give_back(&self, stream: TcpStream, broken: bool) {
        if broken {
            return self.release_slot();
        }
        let mut state = self.state.lock().expect("pool lock");
        state.idle.push(Idle {
            stream,
            since: Instant::now(),
        });
        drop(state);
        self.returned.notify_one();
    }

    fn release_slot(&self) {
        self.state
            .lock()
            .expect("pool lock")
            .open -= 1;
        self.returned.notify_one();
    }

    /// (open connections, idle connections)
    fn sizes(&self) -> (usize, usize) {
        let state = self.state.lock().expect("pool lock");
        (state.open, state.idle.len())
    }
}
impl Pooled<'_> {
    /// Close this connection instead of returning it, after an error.
    fn discard(mut self) {
        self.broken = true;
    }
}

impl Deref for Pooled<'_> {
    type Target = TcpStream;

    fn deref(&self) -> &TcpStream {
        self.stream
            .as_ref()
            .expect("stream until drop")
    }
}

impl DerefMut for Pooled<'_> {
    fn deref_mut(&mut self) -> &mut TcpStream {
        self.stream
            .as_mut()
            .expect("stream until drop")
    }
}

impl Drop for Pooled<'_> {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        if let Some(stream) = self.stream.take() {
            self.pool.give_back(stream, self.broken);
        }
    }
}

give_back pushes the socket onto the idle stack with Instant::now() and invokes notify_one on the Condvar. Calling discard marks the guard as broken so that Drop closes the socket, decrements open, and wakes a waiter instead of returning it to the idle stack. Discarding after any I/O error is mandatory: an aborted request may leave partial response bytes in the kernel receive buffer, which would corrupt framing for the next borrower.

ask composes borrowing, request-response execution, error-triggered discard, and automatic return into a single helper:

/// Send one line, and read one line back.
fn request(stream: &mut TcpStream, line: &str) -> io::Result<String> {
    writeln!(stream, "{line}")?;
    let mut reply = String::new();
    if BufReader::new(&*stream).read_line(&mut reply)? == 0 {
        return Err(io::Error::new(
            ErrorKind::UnexpectedEof,
            "server closed the connection",
        ));
    }
    Ok(reply.trim_end().to_string())
}

/// One request on a pooled connection. A connection that failed is discarded,
/// so the pool does not lend it again.
fn ask(pool: &Pool, line: &str) -> io::Result<String> {
    let mut connection = pool.get()?;
    let reply = request(&mut connection, line);
    if reply.is_err() {
        connection.discard();
    }
    reply
}

29.5 Stale connections

Operating the idle collection as a LIFO stack concentrates traffic onto a small working set of warm sockets during low load. Surplus sockets sink to the bottom of the stack, age past idle_timeout, and are closed on subsequent sweeps. A FIFO queue, by contrast, rotates every socket evenly across requests, resetting every idle timestamp and preventing the pool from shrinking after a traffic spike.

Even within idle_timeout, servers enforce their own idle connection timeouts (commonly 5 seconds to several minutes) by transmitting a TCP FIN. While the socket sits idle in the pool, no thread reads that FIN; without a liveness probe, the next borrower writes a request into the half-closed socket and fails with UnexpectedEof or ECONNRESET (Figure 29.2).

take_idle enforces both idle-timeout eviction and server-close detection before lending a socket:

/// Whether the server has closed `stream`, checked without blocking: a
/// readable socket with nothing to read has seen the server's `FIN`.
fn is_alive(stream: &TcpStream) -> bool {
    if stream.set_nonblocking(true).is_err() {
        return false;
    }
    let alive = match stream.peek(&mut [0]) {
        Err(error) => error.kind() == ErrorKind::WouldBlock,
        Ok(_) => false,
    };
    stream.set_nonblocking(false).is_ok() && alive
}
impl Pool {
    // ...
    /// The most recently returned idle connection that is fresh and open.
    /// Connections idle too long, or closed by the server, are dropped.
    fn take_idle(&self, state: &mut State) -> Option<TcpStream> {
        while let Some(idle) = state.idle.pop() {
            if idle.since.elapsed() > self.config.idle_timeout {
                state.open -= 1;
                self.stats.evicted.fetch_add(1, Relaxed);
            } else if self.config.check_alive && !is_alive(&idle.stream) {
                state.open -= 1;
                self.stats.stale.fetch_add(1, Relaxed);
            } else {
                return Some(idle.stream);
            }
        }
        None
    }
    // ...
}

is_alive temporarily switches the socket to non-blocking mode and executes peek(&mut [0u8; 1]). Because a healthy idle request-response socket should contain zero unread bytes, WouldBlock confirms that the connection remains open and clean. Returning Ok(0) indicates a pending server FIN, and returning Ok(n > 0) indicates unexpected stray bytes; in either case, the pool closes the socket and decrements open.

A pre-lend peek narrows the stale-connection race window but cannot eliminate it completely, because the server’s FIN can arrive in flight between peek and the client’s write. Production clients close the remaining window with two complementary defenses:

  • Configure the pool’s idle_timeout strictly shorter than the server’s keep-alive timeout so the client initiates eviction before the server closes.
  • Retry idempotent requests once on a fresh connection when a reused socket fails with a transport error (Chapter 19).

Animation 29.1 visualizes the complete pool lifecycle across borrowing, capacity blocking, idle eviction, and stale-socket detection.

29.6 Measured

main executes four scenarios against a local line-oriented server. Scenario 1 dispatches 2,000 requests across eight worker threads, comparing unpooled connections against a 4-connection pool:

1. 2000 requests from 8 threads
  a new connection each:   2000 connections,  169.8 ms
  a pool of 4:                4 connections,   80.4 ms, 1996 reuses

Even on loopback where TCP handshakes execute in microseconds, pooling halved elapsed wall-clock latency while eliminating 1,996 handshakes. Without pooling, the run generated 2,000 TIME_WAIT sockets in 0.17 seconds, a rate that exhausts Linux’s 28,232-port ephemeral range in under 3 seconds (Section 27.2.1). Over a real network with TLS, unpooled requests would additionally incur 2 RTT per call.

Scenarios 2 through 4 verify capacity enforcement, idle eviction, and stale-connection detection:

2. The bound: 2 connections, both lent out
  third get after 103 ms: Err(Custom { kind: TimedOut, error: "pool exhausted" })
  after one is returned: Ok(()), sizes (open, idle) = (2, 1)

3. Idle eviction: idle_timeout 100 ms
  connects 2, evicted 1

4. A server that closes idle connections after 50 ms
  check_alive false: Err(Custom { kind: UnexpectedEof, error: "server closed the connection" }), stale discarded 0
  check_alive true : Ok("ok second"), stale discarded 1

When both slots were occupied, the third get waited its 100 ms deadline and returned TimedOut; returning one guard immediately unblocked the next acquisition. Sleeping 150 ms past a 100 ms idle_timeout triggered eviction and a fresh dial. Against a server enforcing a 50 ms idle close, disabling check_alive lent a half-closed socket and failed with UnexpectedEof, whereas enabling check_alive detected the pending FIN, discarded the stale socket, and redialed transparently.

29.7 The complete program

Listing 29.1 A bounded connection pool with automatic return, idle eviction, and a liveness check. src/bin/conn_pool.rs

//! A client connection pool: at most `max` connections to one server, each
//! lent out behind a guard that gives it back when dropped. Idle connections
//! are reused, closed after `idle_timeout`, and checked before reuse in case
//! the server closed them first.
//!
//! Run with: cargo run --release --bin conn_pool

use std::{
    io::{self, BufRead, BufReader, ErrorKind, Write},
    net::{SocketAddr, TcpListener, TcpStream},
    ops::{Deref, DerefMut},
    sync::{
        Arc,
        Condvar,
        Mutex,
        atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering::Relaxed},
    },
    thread,
    time::{Duration, Instant},
};

/// The limits a pool enforces.
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
struct Config {
    /// The most connections open at once, lent out or idle.
    max: usize,
    /// How long `get` waits for a connection before it gives up.
    wait_timeout: Duration,
    /// How long a connection may sit idle before the pool closes it.
    idle_timeout: Duration,
    /// Whether to check that an idle connection is still open before lending it.
    check_alive: bool,
}

/// What the pool has done, for the demonstration.
#[derive(Default)]
struct Stats {
    connects: AtomicUsize,
    reuses: AtomicUsize,
    evicted: AtomicUsize,
    stale: AtomicUsize,
}

struct Idle {
    stream: TcpStream,
    since: Instant,
}

/// The connections the pool owns: the idle ones, and a count of all open ones.
struct State {
    idle: Vec<Idle>,
    open: usize,
}

struct Pool {
    address: SocketAddr,
    config: Config,
    state: Mutex<State>,
    returned: Condvar,
    stats: Stats,
}

/// A connection lent out by the pool. Dropping it gives it back.
struct Pooled<'a> {
    pool: &'a Pool,
    stream: Option<TcpStream>,
    broken: bool,
}

/// Whether the server has closed `stream`, checked without blocking: a
/// readable socket with nothing to read has seen the server's `FIN`.
fn is_alive(stream: &TcpStream) -> bool {
    if stream.set_nonblocking(true).is_err() {
        return false;
    }
    let alive = match stream.peek(&mut [0]) {
        Err(error) => error.kind() == ErrorKind::WouldBlock,
        Ok(_) => false,
    };
    stream.set_nonblocking(false).is_ok() && alive
}

impl Pool {
    fn new(address: SocketAddr, config: Config) -> Self {
        Self {
            address,
            config,
            state: Mutex::new(State {
                idle: Vec::new(),
                open: 0,
            }),
            returned: Condvar::new(),
            stats: Stats::default(),
        }
    }

    /// Lend a connection: an idle one if there is one, a new one if the pool
    /// is below `max`, or the next one returned, waiting up to `wait_timeout`.
    fn get(&self) -> io::Result<Pooled<'_>> {
        let deadline = Instant::now() + self.config.wait_timeout;
        let mut state = self.state.lock().expect("pool lock");
        loop {
            if let Some(stream) = self.take_idle(&mut state) {
                self.stats.reuses.fetch_add(1, Relaxed);
                return Ok(self.lend(stream));
            }
            if state.open < self.config.max {
                state.open += 1;
                drop(state);
                return self.connect();
            }
            let now = Instant::now();
            if now >= deadline {
                return Err(io::Error::new(ErrorKind::TimedOut, "pool exhausted"));
            }
            state = self
                .returned
                .wait_timeout(state, deadline - now)
                .expect("pool lock")
                .0;
        }
    }

    /// The most recently returned idle connection that is fresh and open.
    /// Connections idle too long, or closed by the server, are dropped.
    fn take_idle(&self, state: &mut State) -> Option<TcpStream> {
        while let Some(idle) = state.idle.pop() {
            if idle.since.elapsed() > self.config.idle_timeout {
                state.open -= 1;
                self.stats.evicted.fetch_add(1, Relaxed);
            } else if self.config.check_alive && !is_alive(&idle.stream) {
                state.open -= 1;
                self.stats.stale.fetch_add(1, Relaxed);
            } else {
                return Some(idle.stream);
            }
        }
        None
    }

    /// Open a new connection. The slot was reserved under the lock, and the
    /// connect runs outside it, so other callers are not held up.
    fn connect(&self) -> io::Result<Pooled<'_>> {
        match TcpStream::connect(self.address) {
            Ok(stream) => {
                self.stats
                    .connects
                    .fetch_add(1, Relaxed);
                Ok(self.lend(stream))
            }
            Err(error) => {
                self.release_slot();
                Err(error)
            }
        }
    }

    fn lend(&self, stream: TcpStream) -> Pooled<'_> {
        Pooled {
            pool: self,
            stream: Some(stream),
            broken: false,
        }
    }

    /// Take back a connection. A broken one is closed, and its slot is freed.
    fn give_back(&self, stream: TcpStream, broken: bool) {
        if broken {
            return self.release_slot();
        }
        let mut state = self.state.lock().expect("pool lock");
        state.idle.push(Idle {
            stream,
            since: Instant::now(),
        });
        drop(state);
        self.returned.notify_one();
    }

    fn release_slot(&self) {
        self.state
            .lock()
            .expect("pool lock")
            .open -= 1;
        self.returned.notify_one();
    }

    /// (open connections, idle connections)
    fn sizes(&self) -> (usize, usize) {
        let state = self.state.lock().expect("pool lock");
        (state.open, state.idle.len())
    }
}

impl Pooled<'_> {
    /// Close this connection instead of returning it, after an error.
    fn discard(mut self) {
        self.broken = true;
    }
}

impl Deref for Pooled<'_> {
    type Target = TcpStream;

    fn deref(&self) -> &TcpStream {
        self.stream
            .as_ref()
            .expect("stream until drop")
    }
}

impl DerefMut for Pooled<'_> {
    fn deref_mut(&mut self) -> &mut TcpStream {
        self.stream
            .as_mut()
            .expect("stream until drop")
    }
}

impl Drop for Pooled<'_> {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        if let Some(stream) = self.stream.take() {
            self.pool.give_back(stream, self.broken);
        }
    }
}

/// Send one line, and read one line back.
fn request(stream: &mut TcpStream, line: &str) -> io::Result<String> {
    writeln!(stream, "{line}")?;
    let mut reply = String::new();
    if BufReader::new(&*stream).read_line(&mut reply)? == 0 {
        return Err(io::Error::new(
            ErrorKind::UnexpectedEof,
            "server closed the connection",
        ));
    }
    Ok(reply.trim_end().to_string())
}

/// One request on a pooled connection. A connection that failed is discarded,
/// so the pool does not lend it again.
fn ask(pool: &Pool, line: &str) -> io::Result<String> {
    let mut connection = pool.get()?;
    let reply = request(&mut connection, line);
    if reply.is_err() {
        connection.discard();
    }
    reply
}

/// A line server on loopback that closes a connection idle for `idle_close`.
/// Returns its address and a count of the connections it has accepted.
fn start_server(idle_close: Duration) -> io::Result<(SocketAddr, Arc<AtomicUsize>)> {
    let listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0")?;
    let address = listener.local_addr()?;
    let accepted = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let counter = Arc::clone(&accepted);
    thread::spawn(move || {
        for stream in listener.incoming().flatten() {
            counter.fetch_add(1, Relaxed);
            thread::spawn(move || serve(stream, idle_close));
        }
    });
    Ok((address, accepted))
}

/// Answer each line with "ok", until the client closes or stays quiet too long.
fn serve(stream: TcpStream, idle_close: Duration) -> io::Result<()> {
    stream.set_read_timeout(Some(idle_close))?;
    let mut writer = stream.try_clone()?;
    for line in BufReader::new(stream).lines() {
        let line = line?;
        writeln!(writer, "ok {line}")?;
    }
    Ok(())
}

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    const REQUESTS: usize = 2_000;
    const THREADS: usize = 8;
    let config = Config {
        max: 4,
        wait_timeout: Duration::from_secs(1),
        idle_timeout: Duration::from_secs(30),
        check_alive: true,
    };

    println!("1. {REQUESTS} requests from {THREADS} threads");
    let (address, accepted) = start_server(Duration::from_secs(30))?;
    let start = Instant::now();
    thread::scope(|scope| {
        for _ in 0..THREADS {
            scope.spawn(|| -> io::Result<()> {
                for _ in 0..REQUESTS / THREADS {
                    request(&mut TcpStream::connect(address)?, "ping")?;
                }
                Ok(())
            });
        }
    });
    println!(
        "  a new connection each:  {:>5} connections, {:>6.1} ms",
        accepted.load(Relaxed),
        start.elapsed().as_secs_f64() * 1000.0
    );

    let (address, accepted) = start_server(Duration::from_secs(30))?;
    let pool = Pool::new(address, config);
    let start = Instant::now();
    thread::scope(|scope| {
        for _ in 0..THREADS {
            scope.spawn(|| -> io::Result<()> {
                for _ in 0..REQUESTS / THREADS {
                    ask(&pool, "ping")?;
                }
                Ok(())
            });
        }
    });
    println!(
        "  a pool of {}:            {:>5} connections, {:>6.1} ms, {} reuses",
        config.max,
        accepted.load(Relaxed),
        start.elapsed().as_secs_f64() * 1000.0,
        pool.stats.reuses.load(Relaxed)
    );

    println!("\n2. The bound: 2 connections, both lent out");
    let pool = Pool::new(
        address,
        Config {
            max: 2,
            wait_timeout: Duration::from_millis(100),
            ..config
        },
    );
    let (first, second) = (pool.get()?, pool.get()?);
    let start = Instant::now();
    let third = pool.get().map(|_| ());
    println!(
        "  third get after {:.0} ms: {third:?}",
        start.elapsed().as_secs_f64() * 1000.0
    );
    drop(first);
    let fourth = pool.get().map(|_| ());
    println!(
        "  after one is returned: {fourth:?}, sizes (open, idle) = {:?}",
        pool.sizes()
    );
    drop(second);

    println!("\n3. Idle eviction: idle_timeout 100 ms");
    let pool = Pool::new(
        address,
        Config {
            idle_timeout: Duration::from_millis(100),
            ..config
        },
    );
    ask(&pool, "first")?;
    thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(150));
    ask(&pool, "second")?;
    println!(
        "  connects {}, evicted {}",
        pool.stats.connects.load(Relaxed),
        pool.stats.evicted.load(Relaxed)
    );

    println!("\n4. A server that closes idle connections after 50 ms");
    let (address, _) = start_server(Duration::from_millis(50))?;
    for check_alive in [false, true] {
        let pool = Pool::new(
            address,
            Config {
                check_alive,
                ..config
            },
        );
        ask(&pool, "first")?;
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(100));
        let outcome = ask(&pool, "second");
        println!(
            "  check_alive {check_alive:<5}: {outcome:?}, stale discarded {}",
            pool.stats.stale.load(Relaxed)
        );
    }
    Ok(())
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    fn config(max: usize) -> Config {
        Config {
            max,
            wait_timeout: Duration::from_millis(50),
            idle_timeout: Duration::from_secs(30),
            check_alive: true,
        }
    }

    #[test]
    fn a_returned_connection_is_reused() {
        let (address, accepted) = start_server(Duration::from_secs(5)).unwrap();
        let pool = Pool::new(address, config(2));
        for _ in 0..10 {
            assert_eq!(request(&mut pool.get().unwrap(), "x").unwrap(), "ok x");
        }
        assert_eq!(accepted.load(Relaxed), 1);
        assert_eq!(pool.stats.reuses.load(Relaxed), 9);
    }

    #[test]
    fn the_pool_never_exceeds_max() {
        let (address, _) = start_server(Duration::from_secs(5)).unwrap();
        let pool = Pool::new(address, config(1));
        let held = pool.get().unwrap();
        let error = pool.get().map(|_| ()).unwrap_err();
        assert_eq!(error.kind(), ErrorKind::TimedOut);
        drop(held);
        assert!(pool.get().is_ok());
    }

    #[test]
    fn a_discarded_connection_frees_its_slot() {
        let (address, _) = start_server(Duration::from_secs(5)).unwrap();
        let pool = Pool::new(address, config(1));
        pool.get().unwrap().discard();
        assert_eq!(pool.sizes(), (0, 0));
        drop(pool.get().unwrap());
        assert_eq!(pool.stats.connects.load(Relaxed), 2);
    }
}
